f.d: gsang sngags pha rol phyin lam sbyong bas/[127] / gang yang rung bas sems can kun nam/ / khyad par du yang mir gyur pa la/ / rnam pa kun tu brnyas dang ma gus/ / smad dang skyon nas gleng la sogs pa/ / spang bya gnod pa chen po yin phyir/ /

Whether we follow the Mahayana or the secret mantra, we must never despise sentient beings, humans in particular, and never treat them with disrespect or denigrate them and talk about their faults, because this would cause great harm.

d.div: [127] spyod pas/ mi rigs dpe skrun khang /

f.d: pha rol phyin lam spyod pa'i gnyen por/ / kun rdzob tu ni pha mar mnyam zhing / / don dam stong pa nyid du mnyam pas/ / rtag tu sems can kun la gus bya// gsang sngags tshul spyod rnams kyis gnyen por/ / rang lha'i 'du shes rtag tu gus bya/ /

As an antidote within Mahayana practice, we regard sentient beings as our fathers and mothers on the level of relative truth, and as being identical with emptiness on the level of ultimate truth, and therefore we treat them with respect. As an antidote within tantric practice, we regard ourselves [and others] as deities, and therefore as objects of respect.
sems can skyon gyi bdag po yin phyir/ / skyon rnams gang la'ang mi rigs mi bsam/ / yon tan cung zad su la mthong yang / / ngo mtshar chen pos de la gus bya/ /

Because it is normal for sentient beings to have flaws, we should never think badly of them. When we see even the slightest virtue in others, we should be full of admiration and respect for them, because this is very rare among living beings.

de ni sems can kun la dkon phyir/ / rang gi yon tan gzhan gyi nyes pa/ / brjod 'dod rang sems dang por blta bya/ / lhag pa'i bsam pa kho nas yin na/ / brjod bya 'dres na'ang shing bzhin gnas bya/ / nyon mongs bslangs na smos kyang ci dgos//

We must look at our own minds first if we wish to speak about our own virtues and about other people’s faults. If it is out of a higher motivation [to help others], /35/ we should speak; if it is not out of a pure motivation, we should remain [silent] like a log,[186] particularly when we are afflicted by disturbing emotions.

d.div: [186] This image is taken from Śāntideva’s Guide to the Bodhisattva Way of Life 5:48ff.

f.d: gnod pa spang ba'i thabs kyi skabs nas/ / zla 'od gzhon nus zhus pa'i skabs su/[128] / 'chal sogs sdig pa kun spyod yin yang / / de yi byang chub snying po bsam dang / / sangs rgyas bstan la bya ba mang byas/ / lam ni bstungs pa dag kyang dran nas/ / rgan na gus pas rim gro phyag bya/ /

In the Question of Candraprabha theYouth within the passage on the method for giving up harm [from the Compendium of Trainings],[187] it is stated that we must keep in mind that even though beings commit harmful deeds such as transgressing moral discipline, they have the essence of awakening and follow the teachings of the Buddha in many ways. We should also remember that [these good qualities] make their way [toward buddhahood] shorter. If they are old, we should honor them through respect and material gifts.

d.div: [128] sde dge_127_bka'/ mdo sde/ da_ting nge 'dzin rgyal po'i mdo/ le'u/ 25_shog_85_ba3

[187] This refers to a quotation from the Candraprabha Sutra, more commonly known as the King of Meditation Sutra (Samādhirājasūtra, Toh 127 Kangyur, mdo sde, da, 85b3), in chapter 5 of Śāntideva’s Compendium of Trainings.

f.d: bsten par mi bya brnyas par ma yin/ / bsten na gnyis ka nyams 'gyur snyam nas/ / sems kyis spang bya skyon ni mi bsam//

We should neither imitate them nor despise them. We must keep in mind that if we imitate them, both will get hurt, and therefore we should neither cling to them with our minds nor scrutinize their faults.
mi ni a mra'i 'bras 'dra'i skabs su/[129] / 'di ni mdo dang bstan bcos kun las// shin tu nan tan che bar gsungs pas/ / pha rol ma brtags pa la skyon med/ / brtags pas skyon mang de bas mi brtag /

With respect to the passage on people being like mangos,[188] the same point has been stressed both by sutras and by doctrinal works. If we do not examine the faults in others, no damage will arise; if we do, the damage can be manifold. Therefore we should not examine them.

d.div: [129] sde dge_4182_bstan/ spring yig_nge _mgon po klu sgrub/ bshes spring / sh+loka_20_shog_41_ba4
[188] This refers to stanza 20 of Nāgārjuna’s Letter to a Friend, Toh 4182 Tengyur, spring yig, nge, 41b4.

f.d: rigs su bcad nas skyon brjod sogs kyis/[130] / lan brgyar rnga mor skyes kyang min nam/ / rang la rang rtog gzhan la ma sems/[131] / ci yang min par dmyal bar 'gro bas/ / mi 'gro ba ni cung mi rung ngam/ /

If we are not impartial and talk about [other people’s] faults and the like, [it is as in the example where someone said:] “Even if I will be born a hundred times as a camel—isn’t it [possible to escape this]?”[189] We should examine ourselves and not obsess about others; otherwise we will go to hell, and would we deserve anything different?

d.div: [130] ris su/ mi rigs dpe skrun khang /
[131] rang la rang rtogs gzhan la mi sems/ mi rigs dpe skrun khang /

[189] Lha Drigangpa (p. 421) tells the story of a man who said, “Even if I am reborn as a camel, won’t this have an end at some point?” In the same way, people think, “Even if I am reborn in hell, won’t this be over at some point?”

f.d: gnod pa spong bas bdag lus bsrung ba/ / gtsor bya sems can don ni dran pas/ / khyad par du ni sems dpa' la'o/ /
When we avoid harming others we must take particular care to control our bodies. [This is necessary] when keeping the benefit of others in mind, and especially in the case of bodhisattvas.

de nyid kun la ston pa'i 'du shes/ / rtag tu bya ba do gal chen po/ / ma rmas 'dod pa'i gang zag rnams kyis/[132] / rang gi skyon la dpyad par bya yi/ / gzhan skyon ci 'dra'ang mi brtag btang snyoms/ /

In this respect it is vital that we always regard everyone as a teacher.[190] Persons who wish to avoid harming others must discern their own faults but must be impartial towards others and not examine what their faults are like.

d.div: [132] mi rmas/ mi rigs dpe skrun khang /

[190] Lha Drigangpa (p. 422) elaborates that it is particularly important to never have a harmful or disrespectful attitude toward a bodhisattva, and since we cannot know in which form a bodhisattva may appear, we must generally be full of respect toward all living beings and regard them as teachers.

f.d: ma 'dres sems na bzlog par bya ste// gzhan du na ni thar rgyal kho na'o/ /
When our intentions are not mingled [with selfish thoughts], then we may make them turn away [from their faults]. Otherwise, it is as in the case of the Thargyal.[191]

d.div: [191] Ami Thargyal said: “What are the borders of Tibet?” Dromtönpa said: “Thargyal should forget about the borders of Tibet and examine his own boundaries!” (Lha Drigangpa, p. 423).

d.i: The appropriate view of the Dharma

d.div: [192] This heading has been added for the sake of clarity.

f.d: chos spong sgrib pa'i gnod pa'i skabs su/[133] / chos kun theg pa che la gzhol bas/ / kun la mi smad mnyam par gus bya/ / theg pa che chung khyad par gsungs pa/ /

In the passage on the harm caused by the taint of rejecting the Dharma,[193] it is said that all doctrines are contained in the Mahayana, so we should not revile them but pay respect to them equally. The scriptures speak about a difference between the Hinayana and the Mahayana.

d.div: [133] sde dge_3940_bstan/ dbu ma/ khi_rgyal sras zhi ba lha/ bslab btus/ le'u/ 4_shog_58_na2

[193] This refers to a passage from chapter 4 of Śāntideva’s Compendium of Training (Śikṣāsamuccaya) Toh 3940 Tengyur, dbu ma, khi, 58a2. The Extensive Compendium of All Dharma and Lotus Sutra are quoted to the effect that in reality all the different vehicles are one and the same and have the same purpose (the ekayāna or “one-vehicle” point of view).

f.d: tshul khrims spong ba bdun dang bcur gsungs/ / ched ni rang don gzhan gyi don yin/ / lta ba mi rtag stong pa nyid dang / / 'bras bu mya ngan 'das zad gzod zhi/ / de dag kun kyang snod kyi bye brag / rtogs pa che chung dag gis yin gyi/ / bstan pa la ni bye brag yod min/ /

They declare the transgressions of moral discipline to be either seven or ten.[194] The purpose [of the different vehicles] is benefit for oneself and for others. There are differences between the schools both in terms of the view, for instance regarding impermanence or emptiness, and in terms of the fruit, for instance whether nirvana means extinction [of suffering] or whether [suffering] has been calmed from the very beginning, but although there are great and small ways of understanding, there is no difference in the Dharma itself.

d.div: [194] The seven transgressions are those committed with body and speech (see note 95 above); the ten transgressions include the three committed with the mind.

f.d: de bas kun la mnyam par gus bya/ / chos spong sgrib pa shin tu che phyir/ /
Therefore we must pay equal respect to all schools because rejecting the Dharma is a serious taint.

theg pa thams cad theg chen lam stegs/ / sems dpa'i lam min gang yang yod min/ / sems can blo yi dbye bas gsum bstan/ / ngal la bar du gling sprul bzhin du// re zhig ngal gso'i gnas su gsungs yin/[134] /

All vehicles are a supporting basis for the Mahayana, and there is nothing that does not belong to the path of the bodhisattvas.[195] Because sentient beings have different minds, the Dharma has been taught as three [vehicles]. Like an island that is created magically for the weary, they have been taught as resting-places [for those getting weary on the long path to liberation].

d.div: [134] ngal bso'i/ mi rigs dpe skrun khang /
[195] This and the following verses refer to a passage from the Sutra on Going to Laṅka (Laṅkāvatārasūtra); see Lha Drigangpa, pp. 426–27.

f.d: gtan du thar pa thams cad mkhyen pa/ / de phyir chos dang chos smra kun la/ / mi smad gus pa shin tu cher bya/ / chos spangs pa las sgrib che med phyir//

Because they lead to permanent liberation and the stage of an all-knowing buddha /36/ we must never revile the doctrines and those teaching them but treat them with the greatest respect, since there is no greater fault than abandoning the Dharma.

byang chub sems dpa'i rma 'byin skabs su/[135] / gang la brten nas gnod pa byung ba/ / de nyid la brten gus sogs bzod gsol/ / byas na sdig pa de ni sbyang sla/ / dkon mchog gzhan brten bsags pa'ang de bzhin//

In the passage on having harmed a bodhisattva,[196] it is said that when we have done harm to a certain object or person, we must pay respect to and ask for forgiveness from that very same object or person. When we act like this, it is easy to purify the trespass. It is the same even when we have [committed a transgression] concerning the Three Jewels.

d.div: [135] sde dge_3940_bstan/ dbu ma/ khi_rgyal sras zhi ba lha/ bslab btus/ le'u/ 4_shog_53_na4
[196] In chapter 8 of Śāntideva’s Compendium of Trainings (Śikṣāsamuccaya), Toh 3940 Tengyur, dbu ma, khi, 53a4.

f.d: nyer bzhi pa bar chad spangs nas gzhan don la 'jug tshul ston pa/
24. How to proceed in the preservation of benefit after having averted the obstacles

de ltar rang rgyud yongs su smin pa/ / las dang po yis gtso bor de bya/ / gzhan don gtso bor bya ba ma gnang / / lhag pa'i bsam pa bskul bzhin gnas bya/[136] / sems kyis sems can don las gzhan med/ / lus ngag dag gis dngos su mi 'jug /

Thus beginners [on the path of a bodhisattva] must primarily enable their own minds to mature and not make benefitting others the most important thing just yet. They must live as it is said in the Sutra Encouraging Nobler Intention. In their minds there is nothing but the benefit of sentient beings, but with their body and speech they do not yet embark [on the full bodhisattva practice].

d.div: [136] sde dge_69_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ ca_lhag pa'i bsam pa bskul ba'i mdo/ shog_135_na4

f.d: mngon shes med ring sems can don byed/ / dmus long ri dwags ming gis mda' 'phen/ / de bas tsab tsub nyung ba gtsor bya/[137] /

When they have not achieved the supernatural kinds of knowledge and try to work for the benefit of sentient beings, they are like a blind man who shoots an arrow when he is told that there is a deer. Therefore we should never act too hastily.

d.div: [137] tsam tsub/ mi rigs dpe skrun khang /

f.d: bdag cag thams cad tsan dan bsngags 'tsho/[138] / tsan dan bsngags pas 'tsho ba min zhing / / tsan dan nyid dang ldan par 'dod na/ / tsan dan bsngags pas 'tsho ba spangs la/ / tsan dan btsal phyir rtag tu 'bad bya/ /

We are all like people who live praising sandalwood [without possessing it]. If we don’t want to live praising the sandalwood but want to obtain the sandalwood ourselves, then we must give up just praising the sandalwood and must constantly strive and search for it.

d.div: [138] bdag can/ mi rigs dpe skrun khang /

f.d: mngon shes mi ldan sems can don ni/ / don med dmus long ri dwags mda' bzhin/ / mos pas spyod ring sems can don ni/ / phal cher don med gsungs te de yang // mngon shes ldan par gyur na de yin/ / mi ldan ring la thams cad don med/ / lha cig de gsung da lta 'gro don/ / dngos su mi nus gong gi dpe bzhin/ /

Those who don’t have the supernatural kinds of knowledge cannot achieve the benefit of sentient beings, like the blind man shooting at the deer. As long as we just act out of enthusiasm, our work for the benefit of beings will mostly be fruitless, as the scriptures say. Also our sole lord has said that once we have acquired the supernatural knowledges, we will [be able to help others], but as long as we haven’t, we will be of no use to them. Nowadays we are not truly able to accomplish the benefit of living beings, just as in the example given above.
ci nas byed 'dod sangs rgyas bstan pa/ / 'jig rten yun ring ci gnas bya ste/ / de yang dge 'dun sde la rag las/ / nus pa yod na de gnas thabs bya/ /

If we want to accomplish it, we must try to ensure that the teachings of the Buddha remain in the world for a long time. And because this depends on the monastic community, we must make the monastic community last if we can.[197]

d.div: [197] According to Lha Drigangpa (pp. 431–32) this is what Atiśa said to Dromtönpa, who therefore founded the monastery of Radeng.

f.d: nus med rang rgyud ji ltar khas blangs/ / sems can ched du mi nyams bsrung zhing / / lhag bsam bskul bzhin chos bzhis gnas na/ / las dang po yi sems can don de/ / tshul de las gzhan rang mgo bskor thabs/ / de ni bsdu ba'i dngos po'i skabs su'o/ /

If we cannot do this, we must guard our own minds in accord with our vows for the sake of sentient beings. If we live according to the four instructions from the Sutra Encouraging Nobler Intention,[198] then, as beginner bodhisattvas, we will work for the benefit of beings [by making our own minds more mature]; acting otherwise is simply to deceive ourselves. This is what the passage on the four means of attraction says.

d.div: [198] For the four instructions in the Adhyāśayasaṃcodanasūtra, see note 96 above.

f.d: bslab btus rkyen tshogs tshol ba'i skabs su/[139] / bstan pa 'dzin srung skyong dang gsum ni/ / bslab pa gsum po thos bsam gsum gyis/ / rang rgyud 'dzin pa de ni dang po/ /

In the passage from the Compendium of Trainings on seeking what accumulates the right conditions,[199] it is said that there are three [duties]: maintaining the Dharma, protecting it, and preserving it. The first is that we maintain the Dharma in our minds through the three trainings and by listening, reflecting, and meditating on it.

d.div: [139] sde dge_3940_bstan/ dbu ma/ khi_bslab btus/ le'u/ 1_shog_11_na7
[199] Śāntideva, Śikṣāsamuccaya, chapter 4; Toh 3940 Tengyur, dbu ma, khi, 11a7.

f.d: de 'dzin gang zag gnod srung gnyis pa/ / thabs tshul kun gyis phan 'dogs gsum pa/ / nus pa che chung khyad par min pa/ / srung dang skyong ba kun la nus yod/ /

The second is that we protect from harm the persons who maintain the Dharma. /37/ To assist them by all possible means is the third. Everyone is able to protect and preserve it, no matter whether their abilities are great or small.
tha na sprang po'i bus pa la yang / / spyil po srung sogs nus pa yod bzhin/ / ye nas bsrung skyong rgyal po sogs kyi/ / 'on kyang da lta rang cag la bab/ / sna tshogs tshul gyis gsum la 'bad bya/ /

This is like the begging children who were able to protect the hut.[200] In former times it was persons such as kings who protected and preserved [the Dharma]; now this task has become ours, and we must try to fulfill the three duties in various ways.

d.div: [200] When Potowa was teaching in Trak and Khartok, there were beggars sitting around the assembled Sangha who defended the hut against dogs, brought wood and leaves to feed the fire, and so on (Lha Drigangpa, pp. 433–34).

f.d: nus pa med pa'i yul la nyes med/ / chos mi mthun pas skyong srung ma gnang / / mthu yod bzhin du gzhan dag brlag pa'ang / / yal bar bor na nyan thos kyang min/ / de bas de ni nus med yul la'o//

If, however, we are not able to do so, this is no fault. We are not allowed to preserve or protect [the Dharma] by methods that are contrary to the Dharma. Leaving others to ruin and destruction although we have the power [to help them] is not even allowed for the śrāvakas. All this has been said about those who are not able [to fully act like a bodhisattva].
bdud kyi las kyi gnod pa'i skabs su/[140] / man ngag yin te khrom bos byas na/ / bdud ni gnyis te mi min rnam rtog / re dogs spangs shing ri ltar mi g.yo/ / de la de dag gnyis ka mi 'byung / /

The passage on harm done by the evil spirits[201] is a secret instruction, but we now proclaim it in the marketplace: There are two kinds of evil spirits: nonhuman spirits and imagined spirits. We must give up hope and fear and become as unshakable as a mountain; then these two kinds will not appear.

d.div: [140] sde dge_3940_bstan/ dbu ma/ khi_bslab btus/ le'u/ 4_shog_34_na7
[201] Śāntideva, Compendium of Trainings (Śikṣāsamuccaya), chapter 4, Toh Toh 3940 Tengyur, dbu ma, khi, 34a6.

f.d: zlog la de dag gnyis ka spyan 'dren/ / dang po'i gnyen po gsum ste rjes dran/ / byams dang snying rje sgyu ma nam mkha'/ / gnyis pa'i gnyen por rang sems 'khrul par/ / shes pa nyid yin gzhan du mi btsal/ /

If we need to drive them back, we must first summon them. Then, there are three remedies against the first kind: the recollection [of the Three Jewels], loving kindness and compassion, and [seeing them] as an illusion or [as empty] like the sky. Against the second kind, the remedy is to recognize that they are fabrications of our minds; we need nothing but this.

sgyu ma lta bur tshol ba'i skabs su/[141] / 'di yang man ngag khrom bos byas na// sgom par byed pa'i gang zag rnams la/ / mtshar mtshar du'am yags yags su'am/ / bzang bzang po ni ji ltar byung yang / / nga rgyal mi bya byed na 'dres khyer/ /

The passage on seeing them as an illusion[202] is also a secret instruction, but we now proclaim it in the marketplace: When persons who meditate have wonderful or really good or excellent meditation experiences, they must not become proud. If they do, the demons will carry them away.

d.div: [141] sde dge_4020_bstan/ sems tsam/ phi_byams pa mgon po/ mdo sde rgyan/ le'u/ 12_sh+loka_15_shog_13_ba6
[202] Maitreya, Ornament of Mahayana Sutras 12:15, Toh 4020 Tengyur, sems tsam, phi, 13b6.

f.d: sngar ma khyer yang da gdod spyan 'dren/ / de bas spyir snang sgyu mar shes bya/ / gnyen pos mi mthun phyogs bcom pa yang / / sgyu ma'i rgyal pos de 'dra'i rgyal po/ / bcom pa bzhin du shes bya man ngag /

sems las 'jigs pa gzhan 'ga' med skabs/ / de bas rang gi rnam rtog bgegs yin/ / de med pa la gzhan gyis ci bya/ / ston shes g.yung gis phyags la sdig 'khrul/ / bred pas kun gyis skad ngan bton bzhin/ /

The statement that nothing is to be feared except mind[203] means that our own imagination is an obstacle.[204] If it were not there, what could others do to us?! The teacher Sheyung was afraid of a broom and cried out in fear.[205]

d.div: [203] Śāntideva’s Guide to the Bodhisattva Way of Life 5:8.
[204] The word bgegs used here signifies both an obstruction and an evil spirit that causes obstacles. The following passage deals with both.

[205] The teacher Sherap Yungdrung was a coward. One evening the light of a butter lamp in the temple fell on a broom. Sherap Yungdrung thought that it was a ghost and screamed. Some other monks came to his assistance and discovered what the “ghost” really was (Lha Drigangpa, p. 438). The next two anecdotes run along similar lines.

f.d: thu gar mi yis pha bong 'don dus/ / gzhan gyis nya bcug de nyid kyis brlag / sgom g.yog bag phyes 'bag byas sdigs bzhin/ / gzhan yang de lta bu ni mang yod/ /

When someone from Thugar was digging out a boulder, another person put a fish [underneath it], and both were stupefied. The servant of a meditation master made a mask of wheat dough to scare him; and there are many more similar cases.

de bas rang gi rnam rtog bgegs yin/ / rnam rtog med cing dpa' bar gyur na/ / ci lta bus kyang gnod pa mi 'byung / / sdug dang mi sdug ci ltar snang yang // mi zhig mngon sum 'dug bzhin sems na/ / lha cig rta mgo can bzhin 'jigs med/ / rang sems 'khrul la mngon zhen mi bya/ /

Therefore our own imagination is an obstacle. If imagination is absent and we have become courageous, nothing will be able to harm us. Whatever appears for us, be it pleasant or unpleasant, we should think that it is similar to the appearance of a human being. Thus our sole lord was not even afraid of a being with a horse’s head. We should not cling to the fabrications of our own minds.
sgrub pa gang la 'jug par gyur kyang / / dang po nyid nas re dang dogs spangs/ / re dogs can la gnod pa 'byung nye/ / bu ga yod la rlung 'jug ji bzhin/ /

Whatever appears [when we meditate], we must first of all give up hope and fear, because harm is near when we are possessed by hope or fear.[206] It is as [in the saying that] the wind enters wherever there is a hole.[207] /38/

d.div: [206] This refers to the hope of having good meditation experiences, such as seeing one’s meditation deity, and to the fear that demons and evil spirits might appear.
[207] According to Lha Drigangpa (pp. 439–40), this refers to a passage from the Questions of Gaganagañja Sutra (Gaganagañjaparipṛcchāsūtra).

f.d: zhang zhung rgan ltar glags btsal sla na/ / kun gyi co 'dri min na sus 'dri/[142] /
Like the old monk from Shangshung,[208] we will be ridiculed by everyone if it is easy to find an opportunity to do so. If there is no opportunity, who would do that?!

d.div: [142] kun gyis/ mi rigs dpe skrun khang /

[208] An old monk from Shangshung came to Radeng Monastery and asked, “Whom must I greet respectfully in this monastery?” He was sent from one monk to the other and saluted everyone, and finally he was even sent to greet the dogs.

f.d: de bas dang por re dogs kun spang /[143] / yang zhing srab pa'i sems kyang spangs la/ / bar du ci snang rang sems nyid blta/ / byams dang snying rje byang chub sems sbyang / / rang gis khas blangs tshul khrims gtsang bya/ / sna tshogs tshul gyis tshogs kyang gsog na/ / de lta bu la bar chad mi 'byung / / byung yang myur du nye bar zhi 'gyur/ /

Therefore we must first give up all hopes and fears. When we have left all weak and unstable states of mind behind, we must next regard all appearances as being the mind itself, train ourselves in the thought of awakening endowed with love and compassion, keep a pure discipline with respect to our vows, and gather the accumulations in many ways. Then no hindrances will appear, and even if they do, they will quickly be appeased.

d.div: [143] kun spangs/ mi rigs dpe skrun khang /

f.d: rang gi sems la rma rnams med na/ / bdud kyis bsdigs sogs bar chad byar med/ / des kyang dang po rnyed pa sogs sgrub/ / 'dod chags zhe sdang sogs kyi rkyen sgrub/ /

If our own minds are free from defects, the evil spirits cannot cause obstacles by threatening us and the like. Therefore they first make us gain some profit, and then they can produce causes [for wrong attitudes] like desire or hatred.
de las nyon mongs 'phel bas rgyud sreg / de nas dmyal sogs dag tu nges ltung / / bdud kyis bar chad byed tshul de yin/ /
From these [wrong attitudes] delusion grows, and then our minds will be scorched and we will necessarily fall into bad states like hell. This is how the evil spirits create obstacles.

dper na nyi mas nags bsregs bzhin te/ / nyi ma nyid kyis dngos su mi sreg / me shel la phog 'od kyis bar bur/ / de yis nags te brgyud pas kun sreg / nyi mas nags sreg tshul ni de bzhin/ / dkar po'i chos rnams bdud kyis sreg pas/ / de bas bdud kyis mi brdzi bya phyir/ / rang gi sems la rma med man ngag /

It is like the way the sun burns a forest: The sun itself does not really burn it, but when its rays fall on a lens made of glass, flames will blaze up and eventually incinerate the entire forest. Similarly, our wholesome factors can be burned up by the evil spirits, and thus our minds must be free from defects so that the evil spirits cannot afflict us; that’s the instruction.
dgon par gnas pas 'jigs skrag spang skabs/ / so sor rtog pa'i stobs kyis bdag med/ / rnam gnyis sgom la skrag pa mi 'byung / / de la bar chad dag gis mi brdzi/ /

According to the passage on giving up fear when we are in the wilderness,[209] no fear will arise when we meditate with the power of analytical discrimination on the two kinds of selflessness [of the person and of phenomena]. Then we will not be afflicted by obstacles.

d.div: [209] This refers to a quotation from the Questions of the Layman Ugra Sutra (Gṛhapatyu-graparipṛcchāsūtra) in chapter 11 of Śāntideva’s Compendium of Trainings.

f.d: gang gi gnyen por gang gsungs de yang / / rang gi rgyud la skyer mi btub na/ / de la gnyen por gang bshad pa'ang // gnyen po nyid du 'gyur ba ma yin/ / des ni man ngag the tshom mi bya/ /

Although this has been explained to be the antidote, we may find ourselves unable to produce [this attitude] in our minds. Then what has been taught as an antidote will not really help us. This should not make us doubt the instructions.
rang rgyud ma btub rtags su shes kyis/ / de btub bya phyir tshogs bsag sgrib sbyang / / bla mar gsol btab sna tshogs tshul nas// btub par gyur na gnyen por 'gyur nges/ /

We must know that it is a defect of our own minds. Therefore we must gather the accumulations, remove the obscurations, pray to the teacher, and so on in order to become more capable; and when we have become capable through these methods, [the analytical method outlined above] will become an antidote without fail.

bar chad dag tu gsal ba byung na/ / bsam pa'i khyad par rgyun du gang byed/ / de nyid gnyen po gzhan du mi btsal/ / sangs rgyas rjes dran byams dang snying rje// lha yi sku'am stong nyid bsgoms pa/ / 'dra ste de dus de nyid dran bya/ /

When we have removed the obstacles, we need not seek for any other remedy than the mental fruits of whatever wholesome practice we have done. When [we experience obstructions in our meditation], we must apply the very same practices: recollecting the Buddha, loving kindness and compassion, and reflecting on the form of a meditation deity or on emptiness.
mngon sum bzhugs nas chos rnams ston yang / / dga' ba'i bsam med stong nyid mi g.yo/ / de la sogs la cis kyang mi brdzi/ /

Whatever [deities or spirits] appear in our perception, we should not rejoice, even if they preach the Dharma, but be unwavering in [our meditation on] emptiness. If we [apply methods] like these, nothing will afflict us.

lha dang bdud gnyis shes par bya ba/ / stong nyid bsgoms pas rab tu gsal 'gyur/ / gcig shos de bsgoms myur du med 'gyur/ / de gnyis mtshan nyid gcig ni de yin/ / de mthong rang gi rgyud la nyon mongs/ / zhi dang 'phel las brtag pa'am gcig yin/ /

The method of discerning whether [an apparition] is a deity or an evil spirit is to meditate on emptiness; if it becomes more distinct, [it is a deity, whereas] if it is the other kind of being and you meditate [on emptiness], it will quickly vanish. This is how you can distinguish between the two. Whether the afflictions fade or increase in your mind when you see them, is another way to examine what they are.

dge bshes des gsungs g.yung chung ba la/ / nged rnams tsho la nang na khyod gzhon/ / khyod kyis brgyad cu'i bar du sdod la/ / de yi dus na sgom chen kha cig / ngas ni sangs rgyas zhal mthong zer la/ / nyon mongs 'phel la chung du ma song / /

The spiritual mentor [Dromtönpa] said to Yungchung: /39/ “You are the youngest in our group. Some meditation masters say when they have reached the age of eighty, ‘I have seen the face of the Buddha in person,’ and their delusions increase instead of getting smaller.
de ltar snang na 'dres khyer shes gyis/ / sangs rgyas zhal mthong de las bzlog pa/ / rmi lam sogs na'ang de bzhin shes gyis/ /
You must know that when this happens, they are carried away by the demons. We must dispel the face of the Buddha when we see it and understand that it is just like a dream.
kha cig ngas ni ting 'dzin thob zer/ / nyon mongs cher song de yang de bzhin// ngas ni lta ba rtogs zer las 'bras/ / khyad du gsod cing sdig la 'jug na/ / de yang log lta skyes par shes gyis/ /

Some say, ‘I have reached meditative absorption,’ and their delusions increase, just as in the former case. [Others say,] ‘I perceive the right view [of emptiness],’ and thinking little of the law of deeds and their results, commit bad deeds. We must understand that in this case they have developed a wrong view.
yang dag lta ba'i mtshan nyid dag ni/ / chos rnams nam mkha' lta bur shes kyang / / de rtogs bya phyir kun rdzob las 'bras/ / chung ngu tsam yang khyad du mi gsod/ /
The sign of a right view is that we know phenomena to be [empty] like the sky. Nevertheless, to perceive [this emptiness correctly], we do not think little of the relative truth of cause and effect.
bden pa ma mthong gang zag rnams la/ / sdig pa chung yang 'bras bu 'byin phyir/ / dge bsnyen rgad po de zer gyis la/ / khyod kyis mi la de skad du zlos/ / de skad gsungs pas de ltar shes bya//

For people who have not seen the truth, even a small deed will have results. Therefore the old layperson [Dromtön] has told you this. You should also tell this to someone in the future.” This is what he said, and this is what we must know.
nyer lnga pa chos spyod bcu la sogs pa'i sgo nas tshogs bsag dgos tshul ston pa/
25. The need to gather the accumulations through the ten religious actions[210] and so forth

d.div: [210] The ten religious actions are: (1) writing Buddhist texts, (2) religious worship, (3) generosity, (4) listening to the Dharma, (5) memorizing it, (6) reading it, (7) preaching, (8) recitation, (9) thinking about the Dharma, and (10) meditating on it.

f.d: de lta'i yon tan ma lus ldan dang / / skyon rnams ma lus zad par 'dod na/ / sna tshogs tshul nas tshogs rnams bsag bya/ /
If we wish to be fully endowed with all these good qualities and become free from all faults, we must gather the accumulations in various ways.
de yang gang yang rung ba cig la'ang / / de nyid gcig pu byed pa 'dra ba'i/ / bsod nams las la rtag tu 'bad dgos/ /
Whatever [meritorious deed] we do, we must constantly strive to do nothing but this, as if this meritorious deed were the only thing we do.
tshogs kyis nye bar brtan ma byas na/ / btub btub 'dra yang ci zhig ltar na/ / ci yang rung ba zhig gis med 'gyur/ / gnyen po ci yis bcos thabs kyang med/ / de bas tshogs kyis brtan pa gal che/ /

If we do not work to accumulate merit, but just do this and that—whatever occurs to us—this will not prepare us for anything, and we will be unable to apply any of the methods that might help us. Therefore it is very important to become firm in accumulating [merit].

mdo sde rgyan gyi mos pa'i skabs su/[144] / thabs tshul kun gyis bsod nams bsag bya/ / bsod nams bsags la yon tan kun skye/ / dper na bri sha'i rgyal po bzhin nam/ / slob dpon shes rab 'byung gnas sbas bzhin/ / phyogs glang tshad bltas rang gi lta 'gyur/ / rnal 'byor dbu ma'i bden pa'i sems rnyed/ /

According to the chapter on inclinations from the Ornament of Mahayana Sutras,[211] we must gain merit by all possible means. Someone who has gathered merit will achieve all good qualities, just as the king of Brisha did,[212] and the teacher Prajñākaragupta, who adopted the view of the logical system of Dignāga and attained the understanding of the truth according to the Yogācāra-Madhyamaka system.

d.div: [144] sde dge_4020_bstan/ sems tsam/ phi_byams pa mgon po/ mdo sde rgyan/ le'u/ 11_sh+loka_6_shog_12_ba5
[211] Maitreya, Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra 11:6, Toh 4020 Tengyur, sems tsam, phi, 12b4.

[212] The king of Brisha had a non-Buddhist teacher who taught that if he killed human beings he would gain subjects, and if he killed cattle he would gain wealth. The king had done many meritorious deeds and through this merit was able to recognize this view to be wrong (Lha Drigangpa, p. 450).

f.d: AR+ya pa lo'i brtul zhugs kyang yin/ / klu yi dbu ma ltas pa tsam gyis/[145] / phyi rol lta gyur dbu ma chen po/ / de la sogs pa dpag med gsungs phyir/ / sgrib sbyang bsod nams bsag la 'bad bya/ / lam phran legs 'ong gtam rgyud kyang bsam/[146] /

There was also Avalokitavrata,[213] who through merely seeing the middle way view of Nāgārjuna, changed his non-Buddhist view and adopted the Great Madhyamaka; these and other events have been described. Therefore we must strive to remove the obscurations and to gain merit. /40/ We should also think about the stories of Cūḍapantha and Svāgata.[214]

d.div: [145] bltas pa/ mi rigs dpe skrun khang /
[146] sde dge_3_bka'/ 'dul ba/ ja_lung rnam 'byed/ lam phran gyi gtam rgyud/ shog_67_ba_dang / sde dge_3_bka'/ 'dul ba/ nya_lung rnam 'byed/ legs 'ong gi gtam rgyud/ shog_19_na3

[213] Literally “one who has adopted Avalokiteśara’s habit.” Lha Drigangpa (pp. 450–51) explains that this person was a non-Buddhist who had taken an oath to wear long hair. When he became a Buddhist, he saw that Avalokiteśvara was wearing long hair, so he decided not to cut his hair either.

[214] These stories can be found in the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya and in the Divyāvadāna anthology; see Andy Rotman’s translation in Divine Stories: Divyāvadāna (Boston: Wisdom Publications). The well-known story of Cūḍapantha, who overcomes his slow intellect, is in volume 2 (forthcoming), and the tale of Svāgata, who overcomes his ill-fatedness, is in volume 1 (2008: 289–323).

f.d: rnal 'byor tshogs bsag bar chad srung ba'i/[147] / zhing gi dam pa dge 'dun bsnyen bkur/ / 'byor pa med na de rnams kyis bskor/ /

Also, yogis must pay respect to the noble monastic community, the field for gathering merit that will protect them from obstacles. If they do not have the necessary means,[215] the Sangha can also appoint [a single monk to receive the gifts].

d.div: [147] tshogs bsags/ mi rigs dpe skrun khang /

[215] This is what the root text seems to say. The respective passage in the commentary, however, says that if not all the monks can come, they can also appoint a single monk who receives the offerings (see Lha Drigangpa, p. 545).

f.d: gcig la bsnyen bkur kun la byas mtshungs/ / 'byor med gsol ba btab cing bskos phyir/ /
If they have honored a single monk, it is as if they have honored all of them, as long as they have invited everyone and the Sangha has appointed someone [as their representative].
bsam gtan gzugs med ting 'dzin dag kyang / / dpag med tshogs bsags med par min na/ / 'jig rten kun dang mi mthun sems ni/ / dpag med tshogs la ltos dgos ci smos/ /

If the meditative concentrations and the formless meditative attainments do not arise if we have not gathered immeasurable accumulations, how much more do we need immeasurable accumulations to gain a mind so contrary to the mundane.
[sngags lam]

d.div: [216] This heading has been added for the sake of clarity.

f.d: pha rol phyin pa'i tshul gyi lam las// gsang sngags lam ni nye'am snyam na/ / bya ni rnyi las shor ba bzhin nam/ / mi ni btson las shor ba bzhin du/ / tha mal rnam rtog ma 'dres pa yis/ / bsgrubs na gsang sngags pha rol phyin lam/ / nye ring khyad med shin tu myur yin/ /

You may wonder whether the path of secret mantra is shorter than the path of the perfections. If someone whose mind is free from ordinary conceptions practices them [without looking back] —the way a bird escapes from a net or a man escapes from prison— then the path of secret mantra and the path of the perfections are equal in length: both of them are very fast.
lha nyid de gsungs gsang sngags lam dang / / pha rol phyin lam nye ring khyad med/ / gcig ni nye bar gsungs pa dgongs can/ / dgongs pa'i gzhi ni gang zag bsam pa/ /

The sole lord himself said that the path of secret mantra and the path of the perfections are equal in length. When it was stated that one of them is shorter, it was said with a certain intention, and it was intended for certain personalities.[217]

d.div: [217] Lha Drigangpa (p. 458) explains that this has been said with respect to persons with particularly sharp mental faculties, who are able to use the tantric practices as a fast method for reaching liberation.

f.d: nan tar na ni pha rol phyin nye/ / rtag tu ngu yi gtam gyis de shes/ / dang po tshogs lam sgra las nyan phyir/ / chos rgyun ting 'dzin ma skyes des shes/ /

In reality the path of the perfections can be shorter, as we can see in the story of Sadāprarudita, because in the beginning he heard a voice speaking about the path of accumulation and understood it before he had attained the contemplation of a constant stream of Dharma.
mtho na lo gcig lnga brgya'i lam phyin/ / mthong lam de tsam yun gyis skyes gyur/ / de bas tha mal rnam rtog spangs na/ / 'dra ste lam la nye ring yod min/ /

In less than a year, he traveled 500 [leagues],[218] and within this [brief period of] time reached the path of seeing.[219] Therefore they are the same when the ordinary conceptions have been abandoned; the two paths are equal in length.

d.div: [218] The word “league” (yojana, a distance of several miles) has been added from the commentary (Lha Drigangpa, p. 459), where it is mentioned that he travels the distance of five hundred yojana to the east in order to meet his teacher.

[219] This passage alludes to the legend of Sadāprarudita contained in the Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines (Aṣṭasāhasrikāprajñāpāramitā) and partly quoted in chapter 2 of Śāntideva’s Compendium of Trainings. A voice from the sky told him that he must learn the perfection of wisdom from the bodhisattva Dharmodgata who would be his spiritual mentor. Sadāprarudita sacrificed his own flesh to be able to receive Dharmodgata’s instructions and was later miraculously restored to wholeness.

f.d: bla ma mtshan nyid dag dang ldan pas/ / slob ma snod dang rnal mar ldan la/ / mnyes pas dbang bskur man ngag byin nas/ / bsgrubs na sangs rgyas lag gis byed 'dra/ /

If there is a master who has the necessary qualities and a disciple who is a suitable recipient, the disciple will please the master, and the master will give him tantric initiations and practice instructions, and if he practices accordingly, he holds buddhahood in his hand.
log gis zlog na dmyal ba'i gting rgyu/ / lha cig bshes de'i gsung rjes 'brangs na/ / gsang sngags lam la nged cag ma dga'/ / de ltar mtshan nyid ldan pa'ang rab dka'//

But if he does it in a wrong way, it will bring him to the very bottom of hell. Moreover, if we follow the words of our spiritual mentor, the sole lord, we cannot give preference to the path of secret mantra [over the path of the perfections] [because teachers] with the necessary qualities are extremely rare.
nyer drug pa mjug sdud pa dang dge ba bsngo ba/
26. Brief epilogue and dedication of merit

bla ma'i man ngag brjed byang byas pa/ / tshan tshan du bsdus bsdebs pa 'di yin/ / rang nyid dran pa zhan pas brjed dogs/ / bris pa gsang nas gzhag par 'dod pa/ / chos la ser sna byed 'dod min kyang / / byin rlabs nyams dang snod min lag tu/ / song na brnyas sogs chos spong las gsog / de bas shin tu sbas pa yin kyang / / gal te 'phyugs nas mi lag 'grims na/ / thugs kyi bas na bzod pa mdzod cig /

This is a record of the instructions of my teacher, compiled by me in chapters. I wrote it down because I wished to remember it myself, and because I was afraid to forget it. I intended to keep it hidden, but then I did not want to be stingy with Buddhist teachings. However, it should strictly be kept secret because if it falls into the hands of people who are without blessing or who are not suitable recipients, they might abuse it and accumulate the bad karma of rejecting the Dharma. If I have made mistakes, I beg those who hold this book in their hands to forgive me.
bla ma'i man ngag brjed byang byas pa'i/ / dge ba cung zad bdag gis bsags des/ / bdag dang sems can theg chen lam nas/ / 'gro la phan phyir sangs rgyas 'grub shog /
May the little merit that I have gained by making this record of the instructions of my teacher /41/ help me and all other sentient beings to travel the Mahayana path and reach buddhahood.
bla ma'i man ngag brjed byang byas pa/ / thog ma dang bar dang tha mar dge ba rdzogs so// //
The virtuous deed of recording the instructions of my teacher—beginning, middle, and end—is completed.
@#/ /dam chos yid bzhin gyi nor bu thar pa rin po che'i rgyan zhes bya ba bzhugs so//
Part II. Ornament of Precious Liberation: A Wish-Fulfilling Gem of Sublime Dharma
rje sgam po pas mdzad/
Gampopa (1079–1153) Translated by Ken Holmes and edited by Thupten Jinpa /45/
bstan bcos kyi sngon 'gro bshad pa/
@#/ /'phags pa 'jam dpal gzhon nur gyur pa la phyag 'tshal lo/ /
I prostrate to Youthful Mañjuśrī.[1]

d.div: [1] Youthful Mañjuśrī—Mañjuśrī Kumārabhuta—is one of the names of the great bodhisattva Mañjuśrī. It signifies his status as a tenth-level bodhisattva: one of those who remain ever young, not “aging” into full buddhahood.

rgyal dang de sras rnams dang dam pa'i chos rnams dang / / de'i yang rtsa bar gyur pa bla ma la btud nas/ / yid bzhin nor bu lta bu'i dam chos rin chen 'di/ / mi la rje yi drin la brten nas rang gzhan don du bri/[1] /

Having paid homage to the buddhas, their spiritual heirs, the sublime Dharma, and also to the gurus who are the root of all these, I will now write, through the gracious kindness of revered Milarepa, this Gem of Precious Dharma, a Wish-Fulfilling Jewel for both my own and others’ benefit.

[1] gzhung 'di'i ma phyi rtsib ris dpar mar gzhi bcol zhing / dpar ma bsdur yul dpal spungs dpar ma dang / mi rigs dpe skrun khang nas dpar tu btab pa'i gangs can rig brgya'i sgo 'byed lde mig deb grangs _20_nang bzhugs pa'i dwags po thar rgyan gnyis yin/ des na bsdus yig tu dpal spungs dang / mi rigs dpe skrun khang zhes bkod yod/ bla ma'i gsung la brten nas/ dpal spungs/ mi rje'i drin la brten nas/ mi rigs dpe skrun khang /

f.d: spyir chos thams cad 'khor ba dang mya ngan las 'das pa gnyis su 'dus so/ / de la 'khor ba zhes bya ba ni rang bzhin stong pa nyid yin/ rnam pa 'khrul pa yin/ mtshan nyid sdug bsngal du shar ba yin no/ / mya ngan las 'das pa zhes bya ba ni rang bzhin stong pa nyid yin/ rnam pa 'khrul pa thams cad zad cing yal ba yin/ mtshan nyid sdug bsngal thams cad las grol ba yin no/ /

Generally, phenomena can be subsumed into the two classes of samsara and nirvana. That which is known as samsara is, by nature, emptiness, taking the form of illusions and characterized by suffering. That which is known as nirvana is also, by nature, emptiness, taking the form of the exhaustion, then disappearance, of the illusions and characterized by liberation from all suffering.

de la 'khor bar 'khrul pa 'di yang su 'khrul na/ khams gsum gyi sems can thams cad 'khrul lo// gzhi ci las 'khrul na/ stong pa nyid las 'khrul lo/ / rgyu ci las 'khrul na/ ma rig pa chen pos 'khrul lo/ / tshul ji ltar 'khrul na/ 'gro ba rigs drug gi spyod yul du 'khrul lo/ / dpe ji ltar 'khrul na/ gnyid dang rmi lam ltar 'khrul lo/ / dus nam nas 'khrul na/ 'khor ba thog ma med pa nas 'khrul lo/ / 'khrul pa la skyon ci yod na/ sdug bsngal 'ba' zhig la spyod do/ /

Who is deluded by these illusions of samsara? All sentient beings of its three realms. On what are the illusions based? The illusions are projected onto emptiness. What causes the delusion? It occurs through great ignorance. In what way do they come to be deluded? They come to be deluded with regard to the sphere of experiences of the six classes of beings. What would be a suitable metaphor for such an illusion? This resembles the illusion experienced in one’s sleep and dreams. Since when have these illusions been happening? Since time without beginning. What is wrong with them? One experiences nothing but suffering.
'khrul pa ye shes su nam 'gyur na/[2] bla med kyi byang chub thob tsa na 'gyur ro/[3] / 'khrul pa la rang sangs yod dam snyam na/ 'khor ba mtha' med par grags pa de yin no/ /

When will the delusion become pristine awareness? It does so when highest enlightenment is reached.[2] Those who think that illusion may dissolve on its own should be aware that samsara is renowned for being endless.

d.div: [2] 'khrul ba nam sangs na/ dpal spungs/
[3] thob tsa na sangs so/ dpal spungs/
[2] The Palpung edition has, “When will delusion be fully clarified? It will be clarified when highest enlightenment is reached.”

f.d: de ltar na 'khor ba 'di 'khrul pa yin lugs sam/ sdug bsngal che tshod dam/ yun gyi ring lugs sam/ rang grol med lugs de ltar lags pas dus de ring nas bzung ste bla med kyi byang chub ci thob la 'bad 'tshal lo//

Having, in the above way, carefully considered samsara in terms of it being an illusion, the extent of its suffering, the length of its time, and that there is no self-release, strive in all earnestness and with great diligence, from this very moment onward, to attain unsurpassable enlightenment.

de ltar 'bad pa la ci dgos she na/ sdom ni/
rgyu dang rten dang rkyen dang ni/ / thabs dang 'bras bu phrin las te/ / bla med byang chub spyi sdom drug / blo ldan rnams kyis shes par bya/ / zhes pa ste/

What exactly is needed to strive so? The synopsis[3] is:
Prime cause, basis, condition, means, results, and activity: by these six general key terms should the wise know peerless enlightenment.

d.div: [3] These boldface synopses are an important part of the text. They are memorized by students as a way of recollecting its subject matter. Each of the six headings in this opening synopsis constitutes a chapter of the book, with the exception of the fourth, which is spread over sixteen chapters.

f.d: bla med kyi byang chub de'i rgyu dang / de sgrub pa'i rten gyi gang zag dang / de bsgrub pa la bskul ba'i rkyen dang /[4] de sgrub pa'i thabs dang / de grub pa'i 'bras bu dang /[5] de grub nas sangs rgyas kyi phrin las rnams shes dgos pa'o/[6] /

This means that one needs to know (1) the prime cause for highest enlightenment, (2) the beings whose existence forms a basis for achieving it, (3) the condition that incites /46/ that attainment, (4) the means by which it is attained, (5) the results of it being attained, and (6) the enlightened activity once there has been such attainment.

d.div: [4] sgrub/ dpal spungs/
[5] 'grub/ dpal spungs/
[6] sangs rgyas/ zhes pa dpal spungs dpar mar mi byung /

f.d:
de dag rim par bstan pa ni/
rgyu ni bde gshegs snying po ste// rten ni mi lus rin chen mchog / rkyen ni dge ba'i bshes gnyen yin/ / thabs ni de yi gdams ngag ste/ / 'bras bu rdzogs sangs rgyas kyi sku/ / 'phrin las rtog med 'gro don mdzad/ / ces pa rnams yin no/ / de rnams kyis ni lus rnam gzhag bstan pa tsam yin no/[7] /

These will be explained, in the above order, as being the following:
The prime cause is buddha nature The basis is a most precious human existence. The condition is the Dharma master. The means is the Dharma master’s instruction. The results are the bodies of perfect buddhahood. The activity is to nonconceptually fulfill the welfare of beings. This is merely an outline of the main structure of this text.

d.div: [7] rnam bzhag_dpal spungs/

f.d: da ni yan lag rgyas par 'chad do/ / de la dang po/
What follows is a detailed explanation of each point.
(spyi don dang po bla med byang chub sgrub pa'i rgyu bshad pa/)
I. The Prime Cause
le'u dang po/ rgyu bde bshegs snying po/

rgyu ni bde gshegs snying po ste/ /zhes pa ni/[8] 'o na 'khor ba 'khrul pa'i rang bzhin 'di las grol nas/ bla med kyi byang chub thob dgos pa de/ bdag cag la sogs pa gang zag dman pa dag gis 'bad pa byas kyang thob par cang 'gyur ram snyam na/ 'bad pas bsgrubs na byang chub cis te mi thob ste/ bdag cag la sogs pa'i sems can thams cad la sangs rgyas kyi rgyu de bzhin gshegs pa'i snying po yod pa'i phyir ro/ /

The line “The prime cause is buddha nature” states the following. As mentioned above, you need to gain freedom from the deluded nature of samsara and to attain highest enlightenment. However, you might well wonder, “Even if we or other ordinary people[4] like us were to try very hard, how could we ever possibly attain enlightenment?” In truth, anyone who practices with great effort cannot fail to reach enlightenment. Why? Because all forms of conscious life, including ourselves, possess its prime cause. Within us is buddha nature.

d.div: [8] zhes pa la/ dpal spungs/
[4] The text says “lesser beings,” but since that is comparing them with exalted beings, such as buddhas and realized bodhisattvas, the meaning is that they are regular, worldly beings.

f.d:
de ltar yang ting nge 'dzin gyi rgyal po'i mdo las/
bde gshegs snying pos 'gro kun yongs la khyab/[9] / ces gsungs so/ /

The King of Meditation Sutra states:
Buddha nature totally permeates all beings.[5]

d.div: [9] sde dge_127_bka'/ mdo sde/ da_ting nge 'dzin rgyal po'i mdo/ le'u/ 10_shog_32_ba7_'di la dgongs pa yin nam/
[5] Samādhirājasūtra, Toh 127 Kangyur, mdo sde, da, 32a7.

f.d:
mdo mya ngan las 'das chung las kyang /
sems can thams cad ni de bzhin gshegs pa'i snying po can yin no/[10] / zhes dang / mdo sde mya ngan las 'das pa chen po las kyang /
dper na 'o ma la mar gyis khyab par gnas so/ / de bzhin du de bzhin gshegs pa'i snying pos kyang sems can thams cad la khyab par gnas so/[11] / zhes dang /

The shorter Great [Passing into] Nirvana Sutra says:
All sentient beings possess buddha nature.[6] Further, the longer Great [Passing into] Nirvana Sutra says:
Just as butter, for example, exists in milk as something totally permeating it, so does buddha nature permeate all sentient beings.[7]

d.div: [10] sde dge_120_bka'/ mdo sde/ tha_mdo myang 'das/ le'u/ tha ma/ shog_112_na4
[11] gong mtshungs/ mdo myang 'das/ le'u/ tha ma/ shog_111_ba1
[6] Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra (shorter version), Toh 120 Kangyur, mdo sde, tha, 112a4.
[7] Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra (longer version), Toh 119 Kangyur, mdo sde, tha, 111b1.

f.d:
mdo sde rgyan las kyang /
de bzhin nyid ni thams cad la/ / khyad par med kyang dag gyur pa/ / de bzhin gshegs nyid de yi phyir/ / 'gro kun de yi snying po can/[12] / zhes gsungs so//

The Ornament of Mahayana Sutras also states:
Suchness is the same for all and everyone; it is that which is pure. Since this is the Tathāgata, all beings are endowed with this essence.[8]

d.div: [12] sde dge_4020_bstan/ sems tsam/ phi_byams pa mgon po/ mdo sde rgyan/ le'u/ 10_sh+loka_37_shog_10_na5
[8] Maitreya, Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra 10:37, Toh 4020 Tengyur, sems tsam, phi, 10a5.

f.d: 'o na rgyu mtshan ci'i phyir sems can sangs rgyas kyi snying po can yin zhe na/ chos sku stong nyid kyis sems can la khyab pa'i phyir dang / chos nyid de bzhin nyid la dbye ba med pa'i phyir dang / sems can thams cad la rigs yod pa'i phyir te/ des na rgyu mtshan gsum yod pas/ sems can sangs rgyas kyi snying po can yin te/

If this is so, you may wonder why sentient beings are endowed with buddha nature. /47/ It is because: (1) Dharmakāya, emptiness, pervades all beings. (2) The universal essence (dharmatā), suchness (tathatā), is without differentiation. (3) Every sentient being has the potential to become a buddha.

de ltar yang rgyud bla ma las/
rdzogs sangs sku ni 'phro phyir dang / / de bzhin nyid dbyer med phyir dang / / rigs yod phyir na lus can kun/ / rtag tu sangs rgyas snying po can/[13] / zhes gsungs so/ /

This is just what is stated in the Uttaratantra, where it says:
Because the dharmakāya pervades all, because suchness is without differentiation, and because they possess the potential, every living being at all times has buddha nature.[9]

d.div: [13] sde dge_4024_bstan/ sems tsam/ phi_byams pa mgon po/ rgyud bla ma/ le'u/ 1_sh+loka_27_shog_56_na2
[9] Maitreya, Uttaratantra 1:27, Toh 4024 Tengyur, sems tsam, phi, 56a2.

f.d: de la dang po chos sku stong nyid kyis sems can la khyab pa zhes pa ni/ sangs rgyas ni chos kyi sku yin la/[14] [15] chos sku ni stong nyid yin te/ stong nyid des sems can thams cad la khyab pa'i phyir na yang /[16] sems can sangs rgyas kyi snying po can yin pa'o/ / chos nyid de bzhin nyid la dbye ba med pa zhes pa ni/ sangs rgyas kyi de bzhin nyid dang / sems can gyi de bzhin nyid la bzang ngan nam/ che chung ngam/ mtho dma' yi dbye ba med pas na yang /[17] sems can sangs rgyas kyi snying po can yin pa'o/ / sems can thams cad la rigs yod pa zhes pa ni/ sems can rnams sangs rgyas kyi rigs rnam pa lngar gnas te/ gang zhe na/

To explain the first reason, “dharmakāya, emptiness, pervades all beings,” here the Buddha is the dharmakāya, and the dharmakāya is emptiness. Since emptiness is something pervading all sentient beings, it follows that all those beings have the essence of buddhahood. The second reason, “the universal essence, suchness, is without differentiation,” means that whether it be in terms of good and bad, great and small, or higher and lower, there is no difference between the universal essence in buddhas and the universal essence in sentient beings. Thus sentient beings possess the buddha essence. That “every sentient being has the potential to become a buddha” is explained through the five ways in which they stand in respect to enlightenment potential.

d.div: [14] sangs rgyas kyi/ mi rigs dpe skrun/
[15] chos sku yin la/ dpal spungs/
[16] yang / zhes pa'i rgyan sdud kyi phrad de dpal spungs dpar mar mi byung /

f.d:
sdom ni/
rigs chad rigs dang ma nges rigs/ / nyan thos rigs dang rang rgyal rigs/ / theg pa chen po'i rigs can te/ / lngas ni sangs rgyas rigs can bsdus/ / zhes pa'o//

These are outlined in the following synopsis:
Those with enlightenment potential can be summed up as belonging to five groups: those with severed potential, undetermined potential, śrāvaka potential, pratyekabuddha potential, and those with the Mahayana potential.

de la rigs chad kyi rigs ni/ gang dag khrel med pa/ ngo tsha med pa/ snying rje med pa la sogs pa mtshan nyid drug ldan du slob dpon chen po thogs med kyis gsungs pa de dag ste/ ji skad du/
'khor ba'i skyon rnams mthong yang skyo ba cung zad med/ / sangs rgyas yon tan thos kyang dad pa cung zad med/ / khrel med ngo tsha med cing snying rje cung zad med/ / sdig pa lhag par spyod la 'gyod pa cung zad med/ / med drug 'dzom la sangs rgyas skal ba med/[18] / ces gsungs pa'o/ /

Those with severed potential are characterized by six traits, such as lacking a sense of shame in public, having no dignity in private, lacking compassion, and so forth. The great master Asaṅga has said of them:
Though seeing what is wrong with samsara, they are not in the least put off by it. Though hearing about the qualities of enlightened beings, they feel not the slightest faith in them. Without conscience and shame, and devoid of even a little compassion, they feel not the slightest regret for the unwholesome acts in which they fully indulge. When those these six absences converge, they are far from ready for enlightenment.[10]

d.div: [18] 'dir drangs pa'i tshigs bcad 'di'i khungs ngos 'dzin ma thub mod/ thogs med kyis rigs chad kyi gang zag khyad chos drug ldan du gsungs pa de'i nyan sar byung / sde dge_4036_bstan/ sems tsam/ dzi_nyan thos kyi sa/ shog_7_ba5

[10] Asaṅga’s discussion of the six shortcomings and how the convergence of them deprives one of the spiritual potential is found in his Śrāvaka Levels (Śrāvaka-bhūmi), Toh 4036. Tengyur, sem stam, dzi, 7b5. It is difficult to determine whether Gampopa is here citing from another source or versifying this same citation.

f.d:
mdo sde rgyan las kyang /
la la gcig tu nyes pa spyod nges yod/ / la la dkar po'i chos rnams kun tu bcom/ / la la thar pa cha mthun dge ba med/ / dkar po dman pa yod pa rgyu dang bral/[19] / zhes gsungs so/ /

It also says, in the Ornament of Mahayana Sutras:
It is certain that some are solely engaged in what is harmful. Some are constantly destroying whatever is good. Others lack those virtues conducive to liberation. They are devoid of anything that could in any way be wholesome.[11]

d.div: [19] sde dge_4020_bstan/ sems tsam/ phi_byams pa mgon po/ mdo sde rgyan/ le'u/ 4_sh+loka_11_shog_4_na6
[11] Maitreya, Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra 4:11, Toh 4020 Tengyur, sems tsam, phi, 4a6.

f.d:
lar rtags de dag dang ldan pa rigs chad du gsungs pa de yang / 'khor bar yun ring du 'gor ba la dgongs pa yin gyis/ gtan nas byang chub mi thob pa ni ma yin te/ 'bad pa byas na des kyang byang chub thob pa yin no/ / de ltar yang snying rje pad+ma dkar po'i mdo las/
kun dga' bo/ gal te sems can mya ngan las 'da' ba'i skal ba med pa zhig gis/ sangs rgyas la dmigs nas tha na me tog gcig nam mkha' la 'thor na yang / de mya ngan las 'da' ba'i 'bras bu can yin te/ mya ngan las 'das par klas pa dang / mya ngan las 'das pa'i mthas gtugs par nga smra'o/[20] / zhes gsungs so//

Although those who have the above traits are said to have severed potential, this refers to their having to pass an exceedingly long time in samsara and does not mean that they have definitively cut off any chance of achieving enlightenment. Provided that they make the effort, /48/ they can attain enlightenment. It says of this, in the White Lotus of Compassion Sutra:
Ānanda! Were someone lacking the fortunate circumstances for nirvana merely to cast a flower up in the sky, visualizing the Buddha, then that person thereby possesses the fruit of nirvana. I declare that person to be one who will reach nirvana and who will penetrate to its furthest end.[12]

d.div: [20] sde dge_111_bka'/ mdo sde/ cha_snying rje pad dkar gyi mdo/ le'u/ 7_shog_87_na7
[12] Mahākaruṇāpuṇḍarīkasūtra, Toh 111 Kangyur, mdo sde, cha, 87a7.

f.d: ma nges pa'i rigs can ni/ rkyen la rag las pa can te/ gang dag nyan thos kyi dge ba'i bshes gnyen bsten pa'am/ nyan thos kyi grogs po dang 'grogs pa'am/ nyan thos kyi mdo sde mthong na nyan thos la dad de/ nyan thos kyi rigs su gyur nas nyan thos su mngon par 'byung bar 'gyur la/ de bzhin du rang rgyal lam/ theg chen gyi rkyen dag dang phrad na/ rang rgyal lam/ theg pa chen po par 'gyur ba de dag yin no/ /

The lot of those with undetermined potential depends on the circumstances. Those who train under śrāvaka spiritual teachers, become involved with śrāvakas, or come across śrāvaka scriptures will place their trust in the śrāvaka way and, having entered that way, will actually become śrāvakas themselves. Likewise, those who encounter pratyekabuddha or Mahayana circumstances will embrace the pratyekabuddha or Mahayana ways.

'khor ba'i sdug bsngal mthong nas 'jigs/ / mya ngan 'das la mngon par dad/ / sems can don la mi dga' ba/ / rtags gsum ldan pa nyan thos rigs/[22] / zhes gsungs so/ /

[14] The source of this quote has not been identified.

f.d: nyan rang gi rigs de gnyis theg pa de gnyis la zhugs nas/[26] / rang rang gi 'bras bu thob kyang mya ngan las 'das pa dngos ma yin no/ / 'o na de'i tshe de dag ji ltar gnas na/ ma rig pa'i bag chags kyi sa la brten nas/ zag pa med pa'i las kyis yid kyi rang bzhin gyi lus bzung nas gnas so/ / 'on kyang de'i tshe zag pa med pa'i ting nge 'dzin yod pas/ de la mya ngan las 'das pa yin no snyam pa'i 'du shes kyis gnas pa yin no/ /

The above two groups—those with śrāvaka and those with pratyekabuddha potential—although they may enter these two vehicles and attain their respective results, what they achieve is not true nirvana. At the time of their achievement they will, on account of a latent ignorance, acquire and exist in a subtle mental body brought about by their former untainted karma. They will be convinced that the state of untainted profound absorption they enjoy is nirvana and that they have attained nirvana.

d.div: [26] theg pa de dag_dpal spungs/

f.d: 'o na mya ngan las 'das pa dngos min na/ bcom ldan 'das kyis lam de gnyis ston pa mi rigs she na/ rigs te/ dper na 'dzam bu'i gling nas tshong pa dag phyi'i rgya mtshor nor bu rin po che len du 'gro ba la/ bar skabs su 'brog dgon pa chen por ngal zhing chad nas/ bdag gi nor bu mi lon snyam ste phyir ldog par 'gyur ba rnams la ded dpon chen po'i rdzu 'phrul gyis/[27] grong khyer chen po zhig der sprul nas ngal bsor 'jug pa ltar/ sems can snying stobs chung bas sangs rgyas kyi ye shes thos nas dngangs te/[28] sangs rgyas bsgrub pa 'di nyon mongs so/ / bdag gis mi nus so snyam nas mi 'jug pa'am/ phyir ldog pa rnams la nyan rang gi lam 'di gnyis bstan nas/ nyan rang gi go 'phang du ngal bsor 'jug pa yin no/[29] /

One might object, “If this is not real nirvana, /49/ it would be inappropriate for the Buddha to teach these two paths.” It is, in fact, entirely appropriate for the Buddha to teach them as he did. Let us consider the following example. Some merchants from Jambudvīpa[15] set out to the far-off oceans to obtain precious gems. At one point in their journey, they felt so tired and downhearted while crossing a great wilderness that they began to think they would never manage to get the jewels, and they contemplated turning back. However, through his magical powers, their leader created a great illusory citadel where they were able to rest and recuperate. Like the merchants in this story, beings of weak resolve will feel overwhelmed when they learn of the tremendous wisdom of the buddhas, and they may feel that the task of achieving it is too daunting and far beyond the capacity of the likes of them. On account of the awe they feel, they will either never undertake the task of enlightenment or they will give up easily. By teaching the two paths of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha, the Buddha enables them to attain the refreshing, healing state of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha.

d.div: [27] bdag gis/ dpal spungs/ mi rigs dpe skrun/
[28] thos na/ dpal spungs/
[29] ngal gsor/ dpal spungs/
[15] Jambudvīpa in this context refers principally to India.

f.d:
dam chos pad+ma dkar po las kyang /
de bzhin nyan thos thams cad kyang / / mya ngan 'das thob 'du shes te/ / rgyal bas gsungs pa de dag la/[30] / mya ngan ma 'das de ngal gso/[31] / zhes gsungs so//

In the Lotus Sutra it says:
Likewise all the śrāvakas are under the impression that they have attained nirvana. The Buddha tells them that this is not nirvana but a respite.[16]

d.div: [30] rgyal bas bshad pa/ dpal spungs/
[31] sde dge_113_bka'/ mdo sde/ ja_dam chos pad dkar gyi mdo/ le'u/ 5_sh+loka_74_shog_54_ba1
[16] Saddharmapuṇḍarīkasūtra, Toh 113 Kangyur, mdo sde, ja, 54b1.

f.d: sems can de dag nyan rang gi go 'phang du ngal bsos pa dang / de bzhin gshegs pas mkhyen nas de dag sangs rgyas bsgrub pa la bskul ba'o/ / de yang ji ltar bskul na/ sku gsung thugs kyis bskul ba yin te/ thugs kyis 'od zer spros pas/ nyan rang yid kyi lus can de dag la reg pa tsam gyis zag med kyi ting nge 'dzin las sad par byed do/ / de nas sku'i snang ba bstan te/ gsung gis 'di skad du/ dge slong dag khyed de tsam gyis bya ba byas pa ma yin/ byed pa byas pa ma yin/ khyed kyi mya ngan las 'das pa de mya ngan las 'das pa ma yin te/ dge slong dag da ni khyed de bzhin gshegs pa la nye bar gyur gyis ltos shig / rtogs shig ces bskul ba'o/ /

When they have rested and refreshed themselves in the state of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, the Buddha knows it is time to encourage them to achieve full enlightenment. How is this done? The Buddha inspires them through perfect body, pure speech, and wisdom mind. Light rays stream from his mind. By these beams merely touching their mental bodies, śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are awakened from their untainted meditative concentration. Then the Buddha manifests his own perfect physical presence and declares the following with his pure speech: “O monks! By merely doing what you have done, the task is not accomplished and the work is not yet done. Your nirvana is not nirvana. Monks! Now approach the Tathāgata and pay heed to what he says; understand his instruction.”

de nyid dam chos pad dkar las tshigs su bcad de/ yang gsungs pa/
dge slong khyed cag de ring de phyir ngas/ / 'di tsam gyis ni mya ngan mi 'da' ste/ / khyed cag thams cad mkhyen pa'i ye shes phyir/ / brtson 'grus rlabs chen dam pa bskyed par gyis/ / thams cad mkhyen pa'i ye shes thob par 'gyur/[32] / zhes gsungs so/ /

That he motivates them thus is taught in the verses of the Lotus Sutra:
O monks! I therefore tell you today that by this alone you will not attain nirvana, and that for you to gain the pristine awareness of the omniscient ones, you must give rise to a noble and mighty wave of effort. By so doing, you will achieve all-knowing pristine awareness.[17]

d.div: [32] gong mtshungs/ dam chos pad dkar gyi mdo/ le'u/ 7_shog_75_na3

f.d:
de ltar bskul bas nyan rang de dag de nas byang chub chen por sems bskyed de/[33] bskal pa dpag tu med par byang chub sems dpa'i spyod pa spyad nas 'tshang rgya ba yin no/ / 'phags pa lang kar gshegs pa'i mdo las kyang de bzhin du bshad la/ dam chos pad dkar las kyang /
nyan thos de dag mya ngan ma 'das te/ / de dag byang chub spyod pa rab spyad nas/ / nyan thos 'di dag thams cad sangs rgyas 'gyur/[34] / zhes gsungs so//

Through being exhorted in this way, śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas will cultivate the great bodhicitta.[18] Having conducted themselves as bodhisattvas for countless ages, they will become buddhas. /50/ Thus it is stated in the Sutra on Going to Laṅka as well. In the Lotus Sutra it states:
Those śrāvakas have not attained nirvana; so through having practiced the bodhisattva way of life, all these śrāvakas will become buddhas.[19]

d.div: [33] de dag gdong byang chub chen por byang chub tu/ dpal spungs/
[34] sde dge_113_bka'/ mdo sde/ ja_dam chos pad dkar gyi mdo/ le'u/ 5_shog_50_ba1

[18] The term bodhicitta, or “thought of awakening,” can be used to describe the aspiration of the Hinayana paths. When such is the case, the more familiar bodhicitta of the bodhisattva is known as great bodhicitta.
[19] Saddharmapuṇḍarīkasūtra, Toh 113 Kangyur, mdo sde, ja, 40b1.

f.d:
theg pa chen po'i rigs ni ji lta bu zhe na/ sdom ni/
dbye ba ngo bo rnam grangs dang / / gzhan las khyad 'phags rgyu mtshan dang / / rnam pa rtags dang don drug gis/ / theg pa chen po'i rigs bsdus so/ / zhes pa ste/

The synopsis for those with Mahayana potential is the following:
Mahayana potential is summed up through six topics: its categories, their essential characteristics, its synonyms, the reasons it is particularly outstanding, the forms it takes, and its signs.
de la rigs kyi dbye ba ni gnyis te/ rang bzhin gyis gnas pa'i rigs dang /[35] yang dag par bsgrubs pa'i rigs so/ /
First, there are two main categories: the potential as it exists naturally and the potential as something attained.

d.div: [35] dpal spungs dpar mar skabs mang por/ rang bzhin gyis zhes byed sgra dgos sar rang bzhin gyi zhes 'brel sgra byung /

f.d: rigs de dag so so'i ngo bo 'chad pa la/ dang po rang bzhin gyis gnas pa'i rigs ni/ sangs rgyas kyi chos skyed pa'i nus pa/ thog ma med pa'i dus can/ chos nyid kyis thob pa'o/ / yang dag par bsgrubs pa'i rigs ni/ sangs rgyas kyi chos skyed pa'i nus pa sngon dge ba'i rtsa ba goms par byas pa las thob pa de'o/ / de ltar rnam pa gnyis ka sangs rgyas kyi skal pa can yin no/ /

Second is an analysis of the essential characteristics of each of these. The potential as it exists naturally, since time without beginning, is the innate capacity of suchness to give rise to enlightened qualities. The potential as something attained is the capacity of one’s former cultivation of virtue to give rise to enlightened qualities. Both these aspects of Mahayana potential make a readiness for enlightenment.
rigs kyi ming gi rnam grangs ni/ rigs zhes kyang bya/ sa bon zhes kyang bya/ khams zhes kyang bya/ rang bzhin zhes kyang bya'o/ /
The synonyms for this are potential, seed, element, and essential nature.[20]

d.div: [20] These synonyms are very helpful in understanding the connotations of rigs, the Tibetan translation of the Sanskrit term gotra. It is a potential one is born with, if that term is seen through its meaning of “family,” remembering that caste and profession were so closely linked to birth family. It is like a seed, containing from the outset the genetic information of its fruit; it is like the one prime element permeating all existence; and it is the essential nature of all things, once the veil of illusions has fallen.

f.d: rigs gzhan las khyad par du 'phags pa'i rgyu mtshan ni/ nyan rang rnam gnyis kyi rigs ni dman pa yin te/ nyon mongs pa'i sgrib pa byang ba tsam gyis rigs rnam par dag par 'gyur ba'i phyir ro/ / theg pa chen po'i rigs ni mchog yin te/ sgrib pa gnyis char byang bas rigs rnam par dag par 'gyur ba'i phyir ro/ / des na theg pa chen po'i rigs de rigs thams cad las khyad par du 'phags pa bla na med pa yin no//

The reasons it stands far above the other forms of potential are as follows. The śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha potentials are lesser ones, because to realize them, only the afflictions need be eliminated. The Mahayana potential is outstanding because its total realization involves eliminating both obscurations.[21] This makes the Mahayana potential peerless, better than all the others.

d.div: [21] This is the first mention of the two obscurations (avaraṇa) in this text, the afflictions obscuration (kleśāvaraṇa) and the knowledge obscuration (jñeyāvaraṇa).

f.d: rigs kyi rnam pa ni/ rigs sad pa dang / ma sad pa'o/ / de la rigs sad pa ni/ 'bras bu yang dag par grub pa zhes bya ste rtags dmigs pa'o/ / rigs ma sad pa ni/ 'bras bu yang dag par ma grub pa zhes bya ste rtags mi dmigs pa'o/[36] / 'o na rigs de rkyen cis sad par 'gyur zhe na/ 'gal ba'i rkyen dang ni bral/ mthun pa'i rkyen gyis zin na ni rigs sad par 'gyur te/ de las bzlog na rigs mi sad par gnas so/ / de la 'gal ba'i rkyen bzhi ste/ mi khom par skyes pa dang / bag chags med pa dang /[37] log par zhugs pa dang / sgrib pa'i nyes pa'o/ / mthun pa'i rkyen gnyis te/ phyi dam pa'i chos ston pa gzhan gyi rkyen dang / nang tshul bzhin yid la byed pa dge ba'i chos la 'dun pa la sogs pa'o/ /

The different forms of Mahayana potential are its activated and dormant states. When the potential has been activated, its signs are manifest and “the results have been attained.” While it is dormant, the signs are not manifest and “the results have not [yet] been attained.” What activates the potential? Freedom from adverse conditions and the support of favorable ones activate it. While their contraries prevail, it remains dormant. There are four adverse conditions: (1) birth in an unfavorable existence, (2) a lack of good inclinations,[22] (3) involvement in aberrant ways, and (4) being flawed with obscurations. There are two favorable conditions /51/: (1) Externally, there are Dharma teachers, and (2) within, there is a proper mental attitude, aspiring to what is wholesome and so forth.

d.div: [36] ma dmigs pa'o/ /dpal spungs/
[37] bag med pa dang / dpal spungs/
[22] The Palpung edition has “a lack of care.”

f.d:
rigs kyi rtags ni/ byang chub sems dpa'i rigs mtshon par byed pa'i mtshan ma ste/ ji skad du/ chos bcu pa'i mdo las/
byang chub sems dpa' blo ldan gyi/ / rigs ni mtshan ma dag las shes/ / du ba las ni mer shes dang / / chu skyar las ni chu bzhin no/[38] / zhes gsungs pa lta bu'o/ /

The signs [or evidence] of this potential are found in the Ten Dharmas Sutra, where it describes the indications of its presence:
The bodhisattvas endowed with intelligence, their potential is detected by means of its signs, just as one infers the presence, through smoke, of a fire and through the presence of waterfowl, water.[23]

d.div: [38] sde dge_53_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ kha_chos bcu pa'i mdo/ le'u/ 9_shog_167_ba7
[23] Daśadharmakasūtra, Toh 53 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, kha, 167b7.

f.d:
'o na mtshan ma ji lta bu zhe na/ gnyen po la ma ltos par lus ngag rang bzhin gyis 'jam pa dang / sems g.yo sgyu shas chung ba dang / sems can la byams shing dad pa dag yin no/[39] / de ltar chos bcu pa'i mdo las/
mi rtsub brlang pa ma yin la/ / g.yo dang sgyu ni rnam spangs shing / / sems can kun la rab dang ba/ / de ni byang chub sems dpa' yin/[40] / zhes gsungs so//

What are these signs? Naturally and without contrivance, such beings are peaceful in what they do and say, their minds have little deceit or hypocrisy, and they are loving and joyful in their relations with others. As it says in the Ten Dharmas Sutra:
Never rough or rude, beyond deceit and hypocrisy, and full of love for all beings: They are the bodhisattvas.[24]

d.div: [39] dang ba dag_dpal spungs/
[40] sde dge_53_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ kha_chos bcu pa'i mdo/ le'u/ 9_shog_168_na1

f.d:
yang na sbyor ba ci byed kyi sngon rol nas/ sems can la snying rje skye ba dang / theg pa chen po'i chos la mos pa dang / dka' ba spyod pa la ji mi snyam du bzod pa dang / pha rol tu phyin pa'i rang bzhin gyi dge ba'i rtsa ba yang dag par spyod pa'i/ / de ltar mdo sde rgyan las/
sbyor ba'i sngon du snying rje dang // mos pa dang ni bzod pa dang / / dge ba yang dag spyod pa ni/ / rigs kyi rtags su shes par bya/[41]/ zhes gsungs so//

Further, they engender compassion toward all beings before entering into any activity. Genuinely aspiring to Mahayana Dharma, they undertake difficult tasks with forbearance that is never discouraged by the enormity of the undertaking, and they practice most properly and excellently that which generates virtue and has the nature of the perfections. It says in the Ornament of Mahayana Sutras:
Compassion prior to action, aspiration as well as forbearance, and engaging perfectly in virtues: These should be recognized as signs of their potential.[25]

d.div: [41] sde dge_4020_bstan/ sems tsam/ phi_byams pa mgon po/ mdo sde rgyan/ le'u/ 4_sh+loka_5_shog_4_na3
[25] Maitreya, Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra, Toh 4020 Tengyur, sems tsam, phi, 4a3.

f.d: de ltar na rigs lnga po de las/ theg pa chen po'i rigs yod pa ni/ sangs rgyas kyi nye ba'i rgyu yin no/ / nyan thos dang rang sangs rgyas kyi rigs kyang mthar sangs rgyas thob pas na ring ba'i rgyu yin no/ / rigs ma nges pa ni/ kha cig nye ba'i rgyu/ kha cig ring ba'i rgyu yin no/ / rigs chad pa'i rigs kyang / yun ring ba la dgongs pa tsam las/ gtan nas byang chub mi thob pa ma yin pas shin tu ring ba'i rgyu yin no/[42] /

The above means that of the five types of potential, the Mahayana one is the most direct cause for buddhahood. The śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha potentials are also causes for attaining buddhahood but remoter ones. The undetermined potential is sometimes a direct cause, sometimes a remote cause. The disconnected potential is considered a very remote cause but not a total breach of the possibility of enlightenment: It is therefore an exceedingly far-removed cause for it.

d.div: [42] mi thob pa min pas/ dpal spungs/

f.d: des na sems can la rigs de rnams yod pa'i phyir na yang / sems can sangs rgyas kyi snying po can yin no/ / de ltar rgyu mtshan gsum gyis/ sems can thams cad la sangs rgyas kyi snying po yod par bstan to/ / de yang dpe ji ltar yod na/ dngul rdo la dngul gnas pa'am/ til la til mar gnas pa'am/ 'o ma la mar gnas pa ltar yod do/ / des na dngul rdo la dngul bsgrub tu btub pa'am/ til la til mar bsgrub tu btub pa'am/[43] 'o ma la mar bsgrub tu btub pa ltar/ sems can la sangs rgyas bsgrub tu btub pa yin no/ /

Thus we have seen that, due to having one or another of these types of potential, sentient beings possess buddha nature, and this has also been demonstrated through the three reasons. The actual way they possess it can be exemplified by the way silver is present in silver ore, the way sesame oil is present in sesame, or the way butter is present in milk. Just as it is possible to obtain the silver that is in ore, the oil that is in sesame seeds, and the butter that is in milk, /52/ so it is possible to attain the buddhahood that is in all sentient beings.

d.div: [43] bsgrub pa'am/ dpal spungs/

f.d: dam pa'i chos yid bzhin gyi nor bu thar pa rin po che'i rgyan las rgyu'i le'u ste dang po'o//
This concludes the first chapter, concerning the prime cause, of this Ornament of Precious Liberation, a Wish-Fulfilling Gem of Sublime Dharma.
(spyi don gnyis pa bla med byang chub sgrub pa'i rten bshad pa/)
II. The Basis
le'u gnyis pa/ rten mi lus rin chen/
2. A Precious Human Existence
rten ni mi lus rin chen mchog /ces pa la/

'o na sems can thams cad sangs rgyas kyi snying po can yin na/ dmyal ba yi dwags la sogs pa lnga char gyis sangs rgyas bsgrub tu nus pa zhig yin nam zhe na/ ma yin te/ mi lus rin po che zhes bya ba/ lus dal 'byor rnam gnyis dang ldan pa/ sems dad pa rnam gsum dang ldan pa 'di/ sangs rgyas sgrub pa'i rten gyi gang zag tu bzang ngo / /

Given that all sentient beings have buddha nature, can the five types of nonhuman beings—hell beings, hungry spirits ( preta), and so forth—achieve buddhahood? They cannot. The excellent type of existence that provides a working basis for achieving buddhahood is known as a precious human existence, meaning someone who materially has freedoms combined with assets and who mentally has the three kinds of faith.

de 'chad pa la/ sdom ni/
dal ba dang ni 'byor ba dang / / yid ches 'dod dang dang ba ste/ / lus ni gnyis dang sems ni gsum/ / don lnga yis ni rten mchog bsdus/ / zhes pa ste/

The synopsis of the explanation of this is the following:
The very best basis is summed up in five points: freedoms, assets, conviction, aspiration, and clarity. Two of these are physical and three are mental.

de la dal ba ni mi khom pa brgyad dang bral ba'o/ / mi khoms pa brgyad ni/ mdo dran pa nyer bzhag las/
dmyal ba yi dwags dud 'gro dang / / klu klo tshe ring lha dang ni/ / log lta sangs rgyas kyis stong pa/ / lkugs pa 'di dag mi khoms brgyad/[44] / ces gsungs so/ /

They are freedoms inasmuch as the person is free from eight unfavorable conditions. According to [Prajñākaramati’s Commentary on the Guide to the Bodhisattva Way of Life, in his summary of what is found in the] Attention to Mindfulness Sutra:
The eight unfavorable states are to be a hell dweller, a hungry spirit, an animal, a barbarian, a long-living god, someone with fixed aberrant views, one born in a time without a Buddha, or a person with severe difficulty in understanding.[26]

d.div: [44] tshigs bcad 'di mdo dran pa nyer bzhag tu btsal yang rnyed son ma byung / lung 'di sher 'byung blo gros kyis spyod 'jug 'grel par yang drangs/ sde dge_3872_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_spyod 'jug dka' 'grel/ sher 'byung blo gros/ shog_45_ba4
[26] Prajñākaramati, Commentary on the Guide to the Bodhisattva Way of Life (Bodhicaryāvatārapañjikā), Toh 3872 Tengyur, mdo ’grel, la, 45b5.

f.d: 'di dag ji ltar mi khom pa yin zhe na/ dmyal ba ni rtag tu sdug bsngal ba'i rang bzhin yin pa'i phyir dang / yi dwags ni sems tshig pa'i rang bzhin yin pa'i phyir dang / dud 'gro ni kun tu rmongs pa shas che ba'i phyir/ de dag gsum char yang ngo tsha med pa dang / khrel med pas rgyud ma rungs par gyur ba'i phyir/ chos nyams su len pa'i go skabs med pa yin no//

Why are these states deemed unfavorable for the attainment of enlightenment? Hell is unsuitable because the very character of its experience is constant suffering. The hungry spirit state is unsuitable because of its mental anguish. The animal state is unsuitable because of its generalized benightedness.
