This concludes the third chapter, concerning Dharma masters, of this Ornament of Precious Liberation, a Wish-Fulfilling Gem of Sublime Dharma.
(spyi don bzhi pa bla med byang chub sgrub pa'i thabs bshad pa/)
IV. The Means: The Dharma Master’s Instruction
thabs ni de yi gdams ngag ste/ /zhes pa la/
4. The Impermanence of Conditioned Existence

'o na bdag cag la rgyu sangs rgyas kyi snying po yang yod/ 'khor ba thog ma med pa nas brgyud pa'i mdo mdor rten mi lus rin chen yang rnyed cing /[138] rkyen dge ba'i bshes gnyen dang 'phrad 'ong ba la/ de snga sangs rgyas ma thob pa skyon ci zhig byung ba yin zhe na/ de ni bdag cag la sogs pa rnams sangs rgyas mi thob pa'i gegs bzhi'i dbang du gyur pa'i nyes skyon yin no/ / 'o na sangs rgyas mi thob pa'i gegs bzhi po de gang zhe na/ tshe 'di'i spyod yul la chags pa dang / srid pa'i bde ba la chags pa dang / zhi ba'i bde ba la chags pa dang / sangs rgyas sgrub pa'i thabs mi shes pa'o/[139] / gegs bzhi po de gang gis sel na/ dge ba'i bshes gnyen gyi gdams ngag thos nas de nyams su blangs pas sel lo/ /

We have the cause, buddha nature. Furthermore, because samsara has existed since time without beginning, at some point we must already have had the basis, a precious human existence, through which we met the condition, the Dharma master. What prevented us from becoming buddhas then? It was the harmful mistake of falling under the sway of four blockages that stopped us, and those like us, from attaining buddhahood. The four impediments that have prevented the attainment of buddhahood are: (1) attachment to the experiences of this life, (2) attachment to worldly well-being in general, (3) attachment to the well-being of peace, and (4) ignorance of the means by which buddhahood is achieved. What can eliminate these four impediments? They are eliminated by heeding the instruction of Dharma masters and by putting those instructions into practice.

d.div: [138] brgyud pa'i phyir / mdor/ gsung 'bum dpar ma/
[139] bsgrub/ dpal spungs/ mi rigs dpe skrun/

f.d:
dge ba'i bshes gnyen gyi gdams ngag de ci tsam zhig zhe na/ sdom ni/[140]
mi rtag bsgom dang 'khor ba yi/[141] / nyes dmigs las 'bras bcas pa dang / / byams dang snying rje bsgom pa dang / / byang chub sems bskyed chos rnams te/ / de ltar rnam pa bzhi yis ni/ / de yi gdams ngag thams cad bsdus/ / zhes pa ste/

d.div: [140] ma dper sdoms zhes skabs du mar byung yang mi rigs dpe skrun khangs ltar sdom zhes bcos/
[141] dpal spungs dang mi rigs dpe skrun khang gnyis su bsgom zhes par skabs du mar sgom zhes bas 'phul med par byung/

[79] This is the general synopsis for part IV of the text, and it covers the sixteen chapters to come, each of which has its own synopsis and sometimes consists of internal subchapters, each having its own synopsis. The first teaching mentioned here (on impermanence) is addressed below in the present chapter, the second teaching (on suffering and karma) is covered in chapters 5 and 6, the third teaching (on love and compassion) in chapter 7, and the fourth teaching (on the bodhisattva path) in chapters 8–19.

f.d: mi rtag pa bsgom pa'i gdams ngag dang / 'khor ba'i nyes dmigs las 'bras dang bcas pa bsgom pa'i gdams ngag dang / byams pa dang snying rje bsgom pa'i gdams ngag dang / byang chub mchog tu sems bskyed pa'i gdams ngag rnams yin no/ / de la mi rtag pa bsgoms pas ni tshe 'di'i spyod yul la chags pa'i gnyen por 'gyur ba yin no/ / 'khor ba'i nyes dmigs las 'bras dang bcas pa bsgoms pas ni/ srid pa'i bde ba la chags pa'i gnyen por 'gyur ba yin no/ / byams pa dang snying rje bsgoms pas ni zhi ba'i bde ba la chags pa'i gnyen por 'gyur ba yin no/ / byang chub mchog tu sems bskyed pa'i chos rnams ni sangs rgyas bsgrub pa'i thabs mi shes pa'i gnyen por 'gyur ba yin te/ skyabs 'gro nas bzung nas bdag med rnam gnyis kyi don sgom pa man chad dam/[142] yang na lam lnga sa bcu man chad sems bskyed kyi chos su 'ong ba yin no/ / de yang chos kha cig ni sems bskyed kyi rten/ chos kha cig ni sems bskyed kyi dmigs pa/ chos kha cig ni sems bskyed kyi cho ga[143] / chos kha cig ni sems bskyed kyi bslab bya/ chos kha cig ni sems bskyed kyi phan yon/ chos kha cig ni sems bskyed kyi 'bras bu ste/ theg pa chen po'i chos ni sems bskyed la ma 'dus pa med do/ / des na gdams ngag de dag thams cad dge ba'i bshes gnyen las 'byung zhing / dge ba'i bshes gnyen la rag las pa yin no//

This means that the Dharma masters’ instruction comprises advice on (1) how to meditate on impermanence, (2) how to meditate on the defects of samsara and on actions and their consequences, (3) how to cultivate love and compassion, and (4) how to cultivate bodhicitta. These act as remedies as follows.[80] Meditation on impermanence counteracts attachment to the experiences of this life. Meditation on the defects of samsara counteracts attachment to worldly well-being in general. /67/ The meditations on love and compassion counteract attachment to the well-being of meditative peace. The teachings on cultivating highest enlightenment counteracts ignorance of how to attain buddhahood. These cover all teachings—from taking refuge up to the meaning of the two types of absence of self, or from the five path phases and the ten bodhisattva levels down through all the teachings on bodhicitta. Some of these topics form the basis for bodhicitta, some are its objective, some are the rituals connected with bodhicitta development, some are advice pertinent to bodhicitta, some concern its qualities and benefits, and some present its results. There is no Mahayana topic that is not included in the bodhicitta teachings. Hence all those forms of instruction stem from the Dharma master: they depend on the Dharma master.

d.div: [142] yan chad/ dpal spungs/
[143] sems bskyed kyi chos/ dpal spungs/
[80] The four remedies that follow are repeated as subheadings for individual sections below.

f.d:
'phags pa sdong po bkod pa'i mdo las kyang /
dge ba'i bshes gnyen ni dge ba'i chos thams cad kyi 'byung gnas so/[144] / zhes dang /
thams cad mkhyen pa ni dge ba'i bshes gnyen gyi gdams ngag la rag las/[145] zhes gsungs so//

Therefore the Marvelous Array Sutra says:
The Dharma master is the very source of all the teachings of virtue.[81] and
Omniscience depends on the instruction given by Dharma masters.

d.div: [144] sde dge_44_bka'/ phal chen/ a_sdong po bkod pa'i mdo/ shog_284_ba2
[145] gong mtshungs/ phal chen/ a_sdong po bkod pa'i mdo/ shog_284_na1
[81] Gaṇḍavyūhasūtra (chapter 45 in the Flower Ornament Sutra), Toh 44 Kangyur, phal chen, ā, 284b2.

f.d: le'u bzhi pa/ 'dus byas mi rtag par bstan pa/

de la dang po tshe 'di'i spyod yul la chags pa'i gnyen po mi rtag pa bsgom pa bshad par bya ste/ de yang spyir 'dus byas thams cad mi rtag pa yin no/ / sangs rgyas kyi zhal nas kyang /
dge slong dag 'dus byas thams cad ni mi rtag pa'o/[146] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Of these, I first present impermanence, which is the remedy that counter-acts attachment to the experiences of this life. In general, every composite thing is impermanent. Therefore the Buddha taught:
O monks! All composites are impermanent.[82]

d.div: [146] sde dge_111_bka'/ mdo sde/ cha_snying rje chen po'i pad+ma dkar po/ le'u/ 4_shog_75_na6
[82] White Lotus of Great Compassion Sutra (Mahākaruṇāpuṇḍarīkasūtra), Toh 111 Kangyur, mdo sde, cha, 75a6.

f.d:
de yang ji ltar mi rtag na/ bsags pa'i tha ma ni 'dzad/ bslang ba'i tha ma ni 'gyel/ 'phrad pa'i tha ma ni 'bral/ gson pa'i tha ma ni 'chi ba yin no/[147] / de ltar yang ched du brjod pa'i tshoms las/
bsags pa kun gyi mtha' 'dzad cing/ / bslang ba'i tha ma 'gyel bar 'gyur/ / 'phrad pa'i mtha' ni 'bral ba ste// gson pa'i mtha' ni 'chi bar 'gyur/[148] / zhes gsungs so//

How exactly are they impermanent? What is accumulated will eventually dwindle, what is built up will eventually disintegrate, what comes together will eventually part, and what lives will eventually die. Quoting the Collection of Aphorisms:
The end of all accumulation is dispersal, the end of construction is disintegration, the end of meeting is parting, and the end of life is death.[83]

d.div: [147] 'chi ba'o/ /dpal spungs/
[148] sde dge_326_bka'/ mdo sde/ sa_ched du brjod pa'i tshoms/ tshoms/ 1_sh+loka_20_shog_209_ba6
[83] Udānavarga 1:22, Toh 326 Kangyur, sa, 209b6.

f.d: de yang ji ltar bsgom na/ sdom ni/
dbye ba dang ni sgom thabs dang / / bsgoms pa yi ni phan yon te/ / rnam pa gsum po de dag gis/ / mi rtag sgom pa yongs su bsdus/ / zhes pa'o/ /

d.div: Meditation on impermanence is well summarized in three topics: its categories, the meditation techniques, /68/ and the benefits of having meditated on it.

f.d: de la dbye ba ni gnyis te/ phyi snod kyi 'jig rten mi rtag pa dang / nang bcud kyi sems can mi rtag pa'o/ / phyi snod kyi 'jig rten mi rtag pa la'ang gnyis te/ rags pa'i mi rtag pa dang / phra ba'i mi rtag pa'o// nang bcud kyi sems can mi rtag pa la yang gnyis te/ gzhan mi rtag pa dang / rang mi rtag pa'o//

First, the categories are two: the impermanence of the world and the impermanence of sentient beings. The first of these, the impermanence of the world—the outer vessel—has two subcategories: gross impermanence and subtle impermanence. The second, the impermanence of sentient beings—the inner essence—also has two subcategories: the impermanence of others and the impermanence of oneself.

de dag sgom pa'i thabs la/ dang po phyi snod kyi rags pa mi rtag pa ni/ ma gi rlung gi dkyil 'khor nas ya gi bsam gtan bzhi'i gnas man chad po 'di rtag pa'i rang bzhin sra mkhrang can 'gyur med ma yin te/ res 'ga' ni bsam gtan dang po man chad mes 'jig / res 'ga' ni bsam gtan gnyis pa man chad chus 'jig / res 'ga' ni bsam gtan gsum pa man chad rlung gis 'jig pa yin no/ / de la mes bshig pa'i dus su thal ba tsam yang mi lus te/ dper na mar 'tshig pa bzhin no/ / chus bshig pa'i dus su snyigs ma tsam yang mi lus te/ dper na lan tshwa chu la thim pa bzhin no/ / rlung gis bshig pa'i dus su lhag ma tsam yang mi lus te/ dper na thal ba rlung gis khyer ba bzhin no/ /

Second, the techniques for meditating on these will be discussed in two parts: that of the world and that of its beings. For the world, first we consider its gross level of impermanence. There exists nothing, from the wind mandala below [at the base] up to the four levels of meditative concentration [of the form realm] above, that will not change, that is permanent by its very nature, or that has lasting materiality. At times, everything below the first level of concentration is destroyed by fire. At times, everything below the second level of concentration is destroyed by water. At times, everything below the third level of concentration is destroyed by wind. As these things occur, when there is destruction by fire not even ashes are left, just as when oil is consumed by flame. When there is destruction by water, there is not even sediment left, just as when salt is dissolved by water. When there is destruction by wind, nothing remains, just as when powder is blown away.

de ltar yang chos mngon pa mdzod las/
me yis bdun no chu yis gcig / de ltar chu bdun thal nas kyang / / me yis bdun no de nas ni/[149] / mjug tu rlung gis 'jig pa yin/[150] / zhes gsungs so/ /

d.div: [149] me yi bdun no de nas ni// dpal spungs dpar mar mi gsal/
[150] sde dge_4089_bstan/ mngon pa/ ku_dbyig gnyen/ chos mngon pa mdzod/ gnas/ 3_sh+loka_102_shog_10_ba6
[84] Vasubandhu, Abhidharmakośa 3:102, Toh 4089 Tengyur, mngon pa, ku, 10b6.

f.d:
bsam gtan bzhi pa'i gnas ni/ me chu rlung gsum gyis mi 'jig ste/ nang gi sems can shi 'phos pa dang rang 'jig pa yin no/ / de ltar yang /
mi rtag de yi gzhal med khang / / sems can bcas te 'byung 'jig phyir/[151] / zhes gsungs so/ /

The fourth level of concentration will not be destroyed by fire, water, or air. The beings in that state are subject to death and transmigration, and therefore it ends automatically [at their death]. Thus it says:
The celestial abodes of the impermanent arise and disintegrate along with the conscious beings that inhabit them.[85]

d.div: [151] gong mtshungs/ chos mngon pa mdzod/ gnas/ 3_sh+loka_101_shog_10_ba5

f.d:
de yang da res 'jig rten gyi khams 'di me yis 'jig par mngon te/ dpal sbyin gyis zhus pa'i mdo las/
bskal pa gcig lon nas ni 'jig rten 'di/ / nam mkha' rang bzhin nam mkhar 'gyur ba 'ong /[152] / lhun po dag kyang 'jig cing rnam par 'tshig[153] / ces gsungs so/ /

Also, the destruction of this universe by fire, at a certain point, is foretold in the Questions of the Layman Vīradatta Sutra:
After one eon, this world, the nature of which is space, will become space; even the mountains will be incinerated and destroyed.[86]

d.div: [152] nam mkha'i/ dpal spungs/ mi rigs dpe skrun/
[153] sde dge_72_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ ca_khyim bdag dpas byin gyis zhus pa'i mdo/ shog_201_ba2
[86] Vīradattagṛhapatiparipṛcchāsūtra, Toh 72 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, ca, 201b2.

f.d: gnyis pa phra ba'i mi rtag pa ni/ dus bzhi 'gyur bas mi rtag pa dang /[154] nyi zla shar nub kyis mi rtag pa dang / skad cig mas mi rtag pa'o/ /
The subtle impermanence of the environment is that of the flux of the four seasons, the rising and setting of the sun and the moon, and moment-to-moment change.

d.div: [154] dus bzhi'i/ dpal spungs/

f.d: de la dang po ni/ nam zla dpyid 'byung ba'i stobs kyis snod kyi 'jig rten 'di/[155] sa gzhi yang 'bol po/ kha dog kyang dmar po/ rtswa shing snga sngo yang kha 'bus te/ de yang mi rtag 'gyur ba'i dus shig yod do/ / nam zla dbyar 'byung ba'i stobs kyis sa gzhi yang rlon pa/ kha dog kyang sngon po/ rtswa shing snga sngo yang lo 'dab rgyas te/ de yang mi rtag 'gyur ba'i dus shig 'ong ngo / / nam zla ston byung ba'i stobs kyis sa gzhi yang mkhrang po/ kha dog kyang ser po/ rtswa shing snga sngo yang 'bras bu smin te/ de yang mi rtag 'gyur ba'i dus shig 'ong ngo / / nam zla dgun byung ba'i stobs kyis sa gzhi yang 'khyags pa/ kha dog kyang skya lam/[156] rtswa shing snga sngo yang skam zhing chag ste/ de yang mi rtag 'gyur ba'i dus shig 'ong ngo / /

Let us consider the first of these. Due to the powerful influence of the coming of spring, our environment, the world, changes as follows. The land becomes soft and ruddy in color, and the trees, grasses, and plants bud. /69/ However, this is but the manifestation of a transitory period. Due to the powerful influence of the coming of summer, the land becomes predominantly deep green, and leaves and branches grow on the trees, grasses, and plants. This, too, is but the manifestation of a transitory period. Due to the powerful influence of the coming of autumn, the land then hardens and is predominantly golden. Its trees, grasses, and plants bear fruit. This, too, is but the manifestation of a transitory period. Due to the powerful influence of the coming of winter, the land becomes frozen and whitish, and the trees, grasses, and plants are dried up and brittle. This, too, is but the manifestation of a transitory period.

d.div: [155] dpal spungs dpar mar skabs du mar 'byung la byung zhes snang /
[156] skya glam/ dpal spungs/

f.d: nyi zla shar nub kyis mi rtag pa ni/ nyin mo 'byung ba'i stobs kyis snod kyi 'jig rten 'di yang dkar zhing gsal la/[157] mtshan mo 'byung ba'i stobs kyis nag la thib ste/[158] de yang mi rtag 'gyur ba'i brda'o/ /

Now let us consider impermanence in terms of the rising and setting of the sun and moon. The power of day breaking makes our environment, the world, become light and bright. The power of night falling makes it disappear into darkness. These are also signs of impermanence.

d.div: [157] la/ zhes pa mi rigs dpe skrun khang nang mi byung /
[158] 'thib ste/ dpal spungs/

f.d: skad cig mas mi rtag pa ni/ skad cig ma snga ma'i dus kyi snod kyi 'jig rten de skad cig ma phyi ma'i dus na mi gnas so/ / gnas pa ltar 'dug pa ni 'dra ba gzhan 'byung yin te/ dper na 'bab chu'i rgyun bzhin no//

Finally, let us consider impermanence in terms of moment-by-moment change. Our environment, the world of one small instant of time, does not persist into the next instant of time. It gives the impression of remaining the same, yet in fact something similar has taken its place. Cascading water is an example of this.
nang bcud kyi sems can mi rtag pa la gnyis las/
The second technique of meditation contemplates the impermanence of the inner essence, sentient beings, first considering the impermanence of others and then one’s own impermanence.

dang po gzhan mi rtag pa ni/ khams gsum gyi sems can thams cad mi rtag pa yin te/ 'phags pa rgya cher rol pa las/
srid gsum mi rtag ston kha'i sprin dang 'dra/[159] / zhes gsungs so/ /

The impermanence of others: All conscious beings in the three realms are impermanent. It says in the Vast Manifestation Sutra:
The three realms are impermanent, like autumn clouds.[87]

d.div: [159] sde dge_95_bka'/ mdo sde/ kha_rgya cher rol pa'i mdo/ le'u/ 13_shog_88_na2
[87] Lalitavistarasūtra, Toh 95 Kangyur, mdo sde, kha, 88a2.

f.d: rang mi rtag pa ni/ bdag nyid kyang bsdad dbang med de 'gro dgos pa yin no/[160] / de yang rang rgyud la brtags pa dang /[161] gzhan rgyud la sbyar ba gnyis su shes par bya'o// de la dang po ni 'di ltar bsgom ste/ 'chi ba bsgom pa dang / 'chi ba'i mtshan nyid bsgom pa dang / tshe 'dzad pa bsgom pa dang / 'bral bar bsgom pa'o/ /

One’s own impermanence is based on understanding that “I also have no power to remain in this life and must go on to another.” The way to understand this is twofold: (1) by examining your own existence and (2) by applying to yourself what is observed of others’ existences. The way to meditate on the first of these is as follows: meditate on death, on the specific characteristics of death, on the exhaustion of life, and on separation.

d.div: [160] bdag nyid kyang sdod/ dpal spungs/ mi rigs dpe skrun khang /
[161] brtag pa dang / dpal spungs/

f.d: de la 'chi ba bsgom pa ni/ bdag 'jig rten 'dir yun ring por mi sdod phyi ma phan chad du 'gro ba yin snyam du bsam pa'o/ /
Meditation on death is to contemplate “I will not stay long in this world and will soon be moving into the next.”
'chi ba'i mtshan nyid bsgom pa ni/ bdag gi srog 'di ni zad/ dbugs 'di ni 'gag / lus 'di ni ro'i rnam par 'gyur/ sems 'di ni gzhan zhig na phar 'khyams dgos pa yin snyam du bsam pa'o/ /

Meditation on the specific characteristics of death involves contemplating the thought “This life force of mine will be used up, respiration will stop, and this body will take on the appearance of a corpse, while this mind will be obliged to wander off to another life.”

tshe 'dzad pa bsgom pa ni/ na ning nas da phan chad la lo gcig song ste/ de tsam gyis tshe 'ud kyi thung du song /[162] kha sang nas mdang phan chad la zla ba gcig lon te/ de tsam gyis tshe 'ud kyi thung du song / kha tsang nas de ring bar la zhag gcig lon te/ de tsam gyis tshe 'ud kyi thung du song ngo / / da ci nas da lta phan la dar cig song ste/ de tsam gyis tshe thung du song ba yin snyam du bsam pa'o/ /

Meditation on the exhaustion of life is to contemplate: “Since a year ago, a year has passed, and now my life is precisely that much shorter. Since a month ago, a month has passed, and now my life is precisely that much shorter. /70/ From yesterday until today, a day has gone by, and now my life is precisely that much shorter. A moment has just gone by, and my life is precisely that much shorter.”

d.div: [162] de tsam gyis tshe 'ud kyis/ mi rigs dpe skrun/

f.d:
byang chub sems dpa'i spyod pa la 'jug pa las kyang /
nyin mtshan sdod pa yongs med par/ / tshe 'di rtag tu gud gyur cing / / bsnon pa gud nas yod med na/ / bdag lta 'chi bar cis mi 'gyur/[163] / zhes gsungs so//

It says in Guide to the Bodhisattva Way of Life:
Without ever stopping for even a day or a night, this life is constantly on the wane. Because what is left diminishes and disappears, how could the likes of me not die?[88]

d.div: [163] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_rgyal sras zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 2_sh+loka_40_shog_5_ba2
[88] Śāntideva, Bodhicaryāvatāra 2:39, Toh 3871 Tengyur, dbu ma, la, 5b2.

f.d:
'bral ba bsgom pa ni/ da lta yod pa'i bdag gi nye 'brel dang / nor rdzas dang / lus la sogs pa'i rtsis po che 'di rnams dang yang bdag rtag tu 'grogs su mi 'ong ste/ myur du bral ba yin snyam du bsam pa'o/[164] / byang chub sems dpa'i spyod pa la 'jug pa las/
thams cad bor te chas dgos par/ / bdag gis de ltar ma shes nas/[165] / zhes pa la sogs pa gsungs so//

Meditation on separation is to contemplate: “The friends and relatives, wealth and possessions, body, and so forth that I have at present and that I value so much will not always be able to accompany me. Soon will we be parted.” As it says in Guide to the Bodhisattva Way of Life:
By not knowing that I would have to leave everything behind and depart.[89]

d.div: [164] 'bral/ dpal spungs/ mi rigs dpe skrun/
[165] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 2_sh+loka_35_shog_5_na6

f.d: yang na 'chi ba dgu phrugs kyi tshul du bsgom ste/ bdag nges par 'chi/ nam 'chi cha med par 'chi/ cis kyang mi stongs par 'chi snyam du bsam pa'o/ /

Alternatively, one could engage in the ninefold way of meditating on death. The ninefold technique is centered on three main contemplations: “I will certainly die,” “The time of death is indefinite,” and “When I die, nothing whatsoever can accompany me.”
de yang nges par 'chi ba la rgyu mtshan gsum ste/ sngar ma shi ba lus pa med pa'i phyir dang / lus 'dus byas yin pa'i phyir dang / tshe skad cig gis 'dzad pa'i phyir nges par 'chi'o//
There are three reasons it is certain one will die: (1) No one previously has escaped death. (2) The body is a composite phenomenon. (3) Life is consumed from moment to moment.

de la sngar ma shi ba lus pa med pas nges par 'chi ba ni/[166] slob dpon rta dbyangs kyi zhal nas/
sa 'am 'on te mtho ris na/ / skyes nas la la ma shi ba/ / 'ga' zhig khyod kyis mthong ba'am/ / thos sam 'on te the tshom za/[167] / zhes gsungs so/ /

1. It is certain I will die because there was no one in the past who did not die. The great master Aśvaghoṣa said:
Whether it is on earth or in the upper realms, have you ever seen or heard, or have wondered about someone, who has been born but has not died![90]

d.div: [166] ma 'chi ba/ mi rigs dpe skrun/
[167] sde dge_4177_bstan/ spring yig_nge _slob dpon rta dbyangs/ mya ngan bsal ba/ shog_33_na6
[90] Eliminating Suffering (Śokavinodana), Toh 4177 Tengyur, spring yig, nge, 33a6.

f.d:
des na drang srong rdzu 'phrul can mngon shes dpag tu med pa dang ldan pa rnams kyang / mi 'chi ba'i sa phyogs su 'bros sa dang thar sa mi rnyed par thams cad 'chi ba yin te/ 'o skol lta ci smos/ de ltar yang /
drang srong chen po lnga mngon shes/ / mkha' la rgyang ring 'gro ba yang / / gang na spyod yul 'chi med par/ / sa der 'gro ba mi nus so/[168] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Therefore even “seers of truth”[91] cannot find a place to go to escape death and encounter immortality. They will all die, not to mention the likes of us! It is said:
Even the great rishis endowed with five types of clear cognition who travel far through space, they would be unable to travel to that place where they can enjoy immortality.[92]

d.div: [168] gong mtshungs/ mya ngan bsal ba/ shog_33_ba2

[91] “Seers of truth” (Skt. ṛṣi, Tib. drang srong) were highly accomplished meditators of India, renowned for their supernatural abilities. In early times, the rishis and rishikas (female rishis) were poet-seers; in later times, their name came to mean those who spoke only the truth. Straightforwardness and truthfulness are conveyed by the Tibetan translation.
[92] Aśvaghoṣa, Eliminating Suffering (Śokavinodana), Toh 4177 Tengyur, spring yig, nge, 33a6.

f.d:
der ma zad kyi 'phags pa rang sangs rgyas dang / nyan thos chen po dgra bcom pa rnams kyang mthar sku lus gtong na/ 'o skol lta ci smos/ de ltar yang ched du brjod pa'i tshoms las/
gang yang rang sangs rgyas rnams dang / / sangs rgyas rnams kyi nyan thos kyang / / sku lus 'di ni spong mdzad na/ / skye bo phal pa smos ci dgos/[169] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Besides this, even realized beings such as pratyekabuddha or śrāvaka arhats had to leave their bodies in the end. What, then, for the likes of us! Therefore it says, in the Collection of Aphorisms:
When even the pratyekabuddhas and the śrāvakas [disciples] of the buddhas, if they too have to quit their bodies, what need is there to speak ordinary beings?[93] /71/

d.div: [169] sde dge_326_bka'/ mdo sde/ sa_ched du brjod pa'i tshoms/ tshoms/ 1_sh+loka_25_shog_210_na1
[93] Udānavarga 1:25, Toh 326 Kangyur, mdo sde, sa, 210a1.

f.d:
der ma zad yang dag par rdzogs pa'i sangs rgyas sprul pa'i sku mtshan dang dpe byad kyis brgyan pa rdo rje'i rang bzhin lta bu yang sku lus 'jog na/ 'o skol lta ci smos/ de ltar yang slob dpon dpa' bo'i zhal nas/
ji snyed sangs rgyas rnams kyi sku/ / mtshan dang dpe byad kyis brgyan pa'i/ / rdo rje'i sku yang mi rtag na/ / chu shing snying po med 'dra ba'i/ / lus can gzhan la lta ci smos/[170] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Besides this, if even the totally purified, utterly perfect emanation body (nirmāṇakāya), adorned with the marks and signs of a supreme being, whose very nature was like a vajra, had to leave behind his body, then so much the more is it true of ordinary folk like us. The great master Aśvaghoṣa said:
If even the vajra bodies of the buddhas, adorned with the special marks and signs, are impermanent, then there is no point even mentioning other beings’ bodies, which are like plantain trees.[94]

d.div: [170] sde dge_4177_bstan/ spring yig_nge _slob dpon rta dbyangs/ mya ngan bsal ba/ shog_33_ba3

[94] Aśvaghoṣa, Eliminating Suffering (Śokavinodana), Toh 4177 Tengyur, spring yig, nge, 33b3. The plantain has no heartwood. Sentient beings have no single enduring, central component guaranteeing life.

f.d:
lus 'dus byas yin pa'i phyir nges par 'chi ba ni/ gang 'dus byas thams cad ni mi rtag pa yin la/ 'dus byas thams cad ni 'jig pa'i chos can yin te/ ched du brjod pa'i tshoms las/
kye ma 'dus byas rnams mi rtag / skye zhing 'jig pa'i chos can yin/[171] / zhes gsungs so/ / des na lus 'di 'dus ma byas ma yin zhing / 'dus byas yin pas na mi rtag ste nges par 'chi'o/ /

2. It is certain I will die because my body is something composite. Any composite whatsoever is impermanent, and every composite is destructible by nature. The Collection of Aphorisms says:
Alas, all composites are impermanent, characterized by birth and decay![95] Hence, since this body is not noncomposite but composite, it is impermanent, and so it is certain that it will die.

d.div: [171] sde dge_326_bka'/ mdo sde/ sa_ched du brjod pa'i tshoms/ tshoms/ 3_sh+loka_1_shog_209_na2
[95] Udānavarga 1:3; Toh 326 Kangyur, mdo sde, sa, 209a2.

f.d: tshe skad cig gis 'dzad pa'i phyir na nges par 'chi ba ni/ tshe skad cig ma re re 'das shing 'chi ba'i phyogs su nyer song ba yin te/ de mi mngon yang de dang cha 'dra ba dper na/ rtsal po ches mda' 'phangs pa'am/ ri gzar gyi ngos nas chu 'bab pa'am/ gsod sar khrid pa'i btson bzhin du tshe myur du 'da' ba yin no/ / de la dpe dang po skyes bu rtsal po ches mda' 'phangs pa ni bar snang la gzhi gcig tu skad cig kyang mi sdod de/ bsdis pa'i phyogs su myur du phyin pa ltar/ tshe yang skad cig kyang mi sdod par myur du 'chi ba yin no/[172] /

3. It is certain I will die because life is consumed from moment to moment. Life gets closer to death with the passing of each instant. If this is not obvious, let us examine examples that bear some similarity: an arrow shot by a strong archer, a torrent cascading over the edge of a steep cliff, and a prisoner being led to the place of execution and imminent death. The first example is that of an arrow shot by a strong archer. Not halting even for an instant at any one place in space, it speeds swiftly to its target. Life, too, never stands still even for an instant and heads swiftly toward death.

d.div: [172] bsdig/ mi rigs dpe skrun khang /

f.d:
de ltar yang /
dper na skyes bu rtsal can gyis/ / rgyud la springs nas mda' bskur ba// mi sdod bsdig sar myur du phyin/ / mi rnams tshe yang de bzhin no/[173] / zhes gsungs so/ /

As is said:
An arrow loosed from a bowstring by a mighty archer never hovers but speeds to its target; human life is like that, too.[96]

d.div: [173] dper na skyes bu rtsal can gyis/ /rgyud la springs nas mda' bskur ba/ /zhes sogs kyi gzhung ngos 'dzin ma thub/
[96] Crown Jewel Dhāraṇī Sutra (Ratnaketudhāraṇīsūtra), Toh 138 Kangyur, mdo sde, na, 211b3.

f.d:
yang dpe gnyis pa ri gzar gyi ngos nas chu 'bab pa de dar cig kyang mi sdod par rgyug pa ltar/ mi tshe yang sdod du mi btub pa lhag par gsal ba yin no/ / de ltar yang 'dus pa rin po che'i tog las/
grogs dag tshe 'di myur 'gro ste/ / ri gzar chu drag mgyogs 'dra na/ / byis pa'i skye bos mi shes te// mi mkhas longs spyod dregs pas myos/[174] / zhes gsungs so/ /

The second example is that of a torrent cascading over the edge of a steep cliff. Its waters tumble down without pausing even for an instant. Likewise, it is extremely clear that human life is unable to pause. This is found in the Crown Jewel Dhāraṇī Sutra, where it says:
Friends, this life passes as swiftly as water gushing over a waterfall. Immature beings, unaware of this and living unskillfully, proudly intoxicate themselves with sense pleasures.[97]

d.div: [174] sde dge_138_bka'/ mdo sde/ na_'dus pa rin po che'i tog_le'u/ 3_shog_211_ba3
[97] Ratnaketudhāraṇīsūtra, Toh 138 Kangyur, mdo sde, na, 211b3.

f.d:
tshoms las kyang /
chu klung chen po'i rgyun bzhin du/ / phyir mi ldog par 'gro bar 'gyur/[175] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Furthermore, the Collection of Aphorisms says:
It flows on like the current of a mighty river, never turning back.[98]

d.div: [175] sde dge_326_bka'/ mdo sde/ sa_ched du brjod pa'i tshoms/ tshoms/ 1_sh+loka_13_shog_210_na6
[98] Udānavarga 1:14, Toh 326 Kangyur, mdo sde, sa, 210a6.

f.d:
dpe gsum pa gsod sar khrid pa'i btson ni/ gom pa re re bor zhing 'chi ba la bsnyen pa ltar/ / 'o skol gyi tshe yang de dang 'dra'o/ / de ltar yang 'phags pa ljon shing gi mdo las/
gsod sar khrid pa'i btson bzhin du/ / gom re bor zhing 'chi la nye/[176] / zhes gsungs so/ /

The third example is that of a prisoner being led to the place of execution, whose every step brings death closer. We are just like that. In the Noble Tree Sutra it says:
Just like a prisoner being led to the place of execution, /72/ whose every step brings him closer to death.[99]

d.div: [176] ljon shing gi mdo zhes pa gzhung ngos 'dzin ma thub/ 'chi dang nye/ dpal spungs/ mi rigs dpe skrun khang /
[99] The source of this citation has not been located.

f.d:
tshoms las kyang /
dper na nges par gsod pa dag / gom pa gang dag gang bor ba/ / gsod pa'i drung du bsnyen pa ltar/ / mi rnams srog kyang de bzhin no/[177] / zhes gsungs so//

The Collection of Aphorisms also says:
Just as those on their way to execution draw closer to their death with every step that is taken, so it is with the life force of humans.[100]

d.div: [177] sde dge_326_bka'/ mdo sde/ sa_ched du brjod pa'i tshoms/ tshoms/ 1_shog_209_ba1
[100] Udānavarga 1:14, Toh 326 Kangyur, mdo sde, sa, 209b1.

f.d: nam 'chi cha med pa'i tshul gyis 'chi ba la yang rgyu mtshan gsum ste/ tshe la nges pa med pa'i phyir dang / lus la snying po med pa'i phyir dang / 'chi ba'i rkyen mang ba'i phyir nam 'chi cha med par 'chi'o/ /
There are three reasons why the time of death is not definite: (4) The life-span is uncertain. (5) The body has no single vital essence. (6) There are many possible causes of death.

de la dang po ni 'gro ba gzhan nam/ gling gzhan gyi mi tshe la nges pa yod kyang / 'o skol 'dzam bu gling pa'i tshe la nges pa med de/ chos mngon pa mdzod las kyang /
'di na ma nges tha mar ni// lo bcu dang po dpag tu med/[178] / ces gsungs so/ /

4. The time of death is not definite because lifespan is uncertain. Although the lifespan is fixed for some other sentient beings and for human beings in other parts of the cosmos, the lifespan of ordinary people in this world is not definite. In the Treasury of Higher Knowledge it says:
Here it is not definite: ten years at the end and inestimable at the beginning.[101]

d.div: [178] sde dge_4089_bstan/ mngon pa/ ku_dbyig gnyen/ chos mngon pa mdzod/ gnas/ 3_sh+loka_78_shog_9_ba7
[101] Vasubandhu, Abhidharmakośa 3:78, Toh 4089 Tengyur, mngon pa, ku, 9b7. The “end” and “beginning” are the low points and high points of lifespan in our world system over a cosmic eon.

f.d:
de yang ji ltar nges pa med na/ tshoms las/
kha cig mngal du 'chi bar 'gyur/ / de bzhin kha cig btsas pa'i sar/ / de bzhin kha cig gog tsa na// de bzhin kha cig yongs rgyug na/ / la la rgas dang la la gzhon/ / la la dar la babs pa'i mi/ / rim gyis rab tu 'gro 'gyur te/[179] / zhes gsungs pa ltar ro/ /

Just how it is indefinite is explained in the Collection of Aphorisms:
Some will die in the womb, some when they are born, some when they can only crawl, some when they can run, some when aged, some when young, and some in the prime of life. Eventually they all go.[102]

d.div: [179] sde dge_326_bka'/ mdo sde/ sa_ched du brjod pa'i tshoms/ tshoms/ 1_shog_209_na5
[102] Udānavarga 1:9–10, Toh 326 Kangyur, mdo sde, sa, 209a5.

f.d:
lus la snying po med pa ni/ lus 'di la mi gtsang ba'i rdzas sum cu rtsa drug las ma gtogs pa'i snying po sra mkhrang gcig kyang med/[180] ji skad du spyod 'jug las/
thog mar pags pa'i rim pa 'di/ / rang gi blo yis tha dad phye/ / sha yang rus pa'i dra ba las/ / shes rab mtshon gyis gud du phye/ / rus pa rnams kyang phye byas nas/ / rkang gi bar du blta bya zhing / / 'di la snying po ci yod ces/ / bdag nyid kyis ni blta bar gyis/[181] / zhes gsungs so/ /

5. The time of death is indefinite because the body has no single vital essence. This body has no solid, enduring essence, only its thirty-six impure substances. Thus Guide to the Bodhisattva Way of Life says:
Using the scalpel of discerning awareness, first dissect yourself mentally, peeling away with the layer of skin and going through the flesh to the skeleton. Having even dissected the bones and gotten to the marrow, examining carefully, ask: “What is there that could be its vital essence?”[103] This is what we ourselves ought to investigate.

d.div: [180] med de/ dpal spungs/
[181] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_rgyal sras zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 5_sh+loka_63_shog_12_ba4
[103] Śāntideva, Bodhicaryāvatāra 5:62–63, Toh 3871 Tengyur, dbu ma, la, 12b5.

f.d:
'chi ba'i rkyen mang ba ni/ rang gzhan thams cad la 'chi ba'i rkyen du ma gyur pa med de/ bshes spring las/
tshe 'di gnod mang rlung gis btab pa yis/ / chu yi chu bur bas kyang mi rtag na/ / dbugs 'byung dbugs rngub gnyid kyis log pa nas/ / sad khom gang lags de ni ngo mtshar che/[182] / zhes gsungs so//

6. The time of death is not definite because there are many potential causes of death. There is nothing that could not become a cause of death, either for me or for someone else. It says, in the Letter to a Friend:
There are many things that damage life. As life is more unstable than an air bubble in water, it is a wonder that in-breaths give way to out-breaths or that anyone awakens from sleep.[104]

d.div: [182] sde dge_4182_bstan/ spring yig_nge _mgon po klu sgrub/ bshes spring / sh+loka_55_shog_43_na6
[104] Nāgārjuna, Suhṛllekha verse 55, Toh 4182 Tengyur, spring yig, nge, 43a6.

f.d: cis kyang mi stongs par 'chi ba la yang rgyu mtshan gsum ste/[183] nor zas kyis mi bstongs pa dang / gnyen bshes kyis mi bstongs pa dang / rang gi lus kyis mi bstongs pa'o/ /

There are three contemplations on how, once dead, nothing can accompany you: (7) Wealth and objects cannot accompany you, (8) friends and relatives cannot accompany you, and (9) your own body cannot accompany you.

d.div: [183] yang / zhes pa'i rgyan sdud kyi tshig dpal spungs dpar mar mi byung / de bzhin du dpal spungs dang mi rigs dpe skrun khang gnyis kar/ mi stongs pa/ zhes ba sngon 'jug med pa byung /

f.d:
de la nor zas kyis mi stongs pa ni/ ji skad du spyod 'jug las/
rnyed pa mang po thob gyur te/ / yun ring dus su bde spyad kyang / / chom pos 'phrog pa ji bzhin du/ / sgren mo lag pa stongs par 'gro[184]/ zhes gsungs so/ /

7. Wealth and objects cannot accompany you after death. Guide to the Bodhisattva Way of Life says:
Although you may have obtained so many things, /73/ and have used and enjoyed them for a long time, you depart naked and empty-handed, as though robbed by thieves.[105]

d.div: [184] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_rgyal sras zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 6_sh+loka_59_shog_16_ba7
[105] Śāntideva, Bodhicaryāvatāra 6:59, Toh 3871 Tengyur, dbu ma, la, 16b7.

f.d: de ltar nor zas kyis 'chi ba la mi bstongs par ma zad de 'di phyi gnyis ka ru gnod pa yin no/ / de la tshe 'dir gnod pa ni/ nor zas kyi phyir 'thab rtsod dang / bsrung bran gyi sdug bsngal 'byung la/[185] phyi ma de'i rnam smin gyis ngan song du bskyur ba yin no//

Not only do wealth and possessions not accompany you at death, they also harm both this life and the next. They harm this life on account of the suffering caused through quarrels over them, having to protect them from theft, and enslavement to them. The ripening of karma planted in this way harms future lives, taking one to the lower states.

d.div: [185] srung dran/ dpal spungs/

f.d:
de la gnyen bshes kyis mi bstongs pa ni/ ji skad du spyod 'jug las/
'chi ba'i dus la babs pa na/ / bu rnams skyabs su mi 'gyur zhing / / pha yang ma yin gnyen 'dun min/ / khyod la skyabs su 'gyur ba med/[186] / ces gsungs so/ /

8. Friends and relatives cannot accompany you at death. As it says in Guide to the Bodhisattva Way of Life:
When the time comes to die, children will not be a refuge, nor father and mother, nor friends and loved ones. None could be your refuge.[106]

d.div: [186] ma dper/ spyod 'jug las gsungs kyang tshigs bcad 'di tshoms su bzhugs/ sde dge_326_bka'/ mdo sde/ sa_ched du brjod pa'i tshoms/ tshoms/ 1_sh+loka_42_shog_210_ba3
[106] This is a misattribution in the original. The citation is actually found in the Collection of Aphorisms. See Udānavarga 1:42, Toh 326 Kangyur, mdo sde, sa, 210b:3.

f.d: de ltar gnyen 'dun gyis 'chi ba la mi bstongs par ma zad de 'di phyi gnyis ka ru gnod pa yin no/ / de la tshe 'di la gnod pa ni/ de rnams shi dogs na dogs pham gyis dogs nas sdug bsngal che la/ phyi ma de'i rnam par smin pas ngan song du bskyur ba yin no/[187] /

Not only do relatives and friends not accompany you at death, they also harm both this life and the next. They harm this life through the anguish of worrying about their well-being and their lives. The full karmic ripening of these fears spoils your future lives by taking you to the lower realms.

d.div: [187] skyur/ dpal spungs/

f.d: rang gi lus kyis mi bstongs pa ni/ lus kyi yon tan gyis mi bstongs pa dang / lus rang gi dngos pos mi bstongs pa'o/ / de la dang po ni/ dpa' zhing shed che yang 'chi ba mi bzlog gze zhig bang mgyogs kyang 'chi ba la bros pas mi thar/[188] mdzangs shing smra mkhas kyang bshad byang gis mi lo ste/[189] dper na nyi ma ri'i phag tu 'gro ba la sus kyang bshol 'debs pa'am/ bzung bar mi nus pa dang 'dra'o/ /

9. Your own body cannot accompany you at death, nor can its physical qualities do so. No strong or courageous person can turn death away, no swift athlete can outrun it, and no eloquent speaker or negotiator can dissuade it. That would be like trying to prevent or delay the sun from setting behind a mountain: No one can.

d.div: [188] bze/ mi rigs dpe skrun/
[189] mi lto ste/ dpal spungs/ mi long ste/ mi rigs dpe skrun/

f.d:
lus rang gi dngos pos mi bstongs pa ni/ ji skad du spyod 'jug las/
dka' ba mang pos bsgrubs pa yi/ / zas dang gos kyis bskyangs pa'i lus/ / khyod dang mi 'grogs bya khyis za/ / yang na 'bar ba'i me yis 'tshig / yang na chu yi nang du brul/ / yang na sa yi dong du sba/[190] / zhes gsungs so/ /

The physical substance of the body cannot accompany you, either. Guide to the Bodhisattva Way of Life says:
Your body, which you have clothed and fed at the expense of great hardship, will be unable to help you: It will be eaten by jackals or birds, be burned by fire, rot in water, or be buried in a grave.[107]

d.div: [190] yang na chu yi nang du 'drul/ /yang na sa yi dong du sba/ dpal spungs/ ma dper/ spyod 'jug las gsungs kyang / tshigs bcad 'di da lta bstan 'gyur du bzhugs pa'i spyod 'jug nang mi bzhugs pas rje sgam po pas gang las drangs brtag dgos/

[107] This is a reference to the various ways of disposing of a corpse according to the four elements and astrology. Although Gampopa attributes this quotation to Śāntideva, it is not found in the Bodhicaryāvatara.

f.d: de ltar lus 'dis 'chi ba la mi bstongs par ma zad de 'di phyi gnyis kar gnod pa yin no/ / de la tshe 'dir gnod pa ni/ lus 'di na mi bzod/ tsha mi bzod/ grang mi bzod/ bkres mi bzod/ skom mi bzod/ rgyab kyi dogs/[191] bsad kyi dogs/ bcings kyi dogs/ bshus kyi dogs nas sdug bsngal du che la/ phyi ma lus 'di'i lan cog gis ngan song du bskyur ba yin no//

Not only can your body not accompany you, as just explained, it also harms both this life and the next. It injures this life through the great sufferings that occur when it cannot bear sickness, heat, cold, hunger, or thirst, or when there is fear of being killed, bound, or beaten. [Actions related to] these misfortunes will drag you into the lower states in future lives.

d.div: [191] dpal spungs dang mi rigs dpe skun khang gnyis ka/ rgyab kyis/ bsad/ bcings/ bshus bcas la byed sgra byung /

f.d: gzhan rgyud dang sbyar ba ni/ gzhan shi ba mig gis mthong ba dang / rna bas thos pa dang / sems la dran pa kun kyang rang la sbyar zhing bsgom pa'o/ / de la gzhan shi ba mig gis mthong ba dang sbyar na/ rang gi nye du la sogs pa lus ni stobs dang ldan/ byad bzhin mdangs dang ldan/ tshor ba ni bde ba dang ldan/ 'chi ba yid kyi dgu la mi byed pa zhig / de ring lta bu 'chi nad kyis btab nas/ lus kyi stobs shor nas tsog pu yang mi nus/ byad kyi bkrag shor te/ 'om po bkrag med du song / tshor ba sdug bsngal te na tsha la tshugs thabs med/ zug zer la tshugs pa med/[192] sman dang dpyad kyang ma zug_cho ga dang rim 'gros kyang ma phan/ 'chi bar ni shes/ bya thabs ni med/ gnyen gyi tha mas ni bskor/ zas kyi tha ma ni za/ gtam gyi tha ma ni zlo tsa na/[193] bdag kyang 'di'i rang bzhin can/ 'di'i chos can/ 'di'i mtshan nyid can/ chos nyid 'di las ma 'das pa yin snyam du bsam/

The second way [of contemplating your own impermanence] is by observing what happens to others and applying it to yourself. This means that when actually witnessing others die, hearing of their deaths, or recollecting people dying, you imagine this happening to you and then meditate accordingly. /74/ Applying to yourself the deaths of other people you have witnessed dying is done as follows. Think of those closely related to you who were strong at first, of healthy complexion, feeling happy, and never giving a moment’s thought to death, yet who were then stricken by fatal illness. Their bodily strength waned, they could not even sit up, their complexion lost its luster, becoming pallid and dry, and they suffered distress. There was no way to cure the pain or lessen the emotional burden. Medicines and examinations were of no more help, and even religious ceremonies and special prayers could not make them better. They knew that they were going to die and that nothing that could be done to prevent it. Surrounded by their remaining friends, they ate their last meal and spoke their last words. Evoking these images, think: “I, too, am of the same nature. I will also be subject to this. I, too, have these characteristics and have not transcended this particular phenomenon.”

d.div: [192] gzer/ dpal spungs/ mi rigs dpe skrun khang /
[193] tsam na/ dpal spungs/

f.d: de nas da dbugs chad nas de ring phan chad ji ltar gces pa khyim der med du mi btub pa zhig yin kyang /[194] da ro de khyim der zhag gcig kyang bzhag ma 'os par/ mal du khur thag shar gyis bres nas/ khres po sbrags te ro khur gyis khur nas phyir 'don pa'i tshe/[195] la las ni ro de la 'ju zhing 'phyang ba ltar byed/[196] kha cig ni ngu zhing gum pa ltar byed/ kha cig ni 'bog cing brgyal ba ltar byed la/ gzhan kha cig na re 'di ni sa yin/ 'di ni rdo yin/ khyod de ltar byed pa col chung ba skad zer/ ro de ni them pa thal gyis brgal nas/ da ni rnam pa thams cad du nang du mi ldog pa mthong tsa na/ bdag kyang sngar bzhin du bsam/

Then, from the moment the breath stopped, that person’s body was considered unfit to stay even a day in the very place that had been the beloved home from which the person could not bear to part. Once the corpse was laid on a bier, swathed, and bound, it was lifted up and carried out of the house. At that moment some embraced it and clung to it, some wept and wailed, some fainted and were overcome with grief. Yet others remarked, “This dead body is simply the likes of earth and rock, and you are small-minded to carry on as you do!” Contemplating such scenes as a corpse making its one-way journey over the threshold, think: “I, too, am of the same nature. ”

d.div: [194] de nas de/ dpal spungs/
[195] sgrog ste/ dpal spungs/ spags te/ mi rigs dpe skrun/
[196] 'gyur/ dpal spungs/

f.d: de nas ro de dur khrod du bskyal nas 'bus gzhig pa dang /[197] khyi dang lce spyang la sogs pas zos pa dang / keng rus 'thor ba la sogs pa mthong tsa na/ bdag kyang sngar bzhin du bsam mo/ /

Then, contemplating the corpse once it has been left in the charnel ground, where it is ripped apart by jackals and dogs, decomposed by insects, and where there are the disintegrated remains of skeletons, think: “I, too, will be like this. ”

d.div: [197] zhig_dpal spungs/

f.d: gzhan shi ba rna bas thos pa dang sbyar na/ che ge mo shi'o zer ba'am/ de na shi ba'i ro zhig 'dug go zer ba thos tsa na/[198] bdag kyang sngar bzhin du bsam mo/ /

The way to apply to yourself the instances of other peoples’ deaths that you have heard about is as follows. Whenever people say “Such and such a person died,” or “There is a corpse in such and such a place,” think, as above: “I, too, am like that. ”

d.div: [198] ro cig 'dug lo thos tsam na/ dpal spungs/

f.d: gzhan shi ba sems la dran pa dang sbyar na/ rang gi yul dang / grong dang / khyim du rgan gzhon rang dang 'grogs 'grogs pa ji snyed cig shi ste/ de kun bsams la ring po mi thogs par bdag kyang sngar bzhin du bsam mo/ /[199]

The way to apply to yourself the instances of other peoples’ deaths that you recollect is as follows. Think about all the people—some elderly, some young, and some lifelong friends—who have died in your area, town, or in your own house. Bearing their deaths in mind, think, as above, “I, too, am like this. ,” and reflect on how, before too long, you will also go that way.

d.div: [199] bsam/ dpal spungs/

f.d:
de ltar yang mdo las/
sang dang 'jig rten phyi ma gnyis/ / sngon du gang 'ong gtol med pas/ / sang gi tshis la mi 'bad par/ / phyi ma'i don la 'bad par rigs/[200] / zhes gsungs so//

In the sutras it says:
Since no one knows which will come first— /75/ tomorrow or the next life— it makes sense to strive for what has meaning in the next life and not put a lot of effort into what is just for tomorrow.[108]

d.div: [200] mdo las/ sang dang 'jig rten phyi ma gnyis/ /zhes sogs kyi mdo ngos 'dzin ma thub/
[108] The source of this quote has not been located.

f.d: mi rtag pa bsgoms pa'i phan yon ni/[201] 'dus byas thams cad mi rtag par go nas tshe 'di la mngon zhen ldog pa yin no/ / gzhan yang dad pa'i gsol 'debs/ brtson 'grus kyi grogs byed/ chags sdang dang myur du bral nas chos mnyam pa nyid rtogs rkyen byed pa yin no/ /

The third point discusses the benefits of meditating on impermanence. By understanding that all composite things are impermanent, strong craving for this life will be countered. Further, the seed of trust will be planted, diligence will be reinforced, and this will be an important factor in realizing sameness, since it quickly frees the mind from attraction and rejection.

d.div: [201] bsgom/ dpal spungs/

f.d: dam chos yid bzhin gyi nor bu thar pa rin po che'i rgyan las/ 'dus byas mi rtag par bstan pa'i le'u ste bzhi pa'o// //
This concludes the fourth chapter, concerning the impermanence of composite phenomena, of this Ornament of Precious Liberation, a Wish-Fulfilling Gem of Sublime Dharma.
le'u lnga pa/ 'khor ba'i sdug bsngal/
5. The Suffering of Samsara

de ltar mi rtag pa shi yang ci lto ste/[202] yang skye bar 'gyur ba ma yin nam/ skyes tsa na lha mi'i longs spyod phun sum tshogs pa thob ste 'ong / bdag la des ci ma chog snyam na/ de ni srid pa'i bde ba la chags pa yin no/ /

One might feel, “What does it matter if there is impermanence and death, since I’ll be reborn anyway? In that next life I could experience the very finest that being human or divine has to offer. That is fine by me!” To think thus is to be attached to the pleasures of cyclic existence (samsara).

d.div: [202] ci sto ste/ dpal spungs/ ci lta ste/ mi rigs dpe skrun khang /

f.d:
de'i gnyen por 'khor ba'i nyes dmigs sgom pa bshad par bya ste/ bsdoms ni/
'du byed kyi ni sdug bsngal dang / / de bzhin 'gyur ba'i sdug bsngal dang / / sdug bsngal gyi ni sdug bsngal te/ / gsum gyis 'khor ba'i nyes dmigs bsdus/ / zhes pa ste/

As the remedy for this I shall explain how to become familiar with the defects of samsara. The synopsis is:
The defects of samsara are covered by three topics: the suffering of conditioned existence, the suffering of change, and overt suffering.

de ltar sdug bsngal gsum po de/ dpe'i sgo nas bshad na/ 'du byed kyi sdug bsngal ni 'bras ma smin pa dang 'dra'o/ /'gyur ba'i sdug bsngal ni/ 'bras chan dug dang 'dres pa za ba dang 'dra'o/ / sdug bsngal gyi sdug bsngal ni/ 'bras kyi steng du phol byung ba dang 'dra'o/ /

These three sufferings can be explained through metaphors: the suffering of conditioned existence is like uncooked rice, the suffering of change is like cooked rice mixed with poison, and overt suffering is like stomach pains due to eating the poisoned rice.

yang sdug bsngal gsum po de rang gi ngo bo'i sgo nas bshad na/ 'du byed kyi sdug bsngal ni/ tshor ba btang snyoms pa yin no/ / 'gyur ba'i sdug bsngal ni/ tshor ba bde ba yin no/ / sdug bsngal gyi sdug bsngal ni/ tshor ba sdug bsngal yin no/ /

The three sufferings can also be explained in terms of their character. The suffering of conditioned existence has a neutral feeling, the suffering of change has a feeling of pleasure about it, and overt suffering actually feels like suffering.
yang sdug bsngal de gsum mtshan nyid kyi sgo nas bshad na/
The three sufferings can also be explained in terms of their essential characteristics, as follows.

'du byed kyi sdug bsngal ni/ nye bar len pa'i phung po 'di blangs pa tsam gyis sdug bsngal dang ldan pa yin no/ / de yang so so skye bo rnams kyis 'du byed kyi sdug bsngal 'di ma tshor te/ dper na/ rims nad drag pos zin tsa na/ rna ba la sogs pa lus kyi na tsha khal khol yod pa mi tshor ba bzhin no/ / rgyun du zhugs pa la sogs pa 'phags pa rnams kyis 'du byed kyi sdug bsngal 'di gzigs te/ dper na/ rims nad phal cher sos tsa na/ rna ba la sogs pa lus kyi na tsha khal khol yod pa tshor ba bzhin no/ / dpe gzhan yang / spu nyag ma gcig lag mthil na 'dug na mi bde ba dang / sdug bsngal med de/ de nyid mig tu song na mi bde ba dang sdug bsngal bskyed do/ / de bzhin du 'du byed kyi sdug bsngal 'di so so skye bo la yod kyang sdug bsngal du mi tshor te/ 'phags pa rnams la sdug bsngal du che'o/ /

First, the suffering of conditioned existence: We suffer merely through having taken on [a human life composed of] the aggregates, to which suffering is inherent. /76/ Ordinary people do not feel this suffering of conditioned existence and can be compared to people stricken by raging fevers, who are insensitive to trivial physical ills like an itchy ear. Stream-enterers and the other three types of emancipated being [i.e., once-returners, non-returners, and arhats] can perceive this suffering of conditioned existence. They can be compared to someone virtually cured of the fever and hence now quite aware of minor aches and pains. A small hair put on the palm of the hand causes neither discomfort nor pain, but should that same hair get into the eye, it will cause great irritation and unpleasantness. Similarly, ordinary people are insensitive to the suffering of conditioned existence, whereas realized beings are greatly distressed by it.

de ltar yang mdzod kyi TI ka las/
lag mthil spu nyag gcig 'dug pa/ / de ni mig tu song ba na/ / mi bde ba dang sdug bsngal skyed/ / byis pa lag mthil 'dra ba yis/ / 'du byed sdug bsngal spu mi rtogs/ / 'phags pa mig dang 'dra ba yis/ / 'du byed la ni sdug bsngal gzigs/[203] / zhes gsungs so//

As it says in the Commentary on the Treasury of Higher Knowledge:
When a single hair in our palm enters into our eyes, it engenders discomfort and pain. The childish, akin to the palm, do not recognize the suffering of conditioned existence. The noble ones, akin to the eyes, perceive conditioned existence as suffering.[109]

d.div: [203] sde dge_4090_bstan/ mngon pa/ khu_dbyig gnyen/ mdzod rang 'grel/ gnas/ 6_shog_3_ba3
[109] Yaśomitra, Abhidharmakośaṭīkā, Toh 4092 Tengyur, mngon pa, gu, 3b3.

f.d:
gnyis pa 'gyur ba'i sdug bsngal ni/ 'khor ba'i bde ba ji snyed pa thams cad mthar 'gyur nas sdug bsngal du 'gro bas na/ 'gyur ba'i sdug bsngal zhes bya'o/ / de ltar yang snying rje pad+ma dkar po'i mdo las/
lha'i rgyal srid ni sdug bsngal 'byung ba'i rgyu lags so/ / mi rnams kyi rgyal srid kyang sdug bsngal 'byung ba'i rgyu lags so/[204] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Second, the suffering of change is so called because all the pleasures of samsara, whatever they may be, will eventually change into suffering. As it says in the White Lotus of Compassion Sutra:
The divine realms are a cause for suffering to arise. The human realms are also a cause for suffering.[110]

d.div: [204] sde dge_112_bka'/ mdo sde/ cha_snying rje pad dkar gyi mdo/ le'u/ 3_shog_157_ba6
[110] Karuṇāpuṇḍarīkasūtra, Toh 112 Kangyur, mdo sde, cha, 157b6.

f.d:
des na mi'i rgyal po 'khor lo bsgyur ba lta bu'i spyod yul thob kyang / mthar sdug bsngal du 'gyur te/ bshes spring las kyang /
'khor los bsgyur rgyal nyid du gyur nas kyang / / 'khor ba dag na yang bran nyid du 'gyur/[205]/ zhes gsungs so/ /

Hence even those who attain the human status of a universal monarch (cakravartin) will, in time, change and find themselves in a state of suffering. It says, in the Letter to a Friend:
Even a universal monarch will, in the course of time, become a servant.[111]

d.div: [205] sde dge_4182_bstan/ spring yig_nge _mgon po klu sgrub/ bshes spring / sh+lauka_69_shog_44_na1
[111] Nāgārjuna, Suhṛllekha verse 69cd, Toh 4182 Tengyur, spring yig, nge, 44a1.

f.d:
der ma zad lha'i dbang po brgya byin lta bu'i lus dang longs spyod thob kyang / mthar 'chi 'pho zhing ltung ba yin te/ ji skad du/
brgya byin mchod 'os nyid du gyur nas kyang / / las kyi dbang gis slar yang sa steng lhung /[206] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Furthermore, even someone who achieves the physical form and the experiences of Indra, lord of the gods, will eventually fall from that state, first dying, then transmigrating. It says:
Even having become Indra, worthy of offerings, you fall back to earth through the power of karma.[112]

d.div: [206] gong mtshungs/ bshes spring / sh+lauka_69_shog_43_ba7
[112] Ibid. verse 69ab, 43b7.

f.d:
der ma zad lha'i rgyal po tshangs pa la sogs pa lta bu 'dod pa'i 'dod chags dang bral nas/ bsam gtan snyoms 'jug gi bde ba thob kyang mthar ltung ba yin te/ ji skad du/
tshangs nyid chags bral bde ba thob nas slar/ / mnar med me yi bud shing gyur pa yi/ / sdug bsngal rgyun mi chad pa bsten 'tshal lo/[207] / zhes gsungs so//

Besides this, the likes of the king of the gods, Brahma, who has transcended sensual desire and attained the felicity of evenly resting in meditative concentration, will also eventually fall. It says:
From the pleasures of being Brahma, free of desires, you’ll have to put up with the unceasing suffering of being fuel in the Hell of Relentless Agony.[113] /77/

d.div: [207] gong mtshungs/ bshes spring / sh+lauka_74_shog_44_na4
[113] Ibid. verse 74b–d, 44a4.

f.d: gsum pa sdug bsngal gyi sdug bsngal ni/ spyir nye bar len pa'i phung po 'di blangs pa rang gis sdug bsngal yin pa'i steng du/ sdug bsngal chen por mngon pa rnams yin no/ / de yang ngan 'gro'i sdug bsngal dang / bde 'gro'i sdug bsngal gnyis su shes par bya'o/ /

The third point is that of suffering as overt suffering. This is the significant and quite obvious sufferings experienced above and beyond that of having a life composed of aggregates to which suffering is inherent. They are to be known through two categories: those of the lower states of existence and those of the higher states.

de la dang po bshad na/ ngan song ni/ dmyal ba yi dwags dud 'gro gsum yin no/ / de dag re re bzhin dbye na du yod pa dang /[208] gnas gang na gnas pa dang / sdug bsngal ci myong ba dang / tshe ji srid thub pa dang bzhi bzhis shes par bya'o/ /

The sufferings of the lower states of existence are those of the three lower states: hells, hungry spirits, and animals. Each is to be understood through four points: their respective subcategories, locations, sufferings experienced, and lifespan.

d.div: [208] re re zhing / dpal spungs/

f.d: de la dmyal ba la dbye na/ tsha ba'i dmyal ba brgyad/ grang ba'i dmyal ba brgyad de bcu drug / nyi tshe ba dang / nye 'khor ba gnyis te bco brgyad do/ /
The hells. The subcategories are: the eight hot hells, the eight cold hells, the occasional hells, and the peripheral hells, making eighteen types in all.

tsha ba'i dmyal ba 'di dag gnas gang na gnas na/ 'dzam bu'i gling 'di'i 'og na gnas te/ 'di nas der 'gro ba mang ba'i phyir ro/ / de yang / 'og na mnar med pa'i sems can dmyal ba gnas so/[209] / de'i steng na yar la rab tu tsha ba dang / tsha ba dang / ngu 'bod chen po dang / ngu 'bod dang / bsdus 'joms dang / thig nag dang / yang sos rnams so/[210] /

The [eight] hot hells. Where are these hot hells? They are situated beneath Jambudvīpa, for there are many who go from here to there. In the very lowest live the sentient beings of Relentless Agony Hell. Above them, working upward, are the Exceedingly Hot, Hot, Great Wailing, Wailing, Gathering and Crushing, Black Line, and Reviving hells, respectively.

d.div: [209] nangs kyi 'og na/ dpal spungs/
[210] rnams gnas so/ dpal spungs/

f.d:
de ltar yang chos mngon pa mdzod las/
'di 'og stong phrag nyi shu na/ / mnar med pa'o de tsam mo/ / de yi steng na dmyal ba bdun/[211] / zhes gsungs so//

Therefore the Treasury of Higher Knowledge says:
Twenty thousand [leagues] beneath here is Relentless Agony, with seven other hells above it.[114]

d.div: [211] sde dge_4089_bstan/ mngon pa/ ku_dbyig gnyen/ chos mngon pa mdzod/ gnas/ 3_sh+loka_58_shog_9_na4
[114] Vasubandhu, Abhidharmakośa 3:58 Toh 4089 Tengyur, mngon pa, ku, 9a4.

f.d: de dag gis sdug bsngal ci myong na/ sgra 'jug pa'i rgyu mtshan dang thun mong du bstan par bya ste/ de la dang po yang sos ni/ dmyal ba gcig la gcig phan tshun tal phug bcad cing bsad nas/[212] rlung grang mo langs pas yang sos par 'gyur ro/ / de ltar tshe ma zad kyi bar du'o/ /

The reason for their names will be given, as well as a general explanation for the sufferings endured in those places. The first is the Reviving Hell, where beings are bound, immolated, and hacked to death by each other. Subsequently, a cold wind blows to revive them, and the process resumes. This continues relentlessly throughout their stay there.

d.div: [212] phan tshun btags phug_dpal spungs/

f.d:
thig nag ni gang du thig nag po btab nas/ sog le me rab tu 'bar bas gshog pa dang /[213] sta re me rab tu 'bar bas bzhogs par byed de/ / ji skad du/
kha cig sog les dras te de bzhin gzhan/ / sta re mi zad so rnon rnams kyis bzhogs/[214] / zhes gsungs so/ /

In the Black Line Hell, a black line is traced on the body, which is then sawed with blazing saws and chopped with flaming, red-hot axes. As it says:
Some are cut up with saws, others chopped up by unbearably sharp axes.[115]

d.div: [213] gshag_dpal spungs/
[214] sde dge_4182_bstan/ spring yig_nge _mgon po klu sgrub/ bshes spring / sh+loka_78_shog_44_na6
[115] Nāgārjuna, Letter to a Friend (Suhṛllekha) verse 78cd, Toh 4182 Tengyur, spring yig, nge, 44a6.

f.d: bsdus 'joms ni/ ri'i bar du bsdus shing 'joms pa dang / lcags kyi an 'dar gyi bar du bsdus shing 'joms pa'o/ / de la dang po ni/ gang du phyogs gnyis nas ri bo lug gi gdong pa lta bu gnyis 'ongs nas sems can de dag 'joms par byed do/ / de nas ri de gnyis phyir gyes pa dang rlung grang mo langs pas lus snga ma ltar sos/[215] / yang 'joms te de ka ltar byed pa'o/ /

In the Gathering and Crushing Hell, beings are gathered between mountains and also crushed and squeezed in iron presses. In the first instance, mountains in the form of ram’s heads come together, crushing the trapped beings. The hills then draw apart, and a cold wind arises to restore the people to their former condition. They are crushed and restored time after time.

d.div: [215] gyed/ dpal spungs/

f.d:
de ltar yang slob spring las/
ri dang mnyam lug ru rings 'jigs su rung ba gnyis/ / 'dus pa'i phrag tu lus kun phye mar brlag cing 'joms/[216]/ zhes sogs gsungs so/ /

The Letter to a Student says: /78/
Two terrifying mountains, like rams with long horns, crush all the bodies gathered between them and grind them to powder.[116]

d.div: [216] sde dge_4183_bstan/ spring yig_nge _slob dpon tsan+d+ra go mi/ slob spring / sh+loka_45_shog_49_na1
[116] Candragomin, Śiṣyalekha verse 45, Toh 4183 Tengyur, spring yig, nge, 49a1.

f.d:
kha cig lcags kyi an 'dar gyi bar du btsir bas khrag gi rgyun chu bo bzhi tsam pa 'bab bo/ / de ltar yang /
kha cig til bzhin 'tshir te de bzhin gzhan/ / phye ma zhib mo bzhin du rdul du rlog[217] / ces gsungs so/ /

Some are squeezed between iron presses, their blood squirting out like four rivers. It says:
Some are ground like sesame seeds, others milled to dust like fine flour.[117]

d.div: [217] sde dge_4182_bstan/ spring yig_nge _mgon po klu sgrub/ bshes spring / sh+loka_78_shog_44_na6
[117] Nāgārjuna, Letter to a Friend (Suhṛllekha) verse 78ab, Toh 4182 Tengyur, spring yig, nge, 44a6.

f.d: ngu 'bod ni sems can bsregs pa rnams skrag pa'i nga ro 'byin pa'o/[218] / ngu 'bod chen po ni lhag par nga ro 'byin pa'o/ / tsha ba ni/ me la sogs pas gdung bar byed pa ste/ khro chu khol ma khar blug pas khong pa 'tshig pa dang /[219] yang mtshon rtse gcig pa tsher ma can gyis bshang lam nas spyi bor 'bigs pa'o/[220] / rab tu tsha ba ni/ khyad par du gdung bar byed pa ste/ khro chu khol ma la sogs pas pags pa min pa rnams bsregs nas/ bu ga dgu nas me 'byung ba dang / yang mtshon rtse gsum pas bshang lam dang rkang mthil gnyis nas spyi bo dang dpung pa gnyis su 'bigs pa'o/ /

Beings in the Wailing Hell scream with terror as they are burned. Beings in the Great Wailing Hell scream even louder. In the Hot Hell beings are tortured by fire and the like. Boiling metal poured into their mouths burns their viscera, and they are pierced through with one-pointed spears from the anus to the top of the head. In the Exceedingly Hot Hell they are tortured even more than this. Without skin, they are burned by molten metal poured down their throats so that fire comes out their orifices. Then they, too, are pierced—by tridents that puncture the soles of the feet and the anus and penetrate up through the top of the head and the shoulders.

d.div: [218] sbag_dpal spungs/
[219] tshig pa dang / dpal spungs/ khong la 'tshig pa dang / mi rigs dpe skrun/
[220] gshang lam/ dpal spungs/

f.d:
de ltar yang /
de bzhin gzhan dag khro chu bzhus pa yi/ / khu ba 'bar bas 'khrigs pa ldud par bgyid/ / kha cig lcags kyi gsal shing rab 'bar ba/ / tsher ma can la kun tu brgyus par bgyid/[221] / ces gsungs so//

It says:
Similarly, some are forced to drink a blazing liquid of molten metal while others are impaled on blazing iron stakes bearing many spikes.[118]

d.div: [221] sde dge_4182_bstan/ spring yig_nge _mgon po klu sgrub/ bshes spring / sh+loka_79_shog_44_na7
[118] Ibid. verse 79, 44a7.

f.d:
mnar med pa'i sems can dmyal ba ni/ lcags kyi khang pa me rab tu 'bar ba dang /[222] mchu zheng dang / gnam 'phang du dpag tshad stong phrag nyi shu yod pa'i nang nas lcags zangs dpag tshad du ma yod pa'i nang du khro chu dang zangs chu blugs te/ der bcug nas phyogs bzhi nas mi bzad pa'i mes bskol bar byed pa'o/ / de ltar yang /
kha cig lcags las byas pa'i zangs chen du/ / spyi'u tshugs 'bras kyi thug pa bzhin du 'tshod/[223] / ces gsungs so/ / sdug bsngal bar mtshams med pas na mnar med pa zhes bya'o/ /

Relentless Agony (Avīci) Hell is a blazing iron building, twenty thousand leagues (yojana) in height and breadth, within which are copper and iron cauldrons several leagues wide, into which are poured molten bronze and iron that are kept boiling by unbearable fires coming from the four directions. It says:
Some are cast head first into iron cauldrons and boiled up like rice soup.[119] It is so named because the suffering there is unremitting.

d.div: [222] dpal spungs dpar mar dang mi gsal/
[223] sde dge_4182_bstan/ spring yig_nge _mgon po klu sgrub/ bshes spring / sh+loka_82_shog_44_ba2
[119] Ibid. verse 82cd, 44b2.

f.d:
de dag gi tshe yang ji srid du thub ce na/
yang sos la sogs drug rim bzhin/ / 'dod lha'i tshe dang nyin zhag mnyam/ / des na de dag rnams kyi tshe/ / 'dod pa'i lha dang 'dra ba yin/[224] / zhes gsungs te/

The lifespans of hell beings are taught as:
In the first six, starting with the Reviving Hell, a day and night is equivalent to the life of the sense-dimension gods, and hence their lifespans are calculable working from the lifespans of those gods.[120]

d.div: [224] sde dge_4089_bstan/ mngon pa/ ku_dbyig gnyen/ chos mngon pa mdzod/ gnas/ 3_sh+loka_82_shog_10_na2
[120] Vasubandhu, Treasury of Higher Knowledge (Abhidharmakośa) 3:82, Toh 4089 Tengyur, mngon pa, ku, 10a2.

f.d: rgyal chen rigs bzhi'i tshe tshad gang yin pa de ni dmyal ba yang sos kyi nyin zhag gcig yin la/ de sum cu la zla ba gcig / zla ba bcu gnyis la lor brtsis pa'i yang sos kyis rang lo lnga brgya thub bo/ / mi lo ltar na bye ba phrag 'bum drug khri nyis stong yod do/ /

The lifespan of the class of the Four Great King gods is equivalent to a day and night in the Reviving Hell. Thirty days make a month, and twelve months make a year. Reviving Hell beings live for five hundred of their own years. This makes their lifespan 1,620 billion human years. /79/

de bzhin du lha sum cu rtsa gsum dang / dmyal ba thig nag sbyar bas dmyal ba des rang lo stong thub ste/ mi lo ltar na bye ba 'bum phrag bcu gnyis dang / bye ba phrag dgu khri dgu stong yod do/[225] / lha 'thab bral ba dang dmyal ba bsdus 'joms sbyar bas dmyal ba des rang lo nyis stong thub ste/ mi lo ltar na bye ba gcig dang / bye ba phrag drug khri brgyad stong yod do/[226] / lha dga' ldan pa dang / dmyal ba ngu 'bod sbyar bas dmyal ba des rang lo bzhi stong thub ste/ mi lo ltar na bye ba phrag bye ba brgyad dang / bye ba phrag sa ya bzhi dang /[227] bye ba phrag bzhi 'bum bzhi khri nyis stong yod do/[228] / lha 'phrul dga' ba dang / dmyal ba ngu 'bod chen por sbyar bas dmyal ba des rang lo brgyad stong thub ste/[229] mi lo ltar na bye ba phrag bye ba drug cu rtsa drug dang / bye ba phrag sa ya gsum dang / bye ba phrag lnga 'bum lnga khri nyis stong yod do/ / lha gzhan 'phrul dbang byed pa dang / dmyal ba tsha ba sbyar bas des rang lo khri drug stong thub ste/ mi lo ltar na lo bye ba phrag bye ba lnga brgya dang / bye ba phrag bye ba bcu dang /[230] bye ba phrag sa ya brgyad dang / bye ba phrag bzhi 'bum dang / bye ba phrag stong yod do/[231] / dmyal ba rab tu tsha bas ni tshe bar gyi bskal pa phyed thub bo/[232] / mnar med pas ni tshe bar gyi bskal pa gcig thub bo/ /

In a similar way, lifespan in the Black Line Hell is calculated according to that of the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three. Since beings can live for up to a thousand hell years, their lifespan is the equivalent of 12,990 billion human years.[121] Correlating the Gathering and Crushing Hell with the Aggression-Free god realm then, since beings can be there for two thousand hell years, their lifespan is the equivalent of 100,680 billion human years.[122] Correlating the Wailing Hell with the Joyful god realm then, since beings can stay there for four thousand hell years, their lifespan is the equivalent of 844,420 billion human years.[123] Correlating the Great Wailing Hell with the Delighting in Creation god realm then, since beings can stay there for eight thousand hell years, their lifespan is the equivalent of 6,635,520 billion human years. Correlating the Hot Hell with the Rulers of Others’ Creations god realm then, since beings can stay there for sixteen thousand hell years, their lifespan is the equivalent of 51,084,010 billion human years.[124] Those in the Exceedingly Hot Hell can remain there for half an intermediate cosmic eon, and those in the Relentless Agony Hell for a whole intermediate cosmic eon.

f.d:
de ltar yang /
rab tu tsha phyed mnar med ni/ / bar gyi bskal pa'o/[233] / zhes gsungs so//

As it says:
In the Exceedingly Hot, a half, and in the Relentless Agony, a whole intermediate cosmic eon.[125]

d.div: [233] sde dge_4089_bstan/ mngon pa/ ku_dbyig gnyen/ chos mngon pa mdzod/ gnas/ 3_sh+loka_83_shog_10_na2
[125] From Vasubandhu, Treasury of Higher Knowledge (Abhidharmakośa) 3:83, Toh 4089 Tengyur, mngon pa, ku, 10a2.

f.d: nye 'khor gyi dmyal ba ni/ dmyal ba brgyad po de dag gi phyogs bzhi na yod de/ de yang thog mar me ma mur pus nub tsam yod la/ sems can de dag gnas tshol du 'gro ba na/ de dag gis rkang pa bzhag na ni pags pa dang / sha dang / khrag kun zhig par 'gyur ro/ / rkang pa bteg na de dag sos par 'gyur te/ de ni lhag pa dang po'o/ / de'i drung nyid du ro myags mi gtsang ba'i 'dam rdzab dag tu 'bu lus dkar zhing / mgo nag la mchu rno ba dag gnas shing / de dag gis sems can de dag gi rus pa'i bar du 'bigs par byed pa ste/ de ni lhag pa gnyis pa'o/ / de'i drung nyid na spu gris gtams pa'i lam po che dang / ral gri lo ma'i nags tshal dang / khyi bse bo dang /[234] lcags kyi shal ma li dang / kha lcags kyi mchu can rnams kyis gnod pa byed pa ste/[235] de ni lhag pa gsum pa'o/ / de'i drung na chu bo rab med thal chu 'khol mas gang ba ste/[236] der sems can de dag 'tshod la/ 'gram na skyes bu lag na mtshon thogs pas 'gog ste/ de ni lhag pa bzhi pa'o/ /

The neighboring hells. These are situated in the four cardinal directions around the eight hells mentioned above. The first of these is the Glowing Coals Hell, where there are knee-deep glowing coals. As beings there take a step, seeking escape, the flesh, skin, and blood are completely burned off their legs when they put their feet down, yet restored as they lift them up again. That is the first additional hell. Nearby is the Impure Swamp of Putrefied Corpses Hell, infested by white worms with black heads. With sharp, hard, pointed mouths, they enter the flesh, penetrating to the bone. This is the second additional hell. /80/ Nearby is the Great Razor Highway Hell, where beings are molested by a forest of sword-like leaves, terrifying large black dogs, and iron trees with lacerating leaves and branches, on which perch ravens with iron beaks. This is the third additional hell. Nearby is the Most Extreme River, full of boiling lye in which beings are cooked. They are prevented from leaving the river by beings who stand along the banks brandishing weapons. This is the fourth additional hell.

d.div: [234] khyi sre/ dpal spungs/
[235] khwa lcags/ dpal spungs/ mi rigs dpe skrun/
[236] khol/ dpal spungs/ mi rigs dpe skrun/

f.d:
de ltar yang /
brgyad po kun la lhag bcu drug / de dag gi ni ngos bzhi na/ / me ma mur dang ro myags 'dam/ / spu gri'i lam sogs chu bo yin/[237] / zhes gsungs so/ /

It says, about these:
Besides the eight there are sixteen others, in the four cardinal directions from them: the Glowing Coals, a Swamp of Putrefaction, the Razor Highway, and so on, and the River.[126]

d.div: [237] sde dge_4089_bstan/ mngon pa/ ku_dbyig gnyen/ chos mngon pa mdzod/ gnas/ 3_sh+loka_59_shog_9_na4

f.d: ci skyes bu'i cha byad kyis bsrung ma dang /[238] khwa lcags kyi mchu can la sogs pa dmyal srung gi 'khor de dag sems can yin nam ma yin zhe na/ bye brag tu smra ba rnams ni sems can yin par 'dod/ mdo sde pa rnams sems can ma yin par 'dod/ rnal 'byor spyod pa dang mar pa dang mi la yab sras kyi bzhed pa ni sems can sdig pa byas pa'i dbang gis rang gi sems nyid de ltar snang bar 'dod/[239]

You may wonder whether the guardians of the hells—who appear to be humans or ravens with iron beaks—are actual sentient beings. The Vaibhāṣika schools hold them to be sentient beings, whereas the Sautrāntika schools say they are not. The Yogācāra schools and the lineage transmission of Marpa and Milarepa hold them to be manifestations of their perceiver’s own mind, due to former evils enacted.

d.div: [238] cha byad kyi srung ma/ dpal spungs/
[239] rnal 'byor spyod pa ba rnams ni sems can sdig pa/ dpal spungs/

f.d:
don 'di dang mthun par spyod 'jug las/
sems can dmyal ba'i mtshon cha rnams/ / su zhig gis ni ched du byas/ / lcags bsregs sa gzhi su yis byas/ / me tshogs de dag ci las byung / / de 'dra de dag thams cad kyang / / sdig sems yin par thub pas gsungs/[240] / zhes 'byung ngo //

Guide to the Bodhisattva Way of Life accords with this interpretation:
Who could have created the beings there and their hellish weapons for such purposes? Who made the burning iron ground, and from what are the fires generated? The Great Sage has said that all these sorts of things are due to the existence of an unwholesome mind.[127]

d.div: [240] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_rgyal sras zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 5_sh+loka_7_shog_10_ba1
[127] Śāntideva, Bodhicaryāvatāra 5:7–8ab, Toh 3871 Tengyur, la, 10b1.

f.d: grang ba'i dmyal ba brgyad ni/ chu bur can dang / chu bur rdol pa can dang /[241] so tham tham pa dang / a chu zer ba dang / kyi hud zer ba dang / ut+pal ltar gas pa dang / pad+ma ltar gas pa dang / pad+ma chen po ltar gas pa'o/ /

The eight cold hells. These are: (1) the Cold Sore Hell, (2) the Burst Cold Sore Hell, (3) the Chattering Teeth Hell, (4) the Sneezing Hell, (5) the Alas! Hell, (6) the Hell Where Frostbitten Skin Cracks in the Shape of an Utpala, (7) the Hell with Cracks Like a Lotus, and (8) the Hell with Cracks Like Giant Lotuses.

d.div: [241] dpal spungs dpar mar rdol la brdol zhes ba sngon 'jug skabs du mar byung /

f.d:
de ltar yang /
chu bur can sogs grang brgyad gzhan/[242] / zhes gsungs so/ /

It is said:
There are eight cold hells: the Cold Sore Hell and the others.[128]

d.div: [242] sde dge_4089_bstan/ mngon pa/ ku_dbyig gnyen/ chos mngon pa mdzod/ gnas/ 3_sh+loka_59_shog_9_na4
[128] Vasubandhu, Treasury of Higher Knowledge (Abhidharmakośa) 3:59, Toh 4089 Tengyur, mngon pa, ku, 9a4.

f.d: 'di dag gnas gang na gnas she na/ 'dzam bu gling 'di nyid kyi 'og na dmyal ba chen po rnams kyi thad ka na gnas so/ /
They are located beneath this Jambudvīpa, directly beneath the hot hells.

de dag gis sdug bsngal ci zhig myong zhe na/ sgra 'jug pa'i rgyu mtshan dang thun mong du bstan par bya ste/ dang po gnyis ni grang ba mi bzod pas nyen pas lus la chu bur byung ba dang /[243] chu bur rdol ba lta bur gyur ba ste/ lus 'gyur ba las ming du btags so// gsum pa ni grang ba mi bzod pa'i nyen pas sgra 'gyur ba las btags pa'o/ / pags pa sngo zhing / kha lnga'am drug tu gas pa ni ut+pal ltar gas pa'o/ / sngo ba las thal nas dmar zhing / kha bcu'am de las lhag par gas pa ni pad+ma ltar gas pa'o/ / shin tu dmar bar gyur nas kha brgya'am de las lhag par gas pa ni pad+ma ltar cher gas pa'o/ / phyi ma 'di gsum yang lus 'gyur ba las ming du btags pa'o/ /

Below is a general outline of the sufferings experienced in those states and an explanation of their names. In the first two hells, the cold is so unbearable that the beings have cold sores or [in the second] festering cold sores. The next three are named after the sounds and cries that beings there are heard to make due to the unbearable cold. The last three derive their names from the bodily changes that take place: in the sixth the skin turns blue with cold and cracks open in fivefold or sixfold cracks, looking like an utpala flower; in the seventh it has turned from blue to red, and the cracks have ten or more lips, like a lotus; and in the last the skin is violently inflamed and split into a hundred or more flaps, like an open, giant lotus. /81/

d.div: [243] mi bzad/ dpal spungs/ gsham du'ang de bzhin du byung /

f.d:
de dag gi tshe ji srid thub ce na/ bcom ldan 'das kyis de dag dpe tsam du/
dge slong dag dper na/ 'di na yul ma ga d+ha'i til rdzang khal brgyad cu 'gro ba zhig til gyis byur por bkang ste/[244] de nas la la zhig gis lo brgya brgya 'das shing til re re phyir bor na/ dge slong dag rim pa des na/ yul ma ga d+hA'i til rdzang khal brgyad cu po de ma lus par yongs su zad par 'gyur ba ni ches myur gyi/ chu bur can du skyes pa'i sems can rnams kyi tshe yongs su gtugs par ni nga mi smra'o/ / dge slong dag chu bur can nyi shu ji lta ba de bzhin du chu bur rdol ba can gcig yin no/ / zhes pa nas/
dge slong dag pad+ma ltar gas pa nyi shu ji lta ba de bzhin du/ pad+ma ltar gas pa chen po gcig yin no/[245] / zhes gsungs so/ /

How long does the lifespan of these beings last? Just as an example, the Bhagavan Buddha stated the following:
O monks, here is an example. Say a storehouse able to hold eighty bushels of sesame seeds, like those of this land of Magadha, were to be filled with such seeds. If once every hundred years one grain were to be removed, then after a certain period all the eighty bushels of that Magadha sesame would eventually be emptied from that store. I could not tell you which of the two—that period of time or the lifespan of those in the Cold Sore Hell—would be the longer. O monks! The lifespan in the Open Cold Sore hell is twenty times that of the Cold Sore Hell.
O monks! The lifespan in the Great Open Lotus Hell is twenty times that in the Open Lotus Hell.[129]

d.div: [244] dpal spungs dpar mar 'og tu skabs du mar til rdzang la til sbyang zhes skabs du mar gsal/
[245] sde dge_307_bka'/ mdo sde/ sa_tshe'i mtha'i mdo/ shog_143_ba2
[129] In the Lifespan Sutra (Āyuṣparyantasūtra), Toh 307 Kangyur, mdo sde, sa, 143b2.

f.d:
slob dpon dbyig gnyen gyis de'i don mdor bsdus nas bstan pa ni/
til rdzang nang nas lo brgya bzhin/ / til gcig phyung bas zad gyur pa/ / chu bur can gyi tshe yin te/ / gzhan gyi tshe ni nyi shu 'gyur/[246] / zhes pa ste/

Master Vasubhandu taught this in a briefer form:
The lifespan in the Cold Sore Hell [approximates] the time it would take to empty a store of sesame seeds by removing just one seed every hundred years. The lifespan in the others increases by a factor of twenty.[130]

d.div: [246] sde dge_4089_bstan/ mngon pa/ ku_dbyig gnyen/ chos mngon pa mdzod/ gnas/ 3_sh+loka_84_shog_10_na3
[130] Treasury of Abhidharma (Abhidharmakośa) 3:84, Toh 4089 Tengyur, mngon pa, ku, 10a3.

f.d: des na chu bur can gyis til rdzang gang ngo // chu bur rdol ba can gyis nyi shu'o/ / so tham tham gyis bzhi brgya'o/ / a chu zer bas stong phrag brgyad yin no/ / kyi hud zer bas 'bum phrag gcig dang drug khri yin no/ / ut+pal ltar gas pas sa ya phrag gsum dang / 'bum phrag gnyis so/ / pad+ma ltar gas pas bye ba phrag drug dang / sa ya phrag bzhi yin no/ / pad+ma chen po ltar gas pas til rdzang ther 'bum phrag gcig dang / dung phyur phrag gnyis dang / bye ba phrag bzhi yin no/ /

Therefore the lifespan in the Cold Sore Hell is the time it would take to empty a full sesame store; that of the Open Cold Sore Hell is that multiplied by twenty; that of the Chattering Teeth Hell is that multiplied by four hundred; that of the Sneezing Hell is that multiplied by eight thousand; that of the Alas Hell is that multiplied by 160,000; that of the Utpala Wound Hell is that multiplied by 3,200,000; that of the Lotus-Like Wounds is that multiplied by 64,000,000; and that of the Great Lotus Wounds is that multi-plied by 1,280,000,000.
