nyi tshe ba'i sems can dmyal ba ni mang po'am gnyis sam gcig gam/ so so'i las dag gis grub pa yin te/ de dag gi rnam pa'i bye brag du ma yod do/ / 'di'i gnas la nges pa med de/ chu bo dang / ri dang / mya ngam gyi phyogs dang / gzhan dag dang / sa 'og dang / kha cig mi'i yul na gnas te/[247] 'phags pa mau'u gal gyi bus gzigs pa lta bu'o/[248] / de bzhin du mya ngam gyi phyogs su btsun pa dge 'dun 'tshos gzigs pa lta bu'o/[249] / 'di'i tshe tshad la nges pa med pa'o/ /

The occasional hells. These are created by the karma of one or two people or many people, and depend on the specific action performed. They take many different forms and have no definite location. Some of their hell beings live in rivers, some in the hills, and some in desolate areas or yet other places. Some are in subterranean realms. Some are in the human realm, such as those seen by the realized Maudgalyāyana. Likewise some are in destitute places, like those seen by Saṅgharakṣita.[131] Their lifespan is not fixed.

d.div: [247] lus na/ mi rigs dpe skrun/
[248] sde dge_341_bka'/ mdo sde/ a_mdzangs blun zhes bya ba'i mdo/ le'u/ 15_shog_173_na4_nas _182_ba1
[249] sde dge_1_bka'/ 'dul ba/ ka_'dul ba gzhi/ rab byung gi gzhi/ shog_100_ba3
[131] Vinayavastu, Toh 1, Kangyur, ’dul ba, ka, 100b:3.

f.d: sems can dmyal ba'i sdug bsngal bshad zin to//
This concludes the explanation of hell beings’ sufferings.

yi dwags la dbye na yi dwags kyi rgyal po gshin rje dang / de las 'phros pa'i yi dwags so/ / de dag gang na gnas she na/ yi dwags kyi rgyal po gshin rje ni/ 'dzam bu gling gi 'og dpag tshad lnga brgya bcad pa na yod do/ / 'phros pa'i yi dwags ni mya ngam gyi phyogs la sogs pa nges pa med par gnas so/ / 'phros pa'i yi dwags la dbye na gsum ste/ zas skom la phyi'i sgrib pa yod pa dang / nang gi sgrib pa yod pa dang / zas skom la sgrib pa yod pa'o/ / de dag gis sdug bsngal ci myong zhe na/ yi dwags rdzu 'phrul can kha cig gis ni lha'i dpal lta bu yang nyams su myong ngo / / zas skom la phyi'i sgrib pa yod pas ni/ zas skom la rnag khrag tu mthong ba dang / gzhan gyis 'gog par mthong nas bza' btung gi dbang med pa'o/ / nang gi sgrib pa yod pa ni/ gzhan gyis mi 'gogs kyang /[250] rang gis bza' ba dang btung bar mi nus pa ste/

Hungry spirits. There are two categories: the king of the hungry spirits—Yama, lord of the dead—and the scattered spirits. As for their habitats, Yama, the ruler of the hungry spirits, lives some five hundred leagues beneath this Jambudvīpa world. /82/ His scattered subjects have no set location, living in deserts and the like. There are three types of the latter: those that have an external eating or drinking impediment, those that have an internal impediment, and those with a general eating or drinking impediment. The sufferings endured are as follows. Some anguished spirits have super-natural powers and experience almost god-like splendors. However, those with an external eating or drinking impediment see food and drink as pus and blood. They cannot eat or drink it because they perceive themselves as being prevented from so doing by other beings. Those with an internal impediment are not prevented by others from ingesting the food but are themselves unable to do so.

d.div: [250] mi 'gog kyang / mi rigs dpe skrun/

f.d:
ji skad du/
kha cig kha ni khab kyi mig tsam la/ / lto ba ri yi khyon tsam bkres pas nyen/ / mi gtsang gyi nar bor ba cung zad kyang / / 'tshal ba'i mthu dang ldan pa ma lags so/[251] / zhes gsungs so/ /

It is said:
Some have a mouth the size of a needle but a belly the size of a mountain. Anguished with hunger, those with the strength to look for food cannot find a morsel even among rubbish.[132]

d.div: [251] sde dge_4182_bstan/ spring yig_nge _mgon po klu sgrub/ bshes spring / sh+loka_92_shog_45_na1
[132] In Nāgārjuna’s Letter to a Friend (Suhṛllekha), Toh 4182 Tengyur, spring yig, nge, 45a1.

f.d: zas skom la sgrib pa yod pa la yang gnyis/ me lce'i phreng ba can dang / ljan ljin za ba'o/ / de la dang po ni zos pa dang / 'thungs pa tsam gyis 'tshig par 'gyur ro/ / gnyis pa ni phyis sa dang /[252] gcin 'thung ba dang / rang gi sha bcad cing za ba'o/ / de la yang mya ngam gyi phyogs su gro bzhin skyes rna ba bye ba ris mthong ba lta bu'o/[253] /

Among those with an eating and drinking impediment there are two types: fire garlands and filth eaters. As soon as the first type ingests food or drink, they are burned by it, as if by fire. The second eat excrement, drink urine, and cut off their flesh to eat. This was seen in a wilderness by Koṭikarṇa.[133]

d.div: [252] phyi sa/ dpal spungs/
[253] sde dge_1_bka'/ 'dul ba/ ka_'dul ba gzhi/ ko lpags kyi gzhi/ shog_251_ba3

[133] Koṭikarṇa (“Ten Million in the Ear”) was so called because he was born with a divine jewel worth ten million ounces of gold set in his ear. He set out as a merchant, to please his father, but was abandoned by his servants and then lost in a desert, where he spent twelve years with various types of hungry spirits. They were lucid about the past actions that had caused their plight and gave him messages for the human realm, to which he returned. He became a monk under Mahākatyāyana, gaining deep realization. Basis of Vinaya (Vinayavastu), Toh 1 Kangyur, ’dul ba, ka, 251b3. A translation of this story appears in Rotman, Divine Stories, 39–70.

f.d: yi dwags kyi tshe ji srid thub ce na/[254] mi rnams kyi zla ba gcig gang yin pa yi dwags rnams kyi nyin zhag gcig yin la/ de zla ba dang lor brtsis pa'i lo lnga brgya thub bo/ /

How long does the lifespan of a hungry spirit last? A month of human time is the equivalent of a day and night of hungry spirit time. This enables us to calculate how long, in human terms, they live, because their lives last five hundred of their years.

d.div: [254] kyis/ dpal spungs/ mi rigs dpe skrun/

f.d:
de ltar yang /
yi dwags rnams/ / zla ba nyin zhag gi lnga brgya/[255] / zhes gsungs so//

It is said:
. . . hungry spirits live for five hundred [years]: a day being a month.[134]

d.div: [255] sde dge_4089_bstan/ mngon pa/ ku_dbyig gnyen/ chos mngon pa mdzod/ gnas/ 3_sh+loka_83_shog_10_na3
[134] Vasubandu, Treasury of Higher Knowledge (Abhidharmakośa) 3:83, Toh 4089 Tengyur, mngon pa, ku, 10a3.

f.d: dud 'gro la dbye na/ rkang mang dang / rkang bzhi dang / rkang gnyis dang / rkang med dang bzhi'o/ / 'di dag gang na gnas zhe na/ chu dang / thang dang / nags mtha'i spyod yul dag yin no/ / de yang gnas kyi rtsa ba ni rgya mtsho chen po yin no/ / de dag gi sdug bsngal ci myong zhe na/[256] bkol spyod kyi sdug bsngal dang / bsad bcad kyi sdug bsngal dang / gcig la gcig za ba'i sdug bsngal lo//

Animals. There are four main categories: many-legged ones, quadrupeds, bipeds, and the legless. Their habitat can be water, open land, or forest, but the majority live in the oceans. The sufferings they experience are those of enslavement and being slaughtered and butchered when exploited by humans, or being eaten by each other in the wild.

d.div: [256] de dag gis/ dpal spungs dang mi rigs dpe skrun khang /

f.d:
de la dang po ni/ mi'i dbang du gyur pa'i dud 'gro rnams te/ ji skad du/
dbang med gzhan dag rdog pa lag pa dang / / lcags dang lcags kyus gdab pas btab ste bkol/[257] /[258] zhes gsungs so/ /

It says of domesticated animals:
Powerless, they are exploited: beaten, kicked, chained, and goaded.[135]

d.div: [257] lcags kyu/ dpal spungs/ mi rigs dpe skrun/
[258] sde dge_4182_bstan/ spring yig_nge _mgon po klu sgrub/ bshes spring / sh+loka_90_shog_44_ba7
[135] Nāgārjuna’s Letter to a Friend (Suhṛllekha) verse 90cd, Toh 4182 Tengyur, spring yig, nge, 44b7.

f.d:
gnyis pa ni ri dwags la sogs pa rnams te/ ji skad du/
kha cig mu tig bal dang rus pa khrag / sha dang pags pa'i ched du 'chi bar 'gyur/[259] / zhes gsungs so/ /

And of wild animals, it is said:
They are those slaughtered for their pearls, wool, /83/ bones, blood, flesh, or hides.[136]

d.div: [259] gong mtshungs/ bshes spring / sh+loka_90_shog_44_ba7
[136] Ibid. verse 90ab, 44b7.

f.d:
gsum pa ni/ phal cher phyi'i rgya mtsho la gnas pa rnams te/[260] ji skad du/
zas su gdong du gang bab za/[261] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Concerning those living in the great oceans:
They eat whatever is in front of the face.[137]

d.div: [260] phal po che/ dpal spungs/
[261] gzhung ngos 'dzin ma thub/
[137] The source of this quote has not been identified.

f.d:
dud 'gro'i tshe ji srid thub ce na/[262] nges pa med de/ yun ring shos kyis bar gyi bskal pa re re thub pa yang yod do/ /de ltar yang /
dud 'gro rnams/ mchog ring bskal pa'o/[263]/ zhes gsungs so/ /

Animal lifespan is not fixed. The longest living continue for up to an intermediate cosmic eon. It says:
The lifespan of animals is an eon, at most.[138]

d.div: [262] dud gros/ dpal spungs/ dud 'gros/ mi rigs dpe skrun/
[263] sde dge_4089_bstan/ mngon pa/ ku_chos mngon pa mdzod/ gnas/ 3_sh+loka_83_shog_10_na3
[138] Vasubandhu, Treasury of Higher Knowledge (Abhidharmakośa) 3:83, Toh 4089 Tengyur, mngon pa, ku, 10a3.

f.d: ngan 'gro'i sdug bsngal bshad zin to//
This concludes the section on the sufferings of the lower states.
bde 'gro'i sdug bsngal la gsum ste/ mi'i sdug bsngal dang / lha min gyi sdug bsngal dang / lha'i bsdug bsngal lo/ /
The sufferings of the higher states of existence are considered in three areas: humans, demigods, and gods.

de yang mi la sdug bsngal brgyad yod de/ ji skad du/ mngal 'jug gi mdo las/
de bzhin du skye ba yang sdug bsngal lo/ / rga ba yang sdug bsngal yin no/ / na ba yang sdug bsngal yin no/ / 'chi ba yang sdug bsngal yin no/ / sdug pa dang bral ba yang sdug bsngal yin no/ / mi sdug pa dang 'phrad pa yang sdug bsngal yin no/ / gang 'dod pa btsal te ma rnyed pa yang sdug bsngal yin no/ / yod pa bsrung dka' ba yang sdug bsngal yin no/[264] / zhes gsungs so//

Humans. Humans experience eight principal sufferings. It says in Nanda’s Abiding in the Womb:
Likewise birth is a suffering, aging is a suffering, sickness is a suffering, death is a suffering, to be separated from what one likes is a suffering, to encounter what one dislikes is a suffering, to strive after and obtain what one wants is a suffering, and also to undergo hardship in order to maintain what one has is a suffering.[139]

d.div: [264] sde dge_57_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ ga_dga' bo la mngal gnas bstan pa'i mdo/ bam po/ 3_shog_223_ba7
[139] Nandagarbhāvakrāntinirdeśa, Toh 57 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, ga, 223b7.

f.d: de la skye ba ni gzhan thams cad kyi rtsa ba yang yin la/[265] de yang skye gnas bzhi las skye bar gsungs kyang phal cher mngal nas skye'o/ / 'di'i dbang du byas na/ dang po srid pa bar do nas mngal du 'jug khar yang sdug bsngal 'di ltar yod de/ bar do'i srid pa thams cad rdzu 'phrul dang ldan pa/ nam mkha' la 'gro zhing lha'i mig bzhin du skye gnas thag ring po yang mthong bar nus so// de yang las kyi dbang gis log pa'i snang ba bzhi 'char te/ dper na rlung chen po langs pa dang / char chen po babs pa dang /[266] nam rmug pa dang /[267] skye bo mang po'i sgra ca co 'jigs su rung ba grags pa lta bu'i spyod yul du shar bas/ las bzang ngan ji lta ba bzhin du yang dag pa ma yin pa'i 'du shes bcu 'byung bar 'gyur te/

The first of these is the suffering of birth, which also serves as the source of all the others. Although four possible modes of birth[140] are taught, most humans are born from a womb. When that is the case, various sufferings occur in the period starting from the intermediate state (bardo) and continuing until a womb is entered. In general, bardo beings have certain supernatural abilities. They are able to move through space and to see remote birth states through a type of divine vision. This leads to the subjective experience of four types of hallucinations generated by the force of former actions, such as the stirring of a mighty wind, a heavy fall of rain, a darkening of the sky, and the presence of frightening sounds made by hordes of people. Then, according to how good or bad the person’s karma is, the following ten distorted perceptions will come to arise:

d.div: [265] de yang / dpal spungs/
[266] bab pa/ dpal spungs/
[267] rmus pa/ dpal spungs/
[140] The four modes of birth are: spontaneous, from a womb, from an egg, or from heat and moisture.

f.d: bdag ni gzhal med khang du 'jug go snyam pa dang / khang pa brtsegs pa'i steng du 'dzeg go snyam pa dang / khri la 'dzeg go snyam pa dang / rtswa'i spyil por 'jug go snyam pa dang / lo ma'i khyim du 'jug go snyam pa dang / rtswa gseb tu 'dzul lo snyam pa dang / nags kyi nang du 'jug go snyam pa dang / rtsig pa'i bu gar 'dzul lo snyam pa dang / sog ma'i gseb tu 'dzul lo snyam du sems pa ste/ de ltar sems pa dang / pha ma 'khrig pa spyod pa de thag ring po nas kyang mthong nas der 'gro ste/

“I’m entering a celestial palace,” “I’m going on top of a multistory building,” “I’m approaching a throne,” “I’m entering a thatched hut,” “I’m going into a house made of leaves,” “I’m slipping in between blades of grass,” “I’m entering a forest,” “I’m going through a hole in a wall,” or “I’m slipping in between straws.” /84/ Furthermore, seeing from afar the future parents in sexual embrace, [the bardo being] heads toward them.

de yang bsod nams cher bsags pa dang / skye gnas mthon po 'dzin pa rnams kyis ni gzhal med khang dang / khang pa brtsegs pa la sogs par mthong nas der rgyug go/ bsod nams 'bring du bsags pa dang / skye gnas 'bring du 'dzin pa rnams kyis ni rtswa'i spyil bu la sogs par mthong nas der rgyug go / bsod nams ma bsags pa skye gnas ngan pa 'dzin pa rnams kyis ni/ rtsig pa'i bu ga la sogs par mthong nas der rgyug go / der phyin pa dang / gal te rang phor skye ba yin na ma la chags pa skye la/ pha la zhe sdang skye bar 'gyur ro/ / gal te rang mor skye ba yin na/ pha la chags pa skye la/ ma la zhe sdang skye bar 'gyur ro/ / chags sdang gnyis kyis pha ma'i mi gtsang ba'i rdzas dang bar do'i shes pa 'dres so/ /

Beings who have accumulated a great store of merit and who will have a high rebirth see a celestial palace, multistory building, or the like and head for it. Those with a middling store of merit who will have a middling rebirth see the grass-thatched hut and so forth and head toward that. Those who have gathered no merit and who will have a low rebirth see the hole in the wall and so forth and head toward that. Having reached there, one who is to be born a boy will feel attracted to the mother and averse to the father, whereas one who is to be born a girl will feel attraction for the father and aversion toward the mother. By these feelings of attraction and aversion, the bardo consciousness becomes fused with the impure substances of the parents.[141]

d.div: [141] It is not that the sperm and ovum are particularly impure compared to other bodily substances, but that they form part of the thirty-six impure physical substances of which a human body is composed.

f.d: de nas bzung nas zhag bdun phrag sum cu rtsa brgyad du mngal du gnas par gsungs/[268] kha cig nas zla ba brgyad dam/ zla ba dgu'am/ zla ba bcu'i bar du gnas par yang gsungs so/ / kha cig la ma nges te lo drug cu'i bar du mngal du bsdad pa yang yod do//[269]

It is taught that from that moment on, thirty-eight weeks will be spent in the womb.[142] It is also taught that some spend eight months, some nine, and some ten. Some spend an indefinite period, and there are even some who spend up to sixty years in the womb.[143]

d.div: [268] sde dge_58_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ ga_dga' bo mngal mdo/ bam po/ 3_shog_238_na1
[269] sde dge_343_bka'/ mdo sde/ aM_gang po la sogs pa rtogs brjod brgya pa/ shog_254_na6
[142] Nanda’s Abiding in the Womb (Nandagarbhāvakrāntinirdeśa), Toh 57 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, ga, 238a1.
[143] One Hundred Stories (Avadānaśataka), Toh 343 Kangyur, mdo sde, ām, 254a6.

f.d: de yang zhag bdun phrag dang po'i tshe ma'i mngal du/ zangs tsha ba'i nang du btsos shing brngos pa tsam du/ lus kyi dbang po dang rnam par shes pa lhan cig tu sdug bsngal mi bzad pa myong ste/ de ni mer mer po zhes bya'o/ / de'i dbyibs ni 'bras kyi khu ba'am/ zho'i spris ma dang 'dra'o//

During the first week in the mother’s womb, it is just like being cooked and fried in a hot cooking pot, due to the consciousness combined with the physical constituents causing experiences of unbearable suffering. This stage of the embryo, called the ovoid, is in form like rice jelly or yogurt.

de nas zhag bdun phrag gnyis pa la ma'i mngal nas kyang / kun tu reg pa zhes bya ba'i rlung byung nas mngal la reg pas khams rnam pa bzhi mngon du snang bar 'gyur te/ de ni nur nur po zhes bya'o/ / de'i dbyibs ni zho bska ba'am/ mar 'khyag pa dang 'dra'o/[270] /

In the second week in the mother’s womb, the “all-touching” energy stirs. Its contact with the mother’s womb makes the four elements become manifest. This is called the oblong and is like curds or churned butter in appearance.

d.div: [270] 'khyags/ dpal spungs/ mi rigs dpe skrun/

f.d: de nas zhag bdun phrag gsum pa la ma'i mngal nas/ mdzod ka zhes bya ba'i rlung byung nas/ mngal de la reg pas khams bzhi po dag shin tu mngon du snang bar 'gyur te/ de ni ltar ltar po zhes bya'o/ / de'i dbyibs ni lcags kyi thur ma'am/ srin bu grog ma dang 'dra'o/ /
In the third week in the mother’s womb, the “activator” energy stirs the womb, making the four elements further consolidate. This is known as the lump and looks like a metal spoon or an ant.

de bzhin du sbyar te zhag bdun phrag bdun pa la ma'i mngal nas/ 'khyil bar byed pa zhes bya ba'i rlung byung ste/ rlung de mngal la reg pas lag pa gnyis dang /[271] rkang pa gnyis 'byung bar byed de/ de'i tshe skyes bu stobs dang ldan pas yan lag nas 'then nas skyes bu gzhan zhig gis dbyug pas gdal ba snyam byed pa'i sdug bsngal 'byung ngo /[272] /

Likewise, in the seventh week spent in the mother’s womb, the “twister” energy arises. /85/ Its effect on the child in the womb causes formation of the two arms and two legs. The suffering undergone during this period is as though one strong person were pulling out the limbs while another was using a rolling pin to spread out the body.

d.div: [271] rlung des/ dpal spungs/ mi rigs dpe skrun/
[272] rdeg pa/ dpal spungs/

f.d: de bzhin du sbyar te/ zhag bdun phrag bcu gcig pa la ma'i mngal nas/ bu ga snang ba zhes bya'i rlung byung nas/ mngal la reg pas bu ga dgu po 'byung bar 'gyur te/ de'i tshe rma gsar pa mdzub mos slong ba tsam gyi sdug bsngal yod do/ /

Likewise, in the eleventh week spent in the mother’s womb, the “orifice-forming” energy occurs. Its effect on the child in the womb is to cause the nine bodily orifices to appear. The suffering at that time is like that of a fresh wound being probed by a finger.

gzhan yang mas zas ma snyoms shing grang ba brten na/[273] gcer bu chab rom du bskyur ba tsam gyi sdug bsngal yod do/ / de bzhin du/ kha zas shin tu tsha ba dang / shin tu skyur ba la sogs pas kyang sdug bsngal bskyed do/ / zas shin tu mang ba zos pa'i dus su brag bar du btsir ba lta bu'i sdug bsngal yod do/ / zas nyung ngu zos pa'i dus su nam mkha' la dpyang la btang ba lta bu'i sdug bsngal yod do/[274] / drag tu song ba'am/ mchong ba byas sam/ brdeg 'chos na ri bo'i ngos la 'dril ba lta bu'i sdug bsngal yod do/ / 'khrig chags mang du spyod pa'i tshe/ tsher lcags kyis brabs pa lta bu'i sdug bsngal yod do/ /

Furthermore, when the mother eats irregularly or eats predominantly cold food, one suffers as if one had been thrown naked onto ice. Very hot, sour, or spicy foods will create pain in a similar way. If the mother overeats, the pain is like that of being crushed between rocks. If she does not eat enough, the child also suffers, feeling as if it has been sent spinning through space. When she moves quickly, jumps or turns around sharply, or suddenly bends her body, the child is pained as though it were falling over a precipice. At times of violent intercourse, it suffers as though being beaten by thorny sticks.

d.div: [273] bsten na/ dpal spungs/
[274] nam mkhar dpyangs/ dpal spungs/ nam mkha' la dpyad la/ mi rigs dpe skrun/

f.d: zhag bdun phrag so bdun pa la ni mngal nyid du shes pas gtsang ba'i 'du shes dang / dri mi zhim pa'i 'du shes dang / mun nag gi 'du shes dang / btson ra'i 'du shes dang / yongs su skyo nas phyir 'byung ba'i 'du shes skye bar 'gyur ro/ /
In the thirty-seventh week, the child becomes aware of being in a womb, preceiving it as a dirty, foul-smelling, pitch-black prison. Completely fed up with it, the thought of leaving occurs.

zhag bdun phrag sum cu rtsa brgyad pa la ma'i mngal nas/ me tog sdud pa zhes bya ba'i rlung 'byung ste/ rlung de mngal la gnas pa de bsgyur nas skye ba'i sgo logs su phyogs par byed do/ / de'i tshe lcags kyi 'khrul 'khor la bskyon pa lta bu'i sdug bsngal yod do/ /

In the thirty-eighth week, the “flower-gathering” energy stirs the mother’s womb, turning the fetus around toward the gateway of birth. The suffering at that time is like that of being placed upon a [rapidly rotating] iron machine.

de ltar dus de srid du mngal gyi drod zangs tsha ba dang / rab tu tsha ba lta bus ni btsos shing brngos/ rlung mi 'dra ba nyi shu rtsa brgyad kyis ni reg cing bskyod/ ma'i khrag la sogs pa'i dngas mas ni spel zhing bskyed pas/[275] mer mer po nas bzung nas lus kun rdzogs pa'i bar du 'gyur to/[276] /

Thus, as one develops during the pregnancy from a week-old embryo into a fully developed fetus, one is boiled and stirred around in the womb, as in a hot or even scalding pot; one is affected and shoved about by the twenty-eight different vital energies; and one is nurtured and developed by nutrients coming from the mother’s blood and so forth.

d.div: [275] zas la/ dpal spungs/
[276] gyur to/ dpal spungs/ mi rigs dpe skrun/

f.d:
de ltar yang mngal 'jug gi mdo las/
dang po mer mer po las ni/ / sha yi chu bur skye bar 'gyur/ / chu bur las ni ltar ltar skye/ / ltar ltar po ni mkhrang bar 'gyur/ / mkhrang ba rnam par 'gyur nas ni/ / mgo dang yan lag bzhi skyes pas/ / rus pa 'dus nas lus grub pa/ / thams cad las kyi rgyu las 'byung /[277] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Therefore it says, in Nanda’s Abiding in the Womb:
From the week-old embryo—the ovoid—a flesh bubble arises, and from this arises the oblong, the second-week embryo. This grows more solid, giving rise to the head and four limbs, and once the bones are well formed and connected, the body becomes complete. The cause of all this happening is karma.[144]

d.div: [277] sde dge_57_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ ga_mngal 'jug gi mdo/ bam po/ 3_shog_231_ba2
[144] Nandagarbhāvakrāntinirdeśa, Toh 57 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, ga, 231b2.

f.d: de nas kha thur du blta ba zhes bya ba'i rlung 'byung ste/[278] rlung des lus de mgo thur du bzlog nas lag pa brkyang ste phyir 'byung bar 'gyur ro/ / de'i tshe lcags kyi 'jur mig nas 'dren pa lta bu'i sdug bsngal yod do// kha cig mngal nyid du shi nas 'byung bar 'gyur ro/ / kha cig ma dang mnyam du 'chi bar 'gyur ro// yang de btsas nas sa la ltung ba'i dus su tsher khung du bskyur ba tsam gyi sdug bsngal yod do/ / phyis pa'i dus su pags pa bshus nas rtsig zur la brad pa tsam gyi sdug bsngal yod do/ / der yun de srid du gnas te/ na tsha che chung de 'dra/ dog mi dog de 'dra/ mun pa nag mi nag de 'dra/ gtsang mi gtsang de 'dra ste/ da lta ci tsam 'dod pa che ba zhig yin yang mi gtsang ba'i dong du khyod zhag gsum sdod/ kha bcad la bzhag zhag gsum gyi nangs par gser srang gsum sbyin gyi zer na sus kyang mi nus te/[279] mngal gyi sdug bsngal ni de las thu'o/ /

Then the “heading-downward” /86/ energy stirs, turning the head down-ward. The body leaves the womb, arms outstretched, experiencing pains that feel as though it were being drawn through an iron press. Some die in the process. Sometimes both mother and child die in childbirth. At birth itself, when the child first has contact with surfaces, it suffers as though it has been thrown onto a bed of thorns. A little later, when wiped, it feels as though its skin is being peeled off and its body rubbed against a wall. One’s entire stay [in the womb] is as uncomfortable, confined, dark, and impure as just described: even if a really tough person were offered three measures of gold in return for putting up with being in that kind of an impure, filthy hole for just three days, could such a person manage it? The suffering of being in the womb is even worse than that.

d.div: [278] lta ba/ dpal spungs/
[279] nang par/ dpal spungs/

f.d:
de ltar yang slob spring las/
shin tu mi bzad dri nga mi gtsang gcer bas 'gags/ / rab tu dog pa mun nag 'thibs por 'dug pa yi// mngal gnas dmyal ba lta bu'i nang du de zhugs nas/ / lus yongs bskum la sdug bsngal chen por gnas dgos so/[280] / zhes gsungs so/ / de la yid ches na lan gcig mngal du 'jug pa yang sus nus snyam du bsam mo//

As it says in Letter to a Student:
Stifled by unbearable smells and impurities, totally confined in utter darkness, staying in a womb is like being in hell because one has to put up with great suffering, while the body remains totally constricted.[145] Once convinced of this, think: “Who could possibly enter a womb even one more time?”

d.div: [280] sde dge_4183_bstan/ spring yig_nge _slob dpon tsan+d+ra go mi/ slob spring / sh+loka_19_shog_47_ba3
[145] Candragomin, Śiṣyalekha verse 19, Toh 4183 Tengyur, spring yig, nge, 47b3.

f.d: rga ba'i sdug bsngal yang dpag tu med de/ mdor na bcu tham pa'o/ / de yang gzugs yongs su 'gyur ba dang / skra yongs su 'gyur ba dang / pags pa yongs su 'gyur ba dang / kha dog yongs su 'gyur ba dang / mthu stobs yongs su 'gyur ba dang / gzi brjid yongs su 'gyur ba dang / bsod nams yongs su 'gyur ba dang / nad med pa yongs su 'gyur ba dang / sems yongs su 'gyur ba dang / gnas skabs 'das shing tshe'i mjug brtul ba'o/[281]/

Although the sufferings of aging are also immeasurable, they can be summarized as tenfold: radical change in physique, hair, skin, complexion, abilities, prestige, quality of life, health, mental ability, and the life force itself.

d.div: [281] ma dper/ 'jug_ces byung yang / mjug_ces dpal spungs dang mi rigs dpe skrun khang bzhin bcos/

f.d: de la gzugs yongs su 'gyur ba ni/ sngar gyi gzugs drang zhing brtan la mkhrang ba de 'gyur nas/ dgur po kyog po 'khar bas brten dgos par 'gro ba'o/[282] /
1. There will be marked physical change as the body, previously strong and robust and holding itself erect, becomes bent, twisted, and needing to support itself with a stick.

d.div: [282] sgur po/ dpal spungs/

f.d: skra yongs su 'gyur ba ni/ sngar gyi skra nag sing ba bung ba'i mdog lta bu de 'gyur nas/ skra dkar ba dang / spyi theg la sogs par 'gro ba'o/[283] /
2. There will be marked change in hair. Formerly jet black, it becomes white or is lost.

d.div: [283] spyi ther/ mi rigs dpe skrun/

f.d: pags pa yongs su 'gyur ba ni/ sngar gyi pags pa srab pa 'jam pa/[284] yul wA rA Na sI'i phra ras sam/ rgya'i nang dar lta bu de 'gyur nas/ mthug la gob pa/[285] 'jur mthug dang / gnyer ma'i phung po/ zangs gdub sna ma bzhin du 'gyur ba'o/ /
3. There will be marked change in the skin. Once as fine and smooth /87/ as Benares fine cloth or Chinese silk, it becomes coarse, lined, and heavily wrinkled, looking like braided copper bangles.

d.div: [284] srab la 'jam pa/ mi rigs dpe skrun/
[285] 'thug la kob pa/ dpal spungs/ mthug po gab pa/ mi rigs dpe skrun/

f.d: kha dog yongs su 'gyur ba ni/ sngar gyi kha dog bkrag mdangs dang ldan pa/ me tog pad+ma kha bye ma thag pa lta bu de 'gyur nas/ sngo khog skya khog po me tog rnying pa bzhin du 'gro ba'o/ /
4. There will be marked changes of complexion. Once filled with brightness and luster, like a freshly opened lotus, it now fades, becoming bluish or grayish, like an old, withered flower.

mthu stobs yongs su 'gyur ba ni/ sngar gyi nus pa dang spro sems 'gyur nas 'gro ba ste/ lus kyi shed chad pas dka' las gang yang mi nus/ sems kyi stobs nyams pas bya ba gang la yang spro ba chung / dbang po rnams kyi nus pa zad pas yul mi 'dzin pa'am/ gzhan du 'dzin par 'gro ba'o/ /

5. There will be marked changes in ability and power. The enthusiasm and ability that were previously enjoyed will change, as declining physical strength prevents the harder tasks from being undertaken and as mental decline takes away any enthusiasm for doing things. The sense faculties become blunt and lose their abilities, perceiving their objects in an unclear and confused way.

gzi brjid yongs su 'gyur ba ni/ sngar gzhan gyis bstod cing bkur ba de 'gyur nas/[286] rang bas ngan pas kyang brnyas chos byed/ don med kyi mi'i snying du yang mi sdug /byis pas bsdig mor che/ bu tsha'i rkang 'dren du che bar 'gro'o/ /

6. There will be marked changes in prestige. Although formerly praised and respected by others, the elderly wane in other people’s esteem and become the object of inferiors’ scorn. Even strangers find them unappealing, and they become the object of children’s tricks and become a source of shame for their children and grandchildren.

d.div: [286] khur/ dpal spungs/

f.d: bsod nams yongs su 'gyur ba ni/ sngar gyi longs spyod dang za thang thams cad bri nas/ lus kyis dron po mi myong / khas zhim po mi myong / khyad par du gang med pa de za snying 'dod de/ tshol mkhan dang / ster mkhan yang shin tu dka'o/ /

7. There will be a marked change in quality of life. The pleasure given by possessions, food, and drink deteriorates. The body cannot feel properly warm, nor can the mouth find good taste in anything. There is a fancy for what is not available and difficulty getting others to get supplies or make food.
nad med pa yongs su 'gyur ba ni/ nad che shos rgas nad kyis thebs pas/ nad gzhan thams cad kyang des drangs nas sdug bsngal ba'o/ /
8. There will be marked change in health. Once stricken by old age, the greatest of ailments, there is suffering, for age brings on all the other diseases.
sems yongs su 'gyur ba ni/ smras pa dang / byas pa kun de ma thag tu brjed cing / bcos pa dang 'khrul par 'gyur ba'o/ /
9. There will be a marked change in mental ability. Becoming senile and confused, the elderly forget almost immediately what has just been said or done.
gnas skabs 'das shing tshe'i mjug brtul ba ni/ dbugs kyang brdzangs shing sgra ngar ngar po 'byung /[287] 'du byed thams cad rnying pas 'chi ba la nye ba'o/ /
10. When time is up, life’s end is reached. Short of breath and starting to wheeze since all the component elements of the body have worn out, death is now at hand.

d.div: [287] brdzongs/ dpal spungs/

f.d:
de ltar yang 'phags pa rgya che rol pa las/
rgas pas gzugs sdug gzugs ni mi sdug byed/ / rgas pas gzi brjid 'phrog cing mthu stobs nyams/ / rgas pas bde ba 'phrog cing sdug bsngal skyed/ / rgas pas 'chi byed rgas pas mdangs kyang 'phrog[288] / ces gsungs so//

The Vast Manifestation Sutra says of all this:
Old age turns a pleasant physique into an unpleasant one. Old age steals prestige and damages abilities and strength. Old age steals happiness and increases suffering. Old age is the maker of death and the robber of beauty.[146]

d.div: [288] sde dge_95_bka'/ mdo sde_kha_rgya cher rol pa'i mdo/ le'u/ 13_sh+loka_85_shog_88_ba4
[146] Lalitavistarasūtra, Toh 95 Kangyur, mdo sde, kha, 88b4.

f.d: na ba'i sdug bsngal yang dpag tu med de/ mdor na bdun yod do/ / de yang zug drag pos btab pa'i sdug bsngal dang /[289] dpyad rtsub mo byed pa'i sdug bsngal dang / sman tsha ba brten pa'i sdug bsngal dang / bza' btung snying la 'dod pa 'gog pa'i sdug bsngal dang / sman pa'i ngo bsrung ba'i sdug bsngal dang / yo byad zad pa'i sdug bsngal dang / shi dogs pa'i sdug bsngal rnams yod do/ /

Although the sufferings of sickness are also immeasurable, they can be summed up as sevenfold: (1) being struck down by a powerful disease, (2) undergoing painful physical examinations, (3) having to take strong medicine, (4) being prevented from eating and drinking what is enjoyable, /88/ (5) having to follow the doctor’s orders, (6) the diminution of wealth, and (7) fear of death.

d.div: [289] bzhag pa'i/ dpal spungs/

f.d:
de ltar yang 'phags pa rgya che rol pa las/
nad brgya mang dang nad thibs sdug bsngal gyis// 'gro ba gtsos te mi yi yi dwags bzhin/[290] / zhes gsungs so/ /

The Vast Manifestation Sutra says of this:
Tormented by being prey to—and actually falling victim to— the sufferings of hundreds of maladies, they are like human ghosts.[147]

d.div: [290] sde dge_95_bka'/ mdo sde_kha_rgya cher rol pa'i mdo/ le'u/ 13_sh+loka_86_shog_88_ba_5

f.d:
'chi ba'i sdug bsngal yang dpag tu med de/ rgyal po la gdams pa'i mdo las/
rgyal po chen po/ de bzhin du 'chi bdag gis gsal shing gis zug ste/ rgyags pa dang ni bral/ skyabs ni med/ mgon ni med/ dpung gnyen ni med/ nad kyis ni gdungs/ kha ni skom/ bzhin ni 'gyur/ rkang lag ni g.yob/ las ni mi nus/ kha chu dang / snabs dang / gcin dang / ngan skyugs kyis ni lus la gos/ sgra ngar ngar po ni 'don/ sman pas ni bor/ mal gyi tha ma na ni nyal/ 'khor ba'i rgyun du ni nub/ gshin rje'i mis ni 'jigs skrag / dbugs rgyu ba ni chad/ kha dang sna ni gdangs/ 'jig rten 'di ni 'dor/ 'jig rten pha rol du ni 'gro / skyas chen po ni 'degs/ mun pa chen por ni zhugs/ g.yang sa chen por ni lhung / rgya mtsho chen pos ni 'khyer/ las kyi rlung gis ni bdas/ sa tshugs med pa'i phyogs su ni 'gro / nor bgo bsha' byar ni med/ kyi hud ma/ kyi hud pha/ kyi hud bu zhes ni zer te de'i tshe rgyal po chen po chos ma gtogs pa skyabs dang / mgon dang / dpung gnyen ni gzhan med do/[291] / zhes gsungs so/ /

The sufferings of death are also countless. It says of them, in the Advice to a King Sutra:
Great King! Someone tormented like this, on the torture spike of death, is no longer so arrogant. Protectors, allies, or friends help you no more. Stricken by disease, the mouth is thirsty, the face changes, the limbs give way, you are unable to work, and you soil your body with saliva, snot, urine, and disgusting vomit, and you also wheeze noisily. The doctors abandon hope, and you sleep on your bed for the last time, sinking into the stream of samsara and becoming frightened of the lord of death’s emissaries. The breathing stops, the mouth and nostrils gape. You leave this world behind and head for the next. It is the great departure, the entrance into deepest darkness, the fall over the greatest precipice, and the mighty ocean sweeping you away. Borne away by the winds of karma, you go to the place of no settling, and this without being able to take one iota of your possessions. Though you cry out “O Mother! O Father! Oh, my children!” there is, at that time, Great King, no other protector, no other refuge, no other ally, than Dharma.[148]

d.div: [291] sde dge_221_bka'/ mdo sde_dza_rgyal po la gdams pa'i mdo/ shog_80_ba5
[148] Rājāvavādakasūtra, Toh 221 Kangyur, mdo sde, dza, 10b5.

f.d: sdug pa dang bral ba'i sdug bsngal ni/ pha ma bu tsha la sogs pa yid la bcags pa shi ba'i tshe/[292] mya ngan dang / gdung ba dang / smre sngags dang / ngu 'bod la sogs pa'i sdug bsngal dpag tu med pa yod do/ /

Then there is the suffering of being separated from loved ones. When father, mother, children, or friends die, there is immeasurable suffering, in the form of misery, grief, weeping, wailing, and the like.

d.div: [292] gcags/ dpal spungs/

f.d: mi sdug pa dang 'phrad pa'i sdug bsngal ni/ dgra sdang bas nyen pa'i tshe/ 'thab rtsod kyi sdug bsngal yod de/[293] 'thab rtsod dang / rdeg 'tshog la sogs pa'i sdug bsngal mang po yod do/ /
The suffering of encountering the unwanted is the distress of conflict that occurs when meeting hated enemies. There are many sufferings, such as arguments, physical conflict, and so forth.

d.div: [293] 'thab rtsod kyi sdug bsngal yod de zhes pa'i tshig 'di cha tshang dpal spungs dpar mar mi byung / yod do/ /mi rigs dpe skrun/

f.d: sdug bsngal phyi ma gnyis ni go sla'o//
The last two types of suffering—the strife of obtaining and the difficulty of maintaining—are self-evident.

lha min la lha'i sdug bsngal dang cha mtshungs pa'i steng du nga rgyal dang / phrag dog dang / 'thab rtsod kyi sdug bsngal yod do/ / de ltar yang /
lha min dag ni rang bzhin gyi lha yi/ / dpal la sdang phyir yid kyi sdug bsngal che/[294] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Demigods. Besides having suffering akin to that of the gods, the demigods also suffer from pride, jealousy, fighting, and quarrelling. It says:
Demigods endure great mental torment because they are, by their very nature, resentful of the gods’ splendors and enjoyments.[149]

d.div: [294] sde dge_4182_bstan/ spring yig_nge _mgon po klu sgrub/ bshes spring / sh+loka_101_shog_45_ba1
[149] In Nāgārjuna’s Letter to a Friend (Suhṛllekha) verse 102ab, Toh 4182 Tengyur, spring yig, 45b1.

f.d:
'dod khams kyi lha la yang lha min dang 'thab pa'i sdug bsngal dang / 'dod pas ma ngoms pa'i sdug bsngal dang / dpa' bkong ba'i sdug bsngal dang / bcad pa dang / dral ba dang / gsod pa dang / spyugs pa dang /[295] 'chi 'pho ba dang / ltung ba'i sdug bsngal myong bar 'gyur te/ ji skad du/
lha'i bu 'chi ba na ltas rnam pa lnga 'byung bar 'gyur te/ gos dri ma can du 'gyur/ me tog gi phreng ba rnying par 'gyur/ mchan khung gnyis nas rngul 'byung bar 'gyur/ lus la dri nga ba 'byung bar 'gyur/ rang gi stan la mi dga' bar 'gyur/[296] zhes gsungs so/ /

Gods. Gods of the desire realm suffer through having to fight off the demi-gods, through dissatisfaction due to their endless desires, /89/ and through losing their self-confidence. They also suffer by their limbs being severed and parts of their bodies being amputated, by being killed or expelled, and at the end of their lives, they suffer through death, losing their divine status and going to another existence. It is said:
When death comes, divine child, five signs will appear: Your clothes start to smell bad, flower garlands wither, your two arm-pits begin to sweat, foul smells arise from your body, and you begin to find seats uncomfortable.[150]

d.div: [295] spyug_dpal spungs/
[296] sde dge_119_bka'/ mdo sde/ nya_mdo chen po myang 'das/ le'u/ 7_bam po/ 26_shog_307_na3
[150] In the longer Great Passing into Nirvana Sutra (Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra), Toh 119 Kangyur, mdo sde, nya, 302a3.

f.d: gzugs khams dang / gzugs med kyi khams na ni sdug bsngal de dag med de/ 'on kyang 'chi 'pho ba dang / gnas la rang dbang med pa'i phyir/ gnas ngan len gyi sdug bsngal yod do/ / de lta bu'i bde 'gro dang mtho ris de dag kyang las zad pa dang ngan song du lhung ba yin no// des na 'khor ba'i gnas 'di ni sdug bsngal chen po'i rang bzhin me 'bar ba'i khang pa lta bu yin te/

Gods of the form and formless dimensions do not have the above-mentioned sufferings. However, since they die, transmigrate, and do not have the power to remain in their state, they suffer through having to take birth in a lower state. Likewise, once the good karma of humans or gods of any level is exhausted, they have to fall into states of suffering. Therefore the whole condition of samsara, the very nature of which is suffering, is like that of a house ablaze.

mngal 'jug gi mdo las kyang /
kye ma kye hud/ srid pa 'khor ba'i rgya mtsho 'di ni 'bar ba/ rab tu 'bar ba/ mchog tu 'bar ba/ shin tu mchog tu 'bar ba yin pas/ sems can 'ga' tsam yang des ma bcom pa med do/ / rab tu 'bar bar byed pa'i me gang zhe na/ 'di lta ste/ 'dod chags dang / zhe sdang dang / gti mug gi me dang / skye ba dang / rga ba dang / 'chi ba'i me dang / mya ngan dang / smre sngags 'don pa dang / yid mi bde ba dang / 'khrug pa'i me dag gis rtag tu bsreg cing 'bar bar byed pas/ 'ga' tsam yang de las thar pa med do/[297] / zhes gsungs so// /

To quote Nanda’s Abiding in the Womb:
Woe and alas! Because this immensity of self-perpetuating existence is ablaze, completely flaming, really burning, totally blazing, not even a few remain undefeated by it. What is this raging inferno? It is the fire of aggression, passion, and stupidity; the fire of birth, aging, and death; the fire of sorrow, lamentation, mental unhappiness, and unrest. Because these fires are constantly raging and blazing, no one escapes them.[151]

d.div: [297] sde dge_57_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ ga_dga' bo mngal na gnas pa bstan pa'i mdo/ shog_228_na5
[151] Nandagarbhāvakrāntinirdeśa, Toh 57 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, ga, 228a5.

f.d:
de ltar 'khor ba'i nyes dmigs de dag shes pas/ srid pa'i bde ba las blo ldog pa yin no/ / de ltar yang / yab sras mjal ba'i mdo las/
'khor ba'i nyes dmigs ma_thong ba na/ / skyo ba'i sems ni rab tu skye/ / khams gsum btson rar 'jigs pas na/ / brtson pa'i sems kyis spong bar byed/[298]/ ces gsungs so/ /

Knowing the sufferings of samsara to be just like that will, in itself, turn the mind away from the pleasures of worldly existence. To quote the scriptures, the Meeting of Father and Son Sutra states:
Recognizing the sufferings of samsara, true weariness with it will arise, and fear of its three realms will stimulate a diligent abandoning of it.[152]

d.div: [298] sde dge_61_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ nga _gang pos zhus pa'i mdo/ le'u/ 1_shog_171_na5_ma dper lung 'di yab sras mjal ba'i mdo las zhes drangs kyang mdo der ma bzhugs mod/ dkon brtsegs su mdo de'i mjug de ma thag tu bzhugs pa'i gang pos zhus pa'i mdo byung ba de'i nang du buzhugs/

[152] Although the text attributes this quotation to the Meeting of Father and Son Sutra (Pitāputrasamāgamasūtra), it is actually found in the Questions of Pūrṇa Sutra (Pūrṇaparipṛcchāsūtra), Toh 61 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, nga, 171a5.

f.d:
slob dpon klu sgrub kyis kyang don de ltar gsungs te/ ji skad du/
'khor ba de 'dra lags pas lha mi dang / / dmyal ba yi dwags dud 'gro rnams dag tu/ / skye ba bzang po ma lags skye ba ni/ / gnod pa du ma'i snod gyur lags mkhyen mdzod/[299] / ces gsungs so/ /

The great teacher Nāgārjuna has also said, in a similar vein:
Since samsara is like that, there is no good birth as a god, a human, a hell being, a hungry spirit, or as an animal. So know rebirth to be a vessel for many harms.[153]

d.div: [299] sde dge_4182_bstan/ spring yig_nge _mgon po klu sgrub/ bshes spring / sh+loka_102_shog_45_ba1
[153] Nāgārjuna, Letter to a Friend (Suhṛllekha) verse 103, Toh 4182 Tengyur, spring yig, nge, 45b1.

f.d: dam chos yid bzhin gyi nor bu thar pa rin po che'i rgyan las/ 'khor ba'i sdug bsngal bstan pa'i le'u ste lnga pa'o// //
This was the fifth chapter, explaining the sufferings of samsara, from this Ornament of Precious Liberation, a Wish-Fulfilling Gem of Sublime Dharma. /90/
le'u drug pa/ las rgyu 'bras/
6. Karma and Its Effects

de ltar bshad pa'i sdug bsngal de dag rgyu ci las byung snyam na/[300] zag bcas kyi las las byung bar shes par bya'o/ / de ltar yang mdo sde las brgya pa las/
las rnams kyang ni sna tshogs las/ / de yis 'gro 'di sna tshogs byas/[301] / zhes gsungs so/ /

d.div: [300] de dag thams cad/ dpal spungs/
[301] sde dge_340_bka'/ mdo sde/ ha_las brgya tham pa/ bam po/ 90_shog_106_na7_'di'i thad la dgongs pa yin nam/
[154] Karmaśataka, Toh 340 Kangyur, mdo sde, ha, 106a7.

f.d:
snying rje pad+ma dkar po las/
'jig rten ni las kyis byas pa/ las kyis sprul pa'o/ / sems can rnams ni las kyis byas pa/ las kyi rgyu las byung ba/ las kyis rab tu phye ba'o/[302] / zhes gsungs so/ /

The White Lotus of Compassion Sutra says:
The worlds have been made by actions. Their manifestation is due to actions. Sentient beings have been created by actions and have sprung from actions. Through action arises all their different types.[155]

d.div: [302] sde dge_111_bka'/ mdo sde/ cha_snying rje chen po'i pad+ma dkar po/ le'u/ 1_shog_62_ba3
[155] Mahākaruṇāpuṇḍarīkasūtra, Toh 111 Kangyur, mdo sde, cha, 62b3.

f.d:
chos mngon pa mdzod las kyang /
'jig rten sna tshogs las las skyes/[303] / zhes gsungs so/ /

The Treasury of Higher Knowledge says:
The various worlds were generated by actions.[156]

d.div: [303] sde dge_4089_bstan/ mngon pa/ ku_dbyig gnyen/ chos mngon pa mdzod/ gnas/ 4_sh+loka_1_shog_10_ba7
[156] Vasubandhu, Abhidharmakośa 4:1a, Toh 4089 Tengyur, mngon pa, ku, 10b7.

f.d:
las de yang ci zhig yin zhe na/ sems pa'i las dang / bsam pa'i las gnyis yin no/ / de ltar yang chos mngon pa kun las btus pa las/
las gang zhe na/ sems pa'i las dang / bsam pa'i las te/[304] zhes gsungs so/ /

If you wonder what exactly karma is, know that it falls into two areas: mental activity and activity propelled by thought. The Compendium of Higher Knowledge says of this:
What is karma? It is mental activity [itself] and mentally motivated action.[157]

d.div: [304] sde dge_4049_bstan/ sems tsam/ ri_'phags pa thogs med/ mngon pa kun btus/ le'u/ 2_shog_85_na5
[157] Asaṅga, Abhidharmasamuccaya, Toh 4049 Tengyur, sems tsam, ri, 85a8.

f.d:
mngon pa mdzod las kyang /
las ni sems pa dang des byas/[305] / zhes gsungs so/ /

The Treasury of Higher Knowledge says:
Karma is intention and what is done because of that.[158]

d.div: [305] sde dge_4089_bstan/ mngon pa/ ku_chos mngon pa mdzod/ gnas/ 4_sh+loka_1_shog_10_ba7
[158] Vasubandhu, Abhidharmakośa 4:1b, Toh 4089 Tengyur, mngon pa, ku, 10b7.

f.d:
rtsa she las kyang /
drang srong mchog gis las rnams ni/ / sems pa dang ni bsam par gsungs/[306] / zhes gsungs so//

Furthermore, in the Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way, it says:
The Supreme Sage has taught that karma means mental activity and that which is done because of thought.[159]

d.div: [306] sde dge_3824_bstan/ dbu ma/ tsa_mgon po klu sgrub/ dbu ma rtsa ba shes rab/ rab byed/ 17_sh+loka_2_shog_9_ba2
[159] Nāgārjuna, Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 17:2, Toh 3824 Tengyur, dbu ma, tsa, 9b2.

f.d:
de gnyis rang ji lta bu yin zhe na/ sems pa'i las ni yid kyi las yin no/ / sems pas bskyed pa gang yin pa de ni bsam pa'i las yin te/ lus dang ngag gi las su rig par bya'o/ / de ltar yang mngon pa mdzod las/
sems pa yid kyi las yin te/ / des bskyed lus dang ngag gi las/[307]/ zhes gsungs so/ /

d.div: [307] sde dge_4089_bstan/ mngon pa/ ku_dbyig gnyen/ chos mngon pa mdzod/ gnas/ 4_sh+loka_1_shog_10_ba7
[160] Vasubandu, Abhidharmakośa 4:1cd, Toh 4089 Tengyur, mngon pa, ku, 10b7.

f.d:
de lta bu'i las dang / des bskyed pa'i 'bras bu 'chad pa la/ sdom ni/
dbye ba dang ni mtshan nyid dang / / bdag gir bya dang bgo skal spyod/ / chung las cher smin chud mi za/ / drug po des ni las 'bras bsdus/ / zhes pa'o//

The following synopsis outlines actions and the results they generate:
Actions and their consequences are summed up through six points: their categories, characteristics, ownership, apportionment, inflation, and ineluctability.
de la dang po las 'bras kyi dbye ba ni gsum du shes par bya ste/ bsod nams ma yin pa'i las rgyu 'bras dang / bsod nams kyi las rgyu 'bras dang / mi g.yo ba'i las rgyu 'bras so//
First are its categories: (1) nonvirtuous actions and their effects,[161] (2) virtuous actions and their effects, (3) the action of unwavering karma and its effect.

d.div: [161] The traditional way of describing karma—as “action, cause and effect”—shows an assumption that the consequences of an action are actually part and parcel of that action rather than something else that happens later due to the action.

f.d: gnyis pa dbye ba so so'i mtshan nyid 'chad pa la/ dang po bsod nams ma yin pa'i las rgyu 'bras ni/ spyir mang na yang las kyi lam gyis bsdus pa mi dge ba bcu ste/ lus kyi sgo nas srog gcod pa la sogs pa gsum/ ngag gi sgo nas rdzun la sogs pa bzhi dang /[308] yid kyi sgo nas brnab sems la sogs pa gsum mo/ / de ltar re re la yang don gsum gsum ste/ dbye ba dang / 'bras bu dang / khyad par ro//

The second point concerns the characteristics of these three. Nonvirtuous actions and their effects. Although generally speaking there are very many sorts of nonvirtuous actions, they can be summarized as the ten nonvirtues. Three are physical: killing and so forth. Four are verbal: lying and so forth. Three are mental: greed and so forth. /91/ Each of these is itself treated through three points: its categories, its results, and some particular instances.

d.div: [308] dpal spungs dpar mar skabs du mar rdzun la brdzun zhes ba sngon 'jug yod pa sha stag byung /

f.d: de la dang po srog gcod pa la dbye na gsum ste/ 'dod chags kyi sgo nas srog gcod pa dang / zhe sdang gi sgo nas srog gcod pa dang / gti mug gi sgo nas srog gcod pa'o/ / de la dang po ni/ sha dang / pags pa la sogs pa'i phyir ram/ rtsed mo'i phyir ram/ nor gyi phyir ram/ bdag gam/ mdza' bo yongs su bskyang ba'i phyir srog gcod pa'o/ / gnyis pa ni/ 'khon zhugs pa dang / 'gran zlar gyur pa lta bu la zhe sdang skyes nas srog gcod pa'o/ / gsum pa ni/ mchod sbyin la sogs pa'o//

Killing has three categories: killing through desire and attachment, killing through anger and aversion, and killing through confused ignorance. The first of these is to kill for the sake of meat, hides, and so forth; for sport or financial gain; or to safeguard yourself or loved ones. The second is to murder those you feel aversion for, on account of grudges or competition and the like. The third is done in order to make offerings.

de'i 'bras bu la yang gsum ste/ rnam par smin pa'i 'bras bu dang / rgyu mthun pa'i 'bras bu dang / dbang gi 'bras bu'o/ / de la rnam par smin pa'i 'bras bu ni/ sems can dmyal bar skye bar 'gyur ro/ / rgyu mthun pa'i 'bras bu ni/ gal te mir skyes na yang tshe thung zhing nad mang bar 'gyur ro/ / dbang gi 'bras bu ni/ yul bkra mi shis shing gzi brjid chung ba'i sar skye bar 'gyur ro/ / khyad par ni/ srog gcod pa'i nang nas pha yang yin la/ dgra bcom pa yang yin pa de'i srog gcod pa sdig che ba'o//

The results of killing are also threefold: the ripened result, the result corresponding to the cause, and the dominant result. The ripened result is rebirth as a hell being. The result corresponding to the cause is that even if you are reborn human, you will have a short life and many sicknesses. The dominant result is to be reborn in an ill-fated and unattractive land. The particular instance—the most heinous among all forms of killing—is to kill an arhat who is also your father.

ma byin par len pa la dbye na gsum ste/ mthus ma byin par len pa dang / 'jab bus ma byin par len pa dang / g.yo sgyus ma byin par len pa'o/ / de la dang po ni/ bsnyad med par btsan 'phrog byed pa'o/ / gnyis pa ni/ khang pa 'bigs pa la sogs pas ma tshor bar brku ba'o/ / gsum pa ni/ bre srang la sogs pa la zol zog byed pa'o/ /

Stealing has three categories: stealing by force, stealing by stealth, and stealing through cheating or fraudulence. The first of these is to steal with needless violence; the second is to steal unnoticed, by burglary and the like; and the third is to cheat through corrupt weights and measures.

de'i 'bras bu la gsum las/ rnam par smin pa'i 'bras bu ni/ yi dwags su skye bar 'gyur ro/ / rgyu mthun pa'i 'bras bu ni/ gal te mir skyes na yang longs spyod kyis phongs par 'gyur ro/ / dbang gi 'bras bu ni/ yul sad ser mang ba'i sar skye bar 'gyur ro/ / khyad par ni/ ma byin par len pa'i nang nas bla ma dang / dkon mchog gi nor la ma byin par len pa sdig pa che ba'o//

Of the three types of result, the ripened result is rebirth as a hungry spirit. The result corresponding to the cause is that even if reborn human, you experience poverty. The dominant result is to be reborn in a place where there is much frost and hail. The worst case of stealing, the most pernicious act, is to take wealth belonging to your guru or to the three precious refuges.

'dod pas log par g.yem pa la dbye na gsum ste/ rigs kyis bsrung ba dang / bdag pos bsrung ba dang / chos kyis bsrung ba'o/ / de la dang po ni/ ma dang sring mo la sogs pa la log par spyad pa'o/ / gnyis pa ni/ khyo'am rgyal po la sogs pas bdag tu byas pa'i bud med la log par spyad pa'o/ / gsum pa la lnga ste/ rang gi chung ma yin yang / yan lag ma yin pa dang / yul ma yin pa dang / dus ma yin pa dang / tshod ma yin pa dang / rigs pa ma yin par spyad pa'o/ / de la dang po yan lag ma yin pa ni/ kha dang bshang lam du spyad pa'o/ / yul ma yin pa ni/ bla ma'i nye 'khor ram/ gtsug lag khang ngam/ mchod rten gyi drung ngam/ mang po 'dus pa'i sar spyad pa'o/ / dus ma yin pa ni/ gso sbyong la gnas pa'i dus sam/ sbrum ma'am/ nu zho 'thung ba'am/ snang ba yod pa'i dus su spyad pa'o/ / tshod ma yin pa ni/ grangs ma lnga las lhag par spyod pa'o/[309] / rigs pa ma yin pa ni/ brdeg cing spyod pa'o/ / yang na pho'am/ ma ning gi kha'am bshang lam du spyad pa'o/ /

Sexual misconduct has three categories: sex proscribed by family ties, /92/ sex proscribed by belonging to someone else, and sex proscribed due to religious factors. The first of these is intercourse with parents, siblings, and so forth [blood relations]. The second is intercourse with someone committed to another person or belonging to a monarch. The third includes five areas of improper intercourse because of organs involved, place, time, degree, or manner. Inappropriate organs refers to oral or anal intercourse. An inappropriate place is in the proximity of a guru, temple, stupa, or large gathering. Inappropriate times are those when lay precepts are being observed, during pregnancy, while the mother is breastfeeding, or during daylight hours. An inappropriate degree is five or more times consecutively. Inappropriate forms of intercourse are the likes of rape and anal or oral intercourse with a person of the same sex or with a hermaphrodite.

d.div: [309] grangs ma lnga'am/ dpal spungs/

f.d: de'i 'bras bu ni gsum las/ rnam par smin pa'i 'bras bu ni/ yi dwags su skye bar 'gyur ro/ / rgyu mthun pa'i 'bras bu ni gal te mir skyes na yang dgra sdang ba can gyi chung mar 'gyur ro/ / dbang gi 'bras bu ni/ yul sa rdul shas che sar skye bar 'gyur ro/[310] / khyad par ni/ 'dod log gi nang nas ma yang yin la/ dgra bcom ma yang yin pa de la log par spyad pa sdig che'o/ /

Of the three types of result, the ripened result is rebirth as a hungry spirit. The corresponding result is that even if reborn human, your partner will be like a hateful enemy. The dominant result is to be reborn in a very dusty land. The worst case is the pernicious act of having intercourse with your own mother who also happens to be an arhat.

d.div: [310] che bar/ dpal spungs/ mi rigs dpe skrun/

f.d: rdzun du smra ba la dbye na gsum ste/ pham pa'i rdzun dang / rdzun chen po dang / rdzun phra mo'o// de la dang po ni/ mi chos bla ma'i rdzun smra ba'o/ / gnyis pa ni/ bdag dang gzhan la phan gnod yod pa'i rdzun smra ba'o/ / gsum pa ni/ phan gnod med pa'i rdzun smra ba'o/ /

Lying is of three types: lies that are your undoing, big lies, and trivial lies. The first of these are those of false gurus and involve pretense about spiritual accomplishment. The second are lies told with the intention of self-benefit or harm to others. The third are lies that are neither beneficial nor harmful.

de'i 'bras bu la gsum las/ rnam par smin pa'i 'bras bu ni/ dud 'gror skye bar 'gyur ro/ / rgyu mthun gyi 'bras bu ni/ gal te mir skyes na yang skur ba 'debs pa mang bar 'gyur ro/ / dbang gi 'bras bu ni/ kha dri mi zhim par skye bar 'gyur ro/ / khyad par ni/ rdzun gyi nang nas de bzhin gshegs pa la skur pa btab/ bla ma la yang rdzun tshig smras na nyes pa rnams kyi nang nas de che'o/ /

Of the three types of result, the ripened result is rebirth as an animal. The corresponding result is that, even if reborn human, you are denigrated by others. The dominant result is to have bad breath. The worst case is the pernicious act of lying to your guru when you have slandered the Tathāgata.

phra ma la dbye na gsum ste/ btsan phra dang / gzhogs phra dang / lkog phra'o/ / de la dang po ni/ mdza' bo gnyis ngo rang du bral ba'o/ / gnyis pa ni/ gzhogs slong byas nas mdza' bo dang phral ba'o/[311] / gsum pa ni/ lkog tu dbyen byas te phral ba'o/ /

Divisive speech is of three types: vehement, insinuated, or via third parties. The first separates friends by direct slander; the second separates them through insinuations made in their presence; /93/ and the third does so through rumors.

d.div: [311] ma dper gzhogs smod zhes byung yang dpar ma gzhan ltar gzhogs slong zhes bcos/

f.d: de'i 'bras bu la gsum las/ rnam par smin pa'i 'bras bu ni/ dmyal bar skye bar 'gyur ro/ / rgyu mthun gyi 'bras bu ni/ gal te mir skyes na yang mdza' bo dang 'bral bar 'gyur ro/ / dbang gi 'bras bu ni/ yul mtho dma' can gyi sar skye bar 'gyur ro/ / khyad par ni/ phra ma'i nang nas 'phags pa'i dge 'dun la mi snyan pa brjod pa sdig che'o//

Of the three types of result, the ripened result is rebirth in hell. The corresponding result is that, even if reborn human, you will be separated from friends. The dominant result is birth in a place where the landscape is erratic and dangerous. The worst instance among such divisive speech acts is the pernicious act of causing a schism in the Sangha.

tshig rtsub la dbye na gsum ste/ ngor rtsub pa dang / gzhogs te rtsub pa dang / brgyud de rtsub pa'o/ / de la dang po ni/ pha rol po la dngos su ngan mtshang sna tshogs smra ba'o/ / gnyis pa ni/ ya ma brla'am/ kyal ka dang bsres nas pha rol po la tshig ngan sna tshogs smra ba'o/ / gsum pa ni/ kho'i mdza' bo la sogs pa'i drung du ngan mtshang sna tshogs smra ba'o/ /

Wounding speech is of three types: direct, insinuated, or via third parties. The first is to tell someone openly of their faults and weaknesses. The second means to say hurtful things, in a half-disguised manner mingled with jest, relevant to someone present. The third is to gossip about someone’s faults or weaknesses to their friends and third parties.

de'i 'bras bu la gsum las/ rnam par smin pa'i 'bras bu ni/ dmyal bar skye bar 'gyur ro/ / rgyu mthun gyi 'bras bu ni/ gal te mir skyes na yang yid du mi 'ong ba'i sgra sna tshogs thos par 'gyur ro/ / dbang gi 'bras bu ni/ yul tsha sgo can dang / yul skams can dang / sdig shas can gyi sar skye bar 'gyur ro/ / khyad par ni/ tshig rtsub kyi nang nas pha ma'am/ 'phags pa rnams la gnod pa'i tshig smra ba sdig che'o/ /

Of the three types of result, the ripened result is rebirth in hell. The corresponding result is that, even if reborn a human, the sounds and words you hear will be disturbing. The dominant result is rebirth in a hot and arid place where there is much evil. The worst instance, the most pernicious act of all wounding speech, is to speak harshly to your father or mother or to a realized being.

ngag kyal pa la dbye na gsum ste/ log pa'i ngag kyal dang / 'jig rten pa'i ngag kyal dang / bden pa'i ngag kyal lo/ / de la dang po ni/ mu stegs pa'i bzlas brjod dang kha ton la sogs pa'o/ / gnyis pa ni/ bre mo'i gtam la sogs pa'o/ / gsum pa ni/ ma gus pa dang snod ma yin pa la chos bshad pa'o/ /

Useless speech is of three types: deluded useless speech, useless worldly chatter, and true but useless speech. The first concerns the formulas and recitations of deluded belief systems. The second concerns silly talk, jokes, and the like. The third concerns attempts to explain Dharma to those lacking respect or an appropriate frame of mind.

de'i 'bras bu la yang gsum las/ rnam par smin pa'i 'bras bu ni dud 'gror skye bar 'gyur ro/ / rgyu mthun gyi 'bras bu ni/ gal te mir skyes na yang bdag nyid kyi tshig mi btsun par 'gyur ro/ / dbang gi 'bras bu ni/ dus dbyar dgun log pa can du skye bar 'gyur ro/ / khyad par ni/ ngag kyal gyi nang nas chos 'dod pa rnams g.yeng par byed pa sdig che ba'o/ /

Of the three types of result, the ripened result is rebirth as an animal. The corresponding result is that, even if reborn a human, the person’s words will carry no weight. The dominant result is rebirth in a place where the seasons are completely erratic. The worst instance, the most pernicious type of useless speech, is that which distracts those who are practicing Dharma.

brnab sems la dbye na gsum ste/[312] bdag gi la brnab sems pa dang / gzhan gyi la brnab sems pa dang / gnyis ka ma yin pa la brnab sems pa'o/ / de la dang po ni/ bdag nyid kyi cho rigs dang / gzugs byad dang / yon tan dang / nor rdzas la zhen cing chags pa ste/ bdag lta bu med snyam du sems pa'o// gnyis pa ni/ pha rol po'i phun sum tshogs pa la chags pa ste/ 'di bdag gi yin na ci ma rung snyam du sems pa'o/ / gsum pa ni/ sa 'og gi nor la sogs pa bdag dang gzhan gyis dbang byar med pa la chags pa ste/ bdag dbang na ci ma rung snyam du sems pa'o/ /

Avarice is of three types: avarice concerning your own things, other people’s things, and those things that belong to neither you nor others. The first is a grasping attachment to family status, physical appearance, /94/ qualities, wealth, and possessions, thinking, “There is no one quite like me.” The second is to covet the good things others possess, thinking, “If only this were mine.” The third involves attachment to things that belong to no one, such as the precious substances buried in the earth, thinking, “If only I could own that.”

d.div: [312] dpal spungs dpar mar skabs du mar brnab sems la brnabs sems zhes sa yang 'jug byung /

f.d: de'i 'bras bu la gsum las/ rnam par smin pa'i 'bras bu ni/ yi dwags su skye bar 'gyur ro/ / rgyu mthun gyi 'bras bu ni/ gal te mir skyes na yang 'dod chags shas che bar 'gyur ro/ / dbang gi 'bras bu ni/ yul 'bru ngan pa'i sar skye bar 'gyur ro/ / khyad par ni/ brnab sems kyi nang nas yang dag par spong ba rnams kyi rnyed pa 'phrog par 'dod pa'i sems 'di sdig che'o/ /

Of the three types of result of avarice, the ripened result is to be reborn as a hungry spirit. The corresponding result is that even if reborn human, avarice will dominate the mind. The dominant result is rebirth in a place where the quality of food is poor. Of all the sorts of avarice, the most pernicious is the wish to steal the possessions of those who have truly renounced the world.

gnod sems la dbye na gsum ste/ zhe sdang gi cha las byung ba'i gnod sems dang / phrag dog gi cha las byung ba'i gnod sems dang / 'khon 'dzin gyi cha las byung ba'i gnod sems so/ / de la dang po ni/ g.yul ngo lta bur pha rol po la zhe sdang skyes nas gsod par sems pa'o/ / gnyis pa ni/ 'gran zla lta bu gong du shor gyis dogs pa'i bsam pas gsod pa la sogs par sems pa'o/ / gsum pa ni/ sngar bdag la gnod pa byas pa lta bu la mdud par gzung nas bsad pa la sogs par sems pa'o/[313] /

Malevolence is of three types: that due to hatred, jealousy, and resentment. The first is to contemplate killing another because of hatred, as happens in times of war. The second, due to competition and the like, is to think about killing or harming another through fear of being surpassed. The third, due to long-standing resentment, is to contemplate killing or hurting someone who has previously wronged one, or the like.

d.div: [313] bzung / dpal spungs/

f.d: de'i 'bras bu la gsum las/ rnam par smin pa'i 'bras bu ni/ dmyal bar skye bar 'gyur ro/ / rgyu mthun gyi 'bras bu ni/ gal te mir skyes na yang zhe sdang shas che bar 'gyur ro/ / dbang gi 'bras bu ni/ zas kha zhing rtsub pa'i sar skye bar 'gyur ro/ / khyad par ni/ gnod sems kyi nang nas mtshams med pa gshom par byed pa 'di sdig che'o/[314]/

Of the three types of result of malevolence, the ripened result is rebirth in hell. The corresponding result is that even if reborn human, hatred dominates your mind. The dominant result is rebirth in a place where the food is bitter and coarse. Of all types of malevolence, the worst instance and most pernicious act is to plan to commit one of the five acts that have an immediate consequence.[162]

d.div: [314] shom/ dpal spungs/

[162] The five actions that have immediate result at death (i.e., no intermediate state but immediate rebirth in the worst realms) are parricide, matricide, killing an arhat, creating divisions in the Sangha, and injuring a buddha.

f.d: log par lta ba la dbye na gsum ste/ las 'bras la log par lta ba dang / bden pa la log par lta ba dang / dkon mchog la log par lta ba'o/ / de la dang po ni/ las dge sdig de 'bras bu bde sdug gi rgyur mi 'dod pa'o/ / gnyis pa ni/ lam gyi bden pa nyams su blangs kyang 'gog pa'i bden pa mi thob par 'dod pa'o/ / gsum pa ni/ dkon mchog gsum mi bden par lta zhing skur ba 'debs pa'o/ /

Aberrant belief is of three types: aberrant beliefs about actions and their consequences, about the truth(s), and about the precious refuges. The first of these means not believing that virtuous and nonvirtuous actions produce their respective consequences—happiness and suffering. The second is to consider that the truth of cessation will not be obtained through practice of the truth of the path.[163] The third is to deprecate the three precious refuges, believing them to be untrue.

d.div: [163] The truths of cessation and of the path are the third and fourth of the so-called noble truths, which are more accurately rendered the four truths of the noble ones.

f.d: de'i 'bras bu la yang gsum las/ rnam par smin pa'i 'bras bu ni/ dud 'gror skye bar 'gyur ro/ / rgyu mthun gyi 'bras bu ni/ gal te mir skyes na yang gti mug shas che bar 'gyur ro// dbang gi 'bras bu ni/ 'bras bu ye med pa'i sar skye bar 'gyur ro/ / khyad par ni/ log lta'i nang nas lta bas gzings pa 'di sdig che'o/ / de la rnam smin gyi 'bras bu de dag ni spyir bstan pa'i dbang du byas pa yin no//

Of the three types of result of aberrant belief, the ripened result is rebirth as an animal. /95/ The corresponding result is that even if reborn human, stupidity and confusion dominate your mind. The dominant result is rebirth in a place without harvests. The worst instance and most pernicious act among aberrant beliefs is to become caught up in the “thorn-like” view.[164] The above was a general explanation of the ripened results of such actions.

d.div: [164] The thorn-like view is a view that denies the long-term consequences of actions (karma) on their doer and only acknowledges their immediate consequences.

f.d: bye brag tu dbye na gsum ste/ nyon mongs pa'i sgo nas rnam par gzhag pa dang / grangs kyi sgo nas rnam par gzhag pa dang / yul gyi sgo nas rnam par gzhag pa'o/ /
Three kinds of ripened results of an action can be distinguished according to the affliction present, the frequency of action, or the person acted on:

de la dang po ni/ zhe sdang gi sgo nas mi dge ba de dag spyad na dmyal bar skye bar 'gyur ro/ / 'dod chags kyi sgo nas spyad na yi dwags su skye bar 'gyur ro/ / gti mug gi sgo nas spyad na dud 'gror skye bar 'gyur ro/ / de ltar yang rin chen phreng ba las/
chags pas yi dwags 'gro bar 'gyur/ / zhe sdang gis ni dmyal bar 'phen/ / rmongs pas phal cher dud 'gror 'gyur/[315] / zhes gsungs so/ /

1. If the actions were done through anger or hatred, rebirth in hell is more likely. If they were done through passion or attachment, rebirth as a hungry spirit is more likely. If they were done through stupidity and confusion, rebirth as an animal is more likely. Thus the Precious Garland says:
Through attachment, you will become a hungry spirit, through anger, you will be cast into hell, and through confusion, you become an animal.[165]

d.div: [315] sde dge_4158_bstan/ spring yig_ge_mgon po klu sgrub/ rin chen phreng ba/ le'u/ 3_sh+loka_30_shog_115_ba3
[165] Nāgārjuna, Ratnāvalī 3:29, Toh 4158 Tengyur, spring yig, ge, 115b3.

f.d: grangs kyi sgo nas rnam par gzhag pa ni/ mi dge ba dpag tu med pa spyad pas dmyal bar skye bar 'gyur ro/ / mang po spyad pas yi dwags su skye bar 'gyur ro/ / 'ga' tsam spyad pas dud 'gror skye bar 'gyur ro/ /
2. Innumerable nonvirtuous acts lead to rebirth in hell. A great deal of nonvirtuous acts lead to rebirth as a hungry spirit. A few such harmful actions lead to rebirth as an animal.

yul gyi sgo nas rnam par gzhag pa ni/ yul khyad par can la brten nas spyad na dmyal bar skye bar 'gyur ro/ / yul 'bring po la brten nas spyad na yi dwags su skye bar 'gyur ro/ / yul tha ma la brten nas spyad na dud 'gror skye bar 'gyur ro/ / de dag gis bsod nams ma yin pa'i las rgyu 'bras bstan te/ rin chen phreng ba las/
chags dang zhe sdang gti mug dang / / des bskyed las ni mi dge ba/ / mi dge las ni sdug bsngal kun/ / de bzhin ngan 'gro thams cad do/[316] / zhes gsungs so//

3. If the nonvirtuous act is committed against a very special person, there may be rebirth in hell. If committed against someone of medium importance, there may be rebirth as a hungry spirit. If committed against a lesser person, there may be rebirth as an animal. The above was an explanation of nonmeritorious actions and their consequences. To quote the Precious Garland:
Attachment, anger, ignorance, and the actions to which they give rise are nonvirtue. Nonvirtue brings all the sufferings and hence all the lower states of existence.[166]

d.div: [316] gong mtshungs/ rin chen phreng ba/ le'u/ 1_sh+loka_20_shog_107_ba5
[166] Ibid. 1:20ab and 21ab, 107b5.

f.d: bsod nams kyi las rgyu 'bras la/ las ni/ mi dge ba bcu po de spangs pa ni dge ba bcu yin la/ gzhan yang 'jug pa'i las dang bstun na/ gzhan gyi srog 'don pa dang / sbyin pa rgya chen po gtong ba dang / tshangs par spyod pa la gnas pa dang / bden pa drang por smra ba dang / gzhan mi mdza' ba rnams bzlum pa dang /[317] zhi des dang /[318] gsong por smra ba dang / don dang ldan pa'i tshig smra ba dang / chags pa chung zhing chog shes par bya ba dang / byams pa la sogs pa bsgom pa dang / yang dag pa'i don la 'jug pa'o/ /

Virtuous actions and their effects. First, we consider the actions. The ten virtuous actions consist of renouncing the nonvirtuous ones and, furthermore, engaging in their counterparts, the things that should be done: protecting the lives of others, giving lavishly, maintaining pure sexual conduct, speaking the truth straightforwardly, dispelling discord among people and bringing them into harmony, speaking peacefully and sincerely in a way that pleases others, speaking in a way that is meaningful, reducing desires and being content with what one has, cultivating loving kindness and the like, /96/ and penetrating the highest meaning.

d.div: [317] bsdums pa dang / dpal spungs/ bsdum pa dang / mi rigs dpe skrun/
[318] zhi dul/ mi rigs dpe skrun/

f.d: de'i 'bras bu yang gsum las/ rnam par smin pa'i 'bras bu ni/ 'dod pa'i khams kyi lha dang mi'i nang du skye bar 'gyur ro/ / rgyu mthun gyi 'bras bu ni/ srog gcod pa spangs shing / gzhan gyi srog 'don pas tshe ring bar 'gyur ro/ / zhes pa la sogs pa sbyar ro/ / dbang gi 'bras bu ni/ srog gcod pa spangs pas dngos po rnams bzang zhing mthu che ba'i sar skye bar 'gyur ro/ / zhes pa la sogs pa sbyar ro/ /

These actions have threefold consequences. The ripened result is rebirth in the human or divine planes of the desire realm. The corresponding result will be, for instance, that by abandoning harm to others and by protecting life, longevity is gained, and similarly for the other virtues. The dominant result is that by giving up killing you will be reborn in a very prosperous and powerful place, and so on and so forth, according to the virtue concerned.

de dag gis bsod nams kyi las rgyu 'bras bstan te/ rin chen phreng ba las/
'dod chags zhe sdang gti mug med/ / des bskyed las ni dge ba yin/ / dge las bde 'gro thams cad dang / / skye ba kun du bde ba dag[319] / ces gsungs so/ /

The above was an explanation of beneficial actions and their consequences. The Precious Garland says:
What is generated by non-attachment, non-anger, and non-delusion is virtue. Virtue brings all fortunate rebirths and happiness in all lifetimes.[167]

d.div: [319] sde dge_4158_bstan/ spring yig_ge_mgon po klu sgrub/ rin chen phreng ba/ le'u/ 1_sh+loka_20_shog_107_ba5
[167] Ibid. 1:20cd and 21cd, 107b5.

f.d: mi g.yo ba'i las rgyu 'bras ni/ rgyu snyom 'jug gi bsam gtan bsgoms pas/[320] 'bras bu che ba'i bsam gtan thob pa ste/[321] de la snyom 'jug gi bsam gtan ni nyer bsdogs brgyad dang / bsam gtan gyi dngos gzhi brgyad dang / bsam gtan khyad par can no/ / 'bras bu skye ba'i bsam gtan ni/ gzugs khams gnas rigs bcu bdun gyi lha dang / gzugs med skye mched mu bzhi'i lha'o/ / de dag gi rgyu 'bras thad kar sbyar na/ dge ba bcu spyad pa ni spyir ro/ /

The action of unwavering karma and its effect. Cultivating the meditative attainment creates causes that give rise to rebirth in similar meditative states. These meditative attainments consist of the eight preparatory absorptions, the eight actual absorptions, and the special meditative attainment. Their consequences—birth in the absorption [realms]—consist of the seventeen types of form-realm gods and the four types of formless-realm gods. The general condition for these causes and effects to occur is the practice of the ten virtues.

d.div: [320] snyoms 'jug_dpal spungs/
[321] 'bras bu skye ba'i bsam gtan/ dpal spungs/

f.d: 'phen byed bsam gtan dang po'i nyer bsdogs mi lcogs pa med pa bar chad med pa'i lam bsgoms nas/ rdzogs byed bsam gtan dang po'i dngos gzhi rtog dpyod dang / dga' bde dang bcas pa'i ting nge 'dzin bsgoms pas tshangs ris kyi lhar skye'o/ / bsam gtan khyad par can bsgoms pas tshangs pa chen por skye'o/ /

The first of the meditative concentrations is propelled by meditatively cultivating its obstacle-removing stage. This is the preparatory attainment that removes inability. It leads into the first completing concentration proper, which is a meditative absorption accompanied by investigation, sustained analysis, joy, and bliss. Through cultivating this, there will be rebirth among the gods of the [first two] Brahma realms. By then cultivating the special aspect of this concentration, there will be rebirth in the Great Brahma heaven.

'phen byed bsam gtan gnyis pa'i nyer bsdogs bar chad med pa'i lam bsgoms nas/ rdzogs byed bsam gtan gnyis pa'i dngos gzhi rtog dpyod ni spangs la/ dga' bde dang ldan pa'i ting nge 'dzin bsgoms pas 'od chung la sogs pa bsam gtan gnyis pa'i lhar skye'o/ /

The second meditative concentration is propelled by meditatively cultivating its obstacle-removing stage, the preparatory attainment. This leads into the second completing concentration itself—a meditative absorption accompanied by joy and physical well-being but in which concept and analysis have been abandoned. By cultivating this, there will be rebirth among the gods of the second concentration, in the Small Light, [Limitless Light, and Radiant] heavens.

de bzhin du 'phen byed nyer bsdogs rnams 'gre bar bya'o/[322] / rdzogs byed bsam gtan gsum pa'i dngos gzhi dga' ba spangs la bde ba dang ldan pa'i ting nge 'dzin bsgoms pas dge chung la sogs pa'i bsam gtan gsum pa'i lhar skye'o/ /

It is likewise for the propelling meditative attainment for the third and fourth meditative concentrations. By cultivating the actual meditative absorption of the third completing concentration, in which there is physical well-being but mental joy is abandoned, there will be rebirth among the third concentration gods of the Lesser Virtue, [Limitless Virtue, and Complete Virtue] heavens.

d.div: [322] 'dre/ dpal spungs/

f.d: rdzogs byed bsam gtan bzhi pa'i dngos gzhi rtog dpyod dang dga' bde spangs pa'i ting nge 'dzin bsgoms pas sprin med la sogs pa bsam gtan bzhi pa'i lhar skye'o/ / bsam gtan bzhis dben pa las skyes pa ni nam mkha' mtha' yas skye mched de/ de bsgoms pas nam mkha' mtha' yas skye mched kyi lhar skye'o/ / de las dben pa las skyes pa ni rnam shes mtha' yas skye mched de/ /de bsgoms pas rnam shes mtha' yas skye mched kyi lhar skye'o/ / de las dben pa las skyes pa ni ci yang med pa'i skye mched de/ de bsgoms pas ci yang med pa'i skye mched kyi lhar skye'o/ / de las dben pa las skyes pa ni 'du shes med 'du shes med min skye mched de/ de bsgoms pas 'du shes med 'du shes med min skye mched kyi lhar skye'o/ /

By cultivating the actual meditative absorption of the fourth completing concentration, in which investigation, sustained analysis, joy, and bliss have all been left aside, there will be rebirth among the fourth concentration gods of the Cloudless Heaven and so forth [up to Akaniṣṭha, eight heavens in all]. /97/ That which has arisen out of the transcendence of these four meditative concentrations is the Sphere of Infinite Space, and cultivating this gives rise to rebirth as a god of the Sphere of Infinite Space. That which has arisen out of the transcendence of this is the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, and cultivating this gives rise to rebirth as a god of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness. That which has arisen out of the transcendence of this is the Sphere of Nothing Whatsoever, and cultivating this gives rise to rebirth as a god of the Sphere of Nothing Whatsoever. That which has arisen out of the transcendence of this is the Sphere of Neither Cognition Nor Absence of Cognition, and cultivating this gives rise to rebirth as a god of the Sphere of Neither Cognition Nor Absence of Cognition.

dben pa las skyes pa zhes bya ba yang lam gang yin na/ sa 'og ma la yid 'byung ba yin te/ 'dod chags dang bral bar 'gro ba'i phyir ro/ / ci nam mkha' mtha' yas skye mched sogs pa de dag kyang nam mkha' la sogs pa nyid la dmigs pas de'i phyir de skad du bya ba'am zhe na ma yin te/ dang po gsum ni snyoms par 'jug pa'i tshe nam mkha' mtha' yas so/ /zhes pa la sogs par yid la byed pas de skad ces ming du btags kyi/ phyis snyoms par zhugs zin nas de nyid yid la byed pa ma yin no/ / phyi ma ni 'du shes dman pa'i sgo nas ming du byas pa ste/ 'du shes gsal ba yod pa ma yin med pa kho na yang ma yin no/ / lar dngos gzhi brgyad po thams cad dge ba'i sems rtse gcig pa yin no/ /

What exactly is meant by the phrase “that which has arisen out of transcendence”? It means that the subsequent stage represents a transcendence of the previous mind condition and moves toward another condition that is freer from desire and attachment. Are the spheres of Infinite Space and so forth so called because limitless space itself [and the others] are the actual object of meditation? No. The first three are called Infinite Space and so forth because the mind is anchored by evoking terms such as “infinite space” and so on during the meditative attainment. Later, when the preparatory stage is over, there is no such anchoring of the mind. The last of the four is so called because of its diminished cognition. Although there is barely any lucid cognition, it cannot be said that there is absolutely none at all. All the eight actual absorptions consist of single-pointed, virtuous mind.

de dag gis mi g.yo ba'i las rgyu 'bras bstan te/ rin chen phreng ba las/
bsam gtan tshad med gzugs med kyis/ / tshangs sogs bde ba myong bar byed/[323] / ces gsungs so//

With these the cause and effects of unwavering karma have been presented. The Precious Garland says:
Through the absorptions, the immeasurables, and the formless [states], the happiness of Brahma [heaven] and so forth is experienced.[168]

d.div: [323] sde dge_4158_bstan/ spring yig_ge_mgon po klu sgrub/ rin chen phreng ba/ le'u/ 1_sh+loka_24_shog_107_ba7

f.d: de ltar na 'khor ba'i dngos po 'di bskyed mkhan zag bcas kyi las gsum po de yin no/ / don gsum pa las bdag gir bya ba zhes bya ba ni/ las rang gis byas pa'i 'bras bu la rang spyod pa ste/ byed pa po zin pa'i phung po nyid la smin gyi gzhan la ma yin pa'o/ /

Thus the three kinds of tainted action described above [i.e., nonvirtuous, virtuous, and unwavering] give rise to the substance of samsara. The third point is [ownership—the fact] that actions determine your personal lot. The consequences of the actions that someone has done will be experienced by that person alone: They come to maturity in the aggregates of their doer and in no one else.

de ltar yang mngon pa kun las btus pa las/
las bdag gir bya ba ji lta bu zhe na/ rang gis byas pa'i las kyi rnam par smin pa myong ba'i phyir te/ gzhan dag dang thun mong ma yin pa de ni bdag gi zhes bya'o/[324]/ zhes gsungs so/ / de ltar ma yin na las byas pa chud zos pa dang / ma byas pa dang 'phrad pa'i nyes par yang 'gyur ro/ /

In the Compendium of Higher Knowledge it says:
What does it mean, “Actions determine your personal lot”? Because individuals experience the full maturation of actions they themselves have done, and because that [maturation] shares nothing in common with others, it is called “personal.”[169] Were this not the case, then karma could dwindle or become exhausted, or someone might receive evil consequences from acts committed by someone else.

d.div: [324] sde dge_4049_bstan/ sems tsam/ ri_'phags pa thogs med/ mngon pa kun btus/ le'u/ 2_shog_89_ba6
[169] Asaṅga, Abhidharmasamuccaya, Toh 4049 Tengyur, sems tsam, ri, 89b6.

f.d:
des na mdo las kyang /
lha sbyin nyid kyis byas pa'i las ni/ sa dang / chu la sogs pa la mi smin gyi/ de nyid kyis zin pa'i phung po dang skye mched 'ba' zhig la smin par 'gyur te/ gzhan su zhig la smin par 'gyur/[325] zhes gsungs so//
