This is why the sutra says:
The deeds committed by Devadatta /98/ will not come to maturity in the earth or in water and so forth. They will come to maturity solely in his very own aggregates and sense spheres. In those of whom else could they possibly come to maturity?[170]

d.div: [325] sde dge_1_bka'/ 'dul ba/ ka_'dul ba gzhi/ bam po/ 4_shog_41_na1
[170] Basis of Vinaya (Vinayavastu), Toh 1 Kangyur, ’dul ba, ka, 41a1.

f.d:
don bzhi pa las kyi bgo skal la spyod pa zhes bya ba ni/ las dge sdig byas pa'i 'bras bu bde sdug mi 'khrul bar myong ba ste/ dge ba'i las bsags pas 'bras bu bde ba myong zhing / sdig pa'i las bsags pas 'bras bu sdug bsngal myong ba'o/ / de ltar yang mngon pa kun las btus pa las/
ji ltar na las kyi bgo skal la spyod pa yin zhe na/ rang gis byas pa'i rnam par smin pa myong ba ste/ dge ba dang mi dge ba'i las so so'i bgo skal la spyod pa'i phyir ro/[326] / zhes gsungs so//

The fourth point is [apportionment—the fact] that experiences due to action are strictly apportioned. Happiness or suffering is infallibly experienced as the respective consequence of virtuous or harmful action. By accumulating virtuous action, happiness will be experienced as a result. By accumulating harmful action, suffering will be experienced as a result. The Compendium of Higher Knowledge says of this:
How will experience be apportioned? Subject to the ripened result of actions, a person experiences his own share that corresponds specifically to the virtuous or nonvirtuous actions that have been done.[171]

d.div: [326] sde dge_4049_bstan/ sems tsam/ ri_mngon pa kun btus/ le'u/ 2_shog_89_ba6
[171] Asaṅga, Abhidharmasamuccaya, Toh 4049 Tengyur, sems tsam, ri, 89b6.

f.d:
dran pa nyer gzhag chung ba las kyang /
dge ba yis ni bde ba thob/ / mi dge ba las sdug bsngal 'byung / / de ltar dge dang mi dge ba'i/ / las dang 'bras bu gsal bar bstan/[327] / zhes gsungs so/ /

The Shorter Sutra on Mindfulness says:
Through virtue, one attains happiness. Through nonvirtue, suffering occurs. This is the reason for teaching clearly the virtuous and nonvirtuous actions and their consequences.[172]

d.div: [327] sde dge_119_bka'/ mdo sde/ nya_yongs su mya ngan las 'das pa'i mdo/ le'u/ 7_bam po/ 26_shog_354_na5
[172] This quotation is actually from the longer Great Passing into Nirvana Sutra (Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra), Toh 119 Kangyur, mdo sde, nya, 354a5.

f.d:
des pas zhus pa'i mdo las kyang /
sa bon tsha ba rnams la ni/ / 'bras bu tsha ba skye bar 'gyur// sa bon mngar ba rnams la ni/ / 'bras bu mngar ba skye bar 'gyur/ / dpe zla bya ba 'di yis ni/ / sdig pa'i rnam smin tsha ba dang / / dkar po'i rnam smin mngar ba yang / / mkhas pa yis ni shes par bya/[328]/zhes gsungs so//

And in the Questions of Surata Sutra:
From the seeds of spicy plants, spicy fruits will grow; and from sweet seeds, sweet fruits will come to grow. Wise and skillful people should know through this example the full consequence of evil to be like the spicy [fruit] and bright action to be like the sweet.[173]

d.div: [328] sde dge_71_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ ca_des pas zhus pa'i mdo/ shog_181_ba7
[173] Surataparipṛcchāsūtra, Toh 71 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, ca, 181b7.

f.d:
don lnga pa las chung ngu byas pa las 'bras bu chen por smin pa ni/[329] sdig pa'i las kyi dbang du byas na/ sems kyi skad cig gi grangs kyi bskal par dmyal ba myong bar gsungs pa yang yod do/[330] / byang chub sems dpa'i spyod pa la 'jug pa las kyang /
gang zhig de 'dra'i rgyal sras sbyin bdag la/ / gal te ngan sems bskyed par byed pa ni/ / ngan sems bskyed pa'i grangs bzhin bskal pa ni/ / dmyal bar gnas par 'gyur zhes thub pas gsungs/[331] / zhes gsungs so/ /

The fifth point is [inflation—the fact] that great results can be created by a small cause. It has been taught that it is possible even for a single moment of evil action to cause you to experience an eon in the hells. In Guide to the Bodhisattva Way of Life, it says:
The Sage has said that whoever generates an evil mind against a benefactor such as the bodhisattva will stay in hell for as many eons as there were moments of evil mind.[174]

d.div: [329] byed pa/ mi rigs dpe skrun/
[330] sems skad cig_dpal spungs/
[331] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_rgyal sras zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 1_sh+loka_34_shog_3_ba2
[174] Śāntideva, Bodhicaryāvatāra 1:34, Toh 3871 Tengyur, dbu ma, la, 3b2.

f.d:
ngag gi nyes pa re re tsam gyis skye ba lnga brgya la sogs par sdug bsngal myong bar 'gyur bar gsungs pa yang yod do/ / tshoms las kyang /
sdig pa chung ngu byas pas kyang / / 'jig rten pha rol 'jigs chen dang / / phung khrol chen po byed 'gyur te/ / khong par song ba'i dug bzhin no/[332] / zhes gsungs so//

It is also said that a person will experience suffering for five hundred existences for each instance of bad speech uttered, and so forth. The Collection of Aphorisms says:
Even a small bad action can generate much fear and considerable damage in a future existence: it is like poison that has entered the system.[175]

d.div: [332] sde dge_326_bka'/ mdo sde/ sa_ched du brjod pa'i tshoms/ tshoms/ 28_sh+loka_25_shog_273_na3
[175] Udānavarga 28:25, Toh 326 Kangyur, mdo sde, sa, 273a3.

f.d:
dge ba'i las chung ngus kyang 'bras bu chen po 'byin te/ tshoms las kyang /
bsod nams chung ngu byas pas kyang / / 'jig rten pha rol bde chen 'dren/ / don chen dag kyang byed 'gyur te/ / 'bru rnams phun tshogs smin pa bzhin/[333] / zhes gsungs so//

It is also the case that even a small virtuous act can induce great consequence. The Collection of Aphorisms says /99/:
Even doing a small wholesome act can produce great happiness in future existences and create great consequence, like grains that produce the most abundant harvests.[176]

d.div: [333] gong mtshungs/ ched du brjod pa'i tshoms/ tshoms/ 28_sh+loka_26_shog_273_na3

f.d: don drug pa las chud mi za ba zhes bya ba de ni/ las de'i gnyen po skyes pa ma gtogs pa/ bskal pa mtha' yas par yang 'bras bu ma smin par brlag pa'am/ chud za bar mi 'gyur te/ bag la nyal yun ring du gnas pa dag kyang ci zhig ltar la rkyen dang phrad na 'bras bu 'byin par 'gyur ro/ /

The sixth point is [ineluctability, the fact] that karma never just fades away. Except for the case of action that has been properly remedied, results will not be lost or become any weaker [with time], even though the karma may not ripen for endless eons. Although you may have been in a state of ease for a considerable period, the result will be induced whenever you encounter the requisite circumstances, whatever they may be.

de ltar 'khor ba'i sdug bsngal la 'jigs shing las 'bras la yid ches tsa na/ ji skad du/
srid pa'i bde la rgyab phyogs shing / / sdig pa'i las las bzlog bdag nyid/ / gang zhig rang zhi tsam don gnyer/ / skyes bu de ni 'bring zhes bya/[334] / zhes gsungs pa ltar skyes bu 'bring gi blo skyes pa yin te/ dper na rgyal po kri kri'i bu mo bdun lta bu'o/[335] /

Being convinced about actions and their consequences, as explained above, and fearing the sufferings of samsara, then, as it is said:
Someone who turns away from worldly happiness, turns away from unwholesome action, and strives for their own peace alone, that person is refered to as “middling” type.[177] A “middling” person who cultivates such an approach would be the likes of the seven daughters of King Kṛkin.[178]

d.div: [334] sde dge_3947_bstan/ dbu ma/ khi_jo bo rje mar me mdzad ye shes/ lam sgron/ sh+loka_4_shog_238_ba1

[335] de ltar 'khor ba'i sdug bsngal/ zhes pa nas/ bu mo bdun lta bu'o/ /zhes pa'i bar gyi tshig 'di rnams dpal spungs dpar mar/ las kyi rnam smin bslu mi srid/ /ces pa'i 'og tu byung zhing / gzhung gi go rim dang bstun na'ang de ltar legs par snang mod/ 'on kyang 'dir ma dpe rang sor bzhag yod/
[177] In Atiśa, Lamp for the Path to Awakening (Bodhipathapradīpa) verse 4, Toh 3947 Tengyur, dbu ma, khi, 238b1.

[178] King Kṛkin had seven daughters with powerful karma due to their Dharma practice in former lives. This gave them radical feelings of renunciation. They refused all the royal benefits offered them by their father and eventually obtained his permission to leave palace life to practice Dharma. They later also refused the gifts of the god Indra, who offered them divine substances when he saw them dressed in rags and meditating assiduously in a charnel ground.

f.d:
de ltar yang mdo sde las brgya pa las/
lus can dag gi las rnams ni/ bskal pa brgyar yang chud mi za/ / tshogs shing dus la babs pa na/ / 'bras bu nyid du smin par 'gyur/[336] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Thus it says in the One Hundred [Stories] about Karma:
The karmas of physical beings are not lost or weakened even for a hundred eons. Once they are gathered and when the time comes, their results will ripen.[179]

d.div: [336] sde dge_340_bka'/ mdo sde/ ha_las brgya pa/ bam po/ 1_shog_16_na3
[179] Karmaśataka, Toh 340 Kangyur, mdo sde, ha, 16a3.

f.d:
dran pa nyer gzhag chung ba las kyang /
me ni grang bar 'gyur yang srid/ / rlung ni zhags pas zin yang srid/ / nyi zla thang la lhung yang srid/ / las kyi rnam smin bslu mi srid/[337] / ces gsungs so/ /

In the Shorter Sutra on Mindfulness, it says:
Fire may become cold, the wind may be caught by a lasso, and the sun and moon may fall down, but the consequences of karma are infallible.[180]

d.div: [337] dran pa nyer bzhag chung bar lung 'di 'tshol zhib byas kyang ma rnyed/ mdo myang 'das chen por lung de dang mtshungs pa zhig byung / sde dge_119_bka'/ mdo sde/ nya_yongs su mya ngan las 'das pa chen po'i mdo/ shog_254_na5
[180] This quote actually comes from the longer Great Passing into Nirvana Sutra (Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra), Toh 119 Kangyur, ka, 354a5.

f.d: dam chos yid bzhin gyi nor bu thar pa rin po che'i rgyan las/ las 'bras yongs su bstan pa'i le'u ste drug pa'o// //
This concludes the sixth chapter, concerning actions and their effects, from this Ornament of Precious Liberation, a Wish-Fulfilling Gem of Sublime Dharma.
le'u bdun pa/ byams pa dang snying rje/
7. Loving Kindness and Compassion

da ni zhi ba'i bde ba la chags pa'i gnyen por byams pa dang snying rje bsgom pa bshad par bya ste/ de la zhi ba'i bde ba la chags pa zhes bya ba ni/ bdag nyid 'ba' zhig mya ngan las 'das pa thob par 'dod cing / sems can la brtse ba med pas gzhan don mi byed pa ste/ theg pa dman pa dag yin no/ / de ltar yang /
bdag gi don phyir gzhan don ni/ / mang po dag kyang btang bya ste/ / rang don ched cher shes gyur na/ / rang gi don gyi mchog tu 'gyur/[338] / zhes gsungs so//

Now I present, as the antidote to counteract attachment to solitary peace, the practice of compassion. “Attachment to solitary peace” means longing only for one’s own nirvana and lacking altruistic activity due to absence of loving concern for sentient beings. This is the Hinayana. As it is said:
When personal welfare takes priority, thinking, “To really benefit myself, I must ignore all the various things that need to be done to help others,” then self-interest has taken control.[181]

d.div: [338] bdag gi don phyir gzhan don ni/ /mang po dag kyang btang bya ste/ /zhes sogs kyi gzhung ngos 'dzin ma thub/
[181] The source of this quote has not been identified.

f.d:
byams pa dang snying rje rgyud la skyes na sems can la chags pas rang gcig pu grol bar mi phod do// des na byams pa dang snying rje bsgom par bya ste/ slob dpon 'jam dpal grags pa'i zhal nas kyang /
theg pa chen po pas byams pa dang snying rje dang skad cig kyang 'bral bar mi bya ste/[339] zhes dang /
gzhan gyi don ni byams pa dang snying rje'i rjes su bzung gi zhe sdang gis ni ma yin te/[340] [341] zhes gsungs so//

When loving kindness and compassion become part of you, you have so much care for other conscious beings that personal liberation alone would be unbearable. /100/ Therefore you need to cultivate loving kindness and compassion. Master Mañjuśrīkīrti has said:
A follower of the Mahayana should not be without loving kindness and compassion for even a single moment.[182] and
It is not anger and hatred but loving kindness and compassion that vouchsafe the welfare of others.[183]

d.div: [339] sde dge_2488_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ zi_'jam dpal grags pa/ rdo rje theg pa'i rtsa ba'i ltung ba'i rgya cher bshad pa/ le'u/ 4_shog_210_na5
[340] snying rjes rjes su bzung / dpal spungs/ bzung gis/ mi rigs dpe skrun/ gzung gi_sde dge bstan 'gyur/
[341] sde dge_2488_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ zi_'jam dpal grags pa/ rdo rje theg pa'i rtsa ba'i ltung ba'i rgya cher bshad pa/ le'u/ 4_shog_210_ba2
[182] Extensive Explantion of Root Vajrayana Downfalls (Vajrayānamūlāpattiṭīkā), Toh 2488 Tengyur, rgyud ’grel, thi, 16a5.
[183] Mañjuśrīkīrti, Extensive Explantion of Root Vajrayana Downfalls (Vajrayāna-mūlāpattiṭīkā), Toh 2488 Tengyur, rgyud ’grel, thi, 10b2.

f.d:
de la dang po byams pa la/ sdom ni/
dbye ba dmigs yul rnam pa dang / / sgom thabs 'byongs tshad yon tan de/[342] / de ltar drug po 'di dag gis/ / byams pa tshad med yongs su bsdus/ / zhes pa'o/ /

The first of these two topics is loving kindness. The synopsis for this sub-chapter is:
Limitless loving kindness is well summarized by six topics: its categories, its object of reference, the form it takes, the means of cultivating it, its measure, and its qualities.

d.div: [342] dpal spungs dang mi rigs dpe skrun dpar mar 'og tu skabs du mar sgom la bsgom zhes ba sngon 'jug byung /

f.d:
de la dang po dbye ba ni gsum ste/ sems can la dmigs pa'i byams pa dang / chos la dmigs pa'i byams pa dang / dmigs pa med pa'i byams pa'o/[343] / de dag kyang 'phags pa blo gros mi zad pa'i mdo las/
sems can la dmigs pa'i byams pa ni/ sems dang po bskyed pa'i byang chub sems dpa' rnams kyi'o/ / chos la dmigs pa'i byams pa ni/ spyod pa la zhugs pa'i byang chub sems dpa' rnams kyi'o/ / dmigs pa med pa'i byams pa ni/ mi skye ba'i chos la bzod pa thob pa'i byang chub sems dpa' rnams kyi'o/[344] / zhes gsungs so//

First, there are three categories: (1) loving kindness focused on sentient beings, (2) loving kindness focused on the nature of things, and (3) loving kindness with no objective reference. It says of these, in the Akṣayamati Sutra:
Loving kindness focused on sentient beings is that of bodhisattvas first cultivating bodhicitta; loving kindness focused on the nature of things is that of the bodhisattva engaged in the deeds; and loving kindness without any objective reference is that of bodhisattvas who have attained the patience accepting unborn phenomena.[184]

d.div: [343] ma dpe dang mi rigs dpe skrun khang gnyis kar byams pa dang / zhes byung yang / dpal spungs ltar byams pa'o/ /zhes bcos/
[344] sde dge_175_bka'/ mdo sde/ ma_blo gros mi zad pa bstan pa'i mdo/ bam po/ 4_shog_132_na3

[184] Akṣayamatinirdeśasūtra, Toh 175 Kangyur, mdo sde, ma, 132a3. “The patience accepting unborn phenomena” (mi skye ba’i chos la bzod pa), translated elsewhere also as “acceptance of unoriginated factors,” is a bodhisattva’s stable realization of emptiness.

f.d: de la skabs 'dir byams pa dang po de bshad na/ de'i dmigs pa'i yul ni sems can thams cad do/ / rnam pa ni/ bde ba dang 'phrad par 'dod pa'i blo'o/ / de sgom pa'i thabs ni/ rtsa ba drin dran pa la rag las pas sems can gyi drin bsam mo/ / de la tshe 'di la drin che shos rang gi ma yin te/ ma'i drin ci tsam yod ce na/ lus bskyed pa'i drin dang / dka' ba spyad pa'i drin dang / srog byin pa'i drin dang / 'jig rten bstan pa'i drin dang bzhi yod do/ /

Second, to explain the first category of loving kindness, its object of reference includes all sentient beings. Third, the form it takes is that of a mind longing for [all sentient beings] to find happiness. Fourth, the way to cultivate loving kindness is as follows. Since gratitude is the root of love, bring to mind the kindness of sentient beings. In this respect, the person who has been kindest to you in this life is your own mother. In what way? She has been kind by creating your body, kind through undergoing hardships [on your behalf], kind by nurturing your life, and kind by teaching you the ways of the world.

de ltar yang 'phags pa brgyad stong pa las/
ci'i phyir zhe na/ ma 'dis bdag cag bskyed pa/ 'dis ni dka' ba byed pa/ bdag cag gi srog byin pa/ 'jig rten kun ston pa yin no/[345] / zhes gsungs so//

The Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines says:
Why is this? Mothers gave birth to us, underwent hardships, kept us alive, and taught us all about the world.[185]

d.div: [345] sde dge_12_bka'/ sher phyin/ ka_brgyad stong pa/ le'u/ 12_shog_139_ba4
[185] Aṣṭasāhasrikāprajñāpāramitā, Toh 12 Kangyur, sher phyin, ka, 139b4.

f.d: de la lus bskyed pa'i drin ni/ bdag nyid kyi lus 'di dang po nas bongs tshad rdzogs pa/[346] sha lus rgyas pa/ kha dog legs pa cig byung bar mi gda' ste/ ma'i lto bar mer mer nur nur gyi rang bzhin las khams kyi dwangs ma rim gyis ma'i sha khrag gi bcud kyis ni bskyed/[347] zad kyi dwangs mas ni spel/ ngo tsha dang / na tsha dang / sdug bsngal thams cad bzod par byas pa las grub pa yin/ phyir skyes nas kyang / chung phud bu tsam nas gso skyong byas nas/ che g.yag po tsam du bskyed pa yin no/ /

First consider the kindness of nourishing your body. This body of yours did not start out fully grown, with its flesh fully developed and with a healthy complexion. It developed gradually inside your mother, through the different embryonic and fetal stages, being gradually created and nourished by vital fluids from her very own flesh and blood. /101/ It grew thanks to nourishment from the food she ate. It came into being by her having to put up with all sorts of embarrassment, sickness, and suffering. Furthermore, generally speaking, it was she who helped make this body, which started out a tiny infant, into [its present] bulk as big as a yak.

d.div: [346] bongs tshod/ dpal spungs/
[347] khad kyis dang rims kyis/ dpal spungs/

f.d: dka' ba spyad pa'i drin ni/ bdag cag dang po nas gos gyon/ rgyan btags/ nor skal bzung / rgyags phye khur nas 'ongs par mi gda'/[348] kha grod zung zhig ma lags pa nor rdzas kyi dngos po ci yang med par stong sang nge byas nas/ 'dris pa mi gcig kyang med par ngo mi shes kyi yul du 'ongs pa'i dus su/ mas ltogs su ma bcug par zas byin/ bskom du ma bcug par btung ba blud/ 'khyags su ma bcug par gos bskon/ phongs par ma bzhag par nor byin/ / de yang rang la mi mkho ba bu la byin pa lta bu ma yin te/ rang gis za ma bra/[349] btung ma bra/ gyon ma bra/

Next, consider the kindness of undergoing hardships. You did not come into this world clothed, finely adorned, with money in your pocket and provisions for the journey. When you came into this unfamiliar place, where you knew no one and had nothing, the only wealth you had was your howling mouth and empty stomach. Your mother gave you food so that you would not go hungry, drink to keep you from thirst, clothes to fend off the cold, and wealth to keep you from poverty. It was not as though she just gave you things she no longer needed herself: she herself went without food, without drink, and without new clothes.

d.div: [348] bye/ dpal spungs/
[349] dpal spungs dpar mar/ rang gi zhes 'brel sgra byung /

f.d: tshe 'di'i bde ba'i don du yang spyad ma phod/ phyi ma phan chod kyi longs spyod kyi don du gtong ma phod pa yin te/[350] don la rang gi tshe 'di phyi gnyis ka'i bde ba la ma bltas par bu gsobaskyangs byas pa yin no/[351] / de yang bde dal gyis rnyed pa lta bu ma yin te/ sdig sdug ngal chad sna tshogs kyis bsgrubs nas bu la byin pa yin no/ / sdig pa la song na/ nya pa dang / bshan pa la sogs pa mi dge ba sna tshogs byas nas bu gsos pa yin no/ / sdug bsngal la song na/ tshong spogs dang / zhing las la sogs pa byed byed nas/ nyin mtshan du ba mo l+h+wam du gyon/ skar chen zhwar gyon/ byin pa rtar zhon/ snal ma lcag tu brabs/ / byin sha khyi la byin/ gdong sha mi la byin nas bsags kyin bu la byin pa yin/ gzhan yang rang re'i pha ma dang bla ma la sogs pa drin can gang bas kyang / cir mi 'ong su yin cha med po de la gces par byas te/ byams pa'i mig gis ni bltas/ 'jam pa'i drod kyis ni bsros/ sor bcu'i kha la ni g.yengs/ snyan pa'i ngag gis ni bos te/ dga'o/ /a'o/ /'bar re/ dgos se/ lu lu/ a ma'i skyid po lags sam/ zhes pa la sogs pa smras pa yin no/ /

Furthermore, not only did she sacrifice her happiness as far as this existence is concerned, she also deprived herself of using her assets [as offerings] to provide for her own prosperity in future lives. In brief, without regard for her own happiness in both this life and the next, she devoted herself to rearing and caring for you, her child. Nor did she obtain what was needed easily and pleasurably. To provide for you she was obliged to sin, to suffer, and to toil. She sinned by having to resort to fishing, killing animals, and so on to provide for you. She suffered because what she gave you was the fruit of trading, laboring in the fields, and so forth, wearing the late evening or early morning frost for her boots, the stars as a hat, riding the horse of her calves, beaten by the whip of the long grass, her legs exposed to be bitten by dogs and her face exposed to the looks of men. She also treated this undefined person who had become her child with more love than her own father, mother, or lama, even though she knew not who this being was or what you would become. She looked at you with loving eyes, gave you her gentle warmth, cradled you in her arms, and spoke to you with sweet words, saying, “My joy! Ah my sunshine, my treasure! Coochie coochie, aren’t you Mummy’s happiness?” and so forth.

d.div: [350] don du yang / dpal spungs/ mi rigs dpe skrun/
[351] gso skyong byas pa/ mi rigs dpe skrun khang /

f.d: srog byin pa'i drin ni/ bdag cag dang po nas da lta 'dra ba'i kha lag 'phrod pa/ dka' las ci yang nus pa'i shed po che zhig byung bar mi gda'/ srin bu kho na 'dra ba'i nya re nyo re/ 'khos med po/ bsam brlag po zhig byung ba la/ mas de ma bor bar zhabs tog byas/ /pang du blangs/ me chu las bskyabs/[352] g.yang sa las bzung / gnod pa ni bsal/ rim gro ni byas te/ shi dogs/[353] na dogs nas/ mo dang / rtsis dang / gto dang / klog pa dang /[354] cho ga la sogs pa bsam gyis mi khyab cing / blos mi 'khyud pa byas nas bu'i srog gton pa yin no/[355] /

Next, consider the kindness of keeping you alive. It is not as though you were born as you are now, knowing how to feed yourself and endowed with the necessary ability to accomplish difficult tasks. When you were helpless, useless—a little worm unable to think—your mother did not discard you but did an inconceivable number of things to nurture your existence. She took you on her lap, protected you from fire and water, held you away from dangerous precipices, /102/ got rid of all sources of harm, and prayed for you. At those times when she feared for your life or health, she resorted to divinations, astrology, exorcisms, recitations of texts, special ceremonies, and so on.

d.div: [352] skyabs/ mi rigs dpe skrun/
[353] shis dogs/ dpal spungs/
[354] bklog pad nga / dpal spungs/ klag pa dang / mi rigs dpe skrun/
[355] bton/ dpal spungs/

f.d: 'jig rten bstan pa'i drin ni/ bdag cag dang po nas mi shes dgu shes po/ mthong goms can/ sgo drag po zhig 'dir yong bar mi gda'/ bshes gnyen gyi rigs la cho nges 'bod pa dang / rkang lag g.yob pa cig ma lags pa ci yang mi shes pa cig yin pa la/ za mi shes pa'i dus su za ba bslabs/ gyon mi shes pa'i dus su gyon pa bslabs/ 'gro mi shes pa'i dus su 'gro ba bslabs/ smra mi shes pa'i dus su smra ba bslabs te/ a gyis dang / a ma gyis dang / zhes bya ba la sogs pa dang / bzo rig pa la sogs pa yon tan sna tshogs bslabs nas/ mi mnyam pa dang ni mnyam/ mi mtshungs pa dang ni mtshungs par byas pa yin no// de yang da res kyi ma byas par ma zad de/ 'khor ba thog ma med pa nas 'khor bas na/ lan grangs dpag tu med par ma byas pa yin no/ /

Finally, consider the kindness of teaching you the ways of the world. At first you were not the clever, experienced, strong-minded person you are now. Apart from being able to bawl out to other members of your family and flap your limbs about, you were ignorant. When you did not know how to feed yourself, it was she who taught you how to eat. When you knew not how to dress yourself, it was she who taught you. When you did not know how to walk, it was she who taught you. When you could not even speak, it was she who taught you, repeating “Mama,” “Dada,” and so on. Having taught you various crafts and skills, she helped you become a balanced being, strengthening your weaker points and introducing you to the unfamiliar. Moreover, apart from being your mother in this life, she has also been your mother in previous lives, an inestimable number of times, due to the unending round of existences that has been going on since time without beginning.

de ltar yang 'khor ba thog ma med pa'i mdo las/
'jig rten gyi khams kyi sa rdo dang / rtsi shing dang / nags tshal thams cad rgya shug gi tshig gu tsam du skyes bu gcig gis byas la/ skyes bu gnyis pas de rnams grangs su bgrangs pas zad pa'i dus srid kyi/ sems can gcig gis bdag gi ma byas pa ni bgrangs bar mi nus so/[356] / zhes gsungs so//

The Beginningless Time Sutra says:
Were one person to set down a little jujube kernel for every piece of earth, stone, plant, or forest that there is in the world and a second person to count them, eventually a time would come when the count would be completed. Yet were we to try to count the number of times that one being has been our mother, it would be impossible.[186]

d.div: [356] 'khor ba thog ma med pa'i mdo zhes pa bka' 'gyur du ma bzhugs/ lung tshig 'di dang ches 'dra ba zhig mdo myang 'das bzhugs/ sde dge_119_bka'/ mdo sde/ ta_mdo myang 'das chen po/ bam po/ 29_le'u/ 10_shog_11_ba4

[186] This cannonical text, Beginningless Time Sutra, does not appear to exist in the Tibetan canon. However, the “Questions” chapter of the longer Great Passing into Nirvana Sutra does contain a version extremely similar to this quotation: Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra, Toh 119 Kangyur, mdo sde, ta, 11b4.

f.d:
bshes spring las kyang /
ma yi thug mtha' rgya shug tshig gu tsam/ / ril bur bgrangs kyang sa yis lang mi 'gyur/[357] / zhes gsungs so/ /

The Letter to a Friend says:
If you reduced the earth to little balls the size of jujube kernels, their number would be less than that of the number of times any one being has been your mother.[187]

d.div: [357] sde dge_4182_bstan/ spring yig_nge _mgon po klu sgrub/ bshes spring / sh+loka_68_shog_43_ba7
[187] Nāgārjuna, Suhṛllekha 68cd, Toh 4182 Tengyur, spring yig, nge, 43b7.

f.d: de ltar ma byas res kyis drin snga ma ltar bzhag pa yin no/ / de bas na ma de'i drin dpag tu med pa yod pas/ de snying du sdug cing phan pa dang / bde bar 'dod pa'i blo gsha' ma ci skyer sgom mo/[358] / de nas der ma zad kyi sems can thams cad kyis ma byas la/ ma byas tshad snga ma kho na ltar drin can yin te/ de yang sems can gyi rgya yi tshad ni ci tsam zhe na/ nam mkha'i mthas gar khyab sems can gyis khyab pa yin no/ /

Recalling the kindness shown by her in the ways described above every time she was your mother in the past and contemplating it all, you will recognize that her kindness has been absolutely immeasurable. Bearing this carefully in mind, cultivate as sincerely and as frequently as possible a loving, positive mind longing for her happiness. Furthermore, every sentient being has been your mother, and they have all shown you the same kindnesses enumerated above. Just how many sentient beings are there? Sentient beings are as vast as space itself.

d.div: [358] bsha'/ mi rigs dpe skrun/

f.d:
de ltar yang bzang po spyod pa'i smon lam gyi mdo las/
nam mkha'i mthar thug gyur pa ji tsam pa/ / sems can ma lus mtha' yang de bzhin no/[359] / zhes gsungs so/ /

The Prayer of Excellent Conduct says:
Whatever the farthest end of space may be, that is the limit of sentient beings’ existence.[188]

d.div: [359] sde dge_44_bka'/ phal chen/ a_sdong po bkod pa'i mdo'i nang tshan bzang spyod/ sh+loka_46_shog_361_na6
[188] The Prayer of Excellent Conduct (Bhadracaryāpraṇidhāna) is part of the Flower Ornament Sutra (Avataṃsakasūtra), Toh 44 Kangyur, phal chen, ā, 361a6.

f.d:
des na nam mkhas gar khyab kyi sems can la phan pa dang bde bar 'dod pa'i blo gsha' ma zhig ci skyer sgom mo/ / de skyes na byams pa dngos yin te/ mdo sde rgyan las kyang /
byang chub sems dpa' sems can la/ / bu gcig pa la bya ba bzhin/ / rkang gi khong nas byams pa che/ / de ltar rtag phan byed par 'dod/[360] / ces gsungs so/ /

Therefore, a sincere mind that longs to benefit and bring happiness to all beings throughout space /103/ is to be cultivated as much as possible. When that has arisen, it is true loving kindness. The Ornament of Mahayana Sutras says:
A bodhisattva acts toward sentient beings as though they were an only child, with a love so great coming from the very marrow of their bones, and thereby wishes to benefit them continuously.[189]

d.div: [360] sde dge_4020_bstan/ sems tsam/ phi_byams pa mgon po/ mdo sde rgyan/ le'u/ 14_sh+loka_20_shog_18_ba1
[189] Maitreya, Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra 14:20, Toh 4020 Tengyur, sems tsam, phi, 18b1.

f.d: byams pa'i shugs kyis mig nas mchi ma 'khrugs pa'am/[361] lus kyi ba spu ldang bar byed na byams pa chen po yin no/ / de lta bu sems can thams cad la mnyam nyid kyis skyes tsa na/[362] byams pa tshad med pa yin no//

Great loving kindness is benevolence so strong that it brings tears to your eyes and makes the hairs of your body stand on end. Limitless loving kindness occurs when you no longer discriminate between beings.

d.div: [361] 'khrug/ dpal spungs/ mi rigs dpe skrun/
[362] mnyam kad/ dpal spungs/

f.d: 'byongs pa'i tshad ni rang bde bar 'dod pa'i blo med par sems can kho na bde bar 'dod tsa na byams pa 'byongs pa yin no/ /

The fifth point is the [measure or] gauge of accomplishment. Loving kindness has been achieved when your sole wish is for others’ happiness and your mind no longer yearns for personal happiness alone.

de bsgoms pa'i yon tan ni dpag tu med de/ zla ba sgron ma'i mdo las kyang /
mchod pa tshad med rnam mang ji snyed pa/ / zhing ni bye ba khrag khrig gtam snyed du// skyes bu mchog la mchod pa de byas pas/ / byams pa'i sems dang grangs la char mi phod/[363] / ces gsungs so/ /

Sixth, the [qualities or] benefits of cultivating loving kindness are immeasurable. The Candraprabha Sutra says:
The merit of limitless offerings made to the Supreme Being, even if they fill a hundred quadrillion buddhafields, does not equal the benefit derived from a benevolent mind.[190]

d.div: [363] sde dge_127_bka'/ mdo sde/ da_ting nge 'dzin rgyal po'i mdo/ le'u/ 33_sh+loka_277_shog_115_ba6

[190] Candraprabha Sutra is one of several names for the King of Meditation Sutra (Samādhirājasūtra), Toh 127 Kangyur, mdo sde, 115b6. Gampopa himself is considered an incarnation of the Buddha’s interlocutor in this sutra, Candraprabhakumāra.

f.d:
byams pa dar cig bsgoms pa'i bsod nams kyang dpag tu med de/[364] rin chen phreng ba las kyang /
rje'u tshong sum brgya'i kha zas dag / nyin re dus gsum byin pas kyang / / byams pa yud tsam thang cig gi / bsod nams dag la char mi phod/[365] / ces gsungs so/ /

The good results generated by even an instant’s practice of loving kindness are countless. The Precious Garland says:
The merit of offering, three times a day, every day, three hundred pots of food cannot even begin to compare with that created by one tiny instant of loving kindness.[191]

d.div: [364] bsgom/ mi rigs dpe skrun/
[365] sde dge_4158_bstan/ spring yig_ge_mgon po klu sgrub/ dbu ma rin phreng / le'u/ 3_sh+loka_85_shog_117_ba3
[191] Nāgārjuna, Ratnāvalī 3:83, Toh 4158 Tengyur, spring yig, ge, 117b3.

f.d:
byang chub ma thob kyi bar du yang phan yon brgyad thob ste/ rin chen phreng ba las/
lha mis byams par 'gyur ba dang / / de dag gis kyang bsrung ba dang / / yid bde ba dang bde mang dang / / dug dang mtshon gyis gnod med dang / / 'bad pa med par don thob dang / / tshangs pa'i 'jig rten skye 'gyur te/ / gal te grol bar ma gyur kyang / / byams chos yon tan brgya thob bo/[366] / zhes gsungs so/ /

d.div: [366] gong mtshungs/ dbu ma rin phreng / le'u/ 3_sh+loka_86_shog_117_ba4

[192] In the ITC critical edition as well as the Tsipri edition, it reads “you will derive/ hundredfold benefits from loving kindness.” Here we have chosen to follow the reading of the Beijing and Palpung editions instead.
[193] Nāgārjuna, Ratnāvalī 3:84–85, Toh 4158 Tengyur, spring yig, ge, 117b4.

f.d: yang rang gi bsrung bar yang byams pa bsgom pa 'di bzang ba yin te/[367] bram ze sbyin pa chen po bzhin no/[368]/ gzhan gyi bsrung bar yang byams pa bsgom pa 'di bzang ba yin te/ rgyal po byams pa'i stobs bzhin no//[369] de ltar byams pa la 'byongs pas/ snying rje 'byongs pa la tshegs med pa yin no/ /

The practice of loving kindness also affords excellent protection. This is illustrated in the story of Mahādatta.[194] It also affords excellent protection for others, as illustrated by the example of King Bāla Maitreya.[195] Once loving kindness has been attained, it will not be difficult to cultivate compassion.

d.div: [367] srung / dpal spungs/ gsham du'ang skabs du mar dpal spungs dpar mar srung zhes sngon 'jug med pa byung /
[368] sde dge_341_bka'/ mdo sde/ a_mdzangs blun zhes bya ba'i mdo/ le'u/ 30_shog_223_na3
[369] gong mtshungs/ mdzangs blun zhes bya ba'i mdo/ le'u/ 12_shog_155_ba4

[194] A former incarnation of Buddha Śākyamuni, the brahman Mahādatta was a wealthy prince whose heart was saddened by the poverty he saw in his land and by knowing the harmful thoughts and actions to which poverty gives rise. He set out on an epic and arduous journey to collect wish-fulfilling gems powerful enough to dispel all the poverty in his world. His long quest bore fruit, and he was able to help innumerable beings due to his loving concern for their happiness. This story is found in chapter 3 of the Sage and Fool Sutra, Toh 341 Kangyur, mdo sde, a, 223a3.

[195] King Bāla Maitreya was another former incarnation of Buddha Śākyamuni. His loving mind and prayers were so strong that it protected his subjects from flesh-eating demons. Five such rakṣas, very hungry because of this, came to him to plead their case. He gave them his own flesh and blood. The strong karmic connection created by this selfless act led them eventually to meet him again and again, finally becoming Kauṇḍinya and the four other ascetics who were Śākyamuni’s meditation companions before his enlightenment and subsequently among the first to receive his teachings. Sage and Fool Sutra (Damamūkanāmasūtra), chapter 12, Toh 341 Kangyur, mdo sde, a, 155b4.

f.d: snying rje la

bsdoms ni/
dbye ba dmigs yul rnam pa dang / / sgom thabs 'byongs tshad yon tan te/ / de ltar drug po 'di dag gis/ / snying rje tshad med yongs su bsdus/ / zhes pa'o/ /

The synopsis for this subchapter is:
Limitless compassion is well summarized by six topics: its categories, its object of reference, the form it takes, the means of cultivating it, its measure, and its qualities.
de la dbye na gsum ste/ sems can la dmigs pa'i snying rje dang / chos la dmigs pa'i snying rje dang / dmigs pa med pa'i snying rje'o/ /
First, there are three categories /104/: (1) compassion focused on sentient beings, (2) compassion focused on the nature of things, (3) compassion with no objective reference.

de la dang po ni/ sems can rnams kyi ngan song gi sdug bsngal la sogs pa mthong bas snying rje skye'o/ / gnyis pa ni/ rang 'phags pa'i bden pa bzhi la goms tsa na/ rgyu 'bras rnam gnyis shes nas/ rtag pa dang ril por 'dzin pa las blo bzlog ste/ sems can gzhan rgyu 'bras mi shes par rtag pa dang ril por 'dzin pa rnams la re 'khrul snyam du snying rje skye'o/ /

The first kind is compassion that arises through understanding the sufferings of beings in the lower states of existence. The second occurs when there is familiarity with the meaning of the four truths of the noble ones and hence understanding of both causes and consequences, thereby counteracting belief in permanent, concrete realities. Compassion arises through realizing how much other beings are unaware of karmic cause and effect and how they perceive things as concrete and lasting.

gsum pa ni/ rang mnyam par bzhag nas/ chos thams cad stong pa nyid du rtogs tsa na/ sems can dngos 'dzin can rnams la khyad par du snying rje skye ste/ ji skad du/
byang chub sems dpa' mnyam bzhag pas/ / goms pa'i stobs kyis rdzogs pa na/ / dngos 'dzin gdon gyis zin pa la/ / khyad par du yang snying rje skye/[370] / zhes gsungs so// de gsum las skabs 'dir ni snying rje dang po de bsgom pa'o/ /

The third kind of compassion occurs when meditative penetration has brought realization of the emptiness of all phenomena. Extraordinary compassion then arises toward sentient beings who grasp at essential existence. As it says:
When, through meditative equipoise, a bodhisattva becomes perfected through practice, compassion arises in particular toward those gripped by the demon of grasping at essential existence.[196] Of these three, only the development of the first will be discussed here.

d.div: [370] byang chub sems dpa' mnyam bzhag pas/ /zhes sogs kyi gzhung ngos 'dzin ma thub/
[196] The source of this quotation has not been identified.

f.d: de'i dmigs pa'i yul ni sems can thams cad do/ /
Second, this first type of compassion has every sentient being as its object of reference.
rnam pa ni sdug bsngal rgyu dang bcas pa dang bral bar 'dod pa'i blo'o//
Third, the form it takes is that of a mind longing for [each sentient being] to become free from suffering.

de sgom pa'i thabs ni/ rtsa ba'i ma la sbyar nas sgom pa ste/ de yang bdag gi rtsa ba'i ma de sa phyogs 'di na skyes bu gzhan dag gis bcad cing gtubs pa'am btsos shing bsregs pa'am/[371] yang na shin tu 'khyags nas lus la chu bur du gyur te/ rdol nas kyang gas te 'dug na shin tu snying rje'o/[372] / de bzhin du dmyal bar skyes pa'i sems can 'di rnams bdag gi ma yin nges na/ sdug bsngal de lta bus ni gnad gcod na/ ci ste snying rje mi skye ste/ de dag sdug bsngal rgyu dang bcas pa dang bral bar 'dod pa'i snying rje bsgom mo/ /

Fourth, the way to cultivate compassion is through reflections based on the mother. You imagine her right here, in front of you, being cut up by some people and being beaten, boiled, or burned by others. Or perhaps her body is completely frozen with cold, to a point where is it covered with cold sores, blistered, and cracked open. If this were really the case, would you not experience compassion for her? Since it is a definite fact that those beings suffering in hell have also been our mothers and that they are currently enduring such sufferings, how can compassion not arise toward them, too? Cultivate actual compassion by contemplating in this way and by wishing those beings to be free from suffering and its causes.

d.div: [371] btub/ mi rigs dpe skrun/
[372] brdol/ dpal spungs/

f.d: yang bdag gi ma de sa phyogs 'di na bkres shing skom pas ni nyen/ na zhing tsha bas ni gzir/ 'jigs shing nyam nga bas ni dpa' 'khums nas 'dug na shin tu snying rje'o/[373] / de bzhin du yi dwags su skyes pa'i sems can 'di rnams kyang bdag gi ma yin nges na/ sdug bsngal de lta bus ni g.yen spyo na/ ci ste snying mi rje ste/ de rnams sdug bsngal dang bral bar 'dod pa'i snying rje bsgom mo/ /

Equally, were your own mother to be right in front of you, tormented by hunger and thirst, afflicted by disease and pain, full of fear, utterly terrified and completely disheartened, would you not experience profound compassion for her? It is certain that those hungry spirits who suffer torments like these have all been your own mothers. How can you not feel compassion? Contemplate this and wish them to be freed from their sufferings.

d.div: [373] 'khongs/ dpal spungs/

f.d: yang bdag gi ma de phyogs 'di na rgas shing dman pa'am/[374] gzhan dag gis dbang med par bkol zhing spyad pa'am/ rdeg cing 'tshog pa'am/[375] bsad cing bcad pa la sogs pa byed cing 'dug na snying rje'o/ / de bzhin du dud 'gror skyes pa'i sems can thams cad kyang bdag gi ma yin nges na/[376] sdug bsngal de lta bus ni nyam thag na/[377] ci ste snying mi rje ste/ de rnams sdug bsngal dang bral bar 'dod pa'i snying rje bsgom mo/ /

Equally, were your own mother to be right in front of you, old and withered by age, /105/ and yet other people nevertheless made her labor as a defenseless slave, beat her hard, killed or chopped her up alive, would you not experience great compassion? It is certain that those beings born as animals are subject to these sufferings and that they were formerly your very own mothers. How can you not feel compassion? Contemplate this and wish them to be free from suffering.

d.div: [374] ma de sa phyogs/ dpal spungs/
[375] rdeg cing 'tshog pa'am/ dpal spungs/ brdeg cing 'tshog gam/ mi rigs dpe skrun/
[376] ngan 'gror/ mi rigs dpe skrun/
[377] nyams thag_mi rigs dpe skrun/

f.d: yang bdag gi ma de dpag tshad stong du lhung ba'i g.yang sa chen po na 'dug / zon ni mi shes/[378] g.yang sa la 'gro'o zhes sbron mkhan ni med/ de nas ltung ba dang sdug bsngal chen po myong zhing yar 'thon dus med pa'i g.yang sar lhung la khad 'dug na/ shin tu snying rje'o/ / de bzhin du lha dang mi dang lha ma yin gsum yang ngan song gi g.yang sa chen po na 'dug / zon sdig pa mi dge ba ni spong mi shes/ dge ba'i bshes gnyen gyis ni ma zin/ lhung ba dang ngan song gsum gyi sdug bsngal myong zhing 'thon par dka' bas na ci ste snying mi rje ste/ de rnams sdug bsngal dang bral bar 'dod pa'i snying rje bsgom mo//

Equally, were your own mother to be right in front of you, blind and near the edge of a precipice a thousand miles deep, unaware of her danger and without anyone who could lead her away or cry out, “Hey, be careful of the abyss!” and then she started wandering toward the edge, would you not experience very great compassion? It is certain that gods, demigods, and humans are all three standing at the edge of the abyss that is the lower states of suffering. Unaware of cause and effect, they do not know that to avoid falling they must give up unwholesome action and practice virtue. Because they do not benefit from the support of a Dharma teacher, they fall into and experience the three lower realms. As it is then so hard to get out of those states, how can you not feel great compassion for them, since they, too, were formerly your own mothers? Contemplate compassion thus and wish them all to be free of suffering.

d.div: [378] mi shes so/ mi rigs dpe skrun/

f.d: 'byongs pa'i tshad ni/ rang la gces par 'dzin pa'i gdos thag chod nas/ sems can thams cad la sdug bsngal dang bral bar 'dod pa'i blo tshig tsam ma yin pa skyes na snying rje 'byongs pa yin no/ /

Fifth, the [measure, or] gauge of accomplishment, is that compassion has been achieved when the shackles of cherishing oneself more than others have been cast off and when there is a real, rather than merely verbal, desire that all beings may be liberated from suffering.

de bsgoms pa'i yon tan dpag tu med de/ spyan ras gzigs kyi rtogs pa brjod pa las/
chos gcig yod na sangs rgyas kyi chos thams cad lag mthil du bzhag pa lta bur 'gyur te gcig gang zhe na/ 'di lta ste/ snying rje chen po'o/[379] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Sixth, the [qualities or] benefits of this practice are immeasurable. The Section Discussing the Realization of the Lord of the World [in the Perfectly Gathering the Qualities of Avalokiteśvara Sutra] says:
Were one thing like all enlightened qualities in the palm of your hand, what would it be? Great compassion![197]

d.div: [379] sde dge_238_bka'/ mdo sde/ zha_chos yang dag pa sdud pa'i mdo/ bam po/ 7_shog_84_na6
[197] Perfectly Gathering the Qualities [of Avalokiteśvara] Sutra (Dharmasaṃgītisūtra), Toh 238 Kangyur, mdo sde, zha, 84a6.

f.d:
chos yang dag par sdud pa'i mdo las kyang /
bcom ldan 'das 'di lta ste/ 'khor los sgyur ba'i rgyal po'i 'khor lo rin po che gang du mchis pa der dpung gi tshogs thams cad mchi'o/ / bcom ldan 'das de bzhin du byang chub sems dpa'i snying rje chen po gang du mchis pa der sangs rgyas kyi chos thams cad mchi'o/[380]/ zhes gsungs so/ /

The Perfectly Gathering the Qualities [of Avalokiteśvara] Sutra says:
O Blessed One! It is like this: wherever the precious wheel of the universal monarch goes, it is automatically accompanied by all his attendant hosts. O Buddha! Wherever the great compassion of the bodhisattva goes, all enlightened qualities accompany it.[198]

d.div: [380] gong mtshungs/ chos yang dag pa sdud pa'i mdo/ bam po/ 7_shog_84_na7

f.d:
de bzhin gshegs pa'i gsang ba'i mdo las kyang /
gsang ba'i bdag po thams cad mkhyen pa'i ye shes de ni snying rje'i rtsa ba las byung ba yin no/[381] / zhes gsungs so//

Also, it says in the Sutra of the Tathāgata’s Secrets:
O master of the secret teaching [Vajrapāṇi]! The root of pristine awareness that knows everything lies in compassion.[199]

d.div: [381] de bzhin gshegs pa'i gsang ba'i mdo ngos 'dzin ma thub mod/ lung 'di sde dge_494_bka'/ rgyud/ tha_rnam snang mngon byang gi rgyud/ bam po/ 7_shog_153_na5_nang bzhugs/
[199] The Sutra of the Tathāgata’s Secrets has not been found. However, this quotation was found in the Enlightenment of Vairocana (Vairocanābhisaṃbodhi), Toh 494 Kangyur, rgyud, tha, 143a5.

f.d: de ltar byams pas sems can rnams bde ba thob par 'dod cing / snying rjes sdug bsngal dang bral bar 'dod tsa na/ rang gcig pu zhi bde thob par mi spro ste/ sems can gyi don du sangs rgyas thob par dga' bas zhi ba la chags pa'i gnyen por 'gyur ba yin no/ /

As taught above, loving kindness is the wish for the happiness of all beings, and compassion is the wish for them all to be free from suffering. When these are present, a person can no longer find contentment in striving solely for the happiness of personal peace /106/ and is joyful at the prospect of attaining buddhahood so as to benefit all beings. Therefore love and compassion constitute the remedy to clinging to the well-being of mere peace.

de ltar na byams snying rje rgyud la skyes pas/ rang las gzhan gces par 'dzin tsa na/ ji skad du/
rang rgyud rtogs pa'i sdug bsngal gyis/ / gang zhig gzhan gyi sdug bsngal kun/ / yang dag zad par kun nas 'dod/ / skyes bu de ni mchog yin no/[382] / zhes gsungs pa ltar skyes bu mchog gi blo skyes pa yin te/ dper na bram ze sbyin pa chen po lta bu'o/ /

Once loving kindness and compassion have arisen, others will be cherished more than oneself. It is said:
Someone who, on the basis of his own suffering, aspires to totally eradicate the entire suffering all beings, that person is most excellent.[200] Among those who have become such “excellent beings” were the brahman Mahādatta and so forth.

d.div: [382] sde dge_3947_bstan/ dbu ma/ khi_dpal mar me mdzad ye shes/ byang chub lam sgron/ sh+loka_5_shog_238_ba2
[200] In Atiśa, Lamp for the Path to Awakening (Bodhipathapradīpa) verse 5, Toh 3947 Tengyur, dbu ma, kha, 238b2.

f.d: dam chos yid bzhin gyi nor bu thar pa rin po che'i rgyan las/ byams pa dang snying rje bstan pa'i le'u ste bdun pa'o// //
This concludes the seventh chapter, concerning love and compassion, from this Ornament of Precious Liberation, a Wish-Fulfilling Gem of Sublime Dharma.
(byang chub tu sems bskyed pa'i chos rnams bshad pa/)
8. Taking Refuge

da ni sangs rgyas sgrub pa'i thabs mi shes pa'i gnyen por/ byang chub mchog tu sems bskyed pa'i chos rnams bshad par bya ste/[383] sdom ni/
rten dang ngo bo dbye ba dang / / dmigs pa rgyu dang blang yul dang / / cho ga phan yon nyes dmigs dang / / 'chor rgyu bcos thabs bslab bya ste/ / bcu dang gnyis po 'di dag gis/ / byang chub mchog gi sems bskyed bsdus/ / zhes pa'o//

Now, as an antidote to counter ignorance pertaining to the means for attaining buddhahood, I present the factors associated with generating bodhicitta. For this, the synopsis is the following:
The development of supreme bodhicitta is covered through twelve topics: basis, nature, different types, aim, causes, source from which the vow is taken, ceremony, benefits, failings, causes for breakage, methods of restoration, and instructions.

d.div: [383] ma dper le'u 'di'i dbur/ skyes bu de ni mchog yin no/ /zhes pa byung yang mi rigs dpe skrun khang du mi byung ba bzhin 'dir bcos/

d.i: First topic: The basis for cultivation of bodhicitta

f.d: de la dang po byang chub mchog tu sems bskyed pa'i rten gyi gang zag ni/ theg pa chen po'i rigs dang ldan pa dang / dkon mchog gsum la skyabs su song ba dang / so so thar pa'i sdom pa ris bdun gang rung gcig dang ldan pa dang / smon pa'i sems bskyed pa rnams ni/ 'jug pa'i sems bskyed kyi rten yin la/ dkon mchog gsum la skyabs su song ba man chad dang ldan pa ni/ smon pa'i sems bskyed kyi rten gyi gang zag yin no/ /

First, the sentient beings that constitute a suitable basis for the cultivation of bodhicitta are those who: (1) are endowed with lineage toward Mahayana, (2) have taken refuge in the three most precious refuges, (3) have taken one of the seven classes of prātimokṣa vows, and (4) have developed the aspiring aspect of bodhicitta. Whereas to have taken refuge in the three precious refuges is the minimum requirement for a life becoming a suitable basis for aspiration bodhicitta, the above four conditions make that life also a proper basis for cultivating engaged bodhicitta.

de ci'i phyir zhe na/ 'jug pa bskyed pa la smon pa sngon du 'gro dgos par byang chub sems dpa'i sa las bshad pa dang /[384] smon pa'i sngon du skyabs 'gro dgos par byang chub lam sgron las bshad pa dang / yang 'jug pa'i rten du so so thar pa'i sdom pa dgos par byang chub lam sgron las bshad pa dang / so so thar pa'i sdom pa len pa la yang / skyabs 'gro dgos par chos mngon pa mdzod las bshad pa dang / theg pa chen po'i rigs med par byang chub mchog tu sems bskyed kyang mi skye bar byang chub sems dpa'i sa las bshad pa ste/ des na de dag thams cad 'brel zhing tshogs dgos so/ / de la dang po bshad na/ spyir theg pa chen po'i rigs yod pa/ bye brag tu rigs sad pa cig dgos te/ rgyas par gong du bstan pa bzhin shes par bya'o//

Why is this? It is explained in Bodhisattva Levels that aspiration must precede actual practice, and it is explained in Lamp for the Path to Awakening that one needs to have taken refuge in order to develop aspirational [mind]. Furthermore, the latter text also states that you need one of the prātimokṣa vows as a foundation for the bodhisattva vow, and in the Treasury of Higher Knowledge it says that refuge is the basis on which the prātimokṣa vows are taken. Lastly, Bodhisattva Levels says that bodhicitta development cannot even occur in those who are not of the Mahayana type. /107/ Thus a combination of all these various factors must be present. The first point is that there needs to be the Mahayana potential in general, and more particularly that this needs to have been awakened.[201] These points can be understood from the fuller explanation above.[202]

d.div: [384] 'jug pa byed pa la/ dpal spungs/ 'jug pa skyed pa/ mi rigs dpe skrun/
[201] The Beijing and Palpung texts add “for there to be practice [bodhicitta].”
[202] This fuller explanation is found in chapter 1, on the essence of buddhahood.

f.d: le'u brgyad pa/ skyabs su 'gro zhing sdom pa bzung ba/

don gnyis pa skyabs 'gro bshad na/ skyabs su 'gro sa 'di yang 'jig rten gyi drag rtsal can tshangs pa dang / khyab 'jug dang / ma hA de ba la sogs pa'am/ rang rang gi yul gyi ri'am/ brag gam/ mtsho'am/ ljon shing la sogs pa la gnas pa'i lha klu mthu bo che rnams la skyabs su 'gro bar bya'am zhe na/ de kun gyis kyang skyabs mi thub pas skyabs gnas ma yin te/ ji skad du mdo las/
'jig rten rnams ni ri dang ni/ / nags tshal dang ni mchod gnas kyi/ / kun dga' dang ni rdo ba dang / / ljon shing lha la skyabs 'gro ba/ / skyabs de gtso bo ma yin zhing /[385] / zhes gsungs so/ /

d.div: [385] sde dge_292_bka'/ mdo sde/ sha_mdo chen po rgyal mtshan dam pa/ shog_267_na3
[203] Great Sutra of the Supreme Victory (Dhvajāgranāmamahāsūtra), Toh 293 Kangyur, mdo sde, sha, 267a3.

f.d:
'o na pha ma gnyis dang gnyen grogs la sogs pa rang la brtse zhing phan par dga' ba rnams la skyabs su 'gro'am zhe na/ des kyang skyabs su mi thub ste/ 'jam dpal rnam par rol pa'i mdo las/
pha ma khyod kyi skyabs ma yin/ / mdza' bshes rtsa lag rnams kyang min/ / de dag gis ni khyod bor nas/ / ji ltar 'dod pa bzhin du 'gro[386] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Should you then perhaps seek refuge in your parents, friends, relatives, and so forth—those beings who care about you and are glad to help? In fact, these cannot be a refuge either. It says in the Sutra of the Play of Mañjuśrī:
Parents are not your refuge; neither are loved ones or relatives. Subject to their own wishes, they abandon you and go where they please.[204]

d.div: [386] sde dge_96_bka'/ mdo sde/ kha_'jam dpal rnam par rol ba'i mdo/ bam po/ 2_shog_237_na1
[204] Mañjuśrīvikrīḍitasūtra, Toh 96 Kangyur, mdo sde, kha, 237a1.

f.d:
de kun gyis skyabs su mi thub pa ci'i phyir zhe na/ skyabs thub pa ni kho rang 'jigs pa las thar pa sdug bsngal med pa zhig dgos te/ de kun yang 'jigs pa las ma thar zhing / sdug bsngal dang bcas pa'i phyir ro/ / des na sdug bsngal las gtan du thar pa sangs rgyas las med/ sangs rgyas sgrub pa'i lam chos las med/ chos byed pa'i grogs po dge 'dun las med pas khong gsum la skyabs su 'gro bar bya'o/ / de ltar yang /
'jigs gyur 'jigs pa sel mdzad cing / / skyabs med skyob pa'i sangs rgyas dang / / chos dang tshogs mchog dge 'dun la/ / de ring skyabs su 'gro bar gyis/[387] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Why are none of these able to provide refuge? Because to constitute a refuge, there must be no fear [of samsara] and there must be liberation from its sufferings. None of the above has transcended fear, and they are still subject to suffering. Other than buddhas, no one is definitively liberated from suffering. Other than Dharma, there is no way to achieve buddhahood. Other than the Sangha, there are none who can help us practice Dharma. Hence refuge should be sought in those three. It is said:
Today, take your refuge in the Buddha, in the Dharma, and in the supreme community, the Sangha, for it is they who can dispel fear in the fearful and it is they who can protect the unprotected.[205]

d.div: [387] gong mtshungs/ 'jam dpal rnam par rol ba'i mdo/ bam po/ 2_shog_237_na2
[205] Sutra of the Play of Manjuśrī (Mañjuśrīvikrīḍitasūtra), Toh 96 Kangyur, mdo sde, kha, 237a2.

f.d:
'o na khong la skyob pa'i nus pa mnga' yang / bdag gis skyabs su phyin pas skyob nges sam snyam na the tshom mi za ste/ mdo sde mya ngan 'das chen las/
dkon mchog gsum la skyabs song ba/ / 'jigs pa med pa thob par 'gyur/[388] / zhes gsungs so//

Since they do possess the ability to protect, do not let yourself be devoured by doubt, wondering, “But can they really protect me once I have taken refuge in them?” /108/ The Great [Passing into] Nirvana Sutra says:
One who has taken refuge in the Three Jewels will attain fearlessness.[206]

d.div: [388] sde dge_119_bka'/ mdo sde/ nya_mya ngan las 'das pa chen po'i mdo/ le'u/ 4_shog_120_na7
[206] Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra (longer version), Toh 119 Kangyur, mdo sde, nya, 120a7.

f.d:
des na de gsum la skyabs su 'gro ba 'chad pa la/ sdom ni/
dbye ba rten dang yul dang dus/ / bsam pa cho ga byed pa'i las/ / bslab bya dang ni phan yon te/ / don rnams dgu yis skyabs 'gro bsdus/[389] / zhes pa'o//

The synopsis explaining refuge in those three is:
Taking refuge is summarized through nine topics: categories, basis, source, duration, motivation, ceremony, function, instruction, and benefits.

d.div: [389] don rnam/ dpal spungs/

f.d: de la dang po skyabs 'gro'i dbye ba ni gnyis te/ thun mong gi skyabs 'gro dang / khyad par gyi skyabs 'gro'o/ /
First, there are two different categories of refuge: general and particular.

rten gyi gang zag la yang gnyis las/ thun mong ba'i rten gyi gang zag ni/ 'khor ba'i sdug bsngal gyis 'jigs shing / dkon mchog gsum la lhar 'dzin pa rnams so/ / khyad par can gyi rten gyi gang zag ni/ theg pa chen po'i rigs can lha mi'i lus rnam par dag pa thob pa rnams so/ /

Second, there are two types of person who form a basis for taking refuge: (1) those who constitute the general basis: people who fear samsara’s sufferings and who conceive of the three precious refuges as deities, and (2) those who constitute the particular basis: people of Mahayana potential who have a relatively pure human or divine existence.

yul la yang gnyis las/ thun mong ba'i yul 'chad pa la/ sangs rgyas dkon mchog ni/ spangs pa dang / ye shes dang / che ba'i bdag nyid phun sum tshogs pa dang ldan pa'i sangs rgyas bcom ldan 'das so/ / chos dkon mchog la yang gnyis las/ bstan pa'i chos ni gsung rab yan lag bcu gnyis so/ / rtogs pa'i chos ni lam gyi bden pa dang / 'gog pa'i bden pa'o/ / dge 'dun dkon mchog la gnyis las/ so so'i skye bo'i dge 'dun ni/ dge slong rnam par dag pa bzhi yan chad tshogs pa yin la/ 'phags pa'i dge 'dun ni/ skyes bu zung bzhi gang zag ya brgyad po dag go/

Third, there are also two sources of refuge: 1. The general source: The most precious Buddha is the Blessed One, awakened and complete, who has the most excellent purity, pristine awareness, and greatness of nature. The most precious Dharma has two aspects: the Dharma of teachings, comprising the twelve branches of [the Buddha’s] supreme speech, and the Dharma as realization, comprising the truths of cessation and the path. The most precious Sangha is also twofold: the Sangha composed of worldly people, as a gathering of four or more full monks (bhikṣu) who have properly maintained their vows; and the most excellent Sangha, as the eight types of beings belonging to the four stages of result.[207]

d.div: [207] The “four stages of result” are stream-enterer, once-returner, nonreturner, and arhat.

f.d: khyad par gyi yul ni/ /mdun na bzhugs pa'i yul dang / mngon par rtogs pa'i yul dang / de kho na nyid kyi yul dang gsum mo/ / de la mdun na bzhugs pa'i yul ni/ sangs rgyas ni de bzhin gshegs pa'i sku gzugs/ chos ni theg pa chen po'i po ti/ dge 'dun ni byang chub sems dpa'i dge 'dun/ mngon par rtogs pa'i yul ni/ sangs rgyas sku gsum gyi bdag nyid can no// chos ni dam pa'i chos zhi ba dang mya ngan las 'das pa'o/[390] / dge 'dun ni sa chen po la gnas pa'i byang chub sems dpa'o/ / de kho na nyid kyi yul gyi dbang du byas na/ skyabs su 'gro ba'i yul ni sangs rgyas nyag cig yin no/ /

2. The special source: This is explained as the source actually present, the source that is direct realization, and the ultimate source. For the source actually present, the Buddha is an image of the Tathāgata, the Dharma is the Mahayana scriptures, and the Sangha is the bodhisattva sangha. For the source in terms of direct realization, the Buddha is the one possessing the nature of the three bodies, the Dharma is the sublime Dharma of peace and nirvana, and the Sangha is bodhisattvas who have attained the levels of sublime realization. The ultimate source, in terms of ultimate essence, is the Buddha alone.

d.div: [390] zhi ba mya ngan las 'das pa'o/ /dpal spungs/

f.d:
de ltar yang theg pa chen po rgyud bla ma las/
dam pa'i don du 'gro ba yi/ / skyabs ni sangs rgyas nyag gcig yin/[391] / zhes gsungs so/ /

About this the Uttaratantra says: /109/
In ultimate terms the refuge for beings is the Buddha and the Buddha alone.[208]

d.div: [391] sde dge_4024_bstan/ sems tsam/ phi_byams mgon/ rgyud bla ma/ skabs/ 1_sh+loka_21_shog_55_ba6
[208] Maitreya, Uttaratantra 1:21, Toh 4024 Tengyur, sems tsam, phi, 55b6.

f.d:
'o na sangs rgyas kyis gtan gyi skyabs thub pa ci'i phyir zhe na/
thub pa chos kyi sku can phyir/ / tshogs kyang de yi mthar thug phyir/[392] / zhes gsungs te/ thub pa rnams skye 'gag med pa/[393] rnam par byang ba/ 'dod chags dang bral ba ste/ chos kyi sku can yin pa'i phyir na yang dam pa'i skyabs yin la/ theg pa gsum gyi tshogs kyang chos sku rnam par dag pa mthar thug pa thob pas mthar phyin par 'gyur ba'i phyir dam pa'i skyabs yin no//

Why is the Buddha capable of providing the [only] totally dependable source of refuge?
Because the Sage possesses the dharmakāya and in terms of the Sangha he is the ultimate sangha.[209] Sages (muni), free from generation and cessation, totally pure, and without desire, are the highest refuge because they possess the dharmakāya and because they are the ultimate achievement of the Sangha of the three vehicles, having attained the dharmakāya, the ultimate conclusion of total purity.

d.div: [392] gong mtshungs/ rgyud bla ma/ skabs/ 1_sh+loka_20_shog_55_ba6
[393] 'gags/ dpal spungs/
[209] Ibid.

f.d:
'o na chos dang dge 'dun gnyis gtan gyi skyabs ma yin nam zhe na/ rgyud bla ma las/
chos rnam gnyis dang 'phags pa'i tshogs/ / gtan gyi skyabs mchog ma yin no/[394] / zhes gsungs so/ /

This being the case, are the Dharma and the Sangha lasting refuges or not? The Uttaratantra says:
The two aspects of Dharma and the assembly of noble ones are not the supreme lasting refuge.[210]

d.div: [394] sde dge_4024_bstan/ sems tsam/ phi_byams mgon/ rgyud bla ma/ skabs/ 1_sh+loka_20_shog_55_ba6

f.d: de dag ci'i phyir gtan gyi skyabs gnas ma yin zhe na/ chos la gnyis yod pa las/ bstan pa'i chos ni ming gi tshogs dang yi ge'i tshogs yin pas/ lam bgrod zin nas gzings ltar spang bya yin pas/ gtan gyi skyabs ma yin pa'o/ / rtogs pa'i chos la yang gnyis las/ lam gyi bden pa ni 'dus byas yin pas mi rtag ste/ bslu ba'i chos can yin pa'i phyir skyabs ma yin no/ / 'gog pa'i bden pa ni/ nyan thos pa'i lugs kyi mar me shi ba ltar rgyun chad du 'dod pas/ med pa'i phyir gtan gyi skyabs ma yin pa'o/ / dge 'dun ni kho rang yang 'khor bas 'jigs nas sangs rgyas la skyabs su song ba yin te/ 'jigs bcas yin pas gtan gyi skyabs ma yin no/ /

Why is it that they are not a lasting source of refuge? Of the two types of Dharma, the Dharma as teachings, being a collection of terms and an assembly of letters, is something to be abandoned once it has served its purpose, like a vehicle once the journey is done. Hence it is not a lasting refuge. As for the two aspects of Dharma as realization, the truth of the path is not a refuge because it is by its very nature unreliable, being impermanent on account of being a composite creation. The truth of cessation is not a lasting refuge because, according to the śrāvakas, it is a nonexistence—the end of a continuum—like the extinction of a flame. As for the Sangha, they themselves take refuge in the Buddha through fear of samsara and cannot constitute a supreme and lasting refuge because of having that fear.

de ltar yang rgyud bla ma las/[395]
spang phyir bslu ba'i chos can phyir/ / med phyir 'jigs dang bcas pa'i phyir/ / chos rnam gnyis dang 'phags pa'i tshogs/ / gtan gyi skyabs mchog ma yin no/[396] / zhes gsungs so//

The Uttaratantra says:
Because it is to be abandoned, it’s unreliable, it’s nonexistent, and it’s endowed with fear: the two aspects of Dharma and the assembly of noble ones are not the supreme lasting refuge.[211]

d.div: [395] de ltar na/ mi rigs dpe skrun/
[396] sde dge_4024_bstan/ sems tsam/ phi_byams pa mgon po/ rgyud bla ma/ skabs/ 1_sh+loka_20_shog_55_ba6
[211] Ibid.

f.d:
des na slob dpon thogs med kyi zhal nas kyang /
mi zad pa'i skyabs/ rtag pa'i skyabs/ g.yung drung gi skyabs/ dam pa'i skyabs ni gcig nyid de/ 'di lta ste/ de bzhin gshegs pa dgra bcom pa yang dag par rdzogs pa'i sangs rgyas so/[397] / zhes gsungs so//

Therefore Master Asaṅga said:
The inexhaustible refuge, the permanent refuge, the eternal refuge, the most elevated refuge is one and one only. What is it? It is the Tathāgata, the defeater of the enemy, the totally and utterly perfect Buddha.[212]

d.div: [397] sde dge_4025_bstan/ sems tsam/ phi_'phags pa thogs med/ rgyud bla ma'i rnam bshad/ shog_84_ba7
[212] Detailed Explanation of the Uttaratantra (Mahāyānottaratantraśāstravyākhyā), Toh 4025 Tengyur, sems tsam, phi, 84b7.

f.d:
'o na gong du skyabs gsum du gsungs pa dang 'gal lo zhe na/ de ni gdul bya drang ba'i thabs su byung ba yin te/[398] thar pa chen po'i mdo las/
mdor na skyabs ni gcig ste thabs kyis ni gsum mo/[399] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Well, then, does this not contradict what has been said above about the three refuges? The latter originated as a skillful means for guiding those training as Buddhists. The Great Liberation Sutra says:
In brief, the refuge is one, but in terms of method [it] is three.[213] /110/

d.div: [398] drangs ba'i/ dpal spungs/
[399] sde dge_264_bka'/ mdo sde/ 'a_thar pa chen po'i mdo/ le'u/ 12_shog_229_na3
[213] Mahāmokṣasūtra, Toh 264 Kangyur, mdo sde, ’a, 229a3.

f.d:
thabs kyis gsum du ji ltar bzhag ce na/ theg pa chen po rgyud bla ma las/
ston pa bstan pa bslab don gyis/ / theg pa gsum dang byed gsum dang / / mos pa rnams kyi dbang byas nas/ / skyabs gsum rnam par bzhag pa yin/[400] / zhes gsungs te/ yon tan gsum dang / theg pa gsum dang / byed pa gsum dang / mos pa gsum gyi dbang du byas nas bzhag pa yin no/ /

How are these three refuges presented as skillful means? The Uttaratantra says:
The three refuges are presented as teacher, teaching, and those training, in terms of the three vehicles, three activities, and in accordance with [diverse] aspirations.[214] Thus the refuges are presented in terms of three qualities, three capacities, three modes of action, and three types of aspiration:

d.div: [400] sde dge_4020_bstan/ sems tsam/ phi_byams pa mgon po/ rgyud bla ma/ skabs/ 1_sh+loka_19_shog_55_ba5
[214] Maitreya, Uttaratantra 1:19, Toh 4024 Tengyur, sems tsam, phi, 55b5.

f.d: de yang ston pa'i yon tan bstan pa'i don du/ byang chub sems dpa'i theg pa'i gang zag dang / sangs rgyas la mchog tu bya ba byed par mos pa rnams kyi dbang du byas na sangs rgyas la skyabs yin te/[401] rkang gnyis rnams kyi mchog sangs rgyas la skyabs su mchi'o/ /zhes so/ /

(1) Emphasizing the qualities of the teacher, those of bodhisattva capacity, as well as those who aspire to actions that principally elevate the Buddha, take refuge in the Buddha saying, “I take refuge in the Buddha, the most sublime human.”

d.div: [401] byas nas/ dpal spungs/ mi rigs dpe skrun/

f.d: ston pa'i yon tan bstan pa'i don du/[402] rang rgyal gyi theg pa'i gang zag dang / chos la mchog tu bya ba byed par mos pa rnams kyi dbang du byas na chos skyabs yin te/ 'dod chags dang bral ba rnams kyi mchog chos la skyabs su mchi'o/ /zhes pa'o/ /

(2) Emphasizing the qualities of the teachings, beings of pratyekabuddha capacity, and those aspiring to act in a way that principally elevates the Dharma, take their refuge in the Dharma saying, “I take refuge in the Dharma, the most sublime of all that transcends desire and attachment.”

d.div: [402] bstan/ mi rigs dpe skrun/

f.d: slob pa'i yon tan bstan pa'i don du/ nyan thos kyi theg pa'i gang zag dang / dge 'dun la mchog tu bya ba byed pa'i dbang du byas na dge 'dun skyabs yin te/ tshogs rnams kyi mchog dge 'dun la skyabs su mchi'o/ /zhes pa'o/ /

(3) Emphasizing the qualities of the trainees, those of śrāvaka capacity, and those who aspire to act in a way principally focused on the Sangha, take refuge in the Sangha saying, “I take refuge in the Sangha, the most sublime of communities.”

de ltar don rnam pa gsum gyis gang zag drug gi dbang du byas nas/[403] skyabs gsum rnam par bzhag pa 'di ni/ bcom ldan 'das kyis kun rdzob tsam du sems can rnams theg pa la rim gyis gzhug pa'i don du gsungs pa yin no/ /

Thus the above three points present the three refuges in terms of six types of person. The noble Buddha has taught that these are mere conventional realities, designed to help beings progress gradually through their respective courses of training.

d.div: [403] dpal spungs dpar mar/ drug ces pa mi byung /

f.d: dus la yang gnyis las/ thun mong ba'i dus ni/ dus 'di nas bzung nas ji srid 'tsho'i bar du skyabs su 'gro ba'o/ / khyad par can ni/ dus 'di nas bzung nas ji srid snying po byang chub la mchis kyi bar du skyabs su 'gro ba yin no/ /

Fourth, there are two possible durations. The general duration is to take refuge from the time [of the ceremony] onward for as long as one lives. The special duration is to take refuge from that time onward until the essence, enlightenment, is attained.
bsam pa la yang gnyis las/ thun mong ba ni/ rang gcig pu'i sdug bsngal ba ma bzod pa'i bsam pa'o/[404] / khyad par can ni/ gzhan gyi sdug bsngal ma bzod pa'i bsam pas so/ /
Fifth, there are two possible motivations. The general motivation is to consider personal suffering unbearable. The special motivation is to consider others’ sufferings unbearable.

d.div: [404] sdug bsngal ma bzod/ dpal spungs/ mi rigs dpe skrun/

f.d:
cho ga la yang gnyis las/ thun mong gi cho ga ni dang po slob mas slob dpon la gsol ba gdab/ de nas slob dpon gyis dkon mchog gsum gyi rten gyi spyan sngar mchod pa 'bul ba sngon du btang nas sam/ yang na de ma 'dzom na dkon mchog gsum nam mkha' la dmigs te/ yid kyis phyag dang mchod pa phul nas/[405] slob dpon gyi rjes su slob mas 'di skad brjod par bya ste/[406] [407]
sangs rgyas dang byang chub sems dpa' thams cad bdag la dgongs su gsol/ slob dpon bdag la dgongs su gsol/ bdag ming 'di zhes bgyi ba dus 'di nas bzung nas ji srid 'tsho'i bar du/[408] rkang gnyis rnams kyi mchog / sangs rgyas la skyabs su mchi'o/ / 'dod chags dang bral ba rnams kyi mchog / chos la skyabs su mchi'o/ / tshogs rnams kyi mchog / dge 'dun la skyabs su mchi'o/ / zhes snying thag pa nas lan gsum bzlas pa'o/ /

Sixth, there are two forms of ceremony, general and special. For the general ceremony, the refuge seeker first requests refuge from the teacher. Then the teacher either makes offerings to the three precious refuges as a prelude to the ceremony or, when there are no representations present, visualizes them in space and makes mental homage and offerings. /111/ Then the refuge seeker repeats the following three times, after the teacher, with utmost sincerity:
All buddhas and bodhisattvas, please heed me, I pray. Master, please heed me, I pray. I, [so-and-so] by name, take refuge from now until I reach the essence—enlightenment—in the Buddha, the most sublime of all humans, in the Dharma, the most sublime of all that transcends desire, and in the Sangha, the most sublime of communities.

d.div: [405] phul la/ dpal spungs/ mi rigs dpe skrun/
[406] ma dper/ slob dpon gyis/ zhes byed sgra byung yang dpal spungs dang mi rigs dpe skrun khang ltar 'brel sgrar bcos/
[407] 'di skad ces/ mi rigs dpe skrun/

[408] ji srid 'tsho'i bar du/ dpal spungs/ ma dper/ 'dir ji srid byang chub snying po la mchis kyi bar du/ zhes byung yang 'di thun mong gi skyabs 'gro bzung ba'i cho ga'i skabs yin pas dpal spungs dpar mar byung ba de dag pas de bzhin du bcos/

f.d: khyad par can gyi cho ga ni/ sbyor ba dang / dngos gzhi dang / rjes gsum las/ dang po ni/ dge ba'i bshes gnyen bsten du rung ba la/ maN+Dal me tog dang bcas pa phul la/ gsol ba gdab/ de nas dge ba'i bshes gnyen des/ slob ma de theg pa chen po'i rigs dang ldan zhing / snod ldan du 'dug na khas blangs shing nub dang po dkon mchog gi rten bkram/ mchod pa bshams/[409] skyabs su song ba'i phan yon dang / ma song ba'i nyes dmigs bshad do/ /

The special ceremony is in three parts: a preparation, the actual ceremony, and a conclusion. The preparation involves first offering a mandala, together with flowers, to an appropriate preceptor, after which the preceptor is requested to confer refuge. Provided the supplicant is a suitable person and someone with Mahayana potential, the preceptor, having accepted the request, will, on the first evening, set up representations of the three precious refuges, arrange offerings, and explain both the benefits of taking refuge and the shortcomings of not doing so.

d.div: [409] bsham/ dpal spungs/

f.d:
nub gnyis pa la dngos gzhi'i cho ga byas te/[410] dang po mdun na bzhugs pa'i yul la dkon mchog dngos kyi 'du shes bskyed nas/ phyag dang mchod pa phul la/ slob dpon gyi rjes su 'di skad brjod do/ /
sangs rgyas dang byang chub sems dpa' thams cad bdag la dgongs su gsol/ slob dpon bdag la dgongs su gsol/ bdag ming 'di zhes bgyi ba/ dus 'di nas bzung nas ji srid byang chub snying po la mchis kyi bar du/ rkang gnyis rnams kyi mchog / sangs rgyas bcom ldan 'das rnams la skyabs su mchi'o/ / 'dod chags dang bral ba rnams kyi mchog / zhi ba mya ngan las 'das pa'i chos rnams la skyabs su mchi'o/ / tshogs rnams kyi mchog / 'phags pa byang chub sems dpa' phyir mi ldog pa'i dge 'dun rnams la skyabs su mchi'o/ / zhes lan gsum brjod do/ /

The actual ceremony takes place on the second evening. The supplicant first cultivates the notion that the [symbols of refuge] on the shrine are the real presence of the most precious refuges, and then pays homage and makes prostrations to them. The following words are then repeated three times, after the preceptor:
All buddhas and bodhisattvas, please heed me, I pray. Master, please heed me, I pray. From this moment on, until the essence of enlightenment is reached, I, [so-and-so] by name, take my refuge in the buddhas, the blessed ones who are the most sublime humans. I take refuge in the Dharma that is peace and nirvana, the most sublime of all that is free from desire and attachment. I take refuge in the Sangha of realized bodhisattvas who are beyond turning back, the most sublime of communities.

d.div: [410] cho ga bya ste/ dpal spungs/ mi rigs dpe skrun/

f.d: de nas mngon par rtogs pa'i yul spyan drangs la/ mngon sum dang 'dra bar dmigs te/ phyag dang mchod pa phul la/ da ci byed khyed mkhyen snyam pa'i bsam pas/ gong ltar skyabs 'gro lan gsum bya'o//

Then, inviting the sources of refuge in terms of direct realization and imagining them to be really present, homage is paid to them and offerings made, thinking, “Whatever I do, you are aware of it.” Following this, the refuge prayer, as above, is repeated.

de nas de kho na nyid kyi yul la/ 'khor gsum yongs su dag pa'i tshul gyis phyag dang mchod pa phul la skyabs su 'gro ba ni/ chos thams cad gdod ma nas bdag med cing ci'i ngo bor yang ma grub pas/ sangs rgyas dang / chos dang / dge 'dun yang de bzhin du mthong bar bya ste/ de ni mi zad pa'i skyabs/ rtag pa'i skyabs/ g.yung drung gi skyabs yin no/ /

Next, in terms of the one-and-only essence as a source of refuge, homage is expressed, offerings are made, and refuge is taken in a way in which the three spheres[215] are totally pure. /112/ Since all phenomena have been, from the very beginning, without self and without any truly existing nature, the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha must be envisioned as also being thus. This is the inexhaustible refuge, the permanent refuge, the eternal refuge.

d.div: [215] See glossary. The idea here is that these actions are performed without perceiving any of the elements involved—object, agent, or act—to possess self-existence.

f.d:
de ltar yang ma dros pas zhus pa'i mdo las/
zang zing med pa'i sems kyis skyabs su song ba gang zhe na/ chos thams cad med par shes nas gzugs su ma yin/ mtshan du ma yin/ chos su ma yin par sangs rgyas yang dag par mthong ba ni/ sangs rgyas la skyabs su song ba'o/ / chos thams cad chos kyi dbyings kyi rjes su song bar mthong ba ni/ chos la skyabs su song ba'o/ / 'dus byas dang / 'dus ma byas gnyis su med par mthong ba ni/ dge 'dun la skyabs su song ba'o/[411] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Thus the Questions of Nāga King Anavatapta Sutra says:
What is it to have taken refuge with a mind free from pollution? By knowing all phenomena not to exist, by not envisioning them as being form, as possessing characteristics, or as being something, but by envisioning them as being totally pure awakened realities,[216] refuge has been taken in the Buddha. By envisioning all phenomena as following after dharmadhātu,[217] refuge has been taken in the Dharma. By envisioning them in a way that is nondual and without conceptual elaboration, refuge has been taken in the Sangha.[218]

d.div: [411] sde dge_156_bka'/ mdo sde/ pha_klu'i rgyal po ma dros pas zhus pa'i mdo/ shog_250_na7
[216] This is a gloss of the word buddha.
[217] Tib. chos kyi dbyings kyi rjes su song ba, conveys the idea of sharing the nature of the dharmadhātu.
[218] Anavataptanāgarājaparipṛcchāsūtra, Toh 156 Kangyur, mdo sde, pha, 250a7.

f.d: nub gsum pa la rjes kyi cho ga ste/ dkon mchog la gtang rag gi mchod pa 'bul ba'o/[412] /
On the third evening, there is the concluding ceremony, during which thanksgiving offerings are made to the most precious sources of refuge.

d.div: [412] gtong rag_dpal spungs/

f.d:
byed pa'i las ni/ mdo sde rgyan las/
'tshe ba dag ni thams cad dang / / ngan song dang ni thabs min dang / / 'jig tshogs theg pa dman pa las/ / de phyir skyabs kyi dam pa'o/[413] / zhes gsungs te/ de yang thun mong gi skyabs 'gros ni/ 'tshe ba thams cad dang / ngan song gsum dang / thabs ma yin pa dang / 'jig tshogs la lta ba rnams las skyob pa'o/ / khyad par can gyi skyabs 'gros ni/ theg pa dman pa man chad kun las skyob pa'o//

Seventh, concerning the function of refuge, the Ornament of Mahayana Sutras says:
It is the highest refuge because it protects from all sorts of harm, from the lower states, from unskillful action, from the ego-view of the perishable composite,[219] and from lesser vehicles.[220] The general refuge protects from all harms, from falling into the lower states, from ineffective courses of action, and from false beliefs about the self based on the perishable collection (the aggregates). The particular refuge protects from the lower paths as well.

d.div: [413] sde dge_4020_bstan/ sems tsam/ phi_byams pa mgon po/ mdo sde rgyan/ le'u/ 10_sh+loka_7_shog_9_na1

[219] The view of the “perishable collection” (’jig tshogs; satkāya) is the misconception that self as an individual truly exists. The term refers to mistaken views of one’s own existence and identity as real conceived on the basis of the perishable aggregates (skandha), one’s body and mind.
[220] Maitreya, Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra 10:7, Toh 4020 Tengyur, sems tsam, phi, 9a1.

f.d: bslab bya la/ spyi'i bslab bya gsum/ bye brag gi bslab bya gsum/ cha mthun gyi bslab bya gsum ste dgu yod do/ / de la dang po ni/ dus rtag tu dkon mchog mchod pa la brtson par bya zhing / tha na rang zas ci za ba'i phud kyis kyang mchod pa dang / srog dang / bya dga'i phyir yang dkon mchog mi spang ba dang / dkon mchog gi yon tan rjes su dran pa'i sgo nas yang dang yang du skyabs su 'gro ba la bslab bo/ /

Eighth, the instructions concerning refuge are ninefold: three common instructions, three particular instructions, and three specific instructions. The three instructions common [to all three refuges] are: (1) to strive at all times to make offerings to the three precious refuges, at least dedicating the first mouthful of food when eating; (2) to never abandon the three precious refuges even should this cost life itself or involve personal loss; and (3) to develop the habit of repeatedly calling to mind the qualities of these three most precious things and taking refuge in them.

bye brag gi bslab bya gsum las/ sangs rgyas la skyabs su song bas lha gzhan la skyabs su mi 'gro ba ste/ mdo mya ngan 'das chen las/
sangs rgyas dag la skyabs song ba/ / de ni yang dag dge bsnyen te/ / nam yang lha rnams gzhan dag la/ / skyabs su gsol bar mi 'gyur ro/[414] / zhes gsungs so/ /

The three particular instructions are: (1) Having taken refuge in the buddhas, refuge need no longer be sought in any other divinity. In the Great [Passing into] Nirvana Sutra it says:
The best of all those who love virtue are those who have taken refuge in the buddhas. They will never go soliciting refuge from other divinities.[221]

d.div: [414] sde dge_119_bka'/ mdo sde/ nya_mya ngan las 'das pa chen po'i mdo/ le'u/ 4_shog_120_na5
[221] Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra (longer version), Toh 119 Kangyur, mdo sde, nya, 120a5.

f.d:
chos la skyabs su song bas sems can rnams la rnam par 'tshe ba mi byed pa ste/ mdo las kyang /
dam pa'i chos la skyabs song na/ / gnod cing 'tshe ba'i sems dang bral/[415] / zhes gsungs so/ /

(2) Having taken refuge in the Dharma, harm should no longer be done to any sentient being. /113/ The sutra says:
Having taken refuge in the noble Dharma, a person is removed from a mentality of harm and violence.[222]

d.div: [415] gong mtshungs/ mya ngan las 'das pa chen po'i mdo/ le'u/ 4_shog_120_na6
[222] Ibid.

f.d:
dge 'dun la skyabs su song bas mu stegs can la mi bsten pa ste/[416] mdo las kyang /
dge 'dun la ni skyabs song bas/ / mu stegs can la phyogs mi 'gyur/[417]/ zhes gsungs so/ /
