f.d: dam chos yid bzhin gyi nor bu thar pa rin po che'i rgyan las/ sbyin pa'i pha rol tu phyin pa'i le'u ste bcu gnyis pa'o// //
This then concludes the twelfth chapter, presenting the perfection of generosity, in this Ornament of Precious Liberation, a Wish-Fulfilling Gem of Sublime Dharma.
le'u bcu gsum pa/ tshul khrims kyi pha rol tu phyin pa/
13. The Perfection of Moral Discipline

tshul khrims kyi pha rol tu phyin pa la/ sdom ni/
skyon yon rnam gnyis bstan pa dang / / ngo bo dang ni dbye ba dang / / phye ba so so'i mtshan nyid dang / / spel dang dag par bya ba dang / / 'bras bu dang ni don bdun gyis/ / tshul khrims pha rol phyin pa bsdus/ / zhes pa'o//

de la dang po bshad na/ gang zhig sbyin pa dang ldan yang tshul khrims dang mi ldan na/ des lha mi rnam par dag pa lta bu'i lus phun sum tshogs pa mi thob bo/ / de ltar yang dbu ma 'jug pa las/
skyes bu tshul khrims rkang pa chag gyur na/ / sbyin pas longs spyod ldan yang ngan 'gror ltung /[669]/ zhes gsungs so/ /

To explain the first point, reflections on the drawbacks of its absence and the benefits of its practice, if someone possesses the quality of generosity but lacks moral discipline, he will be unable to obtain the very best physical human or divine existence. In Entering the Middle Way, it says:
If a person has broken his limbs of moral discipline, he may obtain wealth through generosity but will fall into lower realms.[410]

d.div: [669] sde dge_3861_bstan/ dbu ma/ 'a_zla ba grags pa/ dbu ma 'jug pa/ sems bskyed/ 2_sh+loka_4_shog_202_ba3
[410] Candrakīrti, Madhyamakāvatāra 2:4ab, Toh 3861 Tengyur, dbu ma, ’a, 202b3.

f.d:
yang tshul khrims dang mi ldan na dam pa'i chos dang mi phrad do/ / de ltar yang tshul khrims dang ldan pa'i mdo las/
ji ltar mig med gzugs mthong mi 'gyur ba/ / de bzhin tshul khrims med na chos mi mthong /[670] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Further, if one who lacks moral discipline he will not encounter the Buddhadharma. The Sutra on Moral Discipline says:
Just as the blind cannot see form, so those without moral discipline will not see the Dharma.[411]

d.div: [670] sde dge_303_bka'/ mdo sde/ sa_tshul khrims yang dag par ldan pa'i mdo/ shog_127_ba2
[411] Śīlasaṃyuktasūtra, Toh 303 Kangyur, mdo sde, sa, 127b2.

f.d:
yang tshul khrims dang mi ldan na khams gsum 'khor ba las mi thar ro/ / de ltar yang mdo de nyid las/
ji ltar rkang med lam 'jug ga la nus/ / de bzhin tshul khrims med na thar mi 'gyur/[671] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Nor will those without moral discipline become free from existence within the three realms of samsara. That same sutra says:
How can the legless walk along a path? /159/ Likewise those without moral discipline cannot become liberated.[412]

d.div: [671] gong mtshungs/ tshul khrims yang dag par ldan pa'i mdo/ shog_127_ba2
[412] Ibid.

f.d:
yang tshul khrims dang mi ldan na sangs rgyas kyi lam ma tshang bas bla med kyi byang chub mi thob bo/ / de dag las ldog ste tshul khrims dang ldan na lus phun sum tshogs pa thob bo/[672] [673] / de ltar yang 'phags pa sdud pa las/
khrims kyis dud 'gro'i 'gro ba du ma'i ngo bo dang / / mi khom brgyad spong de yis dal ba rtag tu rnyed/[674] / ces gsungs so/ /

Those lacking moral discipline also cannot attain enlightenment because their path to buddhahood is incomplete. In contrast, if someone has the qualities of moral discipline, he will attain the very best physical existence. The Verse Summary of the Perfection of Wisdom says:
Moral discipline eliminates the very nature of [what causes rebirth in] various animal forms and the eight unfavorable rebirths. Through it, a rebirth with freedoms is always encountered.[413]

d.div: [672] de las/ mi rigs dpe skrun/
[673] bzlog te/ dpal spungs/
[674] sde dge_13_bka'/ sher phyin/ ka_mdo sdud pa/ le'u/ 32_sh+loka_2_shog_19_ba2
[413] Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā, Toh 13 Kangyur, sher phyin, ka, 19b2.

f.d:
yang tshul khrims dang ldan na/ bde legs thams cad kyi gzhi things pa yin no/ / de ltar yang bshes spring las/
khrims ni rgyu dang mi rgyu'i sa bzhin du/ / yon tan kun gyi gzhi rten legs par gsungs/[675] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Further, if you possess moral discipline, you lay the very foundation of all that is excellent and joyous. The Letter to a Friend says:
Moral discipline is taught as being the very foundation and basis for every quality, just as the earth is the basis for all animate and inanimate life.[414]

d.div: [675] sde dge_4182_bstan/ spring yig_nge _mgon po klu sgrub/ bshes spring / sh+loka_7_shog_41_na2
[414] Nāgārjuna, Suhṛllekha 7, Toh 4182 Tengyur, spring yig, nge, 41a2.

f.d:
yang tshul khrims dang ldan na zhing sa gshin pa dang 'dra ste/ de la brten nas yon tan gyi lo thog thams cad 'phel bar 'gyur ba yin no/ / de ltar yang dbu ma 'jug pa las/
yon tan tshul khrims zhing du rnam 'phel na/ / 'bras bu nyer spyod chad pa med par 'gyur/[676] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Also, possessing moral discipline is like owning a fertile field from which crop after crop of good qualities can be harvested. Therefore it says in Entering the Middle Way:
Because good qualities develop specifically on the field of moral discipline, the fruition draws nearer, inevitably.[415]

d.div: [676] sde dge_3861_bstan/ dbu ma/ 'a_zla ba grags pa/ dbu ma 'jug pa/ sems bskyed/ 2_sh+loka_6_shog_202_ba5
[415] Candrakīrti, Madhyamakāvatāra 2:6, Toh 3861 Tengyur, dbu ma, ’a, 202b5.

f.d:
yang tshul khrims dang ldan na ting nge 'dzin gyi sgo du ma yang skye'o/ / de ltar yang zla ba sgron ma'i mdo las/
nyon mongs med pa'i ting 'dzin myur thob ste/ / 'di ni tshul khrims rnam dag phan yon no/[677] / zhes gsungs so/ /

d.div: [677] sde dge_127_bka'/ mdo sde/ da_zla ba sgron ma'i mdo 'am ting nge 'dzin rgyal po'i mdo/ le'u/ 28_shog_89_na5
[416] A.k.a. King of Meditation Sutra (Samādhirājasūtra), Toh 127 Kangyur, mdo sde, da, 89a5.

f.d:
yang tshul khrims dang ldan na smon lam ci btab pa 'grub bo/ / de ltar yang yab sras mjal ba'i mdo las/
tshul khrims rnam dag gang bsrungs bas/ / smon lam thams cad 'grub par 'gyur/[678] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Also, if you have moral discipline, whatever prayers are made will be come to be fulfilled. Thus the Meeting of Father and Son Sutra says:
It is through properly maintained moral discipline that every prayer made comes true.[417]

d.div: [678] ma dper lung 'di yab sras mjal ba'i mdo las zhes drangs kyang / bka' 'gyur du mdo de'i mjug de ma thag tu bzhugs pa'i gang pos zhus pa'i mdor byung / sde dge_61_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ nga _gang pos zhus pa'i mdo/ le'u/ 3_shog_187_ba4

[417] This quotation does not seem to be from the Meeting of Father and Son Sutra but from the sutra that immediately follows it in the Kangyur, i.e., the Questions of Pūrṇa Sutra (Pūrṇaparipṛcchāsūtra), Toh 61 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, nga, 187b4.

f.d:
yang tshul khrims dang ldan na byang chub bsgrub par sla ba yin no/ / de ltar yang mdo de nyid las/
khrims gtsang phan 'dogs mang bas na/ / byang chub 'grub pa yongs mi dka'/[679] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Moreover, if you possess moral discipline, you will attain enlightenment more easily. The same sutra says:
Since purity of discipline brings so many benefits, it will not be difficult to achieve enlightenment.[418]

d.div: [679] sde dge_61_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ nga _gang pos zhus pa'i mdo/ le'u/ 3_shog_187_ba4
[418] Questions of Pūrṇa Sutra (Pūrṇaparipṛcchāsūtra), Toh 61 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs,nga, 187b4.

f.d:
de la sogs pa'i yon tan yod de/[680] ji skad du/ tshul khrims dang ldan pa'i mdo las/
tshul khrims ldan pa sangs rgyas 'byung dang phrad/ / tshul khrims ldan pa rgyan rnams kun gyi mchog / tshul khrims ldan pa dga' ba kun gyi gnas/ / tshul khrims ldan pa 'jig rten kun gyis bstod/[681]/ ces pa la sogs pa gsungs so//

d.div: [680] yon tan sna tshogs yod de/ dpal spungs/
[681] sde dge_304_bka'/ mdo sde/ sa_tshul khrims dang ldan pa'i mdo/ shog_127_na7
[419] Śīlasaṃyuktasūtra, Toh 303 Kangyur, mdo sde, sa, 127a7.

f.d:
tshul khrims kyi ngo bo ni yon tan bzhi ldan yin te/ ji skad du byang sa las/
yon tan bzhi dang ldan pa ni tshul khrims kyi ngo bo nyid yin par rig par bya ste/ bzhi gang zhe na/ pha rol las legs par yang dag par blangs pa dang / bsam pa shin tu rnam par dag pa dang / nyams par gyur na phyir gso bar byed pa dang / mi nyams par bya ba'i phyir gus pa bskyed nas dran pa nye bar gnas pa'o/[682] / zhes gsungs te/

The second, the nature of moral discipline is that it is characterized by four qualities. For example, Bodhisattva Levels states:
That which is endowed with the four qualities should be understood to be the essential nature of moral discipline. What are these four? /160/ (1) It has been adopted from another, most properly and purely; (2) the intention is extremely pure in every respect; (3) it is rectified if it deteriorates, and (4) to prevent its deterioration, it is respected and ever borne in mind.[420]

d.div: [682] sde dge_4037_bstan/ sems tsam/ wi_'phags pa thogs med/ byang sa/ shog_74_na3
[420] Asaṅga, Bodhisattvabhūmi, Toh 4037 Tengyur, sems tsam, wi, 74a3.

f.d: yon tan bzhi po 'di dag kyang mdor bsdus na/ len pa dang bsrung ba gnyis so/ / de la len pa ni tshig dang po'o/ / bsrung ba ni tshig phyi ma gsum mo//
The four qualities mentioned above can be summed up as covering two main areas: the correct adoption of moral discipline, which relates to the first, and its proper maintenance—the latter three.

tshul khrims la dbye na gsum ste/ sdom pa'i tshul khrims dang / dge ba chos sdud pa'i tshul khrims dang / sems can don byed pa'i tshul khrims so/ / de la dang po ni sems gnas par byed pa'o// gnyis pa ni rang rgyud kyi chos smin par byed pa'o/ / gsum pa ni sems can yongs su smin par byed pa'o/ /

The third, in terms of its different aspects, moral discipline is threefold: (1) the moral discipline of restraint, (2) the moral discipline of amassing virtues, and (3) the moral discipline of working for the welfare of others. The first pertains to stabilizing the mind, the second brings the elements within the person’s mental continuum to maturity, and the third causes other beings to achieve full maturity.

de dag so so'i mtshan nyid bshad na/ sdom pa'i tshul khrims ni/ thun mong dang thun mong ma yin pa'o/ / de la thun mong ba ni/ so so thar pa ris bdun po'o/ / de ltar yang byang sa las/
de la byang chub sems dpa'i sdom pa'i tshul khrims ni/ so so thar pa'i sdom pa yang dag par blangs pa ris bdun po/ dge slong dang / dge slong ma dang / dge slob ma dang / dge tshul dang / dge tshul ma dang / dge bsnyen dang / dge bsnyen ma'i tshul khrims gang yin pa ste/ de yang khyim pa dang rab tu byung ba'i phyogs la ci rigs par rig par bya'o/[683] / zhes gsungs so/ /

The fourth, to explain the essential characteristics of each aspect, first, the moral discipline of restraint consists of both what is common and what is uncommon. The common vows refer to the seven classes of prātimokṣa vows. Bodhisattva Levels says:
Right bodhisattva conduct related to restraint refers to the seven categories of prātimokṣa of those who have most properly adopted the precepts: those with the moral discipline of a monk, nun, novice monk, trainee nun, novice nun, ordained layman, and ordained laywoman. These should be understood as applying to those who have fully renounced and to laypersons, as appropriate.[421]

d.div: [683] gong mtshungs/ byang chub sems dpa'i sa/ shog_74_ba7

f.d:
'di dag kyang gzhan la gnod pa gzhi dang bcas pa las log pa yin te/ de yang so so thar pa rang skya ba ni rang don du log pa yin la/ byang chub sems dpa' ni gzhan don du log pa yin no/ / de ltar yang sred med kyi bus zhus pa'i mdo las/
de rgyal srid kyi phyir tshul khrims mi bsrung / mtho ris kyi phyir ma yin/ brgya byin gyi phyir ma yin/ tshangs pa'i phyir ma yin/ longs spyod kyi phyir ma yin/ dbang phyug gi phyir ma yin/ gzugs kyi phyir ma yin/ de bzhin du sbyar te/ dmyal ba'i 'jigs pas 'jigs nas tshul khrims bsrung ba ma yin/ de bzhin du dud 'gro'i skye gnas dang / gshin rje'i 'jig rten gyis 'jigs skrag pas tshul khrims bsrung ba ma yin te/ gzhan du na sangs rgyas kyi tshul la dgod pa'i phyir tshul khrims bsrung / sems can thams cad la phan pa dang / bde ba don du gnyer bas tshul khrims bsrung ngo /[684] / zhes gsungs so//

All of these represent turning away from harming others as well as from the bases of such harm. Within this, the prātimokṣa vows on their own turn away [harm] for one’s own sake, while bodhisattvas refrain from harm out of concern for the welfare of others. The Questions of Nārāyaṇa Sutra says that:
Moral discipline is not to be observed in order to gain royal status, nor for the sake of higher rebirth, nor to become like Indra or Brahma, nor for the sake of possessions, nor for the sake of physical well-being, and so on. Likewise moral discipline is not to be observed through fear of the horrors of rebirth in hell, fear of rebirth in animal states, or fear of the terrifying worlds of the Lord of Death. Not for those sorts of things but through considering it as the way to enlightenment is moral discipline observed—and so that every being can be drawn closer to what is beneficial and joyous.[422]

d.div: [684] sde dge_134_bka'/ mdo sde/ na_sred med gyi bus zhus pa'i mdo/ mtshan gzhan bsod nams thams cad bsdus pa'i ting nge 'dzin zhes bya ba'i mdo/ shog_87_ba6
[422] A.k.a. Sutra of the Absorption that Gathers All Merit (Sarvapuṇyasamuccayasa-mādhisūtra), Toh 134 Kangyur, mdo sde, na, 87b6.

f.d: thun mong ma yin pa la/ slob dpon zhi ba lha ni/ nam mkha'i snying po'i mdo'i rjes su 'brangs nas/ rgyal po'i rtsa ba'i ltung ba lnga/ blon po'i rtsa ba'i ltung ba lnga/ las dang po pa'i rtsa ba'i ltung ba brgyad de/ ming du bco brgyad/ rdzas su bcu bzhi po spong ba la bslab pa'o/ /zhes bzhed do//

As for the uncommon vows, in the tradition coming through Master Śāntideva, they follow the Ākāśagarbha Sutra. On this view, there are five root downfalls specific to monarchs, five specific to ministers, and eight specific to Dharma novices. Altogether these make eighteen in number, but in substance there are fourteen root infractions that need to be relinquished. So it is understood.

de ltar yang /
dkon mchog gsum gyi dkor 'phrog pa/ /phas pham pa yi ltung bar 'dod/ / dam pa'i chos ni spong byed pa/ /gnyis par thub pas gsungs pas yin/ /

Thus it says: /161/
1. To steal what belongs to the Three Jewels—this is held to be a downfall and a state of defeat. 2. To make others abandon the Dharma; this and the above were declared by the Sage.

d.div: tshul khrims 'chal ba'i dge slong la'ang / /ngur smrig 'phrog dang brdeg pa dang / /btson rar 'jug par byed pa dang / /rab tu byung las 'bebs pa dang / / mtshams med lnga po byed pa dang / /

3. To take away the robes of a fully ordained monk, to have him beaten or imprisoned, or to oblige him to give up his commitments, even if he has broken vows. 4. To commit one of the five heinous acts.
log par lta ba 'dzin pa dang / / grong la sogs pa 'jig pa dag/ /
5. To adhere to aberrant philosophy. 6. To destroy towns and the like.
rtsa ba'i ltung bar rgyal bas gsungs/ /
These were taught by the Buddha as root downfalls.[423]
[423] Of the above, 1 through 5 are root downfalls associated with a monarch, and 1 through 4, along with 6, are those associated with a minister.
blo sbyangs ma byas sems can la/ /stong pa nyid ni brjod pa dang / / sangs rgyas nyid la zhugs pa dag /rdzogs pa'i byang chub bzlog pa dang / /
1. To speak about emptiness to those inadequately prepared. 2. To turn those who have entered the way to buddhahood away from perfect enlightenment.
so so thar pa yongs spangs te/ /theg pa chen por sbyor ba dang / / slob pa'i theg pas chags la sogs/ /spong bar 'gyur ba min zhes 'dzin/ /pha rol dag kyang 'dzin 'jug dang / /
3. To practice Mahayana yet totally abandon prātimokṣa ethics. 4. To believe that vehicle of the disciples cannot eliminate desire and so forth and to cause others to so believe.
rang gi yon tan brjod pa dang / /rnyed pa dang ni bkur sti dang / /tshigs bcad sgyu yi gzhan smod dang / / bdag ni zab mo bzod pa'o zhes/ /log pa nyid ni smra ba dang / /
5. To extol one’s own qualities in pursuit of wealth, respect, or praise, and to denigrate others. 6. To speak falsely, such as, “I’ve attained forbearance toward profound emptiness.”

dge sbyong chad pas gcod 'jug dang / /dkon mchog gsum gyi sbyin byed dang / /sbyin pa len par byed pa dang / / zhi gnas 'dor bar byed pa dang / /yang dag 'jog gi longs spyod rnams/ /kha ton byed la sbyin pa rnams/ /

7. To have promised to do something virtuous and then go back on the promise, or to make offerings to the Three Jewels and then take them back. 8. To abandon tranquility and immersion in the highest reality in favor of ritual recitations.
de dag rtsa ba'i ltung ba ste/ /sems can dmyal ba chen po'i rgyu/[685] / zhes gsungs so/ /
These then are the root downfalls and a prime cause of the great hells.[424]
[685] sde dge_3940_bstan/ dbu ma/ khi_rgyal sras zhi ba lha/ bslab btus/ tshul khrims kyi le'u/ 5_shog_43_na5
[424] Śāntideva, Śikṣāsamuccaya, Toh 3940 Tengyur, dbu ma, khi, 43a5. Numbering here has been added for clarity.

f.d: jo bo gser gling pa ni/ byang chub sems dpa'i sa'i rjes su 'brangs nas/ pham pa'i gnas lta bu bzhi dang / nyes byas bzhi bcu rtsa drug spong ba la bslab pa'o/[686] /zhes bzhed do/ /

Lord Serlingpa [Dharmakīrti], following [Asaṅga’s] Bodhisattva Levels, states that one needs to train in relinquishing four offenses that are analogous to the grounds of defeat and forty secondary faults.

d.div: [686] 'dir gser gling pa'i gzhung gang la dgongs ngos 'dzin ma thub/

f.d:
de la pham pa'i gnas lta bu bzhi ni/ byang sa'i don bsdus pa sdom pa nyi shu pa las/
rnyed dang bkur stir chags pa yis/ / bdag bstod gzhan la smod pa dang / / sdug bsngal mgon med gyur pa la/ / ser snas chos nor mi ster dang / / gzhan gyis bshags kyang mi nyan par/ / khros nas gzhan la 'tshog pa dang / / theg pa chen po spong byed cing / / dam chos 'drar snang ston pa'o/[687] / zhes gsungs so/ /

d.div: [687] sde dge_4081_bstan/ sems tsam/ hi_slob dpon can+d+ra go mi/ sdom pa nyi shu pa/ shog_166_ba4
[425] Candragomin, Saṃvaraviṃśaka verses 6–7, Toh 4081 Tengyur, sems tsam, hi, 166b4.

f.d:
nyes byas bzhi bcu rtsa drug kyang de nyid las/
dkon mchog gsum la gsum mi mchod/ / 'dod pa'i sems kyi rjes su 'jug[688] / ces pa la sogs pa gsungs so//

As for the forty-six faults, the same text says the following, for example: /162/
Not making offerings to the Three Jewels three times daily, being carried away by desires. [426]

d.div: [688] gong mtshungs/ sdom pa nyi shu pa/ shog_166_ba6
[426] Ibid. verse 9, 166b46.

f.d: dge ba'i chos sdud pa'i tshul khrims ni/ byang chub sems dpa'i sdom pa'i tshul khrims yang dag par blangs pa'i 'og tu byang chub chen po'i phyir lus dang ngag gis dge ba bsags pa gang ci yang rung ba de dag thams cad ni/[689] mdor bsdu na/ dge ba chos sdud kyi tshul khrims yin no/ /

The second, moral discipline of amassing virtues, is as follows. Following a correct adoption of the bodhisattva’s moral discipline of restraint, whatever virtues one might gather through body and speech aimed at great enlightenment, all of these, in brief, constitute the moral discipline of amassing virtue.

d.div: [689] sems dpa'/ dpal spungs/ mi rigs dpe skrun/

f.d:
de yang gang zhe na/ byang sa las/
byang chub sems dpa'i tshul khrims la brten cing gnas nas/ thos pa dang bsam pa dang sgom pa dang gcig pur dga' ba la brtson par byed do/ / bla ma rnams la bkur sti dang rim gro byed pa dang / nad pa la rim gro dang nad g.yog byed pa dang / legs par sbyin zhing yon tan bsgrag pa dang / gzhan gyi bsod nams la yi rang zhing brnyas pa la bzod pa dang / dge ba byang chub tu bsngo zhing smon lam 'debs pa dang / dkon mchog mchod cing brtson 'grus rtsom pa dang / bag yod par gnas pa dang / bslab pa dran pa dang / shes bzhin gyis bsrung ba dang dbang po'i sgo bsrung zhing zas kyi tshod shes pa dang / nam gyi cha stod dang / cha smad la mi nyal bar rnal 'byor la brtson pa dang / skyes bu dam pa dang / dge ba'i bshes gnyen la bsten pa dang / rang gi 'khrul pa la brtags nas de 'chags shing gtong ba ste/ de lta bu'i chos rnams bsgrub pa dang / bsrung ba dang / rnam par 'phel bar byed pa ni/ dge ba chos sdud kyi tshul khrims zhes bya'o/[690]/ zhes gsungs so//

What are they? In Bodhisattva Levels, it says:
The following is to be understood as being the bodhisattva’s moral discipline of amassing what is virtuous. Relying on and abiding within the bodhisattva’s moral discipline, it is to enthusiastically apply yourself to study, contemplation, and meditation and to maintain solitude. It is to respect gurus and to serve them, and to serve and care for the sick. It is to give properly and proclaim good qualities, to appreciate the attributes of others and to be patient with those who are scornful. It is to dedicate virtue to enlightenment and make earnest prayers to that end; to make offerings to the Three Jewels and strive to be diligent; to be ever caring and careful, to be mindful of the training and through awareness to keep to it; to guard the doors of the senses and to know how much to consume; to not sleep in the first and last parts of the night but to persevere in joining the mind with what is wholesome; to rely on holy individuals and Dharma masters and to examine delusions, admit them, and get rid of them. These sorts of qualities need to be practiced, nurtured, and thoroughly increased.[427]

d.div: [690] sde dge_4037_bstan/ sems tsam/ wi_'phags pa thogs med/ byang sa/ le'u/ 5_shog_75_na1
[427] Asaṅga, Bodhisattvabhūmi, Toh 4037 Tengyur, sems tsam, wi, 75a1.

f.d:
sems can don byed kyi tshul khrims ni/ mdor bsdu na rnam pa bcu gcig tu rig par bya ste/ gang zhe na/ byang sa las/
bya ba don dang ldan pa la grogs su 'gro ba dang / sems can sdug bsngal ba rnams kyi sdug bsngal sel ba dang / thabs mi shes pa la rig pa ston pa dang / byas pa bzo zhing tshor te lan du phan 'dogs pa dang / 'jigs pa rnams las srung ba dang / sdug bsngal ba rnams kyi mya ngan sel ba dang / yo byad med pa rnams la yo byad stob pa dang / chos kyi 'khor legs par sdud pa dang / sems dang mthun par 'jug pa dang / yang dag pa'i yon tan gyis dga' bar byed pa dang / legs par tshar gcod pa dang / rdzu 'phrul gyis skrag pa dang / 'dun par byed pa'o/[691] / zhes gsungs so/[692] /

The third, the moral discipline of working for the welfare of others, can be known in brief in terms of eleven. What are they? Bodhisattva Levels states:
To support those doing worthwhile activities; to remove the suffering of beings in torment; to teach those without skill how to deal with things intelligently; to recognize other’s kindness and to render benefit in return; to protect beings from dangers;to alleviate the distress of those who are suffering; to provide those deprived of resources with provisions; to skillfully assemble a Dharma following; to engage them in accordance with their mentalities; to make them happy through the very finest of qualities; /163/ to tame [the wrathful] with firmness, by inspiring awe through extraordinary abilities, and making them long for [the good and wholesome].[428]

d.div: [691] gong mtshungs/ byang sa/ le'u/ 5_shog_79_na3
[692] mi rigs dpe skrun khang du zhes gsungs so/ /zhes pa'i mjug tu/ bcu bzhi pa/ gzhan yang / zhes byung yang nor bar nges/

f.d:
gzhan yang byang chub sems dpa' gzhan dad cing rang mi nyams par bya ba'i ched du/ sgo gsum gyi 'du byed ma dag pa spang zhing / dag pa gsum brten par bya'o/ / de la lus kyi 'du byed ma dag pa ni/ dgos pa dang bral ba'i mchong rgyug la sogs pa dmu rgod kyi spyod pa ste de dag spang ngo /[693] / 'du byed dag pa ni/ dal ba dang 'jam pa la gnas te/ bzhin 'dzum pa dang bcas par bya'o/ / de ltar yang /
de ltar rang dbang yon bgyis te/ / rtag tu 'dzum pa'i bzhin du gyis/ / khro gnyer ngo zum yongs spongs te/ / 'gro ba'i bshes dang gsong por gyis/[694]/ zhes gsungs so/ /

Furthermore, both to instill confidence in others and to prevent their own conduct from degrading, bodhisattvas should get rid of impure physical, verbal, and mental behavior and only resort to what is pure. Concerning impure physical behavior, you should avoid unnecessary wild behavior—running, jumping, and so forth. Purity means you remain relaxed and smooth, with a kind expression on your face. It says:
Having become self-controlled like that, always have a smiling face. Completely rid yourself of that constant frown and those dark looks, and become a friend to beings and treat them sincerely.[429]

d.div: [693] 'tshong rgyug/ dpal spungs/
[694] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 5_sh+loka_71_shog_13_na2
[429] Śāntideva, Guide to the Bodhisattva Way of Life (Bodhicaryāvatāra) 5:71, Toh 3871 Tengyur, dbu ma, la, 13a2.

f.d:
gzhan blta ba'i tshe ji ltar blta na/
mig gis sems can blta na yang / / 'di dag nyid la brten nas bdag / sangs rgyas nyid du 'gyur ro zhes/ / drang zhing byams pa'i tshul du blta/[695] / zhes gsungs pa ltar ro/ /

How should you look at others? It says:
When looking at others, look at them in a pleasant, kind way, knowing that it is through them that you will become a buddha.[430]

d.div: [695] gong mtshungs/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 5_sh+loka_80_shog_13_na2

f.d:
'dug pa'i tshe ji ltar 'dug na/
rkang pa brkyangs te mi 'dug cing / / lag pa mnyam par mi mnye'o/[696] / zhes gsungs pa ltar ro/ /

As to how to sit, it says:
Do not sit with legs outstretched or fidget with the hands.[431]

d.div: [696] gong mtshungs/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 5_sh+loka_92_shog_13_ba6

f.d:
zas za ba'i tshe ji ltar za na/
yang ji skad du/ kha bkang ba dang sgra bcas dang / / kha gdangs nas ni bza' mi bya/[697] / zhes gsungs pa ltar ro/ /

On how should one eat, it says:
When eating, do not overfill your mouth or chew noisily, with the mouth agape.[432]

d.div: [697] gong mtshungs/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 5_sh+loka_92_shog_13_ba6

f.d:
spyod lam gyi tshe ji ltar bya na/
khri la sogs pa bab col du/ / sgra dang bcas pa mi 'dor ro/ / sgo yang drag tu mi dbye ste/ / rtag tu bcom bskyung dga' bar bya/[698] / zhes gsungs pa ltar ro/ /

As to how to move around:
Do not be noisy and hasty when getting up from a seat, for example, and do not slam doors. Take pleasure in being unobtrusive.[433]

d.div: [698] gong mtshungs/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 5_sh+loka_72_shog_13_na2

f.d:
nyal ba'i tshe ji ltar nyal na/ ji skad du/
mgon po mya ngan 'das gzims ltar/ / 'dod pa'i phyogs su nyal bar bya/[699] / zhes gsungs pa ltar ro//

And on how to sleep, it says:
Just like the savior lied down for nirvana, orient whichever direction you prefer.[434]

d.div: [699] gong mtshungs/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 5_sh+loka_96_shog_14_na1

f.d:
ngag gi 'du byed ma dag pa ni/ smra ba mang po dang / smra ba rnon po spangs pa'o/ / de yang smra ba mang po'i nyes pa ni/ 'phags pa dkon mchog sprin las gsungs te/ ji skad du/
byis pa dam pa'i chos las rab tu nyams/ / sems ni mi mnyen rab tu rtsub par 'gyur/ / zhi gnas lhag mthong dag dang rab tu ring / / smra la dga' ba'i nyes pa 'di dag go /
rtag tu bla ma rnams la gus pa med// sbags pa'i gtam dag la ni dga' ba skye/ / snying po med la gnas shing shes rab nyams/ / smra la dga' ba'i nyes pa 'di dag go[700] / zhes pa la sogs pa gsungs so/ /

With regard to impure speech, you should give up excessive or harsh speech. The shorcomings of excessive speech are explained below in the Clouds of Jewels Sutra:
The childish completely undermine the sublime Dharma. Taking away the mind’s flexibility and making it rough, taking one far from tranquility and profound insight— such are the flaws of delighting in excessive speech.
One will have little respect for Dharma masters. People come to enjoy corrupt speech, becoming absorbed in what is of meager value, and wisdom deteriorates— such are the flaws of delighting in excessive speech.[435]

d.div: [700] gzhung du dkon mchog sprin gyi mdo las zhes byung yang lung 'di sde dge_69_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ ca_lhag bsam bskul bar bstan pa'i mdo/ shog_145_ba1_nang bzhugs/
[435] This quotation was not found in the Clouds of Jewels Sutra, but it occurs in the Sutra Encouraging Nobler Intention (Adhyāśayasaṃcodanasūtra), Toh 69 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, ca, 145b1.

f.d:
smra ba rnon po'i nyes pa ni/ zla ba sgron ma'i mdo las/
gang gis 'khrul pa ci mthong yang / / de dag nyes par mi bsgrag ste/ / ci 'dra ba yi las byas pa/ / 'bras bu de 'dra thob par 'gyur/[701] / zhes gsungs so/ /

d.div: [701] sde dge_127_bka'/ mdo sde/ da_ting nge 'dzin rgyal po'i mdo/ le'u/ 25_sh+loka_41_shog_85_ba4
[436] A.k.a. King of Meditation Sutra (Samādhirājasūtra), Toh 127 Kangyur, mdo sde, da, 85b4.

f.d:
chos thams cad 'byung ba med par bstan pa'i mdo las kyang /
byang chub sems dpa' la ltung ba gleng na byang chub dang ring du 'gyur ro/ / phrag dog gis gleng na byang chub dang ring du 'gyur ro/[702] / zhes pa la sogs pa gsungs so/ /

In the Sutra Teaching the Nonorigination of All Things, it says of this, among other things:
If you describe the lapses of a bodhisattva, enlightenment recedes into the distance. If you talk through jealousy, enlightenment recedes far into the distance.[437]

d.div: [702] sde dge_180_bka'/ mdo sde/ ma_chos thams cad 'byung ba med pa bstan pa'i mdo/ shog_274_ba4
[437] Sarvadharmāpravṛttinirdeśasūtra, Toh 180 Kangyur, mdo sde, ma, 274b4.

f.d:
des na smra ba mang po dang / rnon po spong bar bya'o/ / ngag gi 'du byed dag par ji ltar smra zhe na/ ji skad du/
smra na yid phebs 'brel ba dang / / don gsal yid du 'ong ba dang / chags dang zhe sdang spang ba dang / / 'jam zhing ran par smra bar bya/[703] / zhes gsungs pa ltar ro//

Therefore excessive and harsh speech are to be given up. How then should you speak? As stated in the following:
When speaking, say something that is purposeful, clear in meaning and appealing, free from greed and aversion, smooth, and in just the right amount.[438]

d.div: [703] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 5_sh+loka_79_shog_13_na6
[438] Śāntideva, Guide to the Bodhisattva Way of Life (Bodhicaryāvatāra) 5:79, Toh 3871 Tengyur, dbu ma, la, 13a6.

f.d:
yid kyi 'du byed ma dag pa ni/ rnyed pa dang bkur sti la zhen pa dang / gnyid dang rmugs pa la chags pa la sogs yin no/ / de yang rnyed pa dang bkur sti la chags pa'i nyes pa ni/ lhag pa'i bsam pa bskul ba'i mdo las/
byams pa/ byang chub sems dpas rnyed pa dang bkur sti ni 'dod chags bskyed par brtag par bya'o/ / rnyed pa dang bkur sti ni zhe sdang bskyed par rig par bya'o/ / rnyed pa dang bkur sti ni gti mug bskyed par rig par bya'o/ / rnyed pa dang bkur sti ni g.yo ba bskyed par rig par bya'o/ / rnyed pa dang bkur sti ni sangs rgyas thams cad kyis mi gnang bar brtag par bya'o// rnyed pa dang bkur sti ni dge ba'i rtsa ba 'phrog par brtag par bya'o/ / rnyed pa dang bkur sti ni pha rol 'brid pa'i smad 'tshong ma dang 'dra bar brtag par bya'o/[704] / zhes pa la sogs pa gsungs so//

The impurity of mental engagement refers to faults such as clinging to material gifts and honors as well as being attached to sleep and mental dullness. The fault of craving for material gain and honor is explained in the Sutra Encouraging Nobler Intention:
Maitreya! A bodhisattva should examine how gaining material gifts and being honored in such a way gives rise to desire and attachment. He should know how gaining material gifts and being honored give rise to anger and aversion. He should know how material gifts and honors give rise to confused ignorance. He should know how material gifts and honors give rise to underhandedness. He should consider how none of the buddhas ever encouraged material gifts or receiving honors, and he should examine how material gifts and honors steal the roots of virtue. He should consider how material gifts and honors are like a prostitute trying to seduce a potential client.[439]

d.div: [704] sde dge_69_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ ca_lhag pa'i bsam pa bskul ba'i mdo/ shog_142_na5
[439] Adhyāśayasaṃcodanasūtra, Toh 69 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, ca, 142a5.

f.d:
rnyed pa rnyed kyang ngoms par mi 'gyur te/ yab sras mjal ba'i mdo las/
rmi lam rmis pa'i chu lta bur/ / 'thungs kyang ngoms par mi 'gyur ba/ / de ltar 'dod pa'i yon tan rnams/ / bsten na ngoms par mi 'gyur ro/[705] / zhes gsungs so/ /

This and more is said. Even if material things are gained, the thirst for them is never sated. The Meeting of Father and Son Sutra says:
Just as water imagined in a dream does not quench thirst even when drunk, likewise the objects of sensory pleasures even when sought do not satisfy.[440]

d.div: [705] sde dge_60_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ nga _yab sras mjal ba'i mdo/ le'u/ 26_sh+loka_shog_162_na5
[440] Pitāputrasamāgamasūtra, Toh 60 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, nga, 162a5.

f.d:
de ltar brtags nas 'dod pa chung bar bya/ chog shes par bya'o/ / gnyid la dga' ba'i nyes pa yang / ji skad du/
gang zhig gnyid dang rmugs la dgar gyur pa/ / de yis shes rab shin tu nyams chung 'gyur/ / de yis blo yang yongs su nyams par 'gyur/ / ye shes las ni rtag tu de nyams 'gyur/[706] / zhes pa dang /
gang zhig gnyid dang rmugs la dga' gyur pa/ / mi shes le lo snyoms las shes rab 'chal/ / de la mi ma yin pas glags rnyed de/ / nags na gnas pa'i tshe na 'tshe bar 'gyur/[707] / zhes pa la sogs pa gsungs so/ /

Having considered in this manner, reduce your desires and be content with what you have. Of the fault of enjoying sleep, it is said:
Those who are addicted to sleep and indolence will suffer considerable degradation in their understanding. Their mental capacity will deteriorate, too. Whatever arises from pristine awareness will be constantly impaired.[441] and
Those who are addicted to sleep and indolence will disintegrate through ignorance, lassitude, and laziness. Such people become prey to nonhuman forces and may be harmed /165/ by them when meditating alone in the forests.[442]

d.div: [706] sde dge_69_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ ca_lhag pa'i bsam pa bskul ba'i mdo/ shog_147_na4
[707] gong mtshungs/ shog_147_na5
[441] Adhyāśayasaṃcodanasūtra, Toh 69 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, ca, 147a4. Quoted also in Śāntideva, Śikṣāsamuccaya, Toh 3940 Tengyur, dbu ma, khi, 65a2.
[442] Adhyāśayasaṃcodanasūtra, Toh 69 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, ca, 147a5. Quoted also in Śāntideva, Śikṣāsamuccaya, Toh 3940 Tengyur, dbu ma, khi, 65a2.

f.d: des na de dag spang bar bya'o/ / yid kyi 'du byed dag pa ni/ dad pa la sogs pa sngar bstan pa de dag la gnas par bya'o/[708] /
Therefore the above forms of impure mental conduct should be abandoned. Pure mental engagement is abiding with faith and the other qualities mentioned above.

d.div: [708] de dag yin pas de dag la/ dpal spungs/

f.d: tshul khrims spel ba ni/ ye shes dang / shes rab dang / bsngo ba gsum gyis spel ba ste/ gong du bstan pa ltar ro/ /

The fifth, how the power of moral discipline can be increased, refers to enhancing [moral discipline] by means of the three factors already referred to earlier—these being (1) pristine awareness, (2) wisdom, and (3) dedication.[443]

d.div: [443] The cross-reference is to the section on enhancing generosity in the preceding chapter (see p. 261–62).

f.d: tshul khrims dag par byed pa ni/ stong pa nyid dang snying rjes zin pa ste gong du bstan pa ltar ro//
The sixth, making one’s moral discipline pure, refers to it being sustained by emptiness and compassion, as mentioned earlier.

tshul khrims kyi 'bras bu ni/ mthar thug dang gnas skabs gnyis su shes par bya'o/ / de la mthar thug ni bla na med pa'i byang chub thob ste/ de ltar yang byang sa las/
byang chub sems dpa' tshul khrims kyi pha rol tu phyin pa yongs su rdzogs nas/ bla na med pa yang dag par rdzogs pa'i byang chub tu mngon par rdzogs par 'tshang rgya bar 'gyur ro/[709] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Seventh, the fruits of moral discipline, should be understood in terms of two—its temporary and ultimate results. As for its ultimate fruit, you attain the unsurpassed enlightenment. Bodhisattva Levels says:
A bodhisattva who has completely perfected moral discipline genuinely becomes a perfect buddha, with peerless, true, and perfect enlightenment.[444]

d.div: [709] sde dge_4037_bstan/ sems tsam/ wi_'phags pa thogs med/ byang sa/ le'u/ 5_shog_101_na4
[444] Asaṅga, Bodhisattvabhūmi, Toh 4037 Tengyur, sems tsam, wi, 101a4.

f.d:
gnas skabs su ni mi 'dod kyang 'khor ba'i bde skyid phun sum tshogs pa thob ste/ de ltar yang byang chub sems dpa'i sde snod las/
shA ri'i bu de ltar tshul khrims yongs su dag pa'i byang chub sems dpas lha dang mi'i dpal phun sum tshogs pa myong bar mi 'gyur ba gang yang med do/[710]/zhes gsungs so/ /

As for temporary results, whether sought or not, you will obtain greatest happiness and well-being within the samsaric world. The Bodhisattva Collection says:
Śāriputra! There will not be even a single one of the most wonderful splendors known to gods and humans that a bodhisattva who keeps such completely immaculate conduct will not be able to experience.[445]

d.div: [710] sde dge_56_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ ga_byang chub sems dpa'i sde snod/ le'u/ 7_shog_84_na4
[445] Bodhisattvapiṭaka, Toh 56 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, ga, 84a4.

f.d:
'khor ba'i bde skyid des kyang zil gyis mi non par byang chub kyi lam la 'jug par 'gyur te/ sred med kyi bus zhus pa'i mdo las/
tshul khrims kyi phung po de lta bu dang ldan pa'i byang chub sems dpa' de 'khor los sgyur ba'i rgyal srid las yongs su mi nyams te/ de la yang bag yod cing byang chub 'dod pa yin no/ / brgya byin las yongs su mi nyams te/ de la yang bag yod cing byang chub 'dod pa yin/[711] zhes pa la sogs pa gsungs so/ /

There may be these worldly delights and joys, yet the bodhisattva will not be dazzled by them and will enter the path to enlightenment. In the Questions of Nārāyaṇa Sutra, it says:
A bodhisattva endowed with such amassed moral discipline will not become corrupted in any way, even by the possessions of a universal monarch. That bodhisattva will still exercise mindful care and will still long for enlightenment. That bodhisattva will not take a detour even though he becomes Indra. Then, too, the bodhisattva will exercise mindful care and long for enlightenment.[446]

d.div: [711] sde dge_134_bka'/ mdo sde/ na_sred med gyi bus zhus pa'i mdo/ shog_88_ba5
[446] A.k.a. the Sutra of the Absorption that Gathers All Merit (Sarvapuṇya-samuccayasamādhisūtra), Toh 134 Kangyur, mdo sde, na, 88b5.

f.d:
yang tshul khrims dang ldan pa de mi dang mi ma yin pa rnams kyis mchod cing bsnyen bkur bar 'gyur te/ ji skad du/ de nyid las/
tshul khrims kyi phung po la gnas pa'i byang chub sems dpa' la lha rnams kyis rtag tu phyag byas pa yin/ klu rnams kyis rtag tu bsngags pa yin/ gnod sbyin rnams kyis rtag tu bstod pa yin/ dri za rnams kyis rtag tu mchod pa yin/ bram ze dang rgyal rigs dang / tshong dpon dang khyim bdag rnams kyis rtag tu gsol ba yin/ sangs rgyas rnams kyis rtag tu dgongs pa yin/ lha dang bcas pa'i 'jig rten gyis rtag tu dbang bskur ba yin/[712] zhes pa la sogs pa gsungs so/ /

Furthermore, those who are endowed with moral discipline will receive offerings from and be cared for by humans and nonhumans alike. It says, in the same sutra:
The gods always respect those who keep the amassed virtues of moral discipline; the nāgas will constantly express their appreciation of them; the yakṣas will ever praise them; the gandharvas will constantly make offerings to them; brahmans, princes, merchants, and landowners will supplicate them; the buddhas will constantly embrace them with their compassion; and they will gain power over worlds and the divine forces present therein.[447] /166/

d.div: [712] sde dge_134_bka'/ mdo sde/ na_sred med gyi bus zhus pa'i mdo/ shog_89_na3

f.d: dam chos yid bzhin gyi nor bu thar pa rin po che'i rgyan las/ tshul khrims kyi pha rol tu phyin pa'i le'u ste bcu gsum pa'o// //
This then concludes the thirteenth chapter, discussing the perfection of moral discipline, in this Ornament of Precious Liberation, a Wish-Fulfilling Gem of Sublime Dharma.
le'u bcu bzhi pa bzod pa'i pha rol tu phyin pa/
14. The Perfection of Patience

bzod pa'i pha rol tu phyin pa la/ sdom ni/
skyon yon rnam gnyis bsam pa dang / / ngo bo dang ni dbye ba dang / / phye ba so so'i mtshan nyid dang / / spel dang dag par bya ba dang / / 'bras bu dang ni don bdun gyis/ / bzod pa'i pha rol phyin bsdus so/ / zhes pa'o/ /

de la dang po bshad na/ gang zhig sbyin pa tshul khrims gnyis dang ldan yang bzod pa dang mi ldan na/ de la khong khro skye'o/ / khong khro skyes na sbyin pa dang tshul khrims la sogs pa sngar byas kyi dge ba thams cad dus gcig la zad par 'gyur ro/ /

To present the first, reflections on the drawbacks of its absence and the benefits of practicing it, if someone possesses generosity and moral discipline yet lacks patience, anger can still arise. Once anger has arisen, all the virtue created up to that time—through generosity, moral discipline, and so on—can be consumed right there and then.

de lta na/[713] byang chub sems dpa'i sde snod las/
khong khro ba zhes bya ba ni bskal pa brgya stong du bsags pa'i dge ba'i rtsa ba 'joms pa ste/[714] zhes gsungs so/ /

Thus it says in the Bodhisattva Collection:
This thing we call anger can overpower the roots of virtue established over a hundred thousand eons.[448]

d.div: [713] de ltar yang / dpal spungs/ de ltar na/ mi rigs dpe skrun/
[714] sde dge_56_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ ga_byang chub sems dpa'i sde snod/ le'u/ 8_shog_98_ba2
[448] Bodhisattvapiṭaka, Toh 56 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, ga, 98b2.

f.d:
spyod 'jug las kyang /
bskal pa stong du bsags pa yi/ / sbyin dang bde gshegs mchod la sogs/ / legs spyad gang yin de kun kyang / / khong khro gcig gis 'joms par byed/[715] / ces gsungs so/ /

Guide to the Bodhisattva Way of Life also says:
Whatever excellent deeds one may have gathered over a thousand eons— generosity, making offerings to the buddhas, and so forth— they will be destroyed by one burst of anger.[449]

d.div: [715] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 6_sh+loka_1_shog_14_ba3
[449] Śāntideva, Bodhicaryāvatāra 6:1, Toh 3871 Tengyur, dbu ma, la, 14b3.

f.d: yang bzod pa dang mi ldan na/ zhe sdang khong du zhugs pas/ mda' dug khong du zhugs pa dang 'dra ste/ yid zug rngu langs nas dga' bde dang zhi ba mi myong ste/[716] tha ma gnyid kyang mi phebs pa'o/ /

Furthermore, anger that has found a niche inside someone lacking patience is like the festering wound of a poisoned arrow. The mind thus afflicted knows no joy, no peace, and in the end the person cannot even find rest in sleep.

d.div: [716] yid la zug/ dpal spungs/

f.d:
de ltar yang /
zhe sdang zug rngu'i sems 'chang na/ / yid ni zhi ba nyams mi myong / / dga' dang bde ba'ang mi thob la/ / gnyid mi 'ong zhing brtan med 'gyur/[717] / zhes pa dang /
mdor na khro bas bder gnas pa/ / de ni 'ga' yang yod ma yin/[718] / zhes gsungs so//

Thus it is said:
In the grip of anger’s affliction the mind cannot experience peace; it cannot find joy or well-being, and thus a person cannot sleep and becomes unstable.[450] and
In brief, through their anger, those in good circumstances find no joy.[451]

d.div: [717] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 6_sh+loka_3_shog_14_ba4
[718] gong mtshungs/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 6_sh+loka_5_shog_14_ba5

f.d: yang bzod pa dang mi ldan na/ khong du zhe sdang zhugs pas phyi rol du khro gtum 'byung ste/ des mdza' bshes dang g.yog 'khor thams cad skyo zhing sun nas/ nor zas byin yang 'khor du mi btub bo/ /

The anger dwelling within someone lacking patience will also show on the outside as a violent demeanor. Through this, friends, relatives, and employees all become fed up with the angry person; even gifts of money or valuables cannot persuade them to put up with his or her presence any longer.

de ltar yang /
de yis mdza' bshes skyo bar 'gyur/ / sbyin pas bsdus kyang rten mi byed/[719] / ces gsungs so/ /

d.div: [719] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 6_sh+loka_5_shog_14_ba5

f.d:
yang bzod pa dang mi ldan na/ bdud kyis glags rnyed nas bar chad 'jug go / de ltar yang byang chub sems dpa'i sde snod las/
sems sdang bar gyur pa la bdud kyis glags rnyed nas bar chad 'jug go[720] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Furthermore, those lacking patience lay themselves open to harmful forces (māra), which then create obstacles for them. /167/ Therefore the Bodhisattva Collection says:
A mind under the influence of anger is prey to harmful forces and encounters obstacles.[453]

d.div: [720] sde dge_56_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ ga_byang chub sems dpa'i sde snod/ le'u/ 8_shog_98_ba3
[453] Bodhisattvapiṭaka, Toh 56 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, ga, 98b3.

f.d:
yang bzod pa dang mi ldan na/ sangs rgyas kyi lam pha rol tu phyin pa drug tu ma longs pas bla med kyi byang chub mi thob bo/ / de ltar yang 'phags pa sdud pa las/
sdang zhing bzod dang bral la byang chub ga la yod/[721] / ces gsungs so/ /

Moreover, if you lack patience, you will not get the benefit of having all six perfections, the combination of which forms the path to buddhahood. Thus you will not attain enlightenment. Therefore the Verse Summary of the Perfection of Wisdom says:
Where there is anger and no patience, how can there be enlightenment?[454]

d.div: [721] sde dge_13_bka'/ sher phyin/ ka_mdo sdud pa/ le'u/ 24_sh+loka_4_shog_14_ba4
[454] Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā 24:4, Toh 13 Kangyur, sher phyin, ka, 14b4.

f.d:
de las ldog ste bzod pa dang ldan na/ de nyid dge ba'i rtsa ba rnams kyi nang na mchog yin no/ / de ltar yang /
zhe sdang lta bu'i sdig pa med/ / bzod pa lta bu'i dka' thub med/ / de bas bzod la nan tan du/ / sna tshogs tshul gyis bsgom par bya/[722] / zhes gsungs so/ /

In contrast, if you possess patience, it stands supreme among all the roots of virtue. Therefore it is said:
There is no evil comparable to anger and there is no fortitude like patience. Therefore cultivate patience most earnestly by every means available.[455]

d.div: [722] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 6_sh+loka_2_shog_14_ba4
[455] Śāntideva, Guide to the Bodhisattva Way of Life (Bodhicaryāvatāra) 6:2, Toh 3871 Tengyur, dbu ma, la, 14b4.

f.d:
yang bzod pa dang ldan na/ gnas skabs su yang bde legs thams cad thob bo/ / de ltar yang /
gang zhig bsgrims te khro 'joms pa/ / de ni 'di dang gzhan du bde/[723] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Besides this, if you are endowed with patience, all sorts of happiness and well-being are found in everyday circumstances. Therefore it is said:
Whoever, through self-control, overcomes anger, he will be happy in this and other lives.[456]

d.div: [723] gong mtshungs/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 6_sh+loka_6_shog_14_ba6

f.d:
yang bzod pa dang ldan na bla med kyi byang chub thob bo/ / de ltar yang yab sras mjal ba'i mdo las/
khro ba sangs rgyas lam min zhes/ / rtag tu byams pa bsgom pa na/ / byang chub de las skye bar 'gyur/[724] / zhes gsungs so//

Furthermore, if you possess patience, you will attain the unsurpassed enlightenment. Thus it says in the Meeting of Father and Son Sutra:
Saying “Anger is not the way of the buddhas” while constantly cultivating loving kindness, from this enlightenment will arise.[457]

d.div: [724] ma dper yab sras mjal ba'i mdo las zhes drangs kyang / gang pos zhus pa'i mdor bzhugs/ sde dge_61_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ nga _gang pos zhus pa'i mdo/ le'u/ 1_shog_170_ba5

[457] Although our author attributes this quotation to the Meeting of Father and Son Sutra it is actually from the sutra that immediately follows it in the Dergé Kangyur, i.e., the Questions of Pūrṇa Sutra (Pūrṇaparipṛcchāsūtra), Toh 61 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, nga, 170b5.

f.d:
bzod pa'i ngo bo ni/ ji mi snyam pa ste/ byang sa las/
zang zing med pa'i sems dang / snying rje 'ba' zhig gis ji mi snyam pa gang yin pa 'di ni/ mdor bsdus na/ byang chub sems dpa'i bzod pa'i ngo bo nyid yin par rig par bya'o/[725] / zhes gsungs so//

The second, the nature of patience, consists of being unperturbed by anything.[458] Bodhisattva Levels says:
To have no regard for material gains and to remain unperturbed strictly through compassion. Understand this, in brief, to consitute the essence of the bodhisattva’s patience.[459]

d.div: [725] sde dge_4037_bstan/ sems tsam/ wi_'phags pa thogs med/ byang sa/ le'u/ 11_shog_101_ba7
[458] Were one less literal, this definition of patience provided here could be translated as “to be able to cope with anything.”
[459] Asaṅga, Bodhisattvabhūmi, Toh 4037 Tengyur, sems tsam, wi, 101b7.

f.d: bzod pa la dbye na gsum ste/ gzhan gnod pa byed pa la ji mi snyam pa'i bzod pa dang / sdug bsngal dang du len pa'i bzod pa dang / chos la nges pa sems pa la mos pa'i bzod pa'o/ / de la dang po ni/ gnod pa byed pa'i sems can gyi rang bzhin la dpyad nas bzod par byed pa'o// gnyis pa ni/ sdug bsngal gyi ngo bo la dpyad nas bzod par byed pa'o/ / gsum pa ni/ chos rnams kyi phyin ci ma log pa nyid la so sor brtags pa'i sgo nas bzod par byed pa'o/ / yang dang po gnyis kun rdzob kyi dbang du byas nas bzod pa bsgom pa yin/ phyi ma don dam gyi dbang du byas pa'o/ /

The third, to classify its different aspects, patience is threefold: (1) patience when confronted with harmful beings, (2) patience as voluntary acceptance of suffering, and (3) patience as confidence born of definite contemplation of the Dharma. Of these, the first is to be patient through analyzing the nature of the beings who cause harm, the second is to be patient through analyzing the essential nature of suffering itself, and the third is to be patient through a discerning analysis of the correct nature of phenomena. The first two aspects cultivate patience in terms of [contemplating] the relative, the third in terms of the ultimate.

de dag so so'i mtshan nyid bshad na/ de la dang po ni/ bdag gam bdag gi ba la brdeg pa dang / gshe ba dang / khro ba dang / mtshang 'bru ba la sogs pa mi 'dod pa byed pa dang /[726] 'dod pa'i bgegs byed pa bdag gis bzod par byed pa'o/[727] / de dag bzod pa gang zhe na/[728] mi 'khrug pa dang / phyi gnod pa mi byed pa dang /[729] sems la mi 'dzin pa gang yin pa de ni bzod pa zhes bya'o/ /

Fourth is to explain the essential characteristics of each aspect. Of these, the first refers to being patient on your part when confronted with situations where someone does something undesirable—such as strike, insult, show hostility, or defame you or your loved ones—/168/ or obstruct you from obtaining what you want. What does it mean to be patient in such circumstances? Patience means remaining unperturbed, not retaliating in kind, or not holding on to the event in one’s mind.

d.div: [726] 'tshang 'bru/ dpal spungs/
[727] gegs/ dpal spungs/
[728] de la bzod pa/ dpal spungs/
[729] phyir gnod pa/ dpal spungs/ phyis gnod pa/ mi rigs dpe skrun/

f.d: de yang / slob dpon zhi ba lha'i ltar na/ gzhan dag bdag la gnod par byed pa de/ kho la rang dbang med par brtag pa dang / rang gi las kyi nyes par brtag pa dang / lus kyi nyes par brtag pa dang / sems kyi nyes par brtag pa dang / skyon can khyad med du 'gyur bar brtag pa dang / phan 'dogs par brtag pa dang / drin che bar brtag pa dang / sangs rgyas mnyes par brtag pa dang / phan yon che bar brtags la bzod par bya bar gsungs so/ /

According to Master Śāntideva’s teachings, we are taught to cultivate patience on the basis of considering: (1) the fact that the other person, the aggressor, has no control, (2) the fault due to your own karma, (3) the fault of your physical existence, (4) the fault of your mind, (5) how there is no difference of fault, (6) the practical utility, (7) the enormous kindness, (8) that the buddhas will be delighted, and (9) the tremendous benefits.

de la dang po ni/ lha sbyin lta bu bdag la gnod par byed pa de ni zhe sdang gis rang dbang med la/ zhe sdang ni yul yid du mi 'ong bas dbang med de/ des na kho la rang dbang med pa yin pas/ bdag gis lan bya bar mi rigs so/ / de ltar yang /
de ltar thams cad gzhan gyi dbang / / de yi dbang gis de dbang med/ / de ltar shes na brul lta bu'i/ / dngos po kun la mi khro 'gyur/[730]/ zhes gsungs so/ /

For the first, the fact that the aggressor has no control, reflect, “Those who do me harm have lost control of themselves through anger, as did Devadatta toward the Buddha. Anger is such that people lose all restraint when something they do not like occurs. Since they are not in control of their acts, it is inappropriate to retaliate.” Therefore it says:
All beings are thus under some influence, and they are, by that very fact, not in control of themselves. Knowing this, someone will not become angry toward concrete realities that are but mental projections.[460]

d.div: [730] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 6_sh+loka_31_shog_15_ba6
[460] Śāntideva, Guide to the Bodhisattva Way of Life (Bodhicaryāvatāra) 6:31, Toh 3871 Tengyur, dbu ma, la, 15b6.

f.d:
rang gi las kyi nyes par brtag pa ni/ bdag gis da lta myong ba'i gnod pa 'di kho na 'dra ba zhig skye ba snga ma la byas pas gnod pa 'di byung ba yin/ des na rang gi las ngan gyis nyes pas na gzhan la lan bya bar mi rigs so/ / de ltar yang /
bdag gis sngon chad sems can la/ / 'di 'dra ba yi gnod pa byas/ / de bas sems can 'tshe byed pa/ / bdag la gnod pa 'di 'byung rigs/[731] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Considering the fault of your own karma means to reflect, “The harm that I am experiencing now is a hurt arising through something quite similar that I did in a previous existence. Therefore it is not fitting to retaliate against someone else for the mistakes of my own bad karma.” Hence it is said,
Since I harmed sentient beings in former times in just this sort of way, it is fitting that this harm should come to me now for my aggression.[461]

d.div: [731] gong mtshungs/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 6_sh+loka_42_shog_16_na5

f.d:
rang gi lus kyi nyes par brtag pa ni/ rang lus 'di med na pha rol pos mtshon cha la sogs pa brdeg sa mi rnyed de/ /des na lus 'di yod pas gnod pa de byung ba yin la/ gzhan la lan bya bar mi rigs so/ / de ltar yang /
de yi mtshon dang bdag gi lus/ / gnyis ka sdug bsngal rgyu yin te/ / des mtshon bdag gis lus phyung na/ / gang zhig la ni khro bar bya/[732] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Considering the fault of your physical existence means reflecting, “If I did not have this body, then the others’ weapons and so forth would have nothing to harm. The actual hurt occurs through the presence of this body, and from that point of view it is not right to retaliate.” Thus,
His weapon and my body are both causes for this suffering. He brought the weapon and I my body, so who should I be angry at?[462]

d.div: [732] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 6_sh+loka_43_shog_16_na6

f.d:
sems kyi nyes par brtag pa ni/ rang sems 'dis lus bzang po gzhan gyis gnod par mi bya ba mi 'dzin par/[733] lus ngan pa gze re can bzung bas gnod pas tshugs pa yin/[734] des na rang gi sems kyis lan pas/ gzhan la lan bya bar mi rigs so/ / de ltar yang /
shu ba mi yi gzugs 'dra ba/ / reg tu mi bzod sdug bsngal can/ / sred ldongs bdag gis bzung gyur na/ / de la gnod pa su la khro/[735] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Considering the fault of mind involves reflecting, “This mind of mine did not take on a really good body—one that could not be harmed by others. By having taken a lesser and vulnerable body, it is afflicted by harms. Therefore, since it is my own mind that caused such a body to be mine, it is not right to retaliate against someone else.” /169/ Thus it says:
A human body is like a sore: it cannot bear to be touched. As it was I, craving blindly, who took it on, with whom should I get angry for the harms it encounters?[463]

d.div: [733] gnod par bya ba mi nus pa mi 'dzin par/ dpal spungs/
[734] gzer rag can bzung bas/ dpal spungs/ mi rigs dpe skrun/
[735] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 6_sh+loka_44_shog_16_na6

f.d:
skyon can khyad med du 'gyur bar brtag pa ni/ ji skad du/
la la rmongs te nyes pa byed/ / la la rmongs te khros gyur na/ / de la skyon med gang gis bya// skyon dang bcas te gang zhig yin/[736] / zhes gsungs te/ des na skyon la 'dzems la bzod par bya'o/ /

Considering how there is no difference of fault means to reflect,
Some, through ignorance, make harm; others, through ignorance, get angry at them. Who among them is faultless? Who is at fault?[464] As this is the case, you should avoid the faults and practice patience instead.

d.div: [736] gong mtshungs/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 6_sh+loka_67_shog_18_na5

f.d:
phan 'dogs par brtag pa ni/ gnod byed la brten nas bzod pa bsgom/ bzod pa bsgoms pas sdig pa byang /[737] [738] sdig pa byang bas tshogs rdzogs/ tshogs rdzogs pas 'tshang rgya ste/ des na gnod byed 'di don gyis phan 'dogs chen po yin pas bzod par bya'o/ / de ltar yang /
'di dag la ni brten bcas nas/ / bzod pas bdag sdig mang du byang /[739] / zhes pa la sogs pa gsungs so/ /

Considering the practical utility means that to develop patience you need to have a source of harm. Through cultivating patience, wrongdoings are purified and the accumulations are perfected. Through perfecting the accumulations, there will be enlightenment. Therefore, having harm is incredibly useful, and so you should practice patience:
In dependence on them, many wrongs are purified because of my patience.[465]

d.div: [737] bsgom/ mi rigs dpe skrun/
[738] sdig pa 'byang / dpal spungs/
[739] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 6_sh+loka_48_shog_16_ba1

f.d:
drin che bar brtag pa ni/ byang chub sgrub pa la bzod pa'i pha rol tu phyin pa med du mi btub la/[740] bzod pa sgom pa la gnod byed med du mi btub ste/ des na gnod byed 'di chos kyi grogs po drin can yin pas gnod pa la bzod par bya'o/ / de ltar yang /
byang chub spyod pa'i grogs gyur pa/ / bdag gis dgra la dga' bar bya/ / 'di dag bdag gis bsgrubs pas na// de phyir bzod pa'i 'bras bu 'di/ / thog mar 'di la brdar 'os te/ / 'di ltar de ni bzod pa'i rgyu/[741]/ zhes gsungs so/ /

Considering the enormous kindness means to recognize that without the perfection of patience, enlightenment will not be achieved, and to cultivate patience, the presence of perpetrators of harm is indispensable. Therefore this person, the agent of harm, is a most kind Dharma support. Hence I shall be patient toward him. It says
I should be joyful about my enemy because he supports my bodhicitta practice. By achieving patience through him, both of us will receive its results; since he is my patience’s cause, he deserves its results first.[466]

d.div: [740] bsgrub/ dpal spungs/
[741] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 6_sh+loka_107_shog_18_ba7

f.d:
sangs rgyas mnyes par brtag pa ni/ ji skad du/
gzhan yang g.yo med gnyen gyur pa/ / phan pa dpag med mdzad rnams la/ / sems can mgu byas ma gtogs pa/ / gzhan gang zhig gis lan lon 'gyur/[742] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Considering that the buddhas will be delighted:
Furthermore, the buddhas are the most steadfast of friends and benefit us immeasurably. What way is there to repay their kindness other than by respecting beings?[467]

d.div: [742] gong mtshungs/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 6_sh+loka_119_shog_19_na6

f.d:
phan yon che bar brtag pa ni/ ji skad du/
'di dag mgu byas mang po zhig / 'di ltar phun sum pha rol phyin/[743] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Considering the tremendous benefit:
These who show respect in many ways thereby cross excellently to the other shore.[468]

d.div: [743] gong mtshungs/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 6_sh+loka_112_shog_19_na2

f.d:
byang sa las/ 'du shes lnga bskyed la bzod pa bsgom par gsungs te/ ji skad du/
gnod pa byed pa de la snying du sdug pa'i 'du shes dang / chos tsam du rjes su 'brang ba'i 'du shes dang / mi rtag pa'i 'du shes dang / /sdug bsngal ba'i 'du shes dang / yongs su bzung ba'i 'du shes so/[744]/ zhes gsungs so/ /

In Bodhisattva Levels, it teaches us to cultivate patience on the basis of developing five recognitions. It says
Recognize the perpetrator of the harm as someone dear to your heart, recognize him as a mere phenomenal reality, recognize him as impermanent, recognize him as suffering, and recognize him as someone to be utterly cared for.[469]

d.div: [744] sde dge_4037_bstan/ sems tsam/ wi_'phags pa thogs med/ byang sa/ le'u/ 11_shog_102_ba2
[469] Asaṅga, Bodhisattvabhūmi, Toh 4037 Tengyur, sems tsam, wi, 102b2.

f.d: de la dang po ni/ de lta gnod byed kyi sems can 'di sngon gyi tshe rabs gzhan du pha ma'am/ spun zla'am/ slob dpon ma byas pa ni med la/ de dag gis bdag la ngan par byas pa ni grangs kyis mi chod pas/ da lta gnod pa 'di 'dra ba la bdag lan byed pa mi bzod snyam du snying du sdug pa'i 'du shes kyis bzod par bya'o/[745] /

Recognizing the harmer as someone dear to your heart means that these beings who are at present causing harm were not like this in former lives. Then they were parents, relatives, or teachers, and there is not one of them who was not at one time your mother. In that sense they have been helpful and beneficial to a degree that no one could ever calculate, /170/ and hence it is not right to retaliate against the sort of trouble they are making at present. Patience can be found through relating to the situation in these terms.

d.div: [745] mi 'thad snyam du/ dpal spungs/ mi bzad snyam du/ mi rigs dpe skrun/

f.d: chos tsam du rjes su 'brang ba'i 'du shes ni/ gnod par byed pa 'di ni rkyen la rag las pa dang / 'du shes tsam chos tsam du zad do/ /'di la ni gshe bar byed pa'am/ brdeg pa dang / mtshang 'bru ba dang / brgyad bkag byed pa'i bdag gam sems can nam srog gam/ skye ba po gang yang med do/ /snyam du bsams nas bzod par byed pa'o/ /

Recognizing the harmer as a mere phenomenal reality means that the harm that is taking place is dependent on conditions. As such, it is no more than mere notions, mere phenomena. There is not even the slightest trace of an instigator, a life, or a sentient being who is being abusive, strike you, defame you, or obstuct your activities. Practice patience through notions like these.

mi rtag pa'i 'du shes ni/ sems can ni mi rtag ste 'chi ba'i chos can yin la/ gnod pa'i mchog ni srog dang 'bral ba yin te/ de ltar na sems can rang bzhin gyis 'chi bas srog bcad mi dgos snyam du bsams nas bzod par byed pa'o/ /

Recognizing him as impermanent means to contemplate thus. Sentient beings are impermanent; they are mortal, and the greatest harm that can befall them is to lose their lives. Thus you can practice patience by contemplating that there is no need to kill them since they will die anyway, due to the very nature of their existence.

sdug bsngal ba'i 'du shes ni/ sems can thams cad sdug bsngal gsum gyis nyen la/ bdag gis de dag bsal bar bya yi sdug bsngal bsgrub par mi bya'o snyam ste/ de nyid sdug bsngal ba'i 'du shes kyis gnod pa la bzod par byed pa'o/ /

Recognizing him as suffering: Every sentient being is afflicted by the three types of suffering. Think that you should be removing sufferings and not creating further ones. This is practicing patience by seeing suffering.

yongs su bzung ba'i 'du shes ni/ bdag gis byang chub tu sems bskyed pa na sems can thams cad kyi don du bya'o/ /zhes sems can thams cad chung ma'i tshul du yongs su bzung ste/ de ltar yongs su bzung nas gnod pa phran tshegs la lan byed par mi rigs so snyam nas bzod par byed pa'o/ /

Recognizing him as someone to be utterly cared for means thinking, “Since I have taken the bodhisattva vow, I should be working for the welfare of all sentient beings.” Bearing this in mind, hold every sentient being very dear to your heart, with a fondness like you have for your own spouse. Give rise to patience by seeing that it is not fitting to retaliate for trivial harms done by someone treasured so dearly.

gnyis pa sdug bsngal dang du len pa'i bzod pa ni/ bla na med pa'i byang chub bsgrub pa'i sdug bsngal rnams kyis mi skyo bar dga' ba'i sems kyis dang du blang ba'o/ / de yang byang sa las/
gnas la brten pa'i sdug bsngal la sogs sdug bsngal brgyad dang du blang bar gsungs so/[746]/

The second [aspect of patience], patience as voluntary acceptance of suffering, means accepting joyfully and without regret all the sufferings involved in achieving highest enlightenment. It says in Bodhisattva Levels:
It is to accept the eight sorts of suffering, such as those due to one’s dwelling and so forth.[470]

d.div: [746] sde dge_4037_bstan/ sems tsam/ wi_'phags pa thogs med/ byang sa/ le'u/ 11_shog_103_ba7

f.d: de yang don gyis 'di rnams yin te/ rab tu byung nas chos gos dang bsod snyoms la sogs pa'i rtsol ba'i sdug bsngal dang / dkon mchog dang bla ma mchod cing bsnyen bkur ba dang / chos nyan pa dang / bshad pa dang / kha ton dang / bsgom pa dang / nam gyi cha stod cha smad la mi nyal bar rnal 'byor la brtson pa dang / sems can gyi don snga ma bzhin du bcu gcig po de byed pa la sogs pa la rtsol ba las byung ba'i sdug bsngal te/ ngal ba dang / dub pa dang / tsha ba dang / grang ba dang / bkres pa dang /[747] skom pa dang / sems kyi 'khrug pa la sogs pa thams cad kyis mi skyo bar dang du len pa'o/[748] / de yang dper na/ nad drag po'i sdug bsngal zhi bar bya ba'i ched du gtar gyis nad 'chos pa la sogs pa'i sdug bsngal dang du len pa bzhin no/[749] /

The main points here are to accept the sufferings encountered in one’s efforts to acquire Dharma robes, alms, and so forth following becoming a renunciate, the sufferings faced in one’s efforts in making offerings to and respectfully serving the most precious refuges and gurus, in studying the Dharma, in explaining it, in reciting texts, in meditating, in striving in yoga during the first and last parts of the night instead of sleeping, in working for the welfare of others in the eleven ways mentioned above, and so forth, and to do so without being discouraged by such factors as physical hardship, exhaustion, heat, cold, hunger, thirst, or mental anxiety. An analogy of such voluntary acceptance is to be found in the way someone is glad to receive a painful treatment—such as blood-letting or moxibustion—in order to be cured of a serious illness.

d.div: [747] dkres/ dpal spungs/
[748] mi rigs dpe skrun dpar mar 'brel sgra'i kyi mi byung /
[749] gtar gas/ dpal spungs/ mi rigs dpe skrun/

f.d:
de ltar yang spyod 'jug las/
bdag gis byang chub bsgrub pa yi/ / sdug bsngal 'di ni tshod yod de/ / zug rngu khong brlag gnod bsal phyir/ / lus rma gtong pa'i sdug bsngal bzhin/[750] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Guide to the Bodhisattva Way of Life says of this:
The suffering of my achieving enlightenment is confined. It is like the suffering inflicted on the body by surgery to rid it of an unbearably painful internal ailment.[471]

d.div: [750] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_spyod 'jug_le'u/ 7_sh+loka_22_shog_21_na1
[471] Śāntideva, Bodhicaryāvatāra 7:22, Toh 3871 Tengyur, dbu ma, la, 21a1.

f.d: de ltar chos kyi sdug bsngal dang du blangs nas 'khor ba'i g.yul ngo bzlog cing nyon mongs pa'i dgra 'joms pa ni dpa' bo chen po yin no/ / tha mal pa'i dgra rang bzhin gyis 'chi ba bsad pa ni 'jig rten na dpa' bor grags kyang de lta ma yin te/ ro la mtshon brdeg pa dang 'dra'o/ /

Someone who accepts the suffering involved in Dharma development and who manages to swing the battle with samsara and defeat the enemy—the afflictions—is a truly great hero. There are some people renowned in the world as heroes, but there is really no comparison, because they only defeat ordinary enemies, who by their very mortal nature will be slaughtered by death anyway. What they achieve is like striking a corpse with a weapon.

de ltar yang spyod 'jug las/
sdug bsngal thams cad khyad bsad nas/ / zhe sdang la sogs dgra 'joms pa/ / de dag rgyal byed dpa' bo ste/ lhag ma ro la gsod pa yin/[751] / zhes gsungs so//

The Guide to the Bodhisattva Way of Life says:
By slaughtering reservations about any sort of suffering, you defeat the enemies—anger, hatred, and so on. Someone who achieves that victory is a real hero; the rest is akin to slaying a corpse.[472]

d.div: [751] gong mtshungs/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 6_sh+loka_20_shog_15_na7

f.d: gsum pa chos la nges par sems pa la mos pa'i bzod pa ni/[752] byang sa las/ dkon mchog gi yon tan la sogs pa gnas brgyad la mos pa yin par gsungs so/[753] / yang de kho na nyid kyi don bdag rnam pa gnyis kyis stong pa'i rang bzhin la mos shing bzod pa'o/ /

The third [aspect], patience as confidence born of definite contemplation of the Dharma, is explained in Bodhisattva Levels in terms of “confidence with respect to eight factors, such as the qualities of the Three Jewels.”[473] It also relates to the patience born [of contemplating] the meaning of suchness—that is, the emptiness of the two types of selfhood.

d.div: [752] ma dpe dang mi rigs dpe skrun dpar ma gnyis su gsum pa ma byung yang / dpal spungs ltar bkod yod/
[753] sde dge_4037_bstan/ sems tsam/ wi_'phags pa thogs med/ byang sa/ le'u/ 11_shog_105_na5
[473] Asaṅga, Bodhisattvabhūmi, Toh 4037 Tengyur, sems tsam, wi, 105a5.

f.d: bzod pa spel ba ni/ ye shes dang / shes rab dang / bsngo ba gsum gyis spel ba ste/ gong du bstan pa ltar ro/ /

The fifth, how patience can be increased, refers to it being enhanced by means of pristine awareness, wisdom, and dedication. This is as already explained earlier [in the context of the perfection of generosity].
bzod pa dag par byed pa ni/ stong pa dang / snying rjes zin pa ste/ gong du bstan pa ltar ro//
The sixth, how it can be made pure, refers to patience being supported by emptiness and compassion, as explained earlier.

bzod pa'i 'bras bu ni/ mthar thug dang gnas skabs gnyis su shes par bya'o/ / de la mthar thug ni bla na med pa'i byang chub thob ste/ de ltar yang byang sa las/
bzod pa rgya che zhing tshad med la byang chub chen po'i 'bras bu 'byung ba 'di dag la brten na/ byang chub sems dpa' bla na med pa yang dag par rdzogs par 'tshang rgya bar 'gyur ro/[754] / zhes gsungs so/ /

The seventh, the fruits of patience, should be understood in terms of two—temporary and ultimate fruits. As for the ultimate result, you attain the unsurpassed enlightenment. Bodhisattva Levels says:
Vast and immeasurable patience will result in great enlightenment. Relying on this, bodhisattvas will become purely, most excellently, and perfectly enlightened.[474]

d.div: [754] gong mtshungs/ byang sa/ le'u/ 11_shog_107_na3

f.d:
gnas skabs su ni de la ma dmigs kyang / tshe rabs thams cad du gzugs mdzes pa dang / nad med pa dang / snyan grags dang / tshe ring ba dang / 'khor los sgyur ba'i rgyal srid thob bo/ / de ltar yang spyod 'jug las/
'khor tshe bzod pas mdzes sogs dang / / nad med pa dang grags pa yis/ / shin tu yun ring 'tsho ba dang / / 'khor los sgyur ba'i bde rgyas thob/[755] / ces gsungs so/ /

In the meantime the temporary consequences, even though you may not intentionally seek them, you will attain, in every future existence, a beautiful form, no illness, fame and acclaim, a long life, and the attributes of a universal monarch. Thus Guide to the Bodhisattva Way of Life says:
While in samsara, through patience one obtains beauty and so forth and will live long, with absence of illness and with fame; one will attain the delights of a universal monarch.[475]

d.div: [755] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 6_sh+loka_134_shog_20_na3
[475] Śāntideva, Bodhicaryāvatāra 6:134, Toh 3871 Tengyur, dbu ma, la, 20a3.

f.d: dam chos yid bzhin gyi nor bu thar pa rin po che'i rgyan las/ bzod pa'i pha rol tu phyin pa'i le'u ste bcu bzhi pa'o// //
This then concludes the fourteenth chapter, on the perfection of patience, in this Ornament of Precious Liberation, a Wish-Fulfilling Gem of Sublime Dharma.
le'u bco lnga pa/ brtson 'grus kyi pha rol tu phyin pa/
15. The Perfection of Diligence

brtson 'grus kyi pha rol tu phyin pa la/ sdom ni/
skyon yon rnam gnyis bsam pa dang / / ngo bo dang ni dbye ba dang / / phye ba so so'i mtshan nyid dang / / spel dang dag par bya ba dang /[756] / 'bras bu dang ni don bdun gyis/ / brtson 'grus pha rol phyin bsdus so/ / zhes pa'o/ /

d.div: [756] byas pa dang / dpal spungs/

f.d:
de la dang po bshad na/ gang zhig sbyin pa la sogs pa de dag dang ldan yang / brtson 'grus med na le lo can yin te/ le lo yod na dge ba mi 'grub/ gzhan don mi nus/ byang chub mi thob bo/ / de ltar yang blo gros rgya mtshos zhus pa'i mdo las/
le lo can la ni sbyin pa med pa nas shes rab kyi bar du med do/ / le lo can la ni gzhan don bya ba med do/ / le lo can la ni byang chub shin tu ring zhing rnam par ring ngo /[757] / zhes gsungs so/ /

To explain the first, reflection on the drawbacks of its absence and the benefits of its practice. Even if a person possesses the qualities of generosity and so forth, if he is devoid of diligence, then he will remain indolent. When there is indolence, virtue is not accomplished, there is no ability to benefit others, and enlightenment is not attained. Therefore the Questions of Sāgaramati Sutra says:
A person who is indolent is without generosity, moral discipline, patience, meditative concentration, and wisdom. A person is indolent performs no actions to benefit others. For a person who is indolent, enlightenment is far, exceedingly far.[476]

d.div: [757] sde dge_152_bka'/ mdo sde/ pha_blo gros rgya mtshos zhus pa'i mdo/ le'u/ 5_shog_40_na5
[476] Sāgaramatiparipṛcchāsūtra, Toh 152 Kangyur, mdo sde, pha, 40a5.

f.d:
de las ldog ste/ brtson 'grus dang ldan na/ dkar po'i yon tan thams cad mi 'grib cing 'phel bar 'gyur ro/ / de ltar yang / sdud pa las/
brtson 'grus kyis ni dkar po'i yon tan 'grib mi 'gyur/ / ye shes mtha' yas rgyal ba'i bang mdzod rnyed par 'gyur/[758] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Possession of diligence—the opposite of indolence—prevents all the bright qualities from becoming tainted and fosters their increase. The Verse Summary of the Perfection of Wisdom says:
Through diligence the bright qualities will not become tainted, and the buddhas’ treasure of infinite pristine awareness will be found.[477]

d.div: [758] sde dge_13_bka'/ sher phyin/ ka_mdo sdud pa/ le'u/ 32_sh+loka_3_shog_19_ba2
[477] Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā, Toh 13 Kangyur, sher phyin, ka, 19b2.

f.d:
yang brtson 'grus dang ldan na/ 'jig tshogs kyi ri bo las brgal nus pa yin no/[759] / de ltar yang mdo sde rgyan las/
brtson 'grus kyis ni 'jig tshogs 'das nas grol/[760] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Furthermore, if someone is endowed with diligence, he will be able to get across the mountain that is [the ego view of the] perishable composite.[478] Thus the Ornament of Mahayana Sutras says:
Through diligence, someone goes beyond perishable composite and is liberated.[479]

d.div: [759] rgal/ dpal spungs/
[760] sde dge_4020_bstan/ sems tsam/ phi_byams mgon/ mdo sde rgyan/ le'u/ 17_sh+loka_66_shog_24_ba2

[478] The Sanskrit satkāya was freely rendered into Tibetan as ’jig tshogs, which refers to the five aggregates and their nature as being both perishable (’jig) and composite (tshogs). Each aggregate can each be mistaken for a lasting and/or unitary self, as “me” or “mine.” And with four types of mistaken approaches to any of these five, one ends up with the twenty major aberrant views of personhood (satkāyadṛṣṭi), or as sometime rendered from the Tibetan, “view of the transitory collection.”
[479] Maitreya, Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra, Toh 4020 Tengyur, sems tsam, phi, 24b2.

f.d:
yang brtson 'grus dang ldan na bla med kyi byang chub myur du thob pa yin no/ / de ltar yang mdo sde rgyan las/
brtson 'grus kyis ni byang chub mchog 'tshang rgya/[761] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Moreover, if someone possesses diligence, the attainment of enlightenment will be rapid. Therefore the Ornament of Mahayana Sutras says:
Through diligence one will become supremely enlightened as a buddha.[480]

d.div: [761] gong mtshungs/ mdo sde rgyan/ le'u/ 17_sh+loka_66_shog_24_ba2
[480] Maitreya, Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāravṛtti, Toh 4021 Tengyur, sems tsam, phi, 201b5.

f.d:
blo gros rgya mtshos zhus pa'i mdo las kyang /
brtson 'grus brtsams pa rnams kyis ni bla na med pa yang dag par rdzogs pa'i byang chub dka' ba ma yin no/ / de ci'i phyir zhe na/ blo gros rgya mtsho gang na brtson 'grus yod pa de na byang chub yod do/[762] / zhes gsungs so/ /

The Questions of Sāgaramati Sutra also says:
Ultimate, totally pure, and perfect enlightenment is not difficult for those who practice diligence. Why is this? Sāgaramati! Whoever has diligence has enlightenment.[481] /173/

d.div: [762] sde dge_152_bka'/ mdo sde/ pha_blo gros rgya mtshos zhus pa'i mdo/ le'u/ 5_shog_40_na7
[481] Sāgaramatiparipṛcchāsūtra, Toh 152 Kangyur, mdo sde, pha, 40a7.

f.d:
gang pos zhus pa'i mdo las kyang /
rtag tu brtson 'grus gang brtsams pa/ / de la byang chub yongs mi dka'/[763] / zhes gsungs so/ /

The Questions of Pūrṇa Sutra says in a similar vein,
It will not be difficult for enlightenment to come to one who constantly exerts diligence.[482]

d.div: [763] sde dge_61_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ nga _gang pos zhus pa'i mdo/ le'u/ 3_shog_187_ba5
[482] Pūrṇaparipṛcchāsūtra, Toh 61 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, nga, 187b5.

f.d:
brtson 'grus kyi ngo bo ni/ /dge ba la spro ba'o/ / de ltar yang /
chos mngon pa kun las btus pa las/ brtson 'grus gang zhe na/ le lo'i gnyen po ste/ dge ba la sems mngon par spro ba'o/[764] / zhes gsungs so/ /

The second, the nature of diligence is to delight in virtue. Thus the Compendium of Higher Knowledge says:
What is diligence? It is the antidote against indolence, for it makes one’s mind to take genuine delight in virtue.[483]

d.div: [764] sde dge_4049_bstan/ sems tsam/ ri_mngon pa kun btus/ le'u/ 1_shog_49_na1_don mthun yang tshig mi mthun/
[483] This is not verbatim, but the meaning is that found in Asaṅga’s Abhidharmasamuccaya, Toh 4049 Tengyur, sems tsam, ri, 49a1.

f.d:
mdo sde rgyan gyi 'grel pa las kyang /
dge la yang dag spro ba dang / /zhes bya ba ni ngo bo nyid de/[765] zhes gsungs so/ / de yang mi mthun pa'i phyogs le lo'i gnyen po zhes pa la/ le lo la gsum ste/ snyoms las kyi le lo dang / sgyid lug pa'i le lo dang / smad pa'i le lo'o/ /

The Commentary on the Ornament of Mahayana Sutras also says,
“[The line] ‘To take utter delight in virtue’ presents its essential nature.”[484] With respect to the phrase “the antidote against indolence,” which is its opposing force, indolence is threefold: (1) indolence as idleness, (2) indolence as underestimating potential, and (3) indolence in the form of lowly pursuits.

d.div: [765] sde dge_4026_bstan/ sems tsam/ phi_dbyig gnyen/ mdo sde rgyan gyi 'grel pa/ le'u/ 16_shog_201_ba5
[484] Vasubandhu, Sūtrālaṁkārabhāṣya, Toh 4026 Tengyur, sems tsam, phi, 201b5.

f.d:
de la snyoms las kyi le lo ni/ nyal ba dang / gnyes pa dang /[766] gnyid la sogs pa yid dal gyi bde ba la chags pa ste/ de dag spang bar bya'o/ / de ci'i phyir spang zhe na/ tshe la long med pa'i phyir ro/ / de ltar yang mdo las/
dge slong dag shes pa ni 'grib/ srog ni chad/ tshe'i 'du byed ni 'dor/ ston pa'i bstan pa yang nges par 'jig par 'gyur na/ ci'i phyir brtson 'grus dang brtul ba brtan pos sgrub par mi byed/[767] ces gsungs so/ /

Indolence as idleness means being attached to the pleasures of letting the mind drift: through sleep, idling in bed, and lounging around. These are to be given up. Why give them up? Because there is no time for such things in this life. It is said:
Monks! If your cognition will come to dim, your life will be cut off, your will to live will be lost, and if even the Teacher’s doctrine will disappear for certain, why would you not practice with diligence and unflinching discipline?[485]

d.div: [766] gnyer pa dang / dpal spungs/ mnyes pa/ mi rigs dpe skrun/
[767] sde dge_303_bka'/ mdo sde/ sa_tshul khrims yang dag par ldan pa'i mdo/ shog_127_na4
[485] Sutra on Moral Discipline (Śīlasaṃyuktasūtra), Toh 303 Kangyur, mdo sde, sa, 127a4.

f.d:
spyod 'jug las kyang /
myur ba nyid du 'chi 'gyur bas/ / ji srid du ni tshogs bsag bya/[768] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Guide to the Bodhisattva Way of Life says too:
While death is swiftly encroaching, I must gather the accumulations.[486]

d.div: [768] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 7_sh+loka_7_shog_20_na7
[486] Śāntideva, Bodhicaryāvatāra 7:7ab, Toh 3871 Tengyur, dbu ma, la, 20a7.

f.d:
'chi khar tshogs bsags pas chog gam snyam na/ dus thug nas bsag long mi 'ong ste/[769] ji skad du/
de tshe le lo spangs kyang ni/ / dus ma yin pas ci zhig bya/[770] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Someone may think that it will be all right to establish the accumulations [of virtue and wisdom] at the time of death, but when that time comes, there will be no freedom to establish anything. As it says:
