At death, even if you were to relinquish indolence, what is the point, for it is too late![487]

d.div: [769] bsags/ dpal spungs/
[770] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 7_sh+loka_7_shog_20_na7

f.d:
dge ba ma zin gyi bar du bdag ni mi 'chi'o snyam na/ blo ltos med de/ ji skad du/
yid brtan mi rung 'chi bdag 'di/ / byas dang ma byas mi sdod pas/ / na dang mi na kun gyis kyang / / glo bur tshe la yid mi brtan/[771] / zhes gsungs so/ /

You may feel falsely confident, thinking that somehow death will not happen before you have completed your [accumulation of] virtue. That is an unreliable notion. As is said:
It is wrong to feel so confident. My death will not wait for me to finish the things I have to do. As far as this ephemeral life is concerned, it matters not whether I am sick or healthy.[488]

d.div: [771] gong mtshungs/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 2_sh+loka_34_shog_5_na5

f.d:
'o na snyoms las kyi le lo de ji ltar spang na/ pang du sbrul 'ong ba ltar 'dor ba'am/ mgo la me shor ba gsod pa ltar spang ngo / / de ltar yang spyod 'jug las/
de bas pang du sbrul 'ong na/ / ji ltar rings par ldang ba ltar/ / de bzhin gnyid dang snyom 'ong na/ / myur du de dag bzlog par bya/[772] / zhes gsungs so/ /

This being the case, you might ask, “How then do I eliminate the indolence of idleness?” You should relinquish it as you would react to a snake that had slithered onto your lap or if your hair were on fire. Thus Guide to the Bodhisattva Way of Life says:
Just as you would hurriedly jump up if a snake came onto your lap, so when sleep and idleness come along, swiftly counteract them![489]

d.div: [772] gong mtshungs/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 7_sh+loka_71_shog_23_na4

f.d:
bshes spring las kyang /
mgo'am gos la glo bur me shor na/ / de dag phyir bzlog bgyi ba btang nas kyang / / yang srid med par bgyid slad 'bad 'tshal te/ / de bas ches mchog dgos pa gzhan ma mchis/[773] / zhes gsungs so/ /

And Letter to a Friend says:
Even if your hair or clothes suddenly catch fire, instead of doing everything possible to put out the blaze, /174/ strive instead to extinguish future uncontrolled rebirth. Nothing else is as important as that.[490]

d.div: [773] sde dge_4182_bstan/ spring yig_nge _mgon po klu sgrub/ bshes spring / sh+loka_104_shog_45_ba3
[490] Nāgārjuna, Suhṛllekha verse 104, Toh 4182 Tengyur, spring yig, nge, 45b3.

f.d:
sgyid lugs pa'i le lo ni/ bdag lta bu ngan pas 'bad pa byas kyang byang chub ga la thob snyam nas sems zhum pa yin te/[774] [775] de ltar du zhum mi dgos pas sgyid lug de spang bar bya'o// ji ltar zhum mi dgos snyam na/ ji skad du/ /
sbrang bu sha sbrang bung ba dang / / de bzhin srin bur gang gyur pa/ / des kyang brtson pa'i stobs bskyed na/ / byang chub thob dka' bla med thob/ /
bdag ltar rigs kyi mir skyes la/ / phan dang gnod pa ngo shes pas/ / byang chub spyod pa ma btang na/ / bdag gis byang chub cis mi thob/[776] / ces gsungs pa ltar ro/ /

Indolence as underestimating potential refers to a defeatist attitude whereby you feel, “How could a lowly person like me ever achieve enlightenment, even were I to make great efforts?” Such discouragement is unnecessary. In fact, the waste of potential caused by such an attitude needs to annihilated. Those who wonder why such discouragement is unnecessary [should take heart from the scripture] that says:
If they develop the power of diligence, even bees, flies, mosquitoes, or any insect whatsoever will achieve enlightenment, so hard to attain!
That being the case, how could one like me— born human and knowing what is beneficial and what is harmful— not achieve enlightenment, provided I do not abandon the bodhisattva conduct?[491]

d.div: [774] snyam na/ dpal spungs/
[775] yin te/ de ltar du zhum pa yin te/ de ltar/ mi rigs dpe skrun/
[776] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_spyod 'jug_le'u/ 7_sh+loka_18_shog_20_ba6
[491] Śāntideva, Guide to the Bodhisattva Way of Life (Bodhicaryāvatāra) 7:18–19, Toh 3871 Tengyur, dbu ma, la, 20b6.

f.d: smad pa'i le lo ni/ dgra 'dul ba dang rdzas bsags pa la sogs pa mi dge ba la chags pa dag yin te/ / de dag sdug bsngal dngos kyi rgyu yin pas spang bar bya'o/[777] /

Indolence as lowly pursuits means involvement in nonvirtuous activities such as overcoming enemies, amassing possessions, and the like. As those are very real causes of suffering, they are to be abandoned.

d.div: [777] sdug bsngal gyi/ dpal spungs/ mi rigs dpe skrun/

f.d: brtson 'grus la dbye na gsum ste/ go cha'i brtson 'grus dang / sbyor ba'i brtson 'grus dang / chog par mi 'dzin pa'i brtson 'grus so/ / de la dang po ni/ bsam pa phun sum tshogs pa'o// gnyis pa ni/ sbyor ba phun sum tshogs pa'o/ / gsum pa ni/ de gnyis mthar phyin pa'i yan lag go/

Third, the different aspects of diligence. Diligence is threefold: armor-like diligence, applied diligence, and insatiable diligence. The first is the most excellent attitude. The second is the most excellent activity. The third is what carries the first two through to their conclusion.

de dag so so'i mtshan nyid bshad na/ go cha'i brtson 'grus ni/ dus 'di nas bzung nas sems can thams cad bla na med pa'i byang chub la ma 'god kyi bar du/[778] bdag gis dge ba'i brtson 'grus mi 'dor ro snyam du go cha gyon pa ste/ de ltar yang byang chub sems dpa'i sde snod las/
shA ri'i bu bsam gyis mi khyab pa'i go cha bgo bar bya ste/ 'khor ba'i tha ma ci tsam par byang chub kyi phyir brtson 'grus lhod par mi bya ste/[779] zhes gsungs so/ /

The fourth point develops the essential characteristics of each aspect. [First,] you wear the armor[-like diligence] of the attitude, “From this moment onward and until every sentient being has been established in highest enlightenment, I will never lay aside diligence in virtue.” It is said in the Bodhisattva Collection:
Śāriputra! Wear this as inconceivable armor: until the further-most end of samsara, whatever it may be, and never relax your diligence dedicated to enlightenment.[492]

d.div: [778] bkod/ dpal spungs/ mi rigs dpe skrun/
[779] sde dge_56_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ ga_byang chub sems dpa'i sde snod/ le'u/ 9_shog_116_na7
[492] Bodhisattvapiṭaka, Toh 56 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, ga, 116a7.

f.d:
go cha bkod pa bstan pa'i mdo las kyang /
byang chub sems dpas sems can rnams/ / bsdu phyir go cha bgo bar bya/ / sems can tshad ni med pa'i phyir/ / go cha bgos pa tshad med do/[780] / zhes gsungs so/ /

The Sutra Teaching the Wearing of Armor also says:
Bodhisattvas should wear such armor in order to gather beings to them. Since the number of beings is incalculable, the time for wearing of the armor should likewise be limitless.[493]

d.div: [780] sde dge_51_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ kha_go cha'i bkod pa bstan pa'i mdo/ bam po/ 1_shog_76_na7
[493] Varmavyūhanirdeśasūtra, Toh 51 Kengyur, dkon brtsegs, kha, vol. 1, 76a6.

f.d:
'phags pa blo gros mi zad pas zhus pa'i mdo las kyang /
de bskal pa 'di snyed cig tu go cha bgo / de bskal pa 'di snyed cig tu go cha mi bgo zhes bskal pa bgrang bas byang chub mi 'tshol gyi/ bsam gyis mi khyab pa'i go cha gyon par byed do/[781] / zhes gsungs so/ /

The Akṣayamati Sutra also says:
The bodhisattva does not seek enlightenment on the basis of calculating the eons in terms of “I shall wear armor for this many eons and not for this many eons.” He puts on armor for an inconceivable length of time.[494]

d.div: [781] sde dge_175_bka'/ mdo sde/ ma_blo gros mi zad pa bstan pa'i mdo/ bam po/ 2_shog_105_ba7
[494] Akṣayamatinirdeśasūtra, Toh 175 Kangyur, mdo sde, ma, 105b7.

f.d:
byang sa las/
bdag gis sems can gcig sdug bsngal las thar bar bya ba'i phyir bskal pa stong dang mnyam par sems can dmyal ba kho nar gnas dgos na yang bdag spro bar byed de/ dus yun ches thung ba dang / sdug bsngal ches chung ba lta ci smos snyam pa de lta bu ni/ byang chub sems dpa'i go cha'i brtson 'grus yin te/[782] zhes gsungs so//

Bodhisattva Levels says:
“If, to liberate one single being from suffering, /175/ I must abide in hell for a thousand eons, this fills me with joy. It does not matter how much or how little time it takes or how much or how little suffering it involves.” Such an attitude is the bodhisattva’s armor-like diligence.[495]

d.div: [782] sde dge_4037_bstan/ sems tsam/ wi_'phags pa thogs med/ byang sa/ le'u/ 12_shog_107_ba3
[495] Asaṅga, Bodhisattvabhūmi, Toh 4037 Tengyur, sems tsam, wi, 107b3.

f.d: sbyor ba'i brtson 'grus la gsum ste/ nyon mongs pa spangs pa la brtson 'grus bya ba dang /[783] dge ba sgrub pa la brtson 'grus bya ba dang /[784] sems can gyi don bya ba la brtson 'grus bya ba'o/ /
[Second,] applied diligence has three aspects: (1) diligence in getting rid of affliction, (2) diligence in accomplishing virtue, and (3) diligence in working for the welfare of others.

d.div: [783] spang ba/ mi rigs dpe skrun/
[784] bsgrub/ dpal spungs/ mi rigs dpe skrun/ gsham du'ang skabs mang por ma dper/ sgrub/ ces yod sar/ bsgrub/ ces byung /

f.d: de la dang po ni/ 'dod chags la sogs pa nyon mongs pa dang / de dag gis kun nas bslang pa'i las rnams ni sdug bsngal gyi rtsa ba yin pas dus yun ring po dang / sgos gses su byin gyis brlab cing ci mi 'byung byed pa yin no/[785] /

[1] For the first, [diligence in getting rid of affliction,] it is the afflictions—desire and so forth, as well as the actions they motivate—that are the root of suffering. Therefore, to put a stop to its arising, a correspondingly prolonged action that is both specific and global is needed.

d.div: [785] sgo gses/ dpal spungs/ mi rigs dpe skrun/

f.d:
de ltar yang spyod 'jug las/
nyon mongs tshogs kyi khrod gnas na/ / rnam pa stong du sran zugs te/ / wa la sogs pas seng ge bzhin/ / nyon mongs tshogs kyis mi tshugs bya/[786] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Guide to the Bodhisattva Way of Life:
Amid the hordes of the amassed afflictions, keep your stance firm in a thousand ways; like a lion among foxes, do not let the hosts of the afflictions injure you.[496]

d.div: [786] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_spyod 'jug_le'u/ 7_sh+loka_60_shog_22_ba3
[496] Śāntideva, Bodhicaryāvatāra 7:60, Toh 3871 Tengyur, dbu ma, la, 23a3.

f.d:
de yang dpe ji ltar bsgrim na/[787] ji skad du/
yungs mar gang ba'i snod bskur la/ / ral gri thogs la drung bsdad de/ / bo na gsod sdig 'jigs pa ltar/ / brtul zhugs can gyis de ltar bsgrim/[788] / zhes gsungs pa ltar ro/ /

Is there in fact some example of the vigilance and discipline that are needed? It is said:
One observing the discipline should be as vigilant as a terrified person carrying a pot full of mustard oil while being held at sword-point, threatened with death should a drop be spilled.[497]

d.div: [787] sgrim na/ dpal spungs/
[788] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 7_sh+loka_70_shog_23_na3

f.d: gnyis pa dge ba sgrub pa la brtson par bya ba ni/ pha rol tu phyin pa drug la lus dang srog la yang mi lta bar 'bad par byed pa'o/ / de yang ji ltar 'bad na/ brtson 'grus rnam pa lngas 'bad par bya ste/ rtag tu byed pa'i brtson 'grus dang / gus pa byed pa'i brtson 'grus dang / mi g.yo ba'i brtson 'grus dang / mi ldog pa'i brtson 'grus dang / nga rgyal med pa'i brtson 'grus so/ /

[2] Diligence in accomplishing virtue involves striving hard in the practice of the six perfections, without any regard for your life or physical well-being. How to strive? By means of five aspects of diligence: continuous diligence, enthusiastic diligence, unshakeable diligence, diligence as remaining undeterred, and humble diligence.

de la rtag tu byed pa'i brtson 'grus zhes bya ba ni/ rgyun ma chad par byed pa ste/ dkon mchog sprin las kyang /
'di la byang chub sems dpa' spyod lam thams cad du brtson 'grus brtsams pa na/ ci nas lus skyo bar mi 'gyur ba dang / sems skyo bar mi 'gyur ba de ltar rtsom ste/ 'di ni byang chub sems dpa'i rtag pa'i brtson 'grus zhes bya'o/[789] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Continuous diligence means working uninterruptedly. Of this the Clouds of Jewels Sutra says:
Since bodhisattvas apply diligence to every aspect of their daily lives, nothing can cause them regret about their acts of body or mind. Such application is known as “a bodhisattva’s continuous diligence.”[498]

d.div: [789] sde dge_231_bka'/ mdo sde/ wa_dkon mchog sprin gyi mdo/ bam po/ 2_shog_20_ba2
[498] Ratnameghasūtra, Toh 231 Kangyur, mdo sde, wa, 20b2.

f.d:
gus par byed pa'i brtson 'grus ni/ dga' bzhin spro bzhin myur du byed pa ste/ ji skad du/
de ltar las tshar phyin bya'i phyir/ / nyi ma phyed dus gdungs pa yi/ / glang chen mtshor phrad 'jug pa ltar/ / las de la yang 'jug par bya/[790] / zhes gsungs pa ltar ro/ /

Enthusiastic diligence means acting joyfully, appreciatively, and rapidly. As it is said:
Since this task must be completed, plunge into it like an elephant scorched by the midday sun plunges into a pool.[499]

d.div: [790] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 7_sh+loka_65_shog_22_ba7
[499] Śāntideva, Guide to the Bodhisattva Way of Life (Bodhicaryāvatāra) 7:66, Toh 3871 Tengyur, dbu ma, la, 22b7.

f.d: mi g.yo ba'i brtson 'grus ni/ rang rnam rtog dang / nyon mongs pa dang / sdug bsngal gyis gnod pa thams cad kyis mi g.yo bar byed pa'o/ /
Unshakeable diligence means /176/ not being distracted from the task by impediments due to thoughts, afflictions, or sufferings.

mi ldog pa'i brtson 'grus ni/ gzhan gyis 'tshe ba dang / dmu rgod dang / 'khrug pa dang / lta ba'i snyigs ma la sogs pa mthong bas mi ldog pa ste/ 'phags pa rdo rje rgyal mtshan gyi mdo las 'byung ba ltar ro/ /

Diligence as remaining undeterred means not being deterred by witnessing others’ violence, brutishness, aggressiveness, degenerate views, or the like, as is mentioned in the Vajra Victory Banner Sutra.[500]

d.div: [500] Vajraketusūtra. Toh 30 Kangyur, shes rab sna tshogs, ka.

f.d: nga rgyal med pa'i brtson 'grus ni/ brtson 'grus brtsams pa des mtho bar sems pa med pa'o//
Humble diligence means practicing the above forms of diligence without a haughty mind.
gsum pa sems can gyi don bya ba'i brtson 'grus ni/[791] bya ba la grogs med pa'i grogs bya ba la sogs pa bcu gcig po la 'bad par byed pa yin no/ /
[3] Diligence in accomplishing the welfare of others is to make effort in the eleven fields, such as supporting activities that are unsupported and so forth.

d.div: [791] da ni gsum pa / dpal spungs/

f.d:
de dag gis sbyor ba'i brtson 'grus bshad nas/ chog par mi 'dzin pa'i brtson 'grus ni/ byang chub ma thob kyi bar du dge ba la ngoms chog med par 'bad pa ste/ de ltar yang /
spu gri'i sor chags sbrang rtsi lta'i/ / 'dod pa rnams kyis mi ngoms na/ / rnam smin bde la zhi ba yi/ / bsod nams kyis lta ci ste ngoms/[792]/ zhes gsungs so/ /

[Third,] Insatiable diligence is striving after virtue in a way that knows no satisfaction until enlightenment is reached. As it is said:
If you cannot get enough of sense pleasures, which are like honey on a razor’s edge, how could you ever be satisfied by whatever peaceful, happy results ripen from virtue?[501]

d.div: [792] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 7_sh+loka_64_shog_22_ba6
[501] Śāntideva, Guide to the Bodhisattva Way of Life (Bodhicaryāvatāra) 7:65, Toh 3871 Tengyur, dbu ma, la, 22b6.

f.d: brtson 'grus spel ba ni/ ye shes dang / shes rab dang / bsngo ba gsum gyis spel ba ste/ gong du bshad pa ltar ro/ /
The fifth point concerns how diligence can be increased. It is increased by the three powers taught above: pristine awareness, deep understanding, and dedication, as explained before.
brtson 'grus dag par byed pa ni/ stong pa nyid dang snying rjes zin pa ste gong du bstan pa ltar ro//
The sixth point is how it can be made pure. This is accomplished through the two supports—emptiness and compassion—mentioned above.

brtson 'grus kyi 'bras bu ni/ mthar thug dang gnas skabs gnyis su shes par bya'o/ / de la mthar thug ni bla na med pa'i byang chub thob ste/ de ltar byang sa las/
byang chub sems dpa' brtson 'grus kyi pha rol tu phyin pa yongs su rdzogs par bya ste/ bla na med pa yang dag par rdzogs pa'i byang chub tu mngon par rdzogs par sangs rgyas so/ / mngon par rdzogs par 'tshang rgya bar 'gyur ro/ / mngon par rdzogs par 'tshang rgya'o/[793] / zhes gsungs so/ /

The seventh point, the fruits of diligence is to be understood in terms of two: the immediate and ultimate fruits of diligence. As for its the ultimate result, you attain the unsurpassed enlightenment. Bodhisattva Levels says:
Through perfectly completing the perfection of diligence, bodhisattvas truly became perfect buddhas, are truly becoming perfect buddhas, and will truly become perfect buddhas with highest, utterly pure, and perfect enlightenment.[502]

d.div: [793] sde dge_4037_bstan/ sems tsam/ wi_'phags pa thogs med/ byang sa/ le'u/ 12_shog_110_ba6
[502] Asaṅga, Bodhisattvabhūmi, Toh 4037 Tengyur, sems tsam, wi, 110b6.

f.d:
gnas skabs kyi 'bras bu ni/ 'khor ba na gnas pa'i tshe yang srid pa'i bde ba mchog rnams thob bo/ / de ltar yang mdo sde rgyan las/
brtson 'grus kyis ni srid spyod 'dod pa thob/[794] / ces gsungs so/ /

The temporary result consists of achieving the highest happiness even while remaining in cyclic existence. Thus the Ornament of Mahayana Sutras says:
Through diligence, the pleasures of existence are achieved.[503]

d.div: [794] sde dge_4020_bstan/ sems tsam/ phi_byams pa mgon po/ mdo sde rgyan/ le'u/ 17_sh+loka_66_shog_24_ba1
[503] Maitreya, Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra, Toh 4020 Tengyur, sems tsam, phi, 24b1.

f.d: dam chos yid bzhin gyi nor bu thar pa rin po che'i rgyan las/ brtson 'grus kyi pha rol tu phyin pa'i le'u ste bco lnga pa'o// //
This then concludes the fifteenth chapter, on the perfection of diligence, in this Ornament of Precious Liberation, a Wish-Fulfilling Gem of Sublime Dharma. /177/
le'u bcu drug pa/ bsam gtan gyi pha rol tu phyin pa/
16. The Perfection of Meditative Concentration

bsam gtan gyi pha rol tu phyin pa la/ sdom ni/
skyon yon rnam gnyis bsam pa dang / / ngo bo dang ni dbye ba dang / / phye ba so so'i mtshan nyid dang / / spel dang dag par bya ba dang / / 'bras bu dang ni don bdun gyis/ / bsam gtan pha rol phyin bsdus so/ / zhes pa'o/ /

For the presentation of the perfection of meditative concentration, the following is the synopsis:
The perfection of meditative concentration is summarized as sevenfold: reflections on the drawbacks of its absence and the benefits of its practice; its nature; its different aspects; the essential characteristics of each aspect; how it can be increased; how it can be made pure; and its fruits.

de la dang po bshad na/ gang zhig sbyin pa la sogs pa dang ldan yang / bsam gtan dang mi ldan na/ de rnam par g.yeng ba'i dbang du gyur nas sems nyon mongs pa'i mche bas rmas par 'gyur ro/ / de ltar yang spyod 'jug las/
sems ni rnam par g.yeng ba'i mi/ / nyon mongs mche ba'i phrag na gnas/[795] / zhes gsungs so/ /

The first of these, [namely, the drawbacks of its absence and the benefits of its practice,] is as follows. Whoever has the qualities of generosity and so forth, if he lacks meditative concentration he can be overpowered by distractions and so will be wounded by the sharp fangs of the afflictions. Thus Guide to the Bodhisattva Way of Life says:
Humans whose minds are very distracted live between the fangs of the afflictions.[504]

d.div: [795] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 8_sh+loka_1_shog_23_na7
[504] Śāntideva, Bodhicaryāvatāra 8:1, Toh 3871 Tengyur, dbu ma, la, 23a7.

f.d:
yang bsam gtan dang mi ldan na mngon shes mi skye la/ mngon shes ma skyes na sems can gyi don mi nus so/ / de ltar yang byang chub lam sgron las/
zhi gnas grub pa ma yin pas/ / mngon shes 'byung ba ma yin la/ / de bzhin mngon shes stobs bral bas/ / sems can don byed nus pa min/[796] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Furthermore, if you lack meditative concentration, clairvoyance will not arise, and if clairvoyance has not arisen in you, you will not be fully equipped to benefit others. Lamp for the Path to Awakening says:
Without the achievement of tranquility, clairvoyance will not emerge.[505] And without the force of clairvoyance, other’s welfare will not be achieved.[506]

d.div: [796] sde dge_3947_bstan/ dbu ma/ khi_dpal mar me mdzad ye shes/ lam sgron/ sh+loka_35_shog_239_ba5
[505] Atiśa, Bodhipathapradīpa verse 38, Toh 3947 Tengyur, dbu ma, khi, 239b7.
[506] Ibid. verse 35, 239b5.

f.d:
yang bsam gtan dang mi ldan na/ shes rab mi skye la/ shes rab ma skyes na byang chub mi thob bo/ / de ltar yang bshes spring las/
bsam gtan med par yang ni shes rab med/[797] / ces gsungs so/ /

Moreover, if you lacks meditative concentration, wisdom will not arise, and if wisdom has not arisen, enlightenment will not be attained. Thus the Letter to a Friend says:
There is no wisdom where there is no meditative concentration.[507]

d.div: [797] sde dge_4182_bstan/ spring yig_nge _mgon po klu sgrub/ bshes spring / sh+loka_106_shog_45_ba4
[507] Nāgārjuna, Suhṛllekha, Toh 4182 Tengyur, spring yig, nge, 45b4.

f.d:
de las ldog ste bsam gtan dang ldan na dngos po dman pa la zhen pa 'dor/ mngon par shes pa 'byung / ting nge 'dzin gyi sgo mang po rgyud la skye ba'o/ / de ltar yang 'phags pa sdud pa las/
bsam gtan gyis ni 'dod pa'i yon tan smad pa 'dor/ / rigs dang mngon par shes dang ting 'dzin mngon par 'grub/[798] / ces gsungs so/ /

In contrast, if you are endowed with meditative concentration, you will abandon craving for lesser things, clairvoyance will emerge, and many doors of meditative absorption (samādhi) will be opened within you. Thus the Verse Summary of the Perfection of Wisdom says:
Through meditative concentration, craving for lowly sensual pleasures are rejected, and one truly attains intelligence, clairvoyance, and meditative absorption.[508]

d.div: [798] sde dge_13_bka'/ sher phyin/ ka_mdo sdud pa/ le'u/ 32_sh+loka_3_shog_19_ba3
[508] Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā, Toh 13 Kangyur, sher phyin, ka, 19b3.

f.d:
yang bsam gtan dang ldan na des shes rab bskyed nas rang gi nyon mongs pa thams cad 'joms pa yin no/ / de ltar spyod 'jug las/
zhi gnas rab tu ldan pa'i lhag mthong gis/ / nyon mongs rnam par 'joms par shes byas nas/[799] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Furthermore, if you are endowed with meditative concentration, wisdom will develop, and this will cause every affliction to be overcome. Thus Guide to the Bodhisattva Way of Life says:
Understanding that the afflictions are totally vanquished by profound insight (vipaśyanā) conjoined with tranquility. [509]

d.div: [799] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 8_sh+loka_4_shog_23_ba1
[509] Śāntideva, Bodhicaryāvatāra 8:4, Toh 3871 Tengyur, dbu ma, la, 23b1.

f.d:
yang bsam gtan dang ldan na yang dag pa'i don mthong zhing sems can la snying rje skye'o/ / de ltar chos yang dag par sdud pa'i mdo las/
yid mnyam par bzhag pas yang dag pa ji lta ba bzhin mthong bar 'gyur ro/ / yang dag pa ji lta ba bzhin mthong bas/ byang chub sems dpa' sems can rnams la snying rje chen por 'jug go[800] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Moreover, if you are endowed with meditative concentration, you will have insight into the perfect truth and therefore generate compassion for sentient beings. Thus Perfectly Gathering the Qualities [of Avalokiteśvara] says:
Through settling the mind in meditative equipoise, there will be insight into the ultimate just as it is. Through insight into the ultimate just as it is, bodhisattvas will enter into a state of great compassion for sentient beings.[510] /178/

d.div: [800] sde dge_238_bka'/ mdo sde/ zha_chos yang dag pa sdud pa'i mdo/ bam po/ 4_shog_52_na6
[510] Dharmasaṃgītisūtra, Toh 238 Kangyur, mdo sde, zha, 42a6.

f.d:
yang bsam gtan dang ldan na/ gdul bya thams cad byang chub la 'god nus pa yin no/ / de ltar yang mdo sde rgyan las/
bsam gtan de nyid kyis kyang skye bo thams cad byang chub gsum la 'god/[801] / ces gsungs so/ /

Further, if you are endowed with meditative concentration, through it you will establish disciples in enlightenment. Thus the Ornament of Mahayana Sutras says:
Through meditative concentration itself, all individuals will become established in the three types of enlightenment.[511]

d.div: [801] sde dge_4020_bstan/ sems tsam/ phi_byams pa mgon po/ mdo sde rgyan/ le'u/ 16_sh+loka_40_shog_23_na4
[511] Maitreya, Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra, Toh 4020 Tengyur, sems tsam, phi, 23a4. The three types of enlightenment refer to the arhat states of śrāvakas and prateyakabuddhas and to buddhahood.

f.d:
bsam gtan gyi ngo bo ni/ zhi gnas kyi rang bzhin sems nang du dge ba la rtse gcig tu gnas pa'o/ / de ltar yang byang sa'i bsam gtan gyi ngo bo nyid bstan pa'i skabs nas/
sems rtse gcig pa dge ba la sems gnas pa/[802] zhes gsungs so/ /

The second, the nature of meditative concentration, is this: It is characterized by tranquility wherein the mind rests within, focused on virtue. Therefore, in the section dealing with the nature of meditative concentration of the Bodhisattva Levels, it says:
It is a one-pointed mind, abiding in virtue. . . [512]

d.div: [802] sde dge_4037_bstan/ sems tsam/ wi_'phags pa thogs med/ byang sa/ le'u/ 13_shog_111_na2
[512] Asaṅga, Bodhisattvabhūmi, Toh 4037 Tengyur, sems tsam, wi, 111a2.

f.d: de lta bu'i bsam gtan de yang mi mthun pa'i phyogs rnam par g.yeng ba spangs pa las thob pa yin pas/ dang po rnam par g.yeng ba spang bar bya'o/ / de yang rnam par g.yeng ba spang ba ni dben pa ste/[803] lus 'du 'dzi las dben pa dang / sems rnam par rtog pa las dben par bya'o/ /

This kind of meditative concentration is attained through eliminating its opposing force, namely, powerful distractions. Hence the first priority is to overcome distraction. This involves seclusion, inasmuch as the body needs to be secluded from worldly pursuits and the mind needs to be secluded from its habitual thought processes.

d.div: [803] spong / dpal spungs/

f.d:
de ltar yang spyod 'jug las/
lus dang sems ni dben pa yis/ rnam par g.yeng ba mi 'byung ste/[804] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Thus Guide to the Bodhisattva Way of Life says:
With body and mind secluded, distracted thoughts will not arise.[513]

d.div: [804] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 8_sh+loka_2_shog_23_na7
[513] Śāntideva, Bodhicaryāvatāra 8:2ab, Toh 3871 Tengyur, dbu ma, la, 23a7.

f.d: de la dang po lus 'du 'dzi las rnam par dben par bya ba don drug gis shes par bya ste/[805] 'du 'dzi'i mtshan nyid dang / 'du 'dzi'i rgyu dang / 'du 'dzi'i nyes pa dang / dben pa'i mtshan nyid dang / dben pa'i rgyu dang / dben pa'i yon tan no/ /

Of these two, secluding the body from worldly pursuits will be explained on the basis of six points: (1) the nature of distractive activities, (2) the cause of distractive activities, and (3) harmfulness of distractive activities, (4) the nature of seclusion, (5) the cause of seclusion, and (6) the benefits of seclusion.

d.div: [805] bya ba la don/ dpal spungs/

f.d: de la 'du 'dzi'i mtshan nyid ni/ bdag bu dang chung ma dang 'khor dang longs spyod dang lhan cig tu g.yengs pa'o/[806] /
(1) The nature of distractive activities is this: it is to be in a state of distraction due to involvement with children, spouse, acquaintances, or possessions.

d.div: [806] bdag gi bu/ dpal spungs/

f.d: 'du 'dzi'i rgyu ni/ chags pa ste bu smad dang g.yog 'khor la sogs pa sems can la chags pa dang / zas nor la sogs pa rnyed pa la chags pa dang / bstod pa la sogs pa snyan grags la chags pas 'du 'dzi mi spong ba yin no/ /

(2) The cause of distractive activities is attachment, meaning attachment to people, such as spouse, household, and the like; attachment to material things, such as food, clothing, and the like; and attachment to reputation and respect, such as others’ praise and so on. Being attached to such things, it becomes impossible to shake free from worldly busyness.

de ltar yang /
chags pa'i phyir dang rnyed sogs la/ / sred pas 'jig rten mi spongs te/[807] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Thus it is said:
Because of attachment and craving for material possessions, the world is not relinquished.[514]

d.div: [807] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 8_sh+loka_3_shog_23_ba1

f.d:
'du 'dzi'i nyes pa ni/ spyi dang bye brag gnyis su shes par bya'o/ / de la spyi'i dbang du byas na/ lhag pa'i bsam pa bskul ba'i mdo las/
byams pa 'du 'dzi'i nyes dmigs nyi shu po 'di dag yin te/ nyi shu gang zhe na/ lus kyis ma bsdams pa yin/ ngag gis ma bsdams pa yin/ yid kyis ma bsdams pa yin/ nyon mongs pa che ba yin/ 'jig rten pa'i gtam gyis kyang gos pa yin/ bdud kyis glags rnyed pa yin/ bag med pa la brten pa yin/ zhi gnas dang lhag mthong mi thob pa yin/[808] zhes pa la sogs pa gsungs so/ /

(3) The harmfulness of distractive activities should be known in terms of both the general and the specific. The general harm caused by distractive activities is explained in the Sutra Encouraging Nobler Intention:
Maitreya! The twenty shortcomings of distractive activities are these. What are they? There is no restraint of body, there is no restraint of speech, there is no restaint of the mind, the afflictions are strong, one is polluted by mundane talk, one will be vulnerable to negative influences, /179/ one will be given over to heedlessness, one will fail to attain tranquility and insight [515]

d.div: [808] sde dge_69_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ ca_lhag pa'i bsam pa bskul ba'i mdo/ shog_143_ba2
[515] Adhyāśayasaṃcodanasūtra, Toh 69 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, ca, 143b2.

f.d:
bye brag gi dbang du byas na/ sems can la chags pa'i nyes pas ni byang chub mi thob bo/ / de ltar yang / zla ba sgron ma'i mdo las/
'dod pa dag ni rab tu bsten byed cing / / bu dang chung ma dag la sred bskyed nas/ / smad par bya ba'i khyim la brten pa des/ / nam yang bla med byang chub mchog mi thob/[809] / ces gsungs so/ /

With respect to the specific harms of distractive activities, through attachment to people you will not attain enlightenment. The Candraprabha Sutra says:
Indulging in desires thoroughly, you become attached to children and spouse and rely on the pitiable home [life], thereby never attaining the unsurpassed enlightenment.[516]

d.div: [809] sde dge_127_bka'/ mdo sde/ da_ting nge 'dzin rgyal po'i mdo/ le'u/ 5_sh+loka_5_shog_16_na2
[516] A.k.a. King of Meditation Sutra (Samādhirājasūtra), Toh 127 Kangyur, mdo sde, da, 16a2.

f.d:
spyod 'jug las kyang /
sems can nyid la chags byas na/ / yang dag nyid la kun nas bsgribs/[810] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Guide to the Bodhisattva Way of Life also says of this:
Through attachment to those beings, the highest purpose is completely blotted out.[517]

d.div: [810] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 8_sh+loka_7_shog_23_ba3
[517] Śāntideva, Bodhicaryāvatāra 8:8ab, Toh 3871 Tengyur, dbu ma, la, 23b3.

f.d:
des na de la chags pa spang bar bya ste/ ji skad du/
des kyang bdag don mi byed la/ / bdag kyang de don mi 'gyur bas/ / byis las thag ring byol bar bya/[811] / zhes gsungs so/ /

[The meditator] should therefore get rid of attachment to those people. As it is said:
Neither do they benefit you nor do you benefit them, so steer well clear of the immature![518]

d.div: [811] gong mtshungs/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 8_sh+loka_14_shog_24_na1

f.d:
de dag spangs pa'i phan yon yang / zla ba sgron me'i mdo las/
bu dang chung ma dag la sred spangs nas/ / khyim gyis skrag ste khyim las mngon byung ba/ / de dag byang chub mchog ni rnyed mi dka'/[812] / zhes gsungs so/ /

On the benefits of casting off these attachments, the Candraprabha Sutra says:
Perfect enlightenment is not hard to find for those who, having rid themselves of clinging to spouse and offspring and fearing domestic life, have genuinely shaken free from it.[519]

d.div: [812] sde dge_127_bka'/ mdo sde/ da_ting nge 'dzin rgyal po'i mdo/ le'u/ 5_sh+loka_6_shog_16_na3
[519] King of Meditation Sutra (Samādhirājasūtra), Toh 127 Kangyur, mdo sde, da, 16a3.

f.d: rnyed pa dang grags pa la chags pa'i nyes pa yang gnyis te/ rnyed grags de gtan du gzung bar mi nus pa dang / de dag gis sdug bsngal bskyed pa'o/ /
The harm caused by attachment to material possessions and to reputation is twofold: One cannot sustain them permanently, and they give rise to suffering.

dang po ni/ spyod 'jug las/
rnyed dang grags pa'i tshogs bcas te/ / gang du 'gro ba'i gtol med do/[813] / zhes gsungs so/ /

It says of the first, in Guide to the Bodhisattva Way of Life:
What has become of those who have amassed wealth and fame is quite unknown.[520]

d.div: [813] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 8_sh+loka_20_shog_24_na4
[520] Śāntideva, Bodhicaryāvatāra 8:20cd, Toh 3871 Tengyur, dbu ma, la, 24a4.

f.d:
gnyis pa yang de nyid las/
gang dang gang la chags gyur pa/ / de dang de bsdongs stong 'gyur du/ / sdug bsngal nyid du 'gyur zhing ldang /[814] / zhes gsungs so//

Of the second it says:
Whatever you are attached to will come back a thousandfold as suffering.[521]

d.div: [814] gong mtshungs/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 8_sh+loka_18_shog_24_na3

f.d: dben pa'i mtshan nyid ni/ 'du 'dzi de dag dang bral ba'o/ /
(4) The nature of seclusion consists in being free from ditracting pursuits.

dben pa'i rgyu ni/ gcig pur dgon par gnas pa'o/ / de la dgon pa zhes bya ba ni/ dur khrod dam nags gseb bam bya skyibs sam thang la sogs pa gang yin na'ang yin te/ gzhu 'dom lnga brgya srid du yod pa de la rgyang grags bya ba yin la/ grong las rgyang grags gcig phan chad 'das pa de la dgon pa bya ba yin no/ /

(5) The cause of seclusion is to abide in solitude in an isolated place. An isolated place would be the likes of charnal grounds, forests, caves, meadows, and so forth. To qualify as an isolated place, it should be out of earshot of worldly habitations, meaning a distance of some five hundred bow-spans.

chos mngon pa mdzod las kyang /
gzhu 'dom lnga brgya rnams la ni/ / rgyang grags de la dgon par 'dod/[815] / ces gsungs so/ /

It says in the Treasury of Higher Knowledge:
A place is considered secluded when it is out of earshot, which means five hundred bow-spans away [from dwellings].[522]

d.div: [815] sde dge_4089_bstan/ mngon pa/ ku_chos mngon pa mdzod/ gnas/ 3_sh+loka_87_shog_10_na4
[522] Vasubhandu, Abhidharmakośa, Toh 4089 Tengyur, mngon pa, ku, 10a4.

f.d: dben pa'i yon tan ni/ byang chub dang sems can gyi ched du/ 'du 'dzi las bros te dgon pa brten na yon tan mang ste/[816] sangs rgyas rnams la bsnyen bkur gyi mchog tu 'gyur ba dang / 'khor ba la yid dbyung bar 'gyur ba dang /[817] 'jig rten gyi chos brgyad dang bral bar 'gyur ba dang / nyon mongs pa mi 'phel ba dang / ting nge 'dzin rgyud la skye ba'o/ /

(6) The benefits of seclusion is as follows. When someone has abandoned distractive activities and gone to stay in seclusion, for the sake of both enlightenment and other sentient beings, the benefits are manifold: It is the best way to serve and respect enlightened beings; the mind will emerge from its samsara, /180/ there will be freedom from the eight worldly concerns, and afflictions will not increase; and meditative absorption swiftly develops. These will be explained point by point.

d.div: [816] ma dper/ gros/ zhes byung yang dpal spungs dang mi rigs dpe skrun khang ltar/ bros zhes bcos/
[817] 'khor ba las yid 'byung bar/ dpal spungs/ 'khor ba la yid du byung bar/ mi rigs dpe skrun/

f.d:
de la dang po bshad na/ yang dag par rdzogs pa'i sangs rgyas la zas skom dang / me tog la sogs pa'i mchod pa sna tshogs phul ba bas/ byang chub kyi sems kyis sems can gyi don du dgon par bsdad pa'i bsam pas/ dgon pa'i phyogs su gom pa bdun bor ba tsam la mnyes pa yin no/ / zla ba sgron me'i mdo las kyang /
zas dang skom dang de bzhin gos rnams dang / / me tog spos dang phreng ba rnams kyis ni/ / khyu mchog rgyal la bsnyen bkur byas mi 'gyur/ / gang zhig byang chub rab tu 'dod byed cing / / 'dus byas ngan pas yid 'byung sems can gyi/ / don du dgon par gnas te gom bdun bor/ / 'di ni de bas bsod nams khyad par 'phags/[818] / zhes gsungs so/ /

As for the first point, [seclusion being the best way to serve the buddhas:] When, through bodhicitta, just seven paces are taken toward a hermitage with the intention of staying in retreat to benefit beings, it is far more pleasing to the totally pure and perfect buddhas than offering them food, drink, flowers, and so on. Thus the Candraprabha Sutra says:
Food, drink, and robes, flowers, incense, and garlands are not what best serve and honor the Victor, the finest being of all. Whoever, longing for enlightenment and saddened with the evils of conditioned life, takes seven paces toward a place of retreat with the intention of staying there to benefit beings his merit is far greater than those who make such offerings.[523]

d.div: [818] sde dge_127_bka'/ mdo sde/ da_ting nge 'dzin rgyal po'i mdo/ le'u/ 5_sh+loka_10_shog_16_na5
[523] King of Meditation Sutra (Samādhirājasūtra), Toh 127 Kangyur, mdo sde, da, 16a5.

f.d:
'khor ba las yid dbyung ba dang / chos brgyad dang bral ba dang / nyon mongs pa mi 'phel ba yang / mdo sde de nyid las/
de bzhin 'dus byas rtag tu yid 'byung 'gyur/ / de ni 'jig rten ci la'ang 'dod pa med// zag pa rnams ni rnam par 'phel mi 'gyur/[819] / zhes gsungs so/ /

The same sutra explains how the mind will shake free from samsara and from the eight worldly concerns and how afflictions will not be fostered:
Likewise you will definitively transcend [life’s] artifices, you will be without the slightest longing for worldly things, and things that are tainted will not be fostered.[524]

d.div: [819] gong mtshungs/ ting nge 'dzin rgyal po'i mdo/ le'u/ 29_sh+loka_shog_93_ba7_'gyur la khyad che/

f.d:
dgos pa rnams kyi gtso bo ting nge 'dzin myur du skye ba yang / mdo sde de nyid las/
grong dang grong khyer dag la dga' spongs la/ / rtag tu dben zhing nags khrod bsten par gyis/ / bse ru lta bur rtag tu gnyis med byos/ / ring por mi thogs ting 'dzin mchog thob 'gyur/[820] / zhes gsungs so/ /

It also tells how what is needed more than all else—meditative absorption—will swiftly develop. The same sutra states:
Leave enjoyment of towns and village and ever resort to solitude and the forests. Like a rhinoceros, always remain single-pointed, and before long the best meditative absorptions will be attained.[525]

d.div: [820] gong mtshungs/ ting nge 'dzin rgyal po'i mdo/ le'u/ 30_shog_98_na3

f.d: lus 'du 'dzi las dben pa bshad zin to//
This concludes the explanation of the need for physical seclusion, away from distractive activities.

sems rnam par rtog pa las dben par bya ba ni dgon par bsdad la/ bdag dgon par 'ong ba 'di ci'i phyir 'ongs snyam du bsam par bya'o/ / de la bdag dgon par 'ongs ba 'di grong dang grong khyer la sogs pa g.yeng ba'i sa phyogs nas 'jigs shing skrag nas bros te/ dgon par 'ongs pa yin no/ /

To seclude your mind from habitual thought processes, you should abide in a quiet retreats. While staying in retreat, contemplate, “Why exactly did I come to this hermitage? I came to this secluded place in fear and in terror of the places of distraction, such as towns and cities. Fleeing them, I came to retreat.”

de yang cis 'jigs na/ khyim bdag drag shul can gyis zhus pa'i mdo las/
'du 'dzis 'jigs shing skrag go / rnyed pa dang bkur stis 'jigs shing skrag go / sdig pa'i grogs pos 'jigs shing skrag go / mi dge ba'i bshes gnyen gyis 'jigs shing skrag go / 'dod chags dang zhe sdang dang gti mug gsum gyis 'jigs shing skrag go / phung po dang nyon mongs pa dang 'chi bdag dang lha'i bu'i bdud kyis 'jigs shing skrag go / dmyal ba dang yi dwags dang dud 'gro gsum gyis 'jigs shing skrag go / bdag de lta bus 'jigs shing skrag nas dgon par 'ongs so/[821] / zhes gsungs so/ /

What was so frightening there? The Questions of the Layman Ugra Sutra says:
I am afraid and terrified of the distractive activities; I am afraid and terrified of material possessions and honors; I afraid and terrified of corrupting friends; I am afraid and terrified of those who teach bad ways; I afraid and terrified of the dangers of desire, anger, and delusion; /181/ I afraid and terrified of the māra of the aggregates, the māra of afflictions, the māra of death, and the māra of seductive pleasure; I afraid and terrified of the three rebirths—animals, hungry spirits, and hell beings. Through such fear and terror I have I come to the wilderness.[526]

d.div: [821] sde dge_63_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ nga _khyim bdag drag shul can gyis zhus pa'i mdo/ shog_279_ba2
[526] Gṛhapatyugraparipṛcchāsūtra, Toh 63 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, nga, 279b2.

f.d: de ltar 'jigs shing skrag nas/[822] da lta bdag dgon pa na lus ngag yid gsum ci byed cing 'dug snyam du brtag par bya'o/ / de la bdag dgon pa na lus kyis srog gcod pa dang / ma byin par len pa la sogs pa byed cing 'dug na/ 'o na bdag gcan zan dang /[823] rngon pa dang / chom rkun dang yang khyad med na/ des 'dod pa'i don cang 'grub bam snyam du bsams la de las ldog par bya'o/ /

Being afraid and terrified in the manner described above, think, “Here, in this place of solitude, what are my body, speech, and mind doing right now?” Contemplate, “If while in retreat my body is killing, stealing, or the like, then there is no difference between myself and beasts of prey, hunters, thieves, and robbers. Is this really accomplishing my initial purpose in coming here?” In this way counter these behaviors.

d.div: [822] skrag nas 'ongs na/ dpal spungs/
[823] gcan gzan/ dpal spungs/ mi rigs dpe skrun/

f.d: ngag la brtags la bdag dgon pa na ngag 'khyal dang / phra ma dang ngan smras la sogs pa smras zhing 'dug na/[824] 'o na bdag rma bya dang ne tso dang 'jol mo dang co ga la sogs pa dang yang khyad med na/ des 'dod pa'i don cang 'grub bam snyam du bsams la de las ldog par bya'o/ /

Examining your speech, contemplate, “If while in retreat I chatter, slander, misuse speech, and so forth, then there is no difference between myself and peacocks, parrots, songbirds, larks, and the like. Is this really accomplishing my initial purpose in coming here?” In this way, counteract these [inappropriate speech activities].

d.div: [824] smra zhing / dpal spungs/ mi rigs dpe skrun/

f.d: sems la brtags la bdag dgon pa na 'dod chags dang / zhe sdang dang / phrag dog la sogs pa sems shing 'dug na/ 'o na bdag ri dwags dang / spra dang spre'u dang dom dang dred la sogs pa dang khyad med na/ des 'dod pa'i don cang 'grub bam snyam du bsams la de las bzlog par bya'o/ /

Examine your mind and contemplate, “If while here in retreat I have unwholesome thoughts of desire, anger, and jealousy, then I am no different from wild animals, baboons, monkeys, wild bears, northern bears, and the like.[527] Is this really accomplishing my initial purpose in coming here?” In this way, counteract these [inappropriate mental activities].

d.div: [527] Whatever the original Indian sutra alluded to, with these two references to bears, the terms were translated into Tibetan as the generic bear (dom), famous for its savagery, and the bear of the north (dred ), famous for its stupidity.

f.d: sems rnam par rtog pa las dben par bya ba bshad zin to/ /
This concludes the explanation of secluding the mind from unwholesome thoughts.

de ltar lus sems gnyis dben pas rnam par g.yeng ba mi 'byung ngo / / rnam par g.yeng ba med pas bsam gtan la 'jug pa yin no/ / de nas rang gi sems sbyang bar bya ste/ de yang rang nyon mongs pa shas gang che brtags la de'i gnyen po bsam par bya'o/ / de yang 'dod chags kyi gnyen po ni mi sdug pa bsgom pa'o/ / zhe sdang gi gnyen po ni byams pa bsgom pa'o/ / gti mug gi gnyen po ni rten 'brel bsgom pa'o/ / phrag dog gi gnyen po ni bdag gzhan mnyam pa bsgom pa'o// nga rgyal gyi gnyen po ni bdag gzhan rje ba sgom pa'o/ / nyon mongs pa cha mnyam du rags pa'am rnam rtog mang na rlung bsgom pa'o/ /

When body and mind are both secluded, distractions will no longer arise, and once free of distraction, one can enter into meditative concentration. For that, the mind needs to be cultivated. First there should be some reflection with a view to establishing which affliction is the greatest, and then follow this by cultivating its counterforce. As the remedy for desire, meditate on what is unpleasant; as the remedy for anger, meditate on loving kindness; as the remedy for ignorance, meditate on dependent origination; as the remedy for jealousy, meditate on the equality of self and others; as the remedy for pride, meditate on exchanging of self and others; and if all the afflictions are equal in their coarseness, or in the case of excessive thought processes, as the remedy, meditate on your breathing.

de la rang 'dod chags che na mi sdug pa bsgom na 'di ltar bya ste/ dang po rang gi lus 'di sha dang khrag dang / pags pa dang /[825] rus pa dang / rkang dang / chu ser dang / mkhris pa dang / bad kan dang snabs dang / mchil ma dang / phyi sa la sogs mi gtsang ba'i rdzas sum cu rtsa drug yin snyam du bsam/ de nas dur khrod du song ste/ ro dur khrod du bskyal ba shi nas zhag gcig lon pa/ de bzhin du shi nas gnyis dang / gsum dang / bzhi dang / lnga lon pa/ rnam par bam pa dang / rnam par sngo pa dang /[826] rnam par rnag pa dang /[827] rnam par 'bus gzhil pa'i ro mthong nas/[828] [829] bdag gi lus 'di yang de lta bu'i rang bzhin/ de lta bu'i chos can/ chos nyid de las ma 'das pa yin snyam du sbyar ro/ / yang shi ba'i ro dur khrod du bskyal ba keng rus la sha ra ri chags pa dang / rgyus pa'i drwa ba brang breng du 'dug pa dang / keng rus dum bu dum bur gyes pa dang / shi nas lo du ma lon pa rus pa dung gi mdog lta bur 'gyur pa dang / thal ba'i mdog ltar gyur pa mthong na/[830] bdag gi lus 'di yang de lta bu'i rang bzhin/ de lta bu'i chos can/ chos nyid de las ma 'das pa yin snyam du sbyar ro/ /

(1) If, for you, desire is the predominant affliction, and for its remedy you were to meditate on the unpleasant, this is as follows. First contemplate your body as being composed of thirty-six impure substances—flesh, blood, skin, bones, marrow, serum, bile, phlegm, mucus, saliva, urine, and so forth. /182/ Then go to a charnel ground and observe the corpses that were placed there—fresh ones, two-day-old ones, three-day-old ones, four-day-old ones, and five-day-old ones. Observe their decay, their complete transformation, and how they become black and eaten by small worms. Then reflect, “My own body is also of that nature, a similar phenomenon, and I have not yet transcended such a condition.” When observing corpses brought to the charnel ground, skeletons with little flesh left, those where there is just the muscle structure as interwoven fibers, those broken down into many pieces, or skeletons of those dead for many years, of which the bones are shell- or pigeon-colored, meditate as above, thinking, “My own body is also of that nature, a similar phenomenon, and I have not yet transcended such a condition.”

d.div: [825] lpags pa/ dpal spungs/
[826] rnam par sngos pa/ dpal spungs/ rnam par sdos pa/ mi rigs dpe skrun/
[827] gnag pa/ dpal spungs/ mi rigs dpe skrun/
[828] gzhig_dpal spungs/
[829] mthong na/ mi rigs dpe skrun/
[830] thi ba'i mdog ltar gyur pa mthong na yang / dpal spungs/

f.d: yang rang zhe sdang shas che na de'i gnyen por byams pa bsgom pa la/ spyir byams pa gong du bshad pa ltar gsum yod pa las/ 'dir ni sems can la dmigs pa'i byams pa ste/ gang thog mar snying du sdug pa'i sems can la phan pa dang bde ba bsgrub pa bsam par byed cing / de dang mthun pa'i byams pa de nye bar bsgrub pa'o/ / de'i 'og tu 'dris pa rnams la'o/ / de'i 'og tu tha mal pa rnams la'o/ / de'i 'og tu nye 'khor ba rnams la'o/ / de'i 'og tu rang gi grong na gnas pa rnams la'o/ / de nas shar la sogs pa phyogs bcur yang de bzhin du sgom mo/

(2) If, for you, anger is predominant, and for its remedy you were to meditate on loving kindness, this is as follows. In general there are three aspects of loving kindness, as mentioned in an earlier chapter.[528] The aspect developed in this context is loving kindness focused on sentient beings. First consider someone naturally dear to you and start thinking about making that person happy and well cared for. This should generate corresponding feelings of loving kindness [in you for that person]. That feeling of love is then extended toward others who you are familiar with It is next expanded to embrace ordinary people, then to people within your vicinity, then to those living in your town, and finally to include everyone living in all ten directions.

d.div: [528] This is a reference to (1) loving kindness focused on sentient beings, (2) loving kindness focused on the nature of things, and (3) loving kindness with no objective reference. See page 189.

f.d:
yang rang gti mug shas che na de'i gnyen por rten cing 'brel bar 'byung ba sgom pa ni/ sA lu ljang pa'i mdo las/
dge slong gang zhig sA lu ljang pa 'di shes pas rten cing 'brel bar 'byung ba shes so/ / gang gis rten cing 'brel bar 'byung ba shes pa des chos shes so/ / gang gis chos shes pa des sangs rgyas shes so/[831] / zhes gsungs so/ /

(3) If, for you, delusion is predominant, and for its remedy you were to meditate on dependent origination, this is as follows. It says, in the Rice Shoot Sutra:
Monks! Whoever understands this rice shoot understands dependent origination. Whoever understands dependent origination understands the nature of phenomena. Whoever understands phenomena understands buddhahood.[529]

d.div: [831] sde dge_210_bka'/ mdo sde/ tsha_sA lu ljang pa'i mdo/ shog_116_na4
[529] Śālistambasūtra, Toh 210 Kangyur, mdo sde, tsha, 116a4.

f.d: de yang lugs nas 'byung ba ltar 'khor ba'i rten 'brel dang / lugs las bzlog pa mya ngan las 'das pa'i rten 'brel gnyis yod do/ / dang po la yang gnyis te/ phyi rten cing 'brel bar 'byung ba dang / nang rten cing 'brel bar 'byung ba'o/[832] / 'di la yang gnyis te/ nang gi rten cing 'brel bar 'byung ba rgyu dang bcas pa dang / nang rten cing 'brel bar 'byung ba rkyen dang 'brel ba'o/ /

There are two ways of presenting dependent origination: dependent origination of the forward order pertaining to origination of samsara, and the dependent origination of the reverse order pertaining to nirvana. The first, in turn, is twofold: the dependent origination of inner phenomena and dependent origination of outer phenomena.[530] This latter is discussed in terms of two aspects—the dependent origination of inner phenomena in terms of their causes /183/ and the dependent origination of inner phenomena in terms of their conditions.

d.div: [832] nang gi/ dpal spungs/
[530] The dependent origination of external phenomena and the environment is not discussed here in this text.

f.d:
de la dang po ni/
dge slong dag 'di yod pas 'di 'byung / 'di skyes pas 'di skye ste/ 'di lta ste/ ma rig pa'i rkyen gyis 'du byed nas/ skye ba'i rkyen gyis rga shi dang / mya ngan dang smre sngags 'don pa dang / sdug bsngal ba dang / yid mi bde ba dang / 'khrugs pa rnams 'byung bar 'gyur te/ de ltar na sdug bsngal gyi phung po chen po 'ba' zhig pa 'di 'byung bar 'gyur ro/[833] / zhes gsungs so/ /

With respect to the first, [the Buddha stated]:
“Monks! Because this exists, this will come to be. This having arisen, this arises. That is how it is. Conditioned by ignorance, there will be formations[531]. . . ” and so forth, “. . . birth, and through that condition there will be aging and death, sorrow and lamentations, pain, mental stress, and disturbances. That is how this great cluster of nothing but misery is produced.”[532]

d.div: [833] sde dge_210_bka'/ mdo sde/ cha_sA lu ljang pa'i mdo/ shog_116_na7

[531] “Formations” (Skt. saṃskāra, Tib. ’du byed ). This term is often translated as “compositional factors,” “compounded phenomena,” or “mental formations.” Since neither the Sanskrit nor the Tibetan contains a reference to mind, and since mentioning mind creates certain problems, I have omitted “mental.” The second link of dependent origination can also be explained in several ways. Sometimes it refers to the immediate coming into being of the notion of self, then other, and so on. At other times it refers to the whole backlog of conditioning that one has at any given moment: a person’s karmic formations from past conditioning.
[532] Rice Shoot Sutra (Śālistambasūtra), Toh 210 Kangyur, mdo sde, tsha, 116a7.

f.d: de yang 'di ni khams kyi dbang du byas na 'dod khams su'o/ / skye gnas kyi dbang du byas na mngal skyes la'o/ /
This [quotation] relates to the desire realm in terms of dimension of existence, and to a womb birth in terms of mode of birth.[533]

d.div: [533] There are four modes of birth: from an egg, from a womb, spontaneous, and from ambient conditions.

f.d: de yang thog ma kho nar shes bya la rmongs pa'i ma rig pa zhes bya ba grub ste/ des kun nas bslang nas zag bcas kyi las dge ba'am mi dge ba'am mi g.yo ba mngon par 'du byed de/[834] de ni ma rig pa'i rkyen gyis 'du byed ces bya'o/ /

Here, first what is referred to as ignorance, which is confused about the nature of what is to be known, arises. Stirred by this, one comes to form the contaminated actions, such as those that are virtuous and nonvirtuous. This is what is referred to as “Conditioned by ignorance, formations come to be.”

d.div: [834] ma dpe dang dpar ma gzhan gnyis su'ang / mi dge ba'am mi mngon par 'du byed de/ zhes byung yang / mi dge ba'am mi g.yo ba mngon par 'du byed de/ zhes pa yin nges pas bcos yod/

f.d: las de'i sa bon sgos pa'i sems ni 'du byed kyi rkyen gyis rnam par shes pa zhes bya'o/[835] /
The mind that is imbued by the seed of that karma is what is being referred to in the phrase “Conditioned by karma, consciousness comes to be.”

d.div: [835] bgos/ dpal spungs/

f.d: las kyi stobs kyis sems phyin ci log tu bsgyur nas/ ma'i mngal du nying mtshams sbyar nas nur nur po la sogs par 'gyur te de ni rnam par shes pa'i rkyen gyis ming dang gzugs zhes bya'o/ /

Due to the power of karma, one’s mind becomes distorted and joins up with the procreative elements in the mother’s womb to become the various stages of embryo and then fetus. This is what is referred to as “Conditioned by consciousness, name and form come to be.”
ming dang gzugs de nyid 'phel bas mig dang rna ba la sogs pa'i dbang po rnams rdzogs par 'gyur te/ de ni ming dang gzugs kyi rkyen gyis skye mched drug ces bya'o/ /

Through the development of this name and form, the various sense faculties—of sight, smell, and so forth—become complete. This is what is known as the “Conditioned by name and form, the six sense bases come to be.”
mig la sogs pa'i dbang po dang yul dang rnam par shes pa gsum 'dus nas yongs su spyad pa ni/ skye mched drug gi rkyen gyis reg pa zhes bya'o/ /

When these various sense faculties, such as sight and so on, meet up with their corresponding objective fields through the appropriate consciousness, the meeting of the three causes an actual experience of the object. This is known as “Conditioned by the six sense bases, contact comes to be.”
ji ltar reg pa byung ba de ltar bde ba'am sdug bsngal lam btang snyoms su myong ba'i tshor ba 'byung ste/ de ni reg pa'i rkyen gyis tshor ba zhes bya'o/ /
Just as the contact arises, feeling, in the sense of a pleasant, unpleasant, or indifferent experience arises. This is known as “Conditioned by contact, feeling comes to be.”
tshor ba myong ba la dga' ba dang / zhen pa dang / lhag par zhen pa ni tshor ba'i rkyen gyis sred pa zhes bya'o/ /
Taking pleasure in that feeling, craving and intensely craving for it, is known as “Conditioned by feeling, craving comes to be.”
de ltar zhen pa la bral bar ma gyur cig snyam du mi gtong ba dang phyir zhing don du gnyer ba ni sred pa'i rkyen gyis len pa zhes bya'o/ /

On the basis of such clinging, and with the thought “May I never be separated from this,” attachment in the form of not wanting to let go and of longing for it arise. This is known as “Conditioned by craving, grasping comes to be.”
de ltar don du gnyer ba na/ yang srid pa bskyed pa'i las lus dang ngag dang yid kyis kun nas slong ba de ni len pa'i rkyen gyis srid pa zhes bya'o//
Due to this striving, actions are performed—physically, verbally, or mentally—that give rise to rebirth. This is known as “Conditioned by grasping, becoming comes to be.”
las de las skyes pa'i phung po lnga rnams grub pa gang yin pa de ni srid pa'i rkyen gyis skye ba zhes bya'o//
Whatever existence composed of the five aggregates is generated by those actions is known as “Conditioned by becoming, birth comes to be.”
skyes nas mngon du grub pa'i phung po 'phel ba dang / smin pa ni rgas pa dang /[836] 'jig pa ni 'chi ba yin te/ skye ba'i rkyen gyis rga shi zhes bya'o/ /
Through having been born, the development and maturity of the aggregates is aging and their destruction is death. /184/ Thus, “Conditioned by birth, there will be aging and death.”

d.div: [836] rga ba/ dpal spungs/

f.d: 'chi ba na rmongs pas mngon par zhen cing chags pa dang bcas pa'i nang gi yongs su gdung ba ni mya ngan no/ / mya ngan las byung ba'i tshig tu smra ba ni smre sngags so/ / rnam par shes pa lnga'i tshogs dang ldan pa'i mi bde ba myong ba ni sdug bsngal lo/ / yid la byed pa dang ldan pa'i yid kyi sdug bsngal ni yid mi bde ba'o/ / gzhan yang 'di lta bu la sogs pa nye ba'i nyon mongs pa gang yin pa de dag ni 'khrug pa zhes bya'o//

At death, when you manifestly grasp on to things due to ignorance and are thoroughly assailed within by forces such as attachment, this is sorrow. Lamentations are the verbal outcry emerging from such sorrow. Pain means the unpleasant sensations experienced by the five groups of consciousness. Mental distress is the pain in the mind resulting from various sorts of mental activity. The various other forms of distress are the disturbances—a term relating to the secondary afflictions.

de yang dum bu gsum du shes par bya'o/[837] / ma rig pa dang sred pa dang len pa gsum ni nyon mongs pa yin no/ / 'du byed dang srid pa gnyis ni las yin no/ / rnam par shes pa la sogs pa bdun ni sdug bsngal yin no/ /

The above factors of dependent origination should be understood as falling into three distinct groups: Ignorance, craving, and grasping are afflictions; formations and becoming are karma; and the other seven factors—consciousness and so forth—are suffering.

d.div: [837] shes par bya ste/ dpal spungs/

f.d:
de ltar yang dbu ma rten 'byung las/
yan lag bye brag bcu gnyis gang / / dum bu gsum du shes par bya/ / thub pas rten 'byung gsungs de dag / nyon mongs las dang sdug bsngal dang / / gsum po dag tu zad par 'dus/ / dang po brgyad pa dgu nyon mongs/ / gnyis dang bcu pa las yin te/ / lhag ma bdun yang sdug bsngal yin/[838] / zhes gsungs so/ /

The Verses on the Essence of Dependent Origination says:
The twelve specific links should be understood in terms of three groups. These links of dependent origination taught by the Sage are encompassed by three categories: affliction, karma, and suffering. The first, eighth, and ninth are afflictions, the second and tenth are karma, while the remaining seven are suffering.[534]

d.div: [838] sde dge_3836_bstan/ dbu ma/ tsa_klu sgrub/ rten 'brel snying po'i tshig le'ur byas pa/ sh+loka_1_shog_46_ba2
[534] Nāgārjuna, Pratītyasamutpādahṛdayakārikā, Toh 3836 Tengyur, dbu ma, tsa, 46b2.

f.d: yang dper na ma rig pa ni sa bon 'debs mkhan lta bu'o/ / las ni zhing sa lta bu'o/ / rnam par shes pa ni sa bon lta bu'o/ / sred pa ni rlan lta bu'o/[839] / ming dang gzugs ni myu gu lta bu'o/ / gzhan ni yal ga dang lo ma la sogs pa lta bu'o/ /

Furthermore, to illustrate them by means of analogy, ignorance is like the one who sows a seed, karma is like the field, consciousness like the seed itself, craving is like moisture, name and form like a shoot, and the remaining links are like the branches and leaves [of the plant].

d.div: [839] ma dper/ srid pa/ zhes byung / sred pa/ zhes dpal spungs dang mi rigs dpe skrun khang ltar bcos/

f.d: gal te ma rig pa ma byung na 'du byed kyang mi mngon zhing / de bzhin du skye ba ma byung du zin na rga shi'i bar du yang mi mngon pa zhig na/ 'on kyang ma rig pa yod pa las 'du byed rnams mngon par grub par 'gyur bas na/ skye ba yod pa las rga shi'i bar du mngon par grub par 'gyur ro/ /

Now if ignorance did not occur, formations too would not manifest. Likewise, if birth did not happen, then aging and death could not occur. However, it is because of the presence of ignorance that formations and so forth do actually come into being. Therefore because of the existence of birth, aging and death will actually happen.

de la ma rig pa yang 'di snyam du bdag gis 'du byed rnams mngon par bsgrub bo snyam du mi sems so/ / 'du byed rnams ni 'di snyam du bdag cag ni ma rig pas mngon par bsgrubs so snyam du yang mi sems pa nas/[840] de bzhin du skye ba yang 'di snyam du bdag gis rga shi mngon par bsgrub po snyam du mi sems so/ / rga shi yang 'di snyam du bdag ni skye bas mngon par bsgrubs so snyam du mi sems pa'i bar du ste/ 'on kyang ma rig pa yod pa las 'du byed rnams mngon par grub cing 'byung bar 'gyur ba dang / de bzhin du skye ba yod pa las rga shi'i bar du mngon par grub cing 'byung bar 'gyur te/[841] de ltar na nang gi rten cing 'brel bar 'byung ba rgyu dang bcas par blta'o/ /

In these processes, however, it is not the case that ignorance consciously thinks, “I will make formations truly manifest,” nor do the formations have the thought, “We were made to be manifested by, and created by, ignorance.” Likewise birth does not think, “I will make aging and death truly happen,” nor do aging and death consider themselves actually brought into being by birth. Nevertheless, it is through the existence of ignorance that formations and so forth do become manifest realities and will occur, and it is likewise through the existence of birth that aging and death are /185/ made manifest and will happen. This is how to view inner dependent origination in terms of its causes.

d.div: [840] snyam du mi sems/ dpal spungs/

[841] ma dpe dang mi rigs dpe skrun khang gnyis su/ de bzhin du skye ba yod pas rga shi'i bar du mngon par grub cing 'byung bar 'gyur ba nas/ de bzhin du skye ba yod pa las rga shi'i bar du mngon par grub cing 'byung bar 'gyur te/ zhes byung yang / dpal spungs dpar ma ltar/ de bzhin du zhes pa'i tshig sgrub snga ma de med pa dag par mngon pas de bzhin bcos yod/

f.d: yang nang gi rten cing 'brel bar 'byung ba rkyen dang yang 'brel ba yin te/ sa dang chu dang me dang rlung dang nam mkha' dang rnam par shes pa ste khams drug tu 'dus pa'i phyir ro/ / de la lus kyi sra ba'i dngos po mngon par sgrub par byed pa 'di ni sa'i khams zhes bya'o/[842] / lus sdud pa'i bya ba byed pa 'di ni chu'i khams zhes bya'o/ / zos pa dang 'thungs pa la sogs pa 'ju bar byed pa 'di ni me'i khams zhes bya'o/ / dbugs phyi nang du rgyu ba'i bya ba byed pa 'di ni rlung gi khams zhes bya'o// lus kyi nang srubs yod pa 'di ni nam mkha'i khams zhes bya'o/ / rnam par shes pa lnga'i tshogs dang / zag bcas kyi yid kyi rnam par shes pa ni rnam par shes pa'i khams zhes bya'o/ / rkyen 'di dag med par lus skye bar mi 'gyur gyi nang gi khams drug tshang bar gyur pa thams cad 'dus pa de las lus mngon par 'grub par 'gyur ro/ /

The dependent origination of inner phenomena is connected also with conditions. This is because they are comprised of the six elements—earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness. Here, the “earth element” is the body’s firmness and its actual material existence; the “water element” is what holds the body together; the “fire element” transmutes food, drink, and so forth; the “wind element” moves the breath in and out; the “space element” refers to the inner cavities of the body; the “consciousness element” is comprised of the five sense consciousnesses and the tainted[535] mental consciousness. Without these conditions, a body cannot come into being; furthermore, the presence of all six inner elements is universal and hence comprises everything. It is due to them that the body will have its actual manifest existence.

d.div: [842] bsgrub/ dpal spungs/
[535] “Tainted” in the context of karma means tainted by dualistic concepts, be it virtuous or nonvirtuous karma.

f.d: de la khams drug kyang 'di snyam du bdag gis lus kyi sra ba la sogs pa bsgrub bo snyam du mi sems so/ / lus kyang 'di snyam du bdag ni rkyen 'di dag gis bskyed do snyam du mi sems mod kyi/ 'on kyang rkyen 'di dag las yongs su skye bar 'gyur ro/ /

In these [processes], the six elements do not think, “I will establish the body’s firmness,” and so on, and neither does the body think, “I am generated by these specific conditions.” Nevertheless, it is through these specific conditions that the body occurs in all the ways it does.

de yang rten 'brel bcu gnyis po 'di tshe du la rdzogs she na/ 'phags pa sa bcu pa'i mdo las/
ma rig pa'i rkyen gyis 'du byed rnams zhes bya ba ni sngon gyi mtha' la ltos pa'o/ / rnam par shes pa nas tshor ba'i bar ni da lta byung ba la ltos pa'o/ / sred pa dang srid pa'i bar ni phyi ma la ltos pa ste/ de phan chad kyang rab tu 'byung ngo /[843] / zhes gsungs so/ /

In how many lives do these twelve links of dependent origination complete their cycle? In this respect, the Ten Levels Sutra says:
Formations due to the condition of ignorance applies to what happened in past lives. The [links] from consciousness up to feelings apply to the present life. Craving through to becoming apply to the next life. Everything else emerges inexorably from that.[536]

d.div: [843] sde dge_44_bka'/ phal chen/ kha_sa bcu pa'i mdo/ shog_222_ba2
[536] The Ten Levels Sutra (Daśabhūmikasūtra) is the popular name given to chapter 31 of the Flower Ornament Sutra (Avataṃsakasūtra), Toh 44 Kangyur, phal chen, kha, 222b2.

f.d:
lugs las bzlog pa mya ngan las 'das pa'i rten 'brel ni/ chos thams cad kyi chos nyid stong pa nyid du rtogs pas ma rig pa 'gag par 'gyur la/ de 'gags pas rga shi'i bar du rim gyis 'gag ste/ ji skad du/
de nas ma rig pa 'gags pas 'du byed 'gag /ces bya ba nas/ skye ba 'gags pas/ rga shi dang / mya ngan dang smre sngags 'don pa dang / sdug bsngal ba dang / yid mi bde ba dang / 'khrug pa rnams 'gag par 'gyur te/ de ltar sdug bsngal gyi phung po chen po 'ba' zhig po 'di 'gag par 'gyur ro/[844]/ zhes gsungs so//

Dependent origination of the reverse order that pertains to nirvana refers to the following. Through realizing the true nature (dharmatā) of all phenomena to be emptiness, ignorance ceases, and through its cessation, [all the other links] through to aging and death will come to cease in their due order. As is said:
By stopping ignorance, karmic formation is stopped. . . [up to] by stopping birth, aging and death, and sorrow and lamentations, pain, mental stress, and disturbances are stopped. That is how this great cluster of nothing but misery will cease.[537] /186/

d.div: [844] sde dge_210_bka'/ mdo sde/ cha_sA lu ljang pa'i mdo/ shog_116_ba4
[537] Rice Shoot Sutra (Śālistambasūtra), Toh 210 Kangyur, mdo sde, tsha, 116b4.

f.d:
rang phrag dog shas che na de'i gnyen por bdag gzhan mnyam par bsgom pa ni/ bdag bde ba 'dod pa bzhin du sems can gzhan yang bde ba 'dod la/ bdag sdug bsngal mi 'dod pa bzhin du sems can gzhan yang sdug bsngal mi 'dod pas na/ bdag dang sems can gces pa mnyam por bsgom mo/ / de ltar yang spyod 'jug las/
bdag dang gzhan du mnyam pa ni/ / dang po nyid du 'bad de bsgom/ / bde dang sdug bsngal mnyam pas na/ / thams cad bdag bzhin bsrung bar bya/[845] / zhes gsungs so/ /

(4) If, for you, jealousy is predominant, and you were to meditate on the equality of yourself and others as a remedy, this is as follows. Just as you wish for happiness for yourself, so do other beings wish for happiness for themselves. Just as you do not want suffering yourself, neither do other beings want to suffer. Thinking in such a way, cultivate the same care for others as you have for yourself. Guide to the Bodhisattva Way of Life says:
From the very outset make efforts to meditate on the equality of self and others. Protect all beings as you protect yourself, since all are equal in wanting happiness and not suffering.[538]

d.div: [845] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 8_sh+loka_90_shog_27_na2
[538] Śāntideva, Bodhicaryāvatāra 8:90, Toh 3871 Tengyur, dbu ma, la, 27a2.

f.d:
rang nga rgyal shas che na de'i gnyen por bdag gzhan rje ba bsgom pa ni/ byis pa sems can rnams kyis rang kho na gces par bzung nas rang tshis byas pas 'khor ba na sdug bsngal la/ sangs rgyas rnams kyis gzhan gces par bzung nas gzhan don kho na mdzad pas sangs rgyas thob bo/ / de ltar yang /
byis pas rang don byas pa dang / / thub pas gzhan gyi don mdzad pa/ / 'di gnyis kyi ni khyad par ltos/[846] / zhes gsungs so/ /

(5) If, for you, pride is predominant, the remedy is to meditate on substituting self for others, which is as follows. Immature beings suffer in a samsara that they themselves have created through a motivation of caring for self alone. Buddhas, motivated by their care for others and acting solely for the welfare of others, have attained enlightenment. Thus it says:
Immature beings act out of self-interest. The Sages act for the good of others. Consider the difference between these two![539]

d.div: [846] gong mtshungs/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 8_sh+loka_130_shog_28_ba3

f.d:
des na bdag gces par 'dzin pa de ni skyon can du shes par byas la bdag 'dzin dor/ gzhan gces par 'dzin pa de yon tan du shes par byas la gzhan bdag tu bya'o/ / de ltar yang spyod 'jug las/
bdag nyid skyon can gzhan dag la/ / yon tan rgya mtshor shes byas nas/ / bdag tu 'dzin pa dor ba dang / / gzhan blang ba ni bsgom par bya/[847] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Therefore cast off self-grasping by understanding self-cherishing to be a fault. Treat others as yourself by understanding cherishing others to be a positive quality. The Guide to the Bodhisattva Way of Life says:
Through understanding ego to be faulty and others to be an ocean of qualities, cultivate a rejection of self-grasping and a commitment toward others.[540]

d.div: [847] gong mtshungs/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 8_sh+loka_113_shog_28_na1

f.d:
rang nyon mongs pa cha mnyam pa'am/ rnam par rtog pa shas che na rlung la bslab ste/ bgrang ba dang rjes 'gro la sogs pa drug bsgom mo/ / de ltar yang chos mngon pa mdzod las/
bgrang dang rjes 'gro 'jog pa dang / / rtog pa dang ni bsgyur ba dang / yongs dag rnam pa drug tu 'dod/[848]/ ces gsungs so/ /

(6) If, for you, all the afflictions are equally present, or if there is excessive discursive thought, the remedy is to train in breathing, which is as follows. These are the six [main] aspects of practice, such as counting the breaths, following after them, and so on, presented in the Treasury of Higher Knowledge:
There are held to be six: counting, following, resting, thinking, transformation, and utterly purifying them.[541]

d.div: [848] sde dge_4090_bstan/ mngon pa/ khu_dbyig gnyen/ chos mngon pa'i mdzod kyi bshad pa/ gnas/ 6_shog_11_ba1_'di mdzod 'grel du byung ba'i bsdu ba'i tshigs bcad yin/
[541] Vasubandhu, Commentary on the Treasury of Higher Knowledge (Abhidharma-kośabhāṣya), Toh 4090 Tengyur, mngon pa, khu, 11b1.

f.d: nyon mongs pa de dag spang sgrub sgyur gsum med par nyams su len pa gsang sngags kyi lugs sam/ mar pa yab sras kyi phyag srol dang bzhed pa ni zhal las shes par bya zhing / lhan cig skyes sbyor dang dpal nA ro pa'i chos drug rnams shes par bya'o/[849] / de dag ni sems sbyong ba'i rim pa ste bsam gtan la 'jug par byed pa'o//

As for the practice whereby these afflictions are neither eliminated, indulged in, or transmuted, such as according to the way of secret mantra or of the tradition and instructions of Marpa and his spiritual heirs, this is to be learned orally [from a qualified guru]. You should understand the Innate Union [of Mahāmudrā][542] and the Six Dharmas of Nāropa.[543] /187/ All the above represent the various stages of mental training that lead to entering [the practice of] meditative concentration.

d.div: [849] dpal spungs dpar mar/ nyon mongs pa de dag ces pa nas shes par bya'o/ / bar gyi tshig 'di rnams mi byung ba dpyad/

[542] At the heart of the Kagyü lineage lie two major streams of transmission. The first, referred to here, is that of the Mahāmudrā meditations of Saraha, passed down via a lineage including Maitripa and Marpa and here referred to under one of its other names, Innate Union (lhan cig skyes sbyor; sahajayoga). The other stream of transmission is that of the Six Dharmas of Nāropa, which conveys the quintessence of the father, mother, and nondual tantras.

[543] This entire paragraph is absent in the Tshurphu edition of the text. It seems that, unless we treat this paragraph as part of the parenthetical annotation, its inclusion interrupts the flow of the text.

f.d: bsam gtan dngos la dbye na gsum ste/ mthong ba'i chos la bde bar gnas pa'i bsam gtan dang / yon tan sgrub pa'i bsam gtan dang / sems can gyi don byed pa'i bsam gtan no/ / de yang dang po ni rang gi rgyud snod du rung bar byed pa'o/ / gnyis pa ni rang snod du rung nas sangs rgyas kyi chos bsgrub pa'o/[850] / gsum pa ni sems can gyi don byed pa'o/ /

The third point concerns the different aspects of meditative concentration itself. There are three: (1) meditative concentration that procures tangible well-being, (2) meditative concentration that gives rise to good qualities, and (3) meditative concentration that accomplishes the welfare of others. The first of these makes one’s mind a suitable vessel, the second produces enlightened qualities in someone who is already a fit vessel, and the third works for the benefit of beings.

d.div: [850] sgrub/ dpal spungs/

f.d:
de dag so so'i mtshan nyid bshad na/ dang por mthong ba'i chos la bde bar gnas pa'i bsam gtan ni/ byang sa las/
de la byang chub sems dpa' rnams kyi bsam gtan ni/ rnam par rtog pa thams cad dang bral ba/ lus sems shin tu sbyangs pa bskyed pa/ mchog tu rab tu zhi ba/ rlom sems dang bral ba/ ro myong ba med pa/ mtshan ma thams cad dang bral ba gang yin pa 'di ni/ de dag gis tshe 'di la bde bar gnas pa yin par rig par bya'o/[851] / zhes gsungs so/ /

The fourth point concerns the essential characteristics of each aspect. Meditative concentration that procures tangible well-being is described in Bodhisattva Levels:
This is the meditative concentration of bodhisattvas. It is free of all discursive thought. It gives rise to excellent pliancy of mind and body. It is supremely peaceful in the very best way. It is without arrogance, it does not get involved with experiencing the taste of meditation, and it is free from any [clinging to] signs. Such is what should be understood by “well-being during this life.”[544]

d.div: [851] sde dge_4037_bstan/ sems tsam/ wi_'phags pa thogs med/ byang sa/ le'u/ 12_shog_111_na5
[544] Asaṅga, Bodhisattvabhūmi, Toh 4037 Tengyur, sems tsam, wi, 111a5.

f.d: de la rnam par rtog pa thams cad dang bral ba ni/ yod med la sogs par rtog pa'i yid kyi gya gyu med par rtse gcig tu gnas pa'o/ / lus sems shin tu sbyangs pa bskyed pa zhes ces pa ni/ lus dang sems kyi gnas ngan len thams cad 'jig pa'o/ / mchog tu rab tu zhi ba zhes pa ni/ ngang gis 'jug pa'o/ / rloms sems dang bral ba zhes pa ni/ lta ba'i nyon mongs pa dang bral ba'o/ / ro myong ba med pa zhes pa ni/ srid pa'i nyon mongs pa med pa'o/ / mtshan ma dang bral ba zhes pa ni/ gzugs la sogs pa'i longs spyod dang bral ba'o/ /

In the above: “Free of all discursive thought” means that it remains fully concentrated without any interference due to the discursive intellect producing ideas of existence, nonexistence, and so on. “It gives rise to excellent pliancy of mind and body” means the destruction of every bad condition that body or mind might adopt. “Supremely peaceful in the very best way” means that it enters such a condition naturally. “Without arrogance” refers to an absence of the affliction of [false] views. “Does not get involved with experiencing the taste of meditation” refers to an absence of the affliction of craving. “Free from any [clinging to] signs” means free from experiencing sense objects such as form and so on [as though they were independent entities].

yang thams cad kyi sgo ltar na/ bsam gtan bzhi ste/ bsam gtan dang po dang / gnyis pa dang / gsum pa dang / bzhi pa'o/ / de la bsam gtan dang po ni/ rtog pa dang bcas pa dang dpyod pa dang bcas pa'o/ / bsam gtan gnyis pa ni/ dga' ba dang ldan pa'o/ / bsam gtan gsum pa ni/ sim pa'i bde ba dang ldan pa'o/[852] / bsam gtan bzhi pa ni/ btang snyoms dang ldan pa'o/

In terms of the gateway to all [higher qualities], there are four meditative concentrations (dhyāna): the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna. Of these, the first dhyāna is accompanied by investigation and sustained analysis, the second dhyāna is accompanied by bliss, the third dhyāna is accompanied by joy, and the fourth dhyāna is accompanied by equanimity.

d.div: [852] sems pa bde ba/ dpal spungs/

f.d: yon tan bsgrub pa'i bsam gtan la gnyis te/ thun mong ma yin pa dang / thun mong ba'o/ / de la dang po ni/ stobs bcu'i rigs kyis bsdus pa'i ting nge 'dzin rnam pa sna tshogs bsam gyis mi khyab pa tshad med pa nyan thos dang rang sangs rgyas rnams kyis ming tsam yang mi shes na/ snyoms par 'jug par lta ga la 'gyur ba rnams so/ / thun mong ba ni/ rnam par thar pa dang / zil gyis gnon pa dang / zad par gyi skye mched dang / so so yang dag par rig pa la sogs pa nyan thos dang thun mong ba rnams so/ / de yang ming thun mong ba yin gyi rang gi ngo bo mtshungs pa ni ma yin no/ /

Meditative concentration that produces good qualities is of two kinds: the exceptional and the common. The first refers to to the various meditative absorptions encompassed within the ten powers, which are immeasurable and inconceivable. Since śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are not even aware of the names of such meditative attainments, /188/ what need is there to speak of their ever actually engaging in them. The common ones refer to the likes of the “complete liberations,” “surpassings,” “gateways of exhaustion,” “excellent specific intelligences,” and so forth, which are common to both the Mahayana and the śrāvakayāna. It is on the level of their names they share commonality; in actual fact, however, they are not identical at all.
sems can gyi don byed pa'i bsam gtan ni/ bsam gtan gang la brten nas lus dpag tu med pa sprul te/ sems can gyi dgos pa'i grogs byed pa la sogs pa bcu gcig po byed pa'i bsam gtan no//

As for meditative concentration that accomplishes the welfare of others, whichever meditative concentration is resorted to, there can be countless physical emanations. These meditative concentrations operate for the benefit of beings in eleven ways, such as supporting beings according to their needs and so forth.

'o na zhi gnas dang lhag mthong zhes grags pa la/ zhi gnas ni ci tsam/ lhag mthong ni ci tsam zhe na/ de la zhi gnas ni yang dag pa'i ting nge 'dzin la brten nas sems la sems 'jog pa de'o/ / lhag mthong ni de'i rjes la bya ba dang bya ba ma yin par shes pa'i chos rab tu rnam par 'byed pa de'o/ /

You might ask, “Since there are tranquility and insight, which are well known, what is tranquility and what is insight?” Tranquility refers to placing one’s mind within the mind on the basis of perfect meditative absorption. Insight refers to what follows on from this, an excellent discerning awareness of phenomena that understands what is and what is not to be done.

de ltar yang mdo sde rgyan las/
yang dag gnas pa la brten nas/ / sems la sems ni 'jog phyir dang / / chos rab rnam par 'byed pa'i phyir/ / zhi gnas dang ni lhag mthong yin/[853]/ zhes gsungs so/ /

The Ornament of Mahayana Sutras says:
Through abiding in the most excellent, mind is made to rest within mind, and there is supreme discernment of things. These are tranquility and insight.[545]

d.div: [853] sde dge_4020_bstan/ sems tsam/ phi_byams mgon/ mdo sde rgyan/ le'u/ 18_sh+loka_66_shog_31_na2
[545] Maitreya, Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra, Toh 4020 Tengyur, sems tsam, phi, 31a2.

f.d: de yang zhi gnas ni bsam gtan dngos so/ / lhag mthong ni shes rab kyi cha'o/ /
Tranquility is the meditative concentration itself, and insight is the wisdom aspect.
bsam gtan spel ba ni/ ye shes dang / shes rab dang / bsngo ba gsum gyis spel ba ste/ gong du bstan pa ltar ro/ /

The fifth point is how the power of meditative concentration can be increased. It is increased by the three powers described above: pristine awareness, wisdom, and dedication. This is as explained before.
