bsam gtan dag par byed pa ni/ stong pa dang snying rjes zin pa ste/ gong du bstan pa ltar ro//
The sixth point, how it can be made pure, refers to meditative concentration being supported by emptiness and compassion, just as described above.

bsam gtan gyi 'bras bu ni/ mthar thug dang / gnas skabs gnyis su shes par bya'o// de la mthar thug ni/ bla na med pa'i byang chub thob ste/ de ltar yang byang sa las/
byang chub sems dpas ni bsam gtan gyi pha rol tu phyin pa yongs su rdzogs nas/ bla na med pa yang dag par rdzogs pa'i byang chub tu mngon par rdzogs par sangs rgyas so/ / mngon par rdzogs par 'tshang rgya bar 'gyur ro/ / mngon par rdzogs par 'tshang rgya'o/[854] / zhes gsungs so/ /

The seventh point, the fruits of meditative concentration, should be understood in terms of two—the temporary and ultimate results of meditative concentration. As for its ultimate result, one attains the unsurpassed enlightenment. Bodhisattva Levels says:
Through taking the perfection of meditative concentration to its utter completion, bodhisattvas truly became perfect buddhas, are truly becoming perfect buddhas, and will truly become perfect buddhas—with highest, utterly pure, and perfect enlightenment.[546]

d.div: [854] sde dge_4037_bstan/ sems tsam/ wi_'phags pa thogs med/ byang sa/ le'u/ 13_shog_113_na4
[546] Asaṅga, Bodhisattvabhūmi, Toh 4037 Tengyur, sems tsam, wi, 113a4.

f.d:
gnas skabs su 'dod chags dang bral ba'i lha'i lus thob ste/ slob dpon klu sgrub kyi zhal nas kyang /
'dod spyod dga' dang bde dang sdug bsngal dag / rnam par spangs pa'i bsam gtan bzhi po yis/ / tshangs dang 'od gsal dag dang dge rgyas dang / / 'bras bu che lha rnams dang bskal mnyam thob/[855] / ces gsungs so/ /

In the immediate term, one will obtain the existence of birth as a god free of dersire. Master Nāgārjuna says:
Due to the four meditative concentrations, through which sensory experience, physical bliss, mental joy, and suffering are completely shed, /189/ you attain a state similar to that of the gods in the Brahma, Luminous, Complete Virtue, and Great Result heavens.[547]

d.div: [855] sde dge_4182_bstan/ spring yig_nge _mgon po klu sgrub/ bshes spring / sh+loka_41_shog_42_ba4
[547] Nāgārjuna, Letter to a Friend (Suhṛllekha), Toh 4182 Tengyur, spring yig, nga, 42b4.

f.d: dam chos yid bzhin gyi nor bu thar pa rin po che'i rgyan las/ bsam gtan gyi pha rol tu phyin pa'i le'u ste bcu drug pa'o// //
This then concludes the sixteenth chapter, on the perfection of meditative concentration, in this Ornament of Precious Liberation, a Wish-Fulfilling Gem of Sublime Dharma.
le'u bcu bdun pa/ shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa/
17. The Perfection of Wisdom

shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa la/ sdom ni/
skyon yon rnam gnyis bsam pa dang / / ngo bo dang ni dbye ba dang / / phye ba so so'i mtshan nyid dang / / shes dang goms par bya ba dang / / 'bras bu dang ni don bdun gyis/ / shes rab pha rol phyin bsdus so/ / zhes pa'o//

de la dang po bshad na/ byang chub sems dpa' gang zhig sbyin pa la gnas pa nas/ bsam gtan gyi bar du ldan yang / shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa dang bral na/ des thams cad mkhyen pa'i go 'phang mi thob bo/ / de ci'i phyir zhe na/ long khrid med pa'i long ba'i tshogs kyis yid la 'dod pa'i grong khyer du bgrod par mi nus pa dang 'dra'o/ /

The first point is to reflect on the drawbacks of its absence and the benefits of its practice. A bodhisattva may abide within the perfections from gener-osity through to meditative concentration, yet if he lacks the perfection of wisdom, he will never attain the state of omniscience. Why is this so? The [first five perfections] are like a group of blind people without a guide and hence unable to journey to the city they wish to visit.

de ltar yang 'phags pa sdud pa las/
dmus long dmigs bu med pa bye ba khrag khrig rnams/ / lam yang mi shes grong khyer 'jug par ga la nus/ shes rab med na mig med pha rol phyin lnga yis/ / dmigs bu med pas byang chub reg par nus ma yin/[856] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Thus the Verse Summary of the Perfection of Wisdom says:
How could even a trillion blind people know the road or ever reach the city without a guide? Without wisdom, the five sightless perfections, since they are without an eye, cannot reach enlightenment.[548]

d.div: [856] sde dge_13_bka'/ sher phyin/ ka_mdo sdud pa/ le'u/ 7_sh+loka_1_shog_6_na5
[548] Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā, Toh 13 Kangyur, sher phyin, ka, 6a5.

f.d: de las bzlog ste shes rab dang ldan na/ long khrid kyis long ba'i tshogs grong khyer du khrid pa ltar sbyin pa la sogs pa dge ba'i tshogs thams cad sangs rgyas kyi lam du bsgyur nas/ thams cad mkhyen pa'i go 'phang thob bo/ /

In contrast, when they possess wisdom, all the wholesome aspects of virtue—generosity and so on—are transformed into the path to buddhahood, and the state of omniscience will be attained, like a throng of blind people being led by their guide to the city.

de ltar yang / dbu ma 'jug pa las/
ji ltar long ba'i tshogs kun bde blag tu/ / mig ldan skyes bu gcig gis 'dod pa yi/ / yul du khrid pa de bzhin shes rab kyis/ / mig nyams yon tan blangs te rgyal bar khrid/[857] / ces gsungs so//

Thus Entering the Middle Way says:
Just as a whole group of blind people is easily led to the place of their choice by one sighted person, so are the sightless qualities led to the Conqueror’s state by wisdom.[549]

d.div: [857] sde dge_3861_bstan/ dbu ma/ 'a_zla ba grags pa/ dbu ma 'jug pa/ sems bskyed/ 6_sh+loka_2_shog_204_na1
[549] Candrakīrti, Madhyamakāvatāra 6:2, Toh 3861 Tengyur, dbu ma, ’a, 204a1.

f.d:
'phags pa sdud pa las kyang /
shes rab kyis ni chos kyi rang bzhin yongs shes nas/ / khams gsum ma lus pa las yang dag 'da' bar 'gyur/[858] / zhes gsungs so//

The Verse Summary of the Perfection of Wisdom says:
Every aspect of the three realms will be completely transcended by thoroughly understanding the nature of phenomena through wisdom.[550]

d.div: [858] sde dge_13_bka'/ sher phyin/ ka_mdo sdud pa/ le'u/ 32_sh+loka_4_shog_19_ba3
[550] Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā, Toh 13 Kangyur, sher phyin, ka, 19b3.

f.d:
'o na shes rab kho nas chog mod/ sbyin pa la sogs pa'i thabs rnams ci dgos she na/ mi chog ste/ byang chub lam sgron las/
thabs dang bral ba'i shes rab dang / / shes rab bral ba'i thams dag kyang / / gang phyir 'ching ba zhes gsungs pas/ / de bas gnyis ka spang mi bya/[859] / zhes gsungs so/ /

This being so, some may wonder, “Wisdom alone might suffice, and what need is there for the skillful means—generosity and so forth?” /190/ This is not the case. Lamp for the Path to Awakening says:
Wisdom lacking skillful means and skillful means lacking wisdom are both bondage, it has been taught. Therefore do not abandon this combination.[551]

d.div: [859] sde dge_3947_bstan/ dbu ma/ khi_dpal mar me mdzad ye shes/ lam sgron/ sh+loka_44_shog_240_na2
[551] Atiśa, Bodhipathapradīpa verse 43, Toh 3947 Tengyur, dbu ma, khi, 240a2.

f.d: 'o na thabs shes ya bral du nyams su blangs na gang du 'ching zhe na/ byang chub sems dpas thabs dang bral ba'i shes rab brten na/ nyan thos kyi 'dod pa'i zhi ba phyogs gcig pa'i mya ngan las 'das pa der lhung nas bcings pa bzhin du 'gyur te/ mi gnas pa'i mya ngan las 'das pa thob par mi 'gyur ro/ / de yang theg pa gsum du 'dod pa'i lugs kyis ni gtan du der bcings par 'dod la/ theg pa gcig tu 'dod pas kyang bskal pa chen po brgyad khri bzhi stong du der bcings par 'dod do/ / shes rab dang bral ba'i thabs brten na yang byis pa so so skye bo'i sa las mi 'da' bas/ 'khor ba nyid du bcings pa kho nar 'gyur ba'o/ /

Exactly what bondage occurs if either wisdom or skillful means are practiced on their own? A bodhisattva who resorts to wisdom without skillful means will fall into the partial nirvana considered to be peace by the śrāvakas and become utterly bound, never reaching nonabiding nirvana. According to the viewpoint that upholds the ultimacy of the three vehicles, it is maintained that one remains stuck in that [nirvana] state permanently. According to the theory of a single vehicle, too, it is maintained that one will remain in that state for eighty thousand major eons. Now, if a bodhisattva resorts to skillful means without wisdom, he or she will never get beyond the state of childish ordinary being and will be bound to samsara and samsara alone.

de ltar blo gros mi zad pas zhus pa'i mdo las/
thabs dang bral ba'i shes rab kyis mya ngan las 'das par 'ching la/ shes rab dang bral ba'i thabs kyis 'khor bar 'ching bas zung du 'brel ba zhig dgos so/[860] / zhes gsungs so/ /

In the Akṣayamati Sutra, it says:
With wisdom lacking skillful means, one is tied to nirvana. With skillful means lacking wisdom, one is tied to samsara. Therefore the two must be combined.[552]

d.div: [860] sde dge_175_bka'/ mdo sde/ ma_blo gros mi zad pa bstan pa'i mdo/ shog_170_na7_'gyur khyad che/
[552] Akṣayamatinirdeśasūtra, Toh 175 Kangyur, mdo sde, ma, 170a7.

f.d:
'phags pa dri ma med pa grags pas bstan pa'i mdo las kyang /
byang chub sems dpa' rnams kyi 'ching ba ni gang / thar pa ni gang zhe na/ thabs kyis ma zin pa'i shes rab ni 'ching ba'o/ / thabs kyis zin pa'i shes rab ni thar pa'o/ / shes rab kyis ma zin pa'i thabs ni 'ching ba'o// shes rab kyis zin pa'i thabs ni thar pa'o/[861] / zhes gsungs so/ /

It also says, in the Teachings of Vimalakīrti Sutra:
What is bondage for bodhisattvas and what is their liberation? Their bondage is wisdom not supported by skillful means whereas their liberation is wisdom supported by skillful means.[553]

d.div: [861] sde dge_176_bka'/ mdo sde/ ma_dri ma med par grags pas bstan pa'i mdo/ le'u/ 4_shog_201_ba1
[553] Vimalakīrtinirdeśasūtra, Toh 176 Kangyur, mdo sde, ma, 201b1.

f.d:
des na thabs dang shes rab ya bral du nyams su len pa ni bdud kyi las la spyod pa yin te/ klu'i rgyal po rgya mtshos zhus pa'i mdo las kyang /
bdud kyi las ni gnyis te/ shes rab dang bral ba'i thabs dang / thabs dang bral ba'i shes rab ste/ bdud kyi las su shes pas spang bar bya'o/[862] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Hence, to practice either skillful means or wisdom on its own is to engage in the work of Māra. The Questions of Nāga King Anavatapta Sutra says:
The works of Māra are two: skillful means without wisdom and wisdom without skillful means. Those should be recognized as the work of Māra and rejected.[554]

d.div: [862] ma dper klu'i rgyal po rgya mtshos zhus pa'i mdo las zhes byung yang / lung 'di sde dge_156_bka'/ mdo sde/ pha_klu'i rgyal po ma dros pas zhus pa'i mdo/ le'u/ 4_shog_228_ba3_nang bzhugs/
[554] Anavataptanāgarājaparipṛcchāsūtra, Toh 156 Kangyur, mdo sde, pha, 228b3.

f.d:
yang dper na/ yid la 'dod pa'i grong khyer du 'gro bar 'dod pa la lam brtag pa'i mig dang / sa gcod pa'i rkang pa gnyis 'dzom dgos pa ltar/ mi gnas pa'i mya ngan las 'das pa'i grong khyer du 'gro ba la/ shes rab kyi mig dang thabs kyi rkang pa gnyis zung du 'brel dgos pa yin no/ / ga ya go ri'i mdo las kyang /
theg pa chen po'i lam mdor bsdu na gnyis te/ thabs dang shes rab bo/[863] / zhes gsungs so//

Further, to give an analogy, just as someone wishing to reach the town of his choice needs a combination of eyes to survey the way and legs to cover the distance, so those going to the city of nonabiding nirvana need the union of the eyes of wisdom and the legs of skillful means. The Gayāśīrṣa Hill Sutra says:
In brief, Mahayana is twofold: means and wisdom.[555] /191/

d.div: [863] sde dge_109_bka'/ mdo sde/ ca_ga yA mgo ri'i mdo/ shog_290_na1
[555] Gayāśīrṣasūtra, Toh 109 Kangyur, mdo sde, ca, 290a1.

f.d: yang shes rab de yang rang dgar mi skye ste/ dper na shing nyung zad tsam la me sbar yang / me che la yun ring ba mi 'byung la/ shing shin tu skam zhing mang ba bsags nas me sbar na/ me che la yun ring ba bsad kyang mi sod pa 'byung ngo / / de bzhin du bsod nams nyung zad tsam las ma bsags pa la shes rab chen po mi skye la/ sbyin pa dang tshul khrims la sogs pa'i bsod nams chen po bsags pa la shes rab chen po 'byung ste/ sgrib pa thams cad bsreg go /

Wisdom will not arise of its own accord. For example, while a small amount of wood may be ignited but never becomes a powerful, enduring blaze, a great quantity of extremely dry branches stacked together can be ignited to make a mighty, long-lasting blaze that is inextinguishable. Similarly, if only a small amount of wholesome action has been established, great wisdom will not arise, but when vast amounts of the great merits of generosity, moral discipline, and so forth have been established, a great wisdom will emerge, and this will burn away all the obscurations.

des na shes rab nyid kyi ched du sbyin pa la sogs pa brten dgos so/ / de ltar yang spyod 'jug las/
yan lag 'di dag thams cad ni/ / thub pas shes rab don du gsungs/[864] / zhes 'byung ngo //

Therefore it is for the sake of wisdom alone that one must resort to generosity and so forth. The Guide to the Bodhisattva Way of Life says:
The Victor has taught that all these factors are for the sake of wisdom.[556]

d.div: [864] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_rgyal sras zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 9_sh+loka_1_shog_30_ba7
[556] Śāntideva, Bodhicaryāvatāra 9:1ab, Toh 3871 Tengyur, dbu ma, la, 30b7.

f.d:
shes rab kyi ngo bo ni/ chos rab tu rnam par 'byed pa'o/ / de ltar yang mngon pa kun las btus pa las/
shes rab gang zhe na/ chos rab tu rnam par 'byed pa'o/[865] / zhes gsungs so//

The second point, the nature of wisdom consists of an accurate, discerning appreciation of phenomena. Thus the Compendium of Higher Knowledge says:
What is wisdom? It is an accurate, discerning appreciation of phenomena.[557]

d.div: [865] sde dge_4049_bstan/ sems tsam/ ri_'phags pa thogs med/ mngon pa kun btus/ le'u/ 1_shog_48_ba3
[557] Asaṅga, Abhidharmasamuccaya, Toh 4049 Tengyur, sems tsam, ri, 48b3.

f.d: shes rab la dbye na/ mdo sde rgyan gyi 'grel pa las rnam pa gsum gsungs te/ 'jig rten pa'i shes rab dang / 'jig rten las 'das pa dman pa'i shes rab dang / 'jig rten las 'das pa chen po'i shes rab bo//

The third point concerns its various aspects. The commentary to the Ornament of Mahayana Sutras speaks of three types of wisdom: mundane wisdom, lesser supramundane wisdom, and greater supramundane wisdom.

de dag so so'i mtshan nyid bshad na/ 'jig rten pa'i shes rab ni/ gso ba rig pa dang / gtan tshigs rig pa dang / sgra rig pa dang / bzo rig pa ste/ rig pa'i gnas bzhi po dag la brten nas skyes pa'i shes rab gang yin pa de'o/ /

The fourth point explains the essential characteristics of each aspect. Mundane wisdom is the wisdom emerging from the four domains of knowledge: the sciences of healing, logic and epistemology, linguistics, and creative skill.[558]

d.div: [558] “Creative skill” is used here for the Tibetan bzo ba rig pa. This is often translated as “arts and crafts,” yet covers the much wider scope of all knowledge of how things come into being. The field so often translated as “medicine” also has a broader sense: It is the knowledge of how to act on the causal processes to prevent or reduce the harm they would normally cause.

f.d: 'jig rten las 'das pa'i shes rab gnyis po nang rig pa zhes bya ba dam pa'i chos la brten nas skyes pa'i shes rab gang yin pa'o/ /

de yang dang po 'jig rten las 'das pa dman pa'i shes rab ni/ nyan thos dang rang rgyal ba dag gi thos bsam sgom gsum las byung ba'i shes rab ste/ nye bar len pa'i phung po 'di mi gtsang ba dang / sdug bsngal ba dang / mi rtag pa dang / bdag med par rtogs pa'o/ /

Lesser supramundane wisdom is the wisdom that arises through the study, contemplation, and meditation of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. It is to realize the self-perpetuating aggregates to be impure, ridden with suffering, impermanent, and devoid of any entity.

gnyis pa 'jig rten las 'das pa chen po'i shes rab ni/ theg pa chen po pa'i thos bsam sgom gsum las byung ba'i shes rab ste/ chos thams cad rang bzhin gyis stong nyid skye ba med pa/ gzhi med rtsa bral du shes pa'o/[866] /

Greater supramundane wisdom is the wisdom that arises from Mahayana study, contemplation, and meditation. It is the awareness that each and every phenomenon is, by its very nature, empty, unborn, without foundation, and without root. /192/

d.div: [866] stong nyid skye med du shes pa'o// dpal spungs/

f.d:
de ltar yang shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa bdun brgya pa las/
chos thams cad skye ba ma mchis par shes pa gang lags pa de ni shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa lags so/[867] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Thus it says in the Perfection of Wisdom in Seven Hundred Lines:
To understand that every phenomenon has no existence as something arisen—that is the perfection of wisdom.[559]

d.div: [867] sde dge_90_bka'/ dkon rtsegs/ cha_bdun brgya pa/ shog_197_ba6
[559] Saptaśatikāprajñāpāramitā, Toh 90 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, cha, 197b6.

f.d:
'phags pa sdud pa las kyang /
chos rnams rang bzhin med par yongs su shes gyur pa/ / 'di ni shes rab pha rol phyin mchog spyod pa yin/[868] / zhes gsungs so/ /

The Verse Summary of the Perfection of Wisdom also says:
To understand every phenomenon to be without own-nature is to engage in the practice of excellent perfection of wisdom.[560]

d.div: [868] sde dge_13_bka'/ sher phyin/ ka_mdo sdud pa/ le'u/ 1_sh+loka_28_shog_3_ba1
[560] Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā, Toh 13 Kangyur, sher phyin, ka, 3b1.

f.d:
byang chub lam sgron las kyang /
phung po khams dang skye mched rnams/ / skye ba med par rtogs gyur pa'i/ / rang bzhin stong nyid shes pa la/ / shes rab ces ni yongs su bshad/[869] / ces gsungs so//

Lamp for the Path to Awakening says:
To understand emptiness, the essential nature, in terms of perceiving the aggregates, the sense bases, and elements as devoid of arising, this is clearly stated to be wisdom.[561]

d.div: [869] sde dge_3947_bstan/ dbu ma/ khi_dpal mar me mdzad ye shes/ lam sgron/ sh+loka_47_shog_240_na5
[561] Atiśa, Bodhipathapradīpa verse 47, Toh 3947 Tengyur, dbu ma, khi, 240a5.

f.d: shes rab shes par bya ba ni/ shes rab la gsum yod pa las/ 'jig rten las 'das pa chen po'i shes rab de shes par bya dgos pa yin no/ / de 'chad pa la don rnam pa drug gis ston te/ dngos par 'dzin pa dgag pa dang / dngos med du 'dzin pa dgag pa dang / med par 'dzin pa'i skyon dang / 'dzin pa gnyis char gyi skyon dang / grol bar 'gyur ba'i lam dang / grol ba'i rang bzhin mya ngan las 'das pa'o//

The fifth point concerns that which is to be understood. Of the three types of wisdom mentioned above, it is the third type—greater supramundane wisdom—that one needs to understand. I shall present this by means of six topics: A. Refutation of belief in substantial reality B. Refutation of belief in unreality C. The mistake of believing in nonexistence D. The mistake of both beliefs E. The path to liberation F. The nature of liberation—nirvana
de la dang po dngos por 'dzin pa dgag pa ni/

d.i: A. Refutation of belief in substantial reality

f.d:
jo bo'i byang chub lam sgron du/[870] /
yod pa skye bar rigs min te/ / med pa'ang nam mkha'i me tog bzhin/[871] / zhes pa la sogs pa gtan tshigs chen po rnams kyis dpyad nas gsungs te/

d.div: [870] dpal spungs dpar mar jo bo'i zhes pa'i tshig 'di mi byung /
[871] sde dge_3947_bstan/ dbu ma/ khi_dpal mar me mdzad ye shes/ lam sgron/ sh+loka_48_shog_240_na5
[562] Ibid. verse 48, 240a5.

f.d: lam rim du gsung tsa na/ dngos po'am dngos 'dzin thams cad bdag gnyis su 'dus la/ bdag gnyis po de rang bzhin gyis stong nyid yin par gsungs so/ / 'o na bdag rnam pa gnyis sam/[872] sems zhes bya ba gang yin na/ gang zag gi bdag ces bya ba dang / chos kyi bdag ces bya ba'o/ / de la gang zag gi bdag gam sems zhes bya ba de gang yin na/[873] 'di la'ang 'dod lugs mang ste/ don la gang zag ces bya ba ni/ rig pa dang bcas pa'i nye bar len pa'i phung po'i rgyun nam mi byed dgu byed rig rig gyu gyu po 'di yin no/[874] /

As he explains in the teachings on the gradual path, all substantial realities, or beliefs in substantiality, are included within the two kinds of self, and that both those entities are by their very nature emptiness. What, then, are the two kinds of self ? They are known as the self of persons and the self of phenomena. What is the self of persons?[563] There are many views on this. In fact, what is referred to as a “person” is the continuum of aggregates accompanied by awareness; it is that which does all sorts of things, always thinking this and that, moving and hopping about.

d.div: [872] rnam pa gnyis zhes bya ba de gang yin na/ dpal spungs/
[873] gang zag gi bdag ces bya ba/ dpal spungs/
[874] dpal spungs dpar mar/ nam mi byed dgu byed rig rig gyu gyu po/ zhes pa'i bar gyi tshig 'di rnams mi byung ba dpyad/

[563] In the critical Tibetan edition, the Beijing edition, as well as the Tsipri edition, there is the following reading: “What then are the two kinds of self or mind?. . . What is the self or mind of persons?” In these editions, in these two instances self (bdag) is equated with mind (sems), thus giving rise to a somewhat awkward reading of the text. Here, we have chosen to follow the reading of the Palpung edition.

f.d:
de ltar yang mdo sil bu las/
rgyun la gang zag ces bya ste/ / gya gyu 'phro ba 'di rang yin/[875]/ zhes gsungs so/ /

d.div: [875] 'di 'phags pa gnas brtan sde pa'i mdo bye brag pa zhig yin cing / bod 'gyur ma bzhugs shing / pA li'i gsung rab nas kyang khungs 'tshol zhu ma thub/

f.d: gang zag de la rtag pa dang gcig pur gzung nas nga dang bdag tu zhen cing chags pa de la gang zag gi bdag gam sems zhes bya ste/ bdag des ni nyon mongs pa bskyed do/ / nyon mongs pa des las bskyed do/[876] / las kyis sdug bsngal bskyed do/ / des na sdug bsngal dang nyes pa thams cad kyi rtsa ba ni bdag gam sems de yin no/[877] /

Believing such a person to be eternal and unitary entity, and grasping onto it and being attached to it, this is called the “selfhood of person” or of mind. Through the notion of self, afflictions will be generated; /193/ through the afflictions, karma will be generated; and through karma, suffering will be generated. Thus the root of all sufferings and faults is the self or mind.

d.div: [876] dpal spungs dpar mar nyon mongs pa des las bskyed do// zhes pa'i tshig 'di mi byung /
[877] bdag de yin no/ /dpal spungs/

f.d:
de ltar yang rnam 'grel las/
bdag yod na ni gzhan du shes/ / bdag gzhan cha las 'dzin dang sdang / / 'di dag dang ni yongs 'brel las/ / nyes pa thams cad 'byung bar 'gyur/[878] / zhes gsungs so//

Therefore the Thorough Exposition of Valid Cognition says:
When “I” exists, “other” is known. Through the I-and-other pair comes clinging and aversion. Through the complex interaction of these arises all harm.[564]

d.div: [878] sde dge_4210_bstan/ tshad ma/ ce_rnam 'grel/ tshad ma grub pa'i le'u/ 1_sh+loka_221_shog_116_na1
[564] Dharmakīrti, Pramāṇavārttika, “Pramāṇasidhi” chapter, verse 221, Toh 4210 Tengyur, tshad ma, che, 116a1.

f.d: chos kyi bdag de gang yin na/ de la chos zhes pa ni/ phyi gzung ba'i yul dang / nang 'dzin pa'i sems so/ / ci'i phyir de dag la chos zhes bya zhe na/ de dag rang gi mtshan nyid 'dzin pa'i phyir ro/ /

What is self of phenomena? Here, phenomena refers to the outer perceived world and the inner perceiving mind. Why are those two aspects called phenomena (dharma)? Because they possess their own defining characteristics.[565]

d.div: [565] This is reference to the etymology of dharma, the root dhr of which gives a sense of “holding,” “possessing.” Thus each distinct phenomenon known by the mind has its own characteristics.

f.d:
de ltar yang mdo sil bu las/
mtshan nyid 'dzin la chos zhes bya/[879] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Thus the Sutra of Fragments says,
That which holds defining characteristics is called dharma.

d.div: [879] 'di yang gong du drangs pa ltar gnas brtan sde pa'i mdo zhig yin/

f.d:
de ltar gzung 'dzin gnyis po dngos por bzung nas zhen pa ni chos kyi bdag ces bya'o/[880]/ bdag de gnyis rang bzhin gyis stong nyid yin par 'chad pa la/ dang por gang zag gi bdag dgag ste/ slob dpon klu sgrub kyis mdzad pa'i rin chen phreng ba las/
bdag yod bdag gir yod ces pa/ 'di ni dam pa'i don du log[881] / ces gsungs te/ bdag de don dam par ma grub pa'i don to/ /

Thus holding the two—the objective perceived world and the subjective perceiving world—to possess substantial reality and clinging to them is called self of phenomena. (1) To present how these two types of self are empty by nature, first there is the refutation of the self of persons. Master Nāgārjuna says, in his Precious Garland:
The notions “I” and “mine” deviate from what is ultimately true.[566] This means that, from the point of view of ultimate reality, those aspects of self do not exist.

d.div: [880] gnyis po de la/ dpal spungs/
[881] sde dge_4158_bstan/ spring yig_ge_mgon po klu sgrub/ rin chen phreng ba/ le'u/ 1_sh+loka_28_shog_108_na2
[566] Nāgārjuna, Ratnāvalī 1:28ab, Toh 4158 Tengyur, spring yig, ge, 108a2.

f.d: gal te bdag gam sems don dam par grub nas yod na/[882] bden pa mthong ba'i dus na yang yod dgos pa la/ bden pa mthong ba'i sems kyis ngo bo mthong ba'i dus na bdag de med pas na ma grub pa yin no/[883] /

If such a self existed as an ultimate reality, it should equally be there when ultimate truth is “seen”; yet when a mind with insight into the truth sees the essential nature, there is no such self. Therefore it does not have any true existence.

d.div: [882] gal te bdag de don dam par grub nas bden par yod na/ dpal spungs/
[883] sems kyis ngo bo mthong ba'i/ dpal spungs dpar mar mi gsal/

f.d:
de ltar yang rin chen phreng ba las/
gang phyir yang dag ji lta ba/ / yongs su shes pas gnyis mi 'byung /[884] / zhes gsungs te/

The Precious Garland says:
For when the ultimately pure is fully recognized just as it is, these two will not arise.[567]

d.div: [884] sde dge_4158_bstan/ spring yig_ge_mgon po klu sgrub/ rin chen phreng ba/ le'u/ 1_sh+loka_28_shog_108_na2

f.d: de la yang dag pa ji lta ba zhes pa ni bden pa mthong ba'am sems sam/[885] gnyis mi 'byung ba ni bdag dang bdag gir 'dzin pa mi 'byung ba'o/ /
In that text, “the ultimately pure is fully recognized just as it is” refers to insight into the truth. “These two will not arise” means that there will be not grasping at “I” or “mine.”

d.div: [885] bden pa mthong ba'o// dpal spungs dpar mar/ ba'am sems sam/ zhes pa mi byung /

f.d: yang gal te bdag gam sems de yod par gyur na rang las skye ba'am/ gzhan las skye ba'am/ gnyis ka las skye ba'am/ dus gsum las skye zhes brtags par bya'o/ /
[a] Were a mind or self to truly exist, it could be examined as originating from itself, from something else, or through the three phases of time.
de la rang las mi skye ste/ rang grub zin nam ma zin/ grub ma zin na rgyur mi rung zhing /[886] grub zin na 'bras bur mi rung zhing / rang la rang byed pa 'gal bas so/ /

It does not arise from itself because [as far as the process of origination is concerned] its production must have either already happened or have not yet happened. If it does not yet exist, it cannot possibly serve as a cause [for its own production,] and if it does already exist, it cannot possibly become [its own] result. Thus something producing itself is a contradiction.

d.div: [886] mi rung la/ dpal spungs/

f.d: gzhan las kyang mi skye ste/ de ni rdzas yin pa'i phyir ro/[887] / rgyu ji ltar ma yin na/ 'di ltar rgyu ni 'bras bu la ltos pa yin pas ji srid 'bras bu ma byung ba de srid ni rgyu ma yin no/ / gang gi tshe rgyu ma yin pa de'i tshe 'bras bu yang mi skyed bas snga ma kho na bzhin no/[888] /

It does not arise from others because they are substances [other than itself]. Why can they not be causes? A “cause” only exists with respect to a result, and as long as there is no result, there is no cause. As long as there is no cause, no result can manifest either. /194/ This is similar to the previous argument.[568]

d.div: [887] de ni rgyu ma yin pa'i phyir ro/ /dpal spungs/
[888] mi bskyed pas/ dpal spungs/

[568] This passage is a summary of well-rehearsed arguments found in the Perfection of Wisdom literature. It consists of a minute examination of the successive moments of time of a supposed creation and an exploration of the very notion of “cause”: one thing disappearing and another occurring.

f.d: gnyis ka las kyang mi skye ste/ phyogs gnyis ka sngar bshad pa ltar skyon can yin pa'i phyir ro/ /
It does not arise from both [self and others] of the above since both concepts are faulty, as explained above.

dus gsum las kyang mi skye ste/ 'das pas mi bskyed pa ni de nyid sa bon rul ba nus pa zad pa bzhin no/ / ma 'ongs pas mi skye ba ni mo gsham gyi bu bzhin no/ / da ltar bas mi skye ba ni phan gdags bya 'dogs byed mi 'thad pas so/ /

It does not arise from the three phases of time: It is not a product of the past because the past, like a seed gone rotten, no longer has any power. It is not produced by the future—that would be like the child of a barren woman. It is not a product of the present because it is illogical that it could be both creation and creator [in the same instant].

de ltar yang rin chen phreng ba las/
de ni rang gzhan gnyis ka dang / / dus gsum nyid du ma thob phyir/ / ngar 'dzin pa ni zad par 'gyur/[889]/ zhes gsungs te/ ma thob pa ni mi skye ba'i don to//[890]

Thus the Precious Garland says:
As it is not being obtained from itself, something other, a combination, or the three times, belief in a self will be consumed.[569] “Not being obtained from” means not generated by.

d.div: [889] sde dge_4158_bstan/ spring yig_ge_mgon po klu sgrub/ rin chen phreng ba/ le'u/ 1_sh+loka_37_shog_108_na6
[890] don no/ /mi rigs dpe skrun/
[569] Nāgārjuna, Ratnāvalī 1:37a–c, Toh 4158 Tengyur, spring yig, ge, 108a6.

f.d: yang na 'di ltar go bar bya ste/ bdag ces bya ba de rang gi lus la yod dam/ sems la yod dam/ ming la yod ces brtags par bya'o/ /
[b] Alternatively, one should understand it in the following manner. Examine whether or not this “self” exists in the body, in the mind, or in a name.

lus 'di 'byung ba bzhi'i rang bzhin yin te/ de la lus kyi sra ba ni sa yin/ gsher ba ni chu yin/ drod ni me yin/ dbugs dang g.yo 'gul ni rlung yin no/ / de ltar 'byung ba bzhi la bdag gam sems med de/ dper na phyi rol gyi sa chu la sogs pa'i 'byung ba bzhi la bdag gam sems med pa bzhin no/ /

The nature of the body is that of the four elements: the body’s solidity is the earth element, its fluids are the water element, its warmth is the fire element, and its breathing and movement constitute the wind element. The four elements possess neither self nor mind, just as the four outer elements—earth, water, and so on—are without mind or self.
sems la bdag yod do zhe na/ sems ni cir yang ma grub ste rang gzhan gnyis kas ma mthong ba'i phyir ro/ / des na sems rang ma grub pas/ bdag grub pa med do/ /

Does the self exist in the mind, then? Mind has no existence whatsoever, for neither you nor anyone else has ever seen it. If mind has no actual existence, then self as mind can have no actual existence either.
ming la bdag gam sems yod do zhe na/[891] ming ni glo bur du btags pa yin te/ rdzas su yang ma grub la/ bdag dang yang 'brel ba med do/[892] /
Does self or own mind exist in the name? A name is merely something given arbitrarily; it has no substantial existence and bears no relation to a self.

d.div: [891] ming la'ang bdag yod do zhe na/ dpal spungs /
[892] yang / dpal spungs dpar mar med/

f.d: de ltar na rgyu mtshan gsum gyi sgo nas gang zag gi bdag gam sems ma grub par bstan to//
Thus the three reasons presented above demonstrate that the self or mind of persons has no true existence.
da ni chos kyi bdag dgag pa la gnyis te/ phyi gzung ba'i yul ma grub par bstan pa dang / nang 'dzin pa'i sems ma grub par bstan pa'o/ /

(2) [Second there is] the refutation of the self of phenomena. This is in two parts, demonstrating the nonexistence of the objective perceived world and the nonexistence of the subjective perceiving mind.

de la dang po bshad na/ kha cig phyi gzung ba'i yul dngos por grub par 'dod de/ de yang bye brag tu smra ba na re/ rdul phra rab kyi ngo bo zlum gong cha shas med pa zhig rdzas su yod/ de dag tshogs pa ni gzugs la sogs pa'i yul 'di yin te/ de yang rdul de rnams sil bur so sor bskor ba bar dang bcas par yod de/[893] da lta phyogs gcig tu snang ba ni dper na g.yag rnga dang ne'u sing gi tshul ltar yin/ mi gyes pa ni sems can gyi las kyis bsdus pa yin/[894] zhes zer ro/ /

[a] As for the first, [the nonexistence of the objective perceived world,] some believe in the substantial existence of the objective perceived world. Vaibhāṣikas, for example, hold there to be minute particles of matter that exist substantially; they are round and partless. The aggregation of these particles constitutes objects such as material form and so forth. As the particles agglomerate, there are interstices between them. They presently appear as something homogeneous, just as a yak’s tail or a pasture of grass does. /195/ The minute particles do not drift apart because the karma of beings causes them to bond as they do.

d.div: [893] so so/ dpal spungs/
[894] mi 'gyes/ dpal spungs/

f.d: mdo sde pa na re/ rdul de dag kyang bskor ba bar med pa 'byar la ma reg par yod ces zer ro/ / de ltar 'dod kyang de ma grub ste/

Sautrāntikas hold that when such partless particles conglomerate, they are without interstices yet do not actually touch. These are the views of those [two main Hinayana traditions,] but neither is really the case.

rdul de gcig tu yod dam du mar yod/ gcig yin na rdul de la phyogs cha'i dbye ba yod dam med/ phyogs cha'i dbye ba yod na shar nub dang lho byang dang steng 'og gi cha ste/ cha drug tu song bas gcig tu 'dod pa nyams so// phyogs cha'i dbye ba med na dngos po thams cad kyang rdul gcig gi ngo bor 'gyur dgos na de ltar yang ma yin te/ mngon sum gyi bsal ba yod do/ /

Were such a particle to be unitary, then would it not have sides? If so, would it not have relative east, west, north, south, top and, bottom areas? This makes six sides and destroys the contention of it being unitary. If it had no spatial dimension, all matter would be, by nature, a sole atom. This is obviously not the case either.

de ltar yang / nyi shu pa'i rab tu byed pa las/
drug gis gcig char sbyar ba na/ / phra rab rdul cha drug tu 'gyur/ / drug po dag ni go gcig na/ / gong bu rdul phran tsam du 'gyur/[895] / zhes gsungs so/ /

The Twenty Stanzas says:
If the six are applied to what is one, the ultimate particle has six different parts. If those six are one, then substance is only one particle.[570]

d.div: [895] sde dge_4056_bstan/ sems tsam/ shi_slob dpon dbyig gnyen/ nyi shu pa/ sh+loka_12_shog_3_ba3
[570] Vasubandhu, Viṃśatikā, Toh 4056 Tengyur, sems tsam, shi, 3b3.

f.d: du ma yin no zhe na/ gcig grub na gcig bsags pa'i du ma grub tu rung ba las/ gcig ma grub pas de bsags pa'i du ma yang ma grub bo/ / des na rdul phra rab rdzas su ma grub pas de'i rang bzhin phyi'i yul 'di yang ma grub bo// 'o na da lta mngon sum du snang zhing 'dug pa 'di ci yin snyam na 'di ni rang sems nyid 'khrul nas phyi rol gyi yul du snang ba 'di rang gi sems la de ltar du shar bas snang ba yin no/[896] [897]/ de ltar yin par cis shes na/ lung dang / rigs pa dang / dpe dang gsum gyis shes par bya'o/ /

Are particles multiple? If one partless particle could be proved to exist, it would be reasonable to propose that many of them could conglomerate to make multiple entities, but since the existence of a partless unit cannot be proved, multiples of them cannot be proved to exist either. As a consequence, since particles have no substantial existence, an outer substantial reality composed of particles of such a nature cannot exist either. You may wonder, “What is actually manifesting right now?” It is an image in the mind that appears to the mind as being an outer world. This occurs through delusion. If you ask, “How can we know that is so?” the answer is that it can be known through scriptural authority, reason, and examples:

d.div: [896] rang gi sems nyid/ dpal spungs/
[897] dpal spungs dpar mar/ 'di rang gi sems la de ltar du shar bas snang ba/ zhes pa'i tshig rnams mi byung /

f.d:
de la lung ni/ phal po che'i mdo las/
kye rgyal ba'i sras dag / khams gsum po 'di ni sems tsam mo/[898] / zhes gsungs so/ /

The scriptural authority can be found in the Flower Ornament Sutra, where it says,
Children of good family! This world of the three realms is mind only.[571]

d.div: [898] sde dge_44_bka'/ phal chen/ kha_sa bcu pa'i mdo/ shog_220_ba4
[571] Avataṃsakasūtra, Toh 44 Kangyur, phal chen, kha, 220b4.

f.d:
lang kar gshegs pa'i mdo las kyang /
bag chags kyis ni dkrugs pa'i sems/ / don du snang ba rab tu 'byung / / don yod ma yin sems nyid de/ / phyi rol don mthong log pa'o/[899] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Also in the Sutra on Going to Laṅka, where it says:
Mind agitated by its imprints will manifest thoroughly as objective realities.[572] There are no objective realities but mind alone; the perception of external reality is erroneous.[573]

d.div: [899] sde dge_107_bka'/ mdo sde/ ca_lang kar gshegs pa'i mdo/ le'u/ 10_sh+loka_153_shog_165_na5
[572] Laṅkāvatārasūtra, Toh 107 Kangyur, mdo sde, ca, 165a6.

f.d: rigs pa ni/ phyi snang ba 'di chos can sems kyi 'khrul snang yin par dam bca'/ med pa snang zhing 'dug pa'i phyir/[900] zhes pa ni gtan tshigs so/ /(mi'i rwa'am bsgom pa'i ljon shing lta bu/)[901] de bzhin du yod pa mi snang ba'i (snang ba rkyen gyi stobs kyis 'gyur ba dang /) phyir dang /[902] snang ba 'gyur zhing /(goms pa'i stobs kyis 'gyur/)'gro ba'i phyir dang / (rigs drug gi/)tha dad pa'i phyir snang ba 'di sems kyis 'khrul snang kho na yin no/[903] / dpe ni/ rmi lam dang sgyu ma la sogs bzhin no/ /

[Refutation of external reality through] reason can be presented in the form of the syllogism: “Those things that appear as external” is the logical subject; “they are illusory manifestations of mind” is the proposition; “because that which has no true existence is being perceived” is the reason. (For instance, human horns or a visualized tree.)[574] Such manifestations (the subject) are also simply illusory projections of the mind (the proposition) because they do not appear as what they really are—changing appearances brought about by certain causes and conditions, or appearances that can transmute and disappear through the power of imagination and familiarization, the way things manifest being different according to the projections of each of the six types of sentient being (the reason). Examples of such a process would be dreams, magical illusions, and the like.

d.div: [900] dpal spungs dpar mar/ med pa snang zhing 'dug_zhes pa'i tshig 'di mi byung /
[901] ma dpe dang mi rigs dpe skrun dpar mar yig chung du byung ba 'dari rnams dpal spungs dpar mar yig chen tu gzhung dkyus la byung bas brtag/
[902] phyir dang / zhes pa dpal spungs dpar mar mi byung /
[903] 'di/ zhes pa dpal spungs dpar mar med/
[574] This parenthetical sentence appears as an annotation, written in a small font, embedded in the original Tibetan text.

f.d: de dag gis phyi gzung ba'i yul ma grub par bstan no//
Thus these above presents how the external perceived world is devoid of [substantial] existence. /196/
gnyis pa bshad na/ kha cig nang 'dzin pa'i sems rang rig(rang rgyal ba dang sems tsam pas/)[904] rang gsal du dngos su grub par 'dod do/ /

[b] The second point [is the nonexistence of a perceiving mind]. Some—pratyekabuddhas and Cittamātrins—consider the subjective, perceiving mind really to exist, as something apperceptive and self-illuminating.

d.div: [904] yig chung 'di dag dpal spungs dpar mar med/

f.d: de ltar 'dod kyang de ma grub pa'i rgyu mtshan gsum ste/ sems de skad cig mar brtags pas ma grub pa dang / sems de sus kyang mthong ba med pas dngos su ma grub pa dang / yul med pas sems ma grub pa'o//

They hold such a view, but it is inaccurate for three reasons: 1. Mind does not exist when examined in terms of moments of time. 2. Mind does not exist because no one has ever witnessed it. 3. Mind does not exist because there is no objective reality.

de la dang po ni/ khyod 'dod pa'i sems rang rig rang gsal de skad cig tu yod dam/ du mar yod/ skad cig tu yod ce na/ de la dus gsum gyi cha shas yod dam de la dus gsum gyi cha shas med/[905] dang po ltar na skad cig ma ma grub ste du mar thal lo/ /

(1) Concerning the first of these, [nonexistence in terms of moments of time]: “Is the apperceptive, self-illuminating mind that you postulate present in one instant or several? Were it truly to exist in each instant, would that instant have past, present, and future?[575] If it were so, this would refute its existence as a unique existing unit of mind. If it were not so, [the idea of sequences of] many instants becomes absurd.”

d.div: [905] de la dus gsum gyi cha shas/ shes pa dpal spungs dpar mar med/
[575] Literally, “Does it have the three times?”

f.d:
de ltar yang rin chen phreng ba las/
ji ltar skad cig mtha' yod pa/ / de bzhin thog tha dbus brtags dgos/ / de ltar skad cig gsum brtags phyir/ / 'jig rten skad cig la mi gnas/[906] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Thus the Precious Garland says:
One must examine the instant: just as it has an end, it must also have a middle and a beginning. Since an instant is thus threefold, the world cannot exist as an instant.[576]

d.div: [906] sde dge_4158_bstan/ spring yig_ge_mgon po klu sgrub/ rin chen phreng ba/ le'u/ 1_sh+loka_69_shog_109_na1
[576] Nāgārjuna, Ratnāvalī 1:69, Toh 4158 Tengyur, spring yig, ge, 109a1.

f.d: de la dus gsum gyi cha shas med na skad cig ma de dngos med du thal lo/ / des na skad cig ma ma grub pas sems kyang ma grub bo/ / du mar yod do zhe na/ skad cig grub na skad cig bsags pa'i du ma grub tu rung ba la/ skad cig ma grub pas de bsags pa'i du ma yang ma grub bo/ / du ma ma grub pas sems kyang ma grub bo//

Without the existence of the threefold division of time, the [true existence of the] instant is refuted by its being insubstantial. Through the instant being unproven, the existence of mind [composed of such instants] is also unproven. Does mind exist as multiple instants? Were one instant to be proven, it would be reasonable to postulate an accumulation of many instants, but since the existence of one instant is not proven, the idea of mind as multiple instants is not demonstrated either.

don gnyis pa bshad na/ sems zhes bya ba 'di lus kyi phyi nang bar gsum stod smad gang du gnas pa btsal/[907] gzugs sam kha dog ci ltar 'dug pa legs par brtags la/ nges shes skye skye su 'tshol ba dang / dmigs rim spo ba la sogs pa zhal las shes pa ltar 'tshol/ / de ci ltar btsal yang ma mthong ma rnyed na/ mthong rgyu'am kha dog dngos po'i mtshan ma cung zad kyang med/ yod pa de ma mthong ma rnyed pa ma yin/ btsal ba po rang 'tshol rgyu'am/ 'tshol mkhan rang blo'i yul las 'das pa/ smra bsam shes brjod kyi yul las 'das pa yin pas gang du'ang btsal bas mi mthong ste/ ji skad du 'od srungs kyis zhus pa'i mdo las/
'od srungs sems ni nang na yang med/ phyi rol na yang med/ gnyis ka'i bar la yang mi dmigs so/ / 'od srungs sems ni dpyad du med pa/ bstan du med pa/ brnyed du med pa/ snang ba med pa/ rnam par rig pa med pa/ gnas pa med pa'o// 'od srungs sems ni sangs rgyas thams cad kyis kyang ma gzigs mi gzigs gzigs par mi 'gyur ro/[908] /zhes gsungs so/ /

(2) Now for the second point, the nonexistence of the perceiving mind because it has never been witnessed. Seek out the location of “mind”—in the body, outside it, or between the two; seek it high and low. Examine most thoroughly to determine whether it has any form or color whatsoever. Seek until there is a sense of conviction, whatever it may be. Search for it according to the master’s instructions—such as how to vary the object of inspection. When, no matter how you seek, mind is never seen, never encountered, and no substantial characteristic such as color or something visible is to be found, it is not the case that mind exists but you have not yet been able to find it or witness it. If it cannot be seen, no matter where it is sought, it is because the investigator is the investigated and the seeker is beyond the scope of his or her own intellect—beyond the scope of words, thoughts, ideas, or expression. That is why in the Kāśyapa Chapter Sutra it says:
Kāśyapa! Mind is found neither within, without, nor in between. Kāśyapa! Mind cannot be investigated, cannot be shown, cannot be used as a basis, cannot appear, cannot be known, and has no abiding. /197/ Kāśyapa! Mind has never, is never, and will never be seen, even by any of the buddhas.[577]

d.div: [907] phyi nang gang du'ang btsal/ dpal spungs/ bar gsum stod smad gang du gnas pa btsal/ zhes pa nas / smra bsam shes brjod kyi yul las 'das pa yin pas/ zhes pa'i bar gyi tshig rnams dpal spungs dpar mar mi byung ba brtag
[908] sde dge_87_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ cha_'od srung gis zhus pa'i le'u/ bam po/ 2_shog_139_na2
[577] Kāśyapaparivartasūtra, Toh 87 Kangyur, dkon brtseg, cha, 139a2.

f.d:
dam pa'i chos yongs su 'dzin pa'i mdo las kyang /[909]
de phyir sems ni gsog dang gsob/ / yod pa min par rab shes nas/ / de la snying por mi bzung ste/ / de dag ngo bo nyid kyis stong / / ngo bo nyid kyis stong pa'i chos/ / de dag la ni grub pa med/ / chos rnams thams cad btags pa ste/ / rang bzhin de ltar rab tu bstan/ / mtha' gnyis zil gyis mnan nas su/ / mkhas rnams dbu mar spyod par byed/ / ngo bo nyid kyi chos stong pa/ / de ni byang chub lam yin te// ngas kyang de ni bstan pa yin/[910] / zhes gsungs so/ /

In the Sutra That Perfectly Seizes Sublime Dharma it says:
Therefore, by coming to understand perfectly the various degrees to which mind is a contrivance, a fake, one will no longer perceive it as an essence. Devoid of any essence, phenomena are without any real existence. All phenomena are imputed [by the mind]; I have taught their nature to be such. Outshining the two extremes, the wise practice the middle way; this emptiness of essential reality, this is the path to enlightenment; I too have taught this path.[578]

d.div: [909] dam pa'i chos yongs su 'dzin pa'i mdo las kyang / zhes pa nas/ rtog pa dang mi rtog pa'i yul las 'das pa'o// zhes pa'i bar gyi tshig rnams dpal spungs dpar mar mi byung ba brtag/
[910] mdo 'di bka' 'gyur du ma bzhugs la ma dper gang las drangs ngos 'dzin ma thub/
[578] Dam pa’i chos yongs su ’dzin pa’i mdo. The source of this quotation has not been identified.

f.d:
chos nyid mi g.yo ba'i mdo las kyang /
chos thams cad rang bzhin gyis ma skyes pa/ ngo bo nyid kyis mi gnas pa/ las dang bya ba'i mtha' thams cad dang bral ba/ rtog pa dang mi rtog pa'i yul las 'das pa'o/[911] / zhes gsungs so/ /

The Unwavering Suchness Sutra says:
Every phenomenon is, by its very nature, unborn, essentially nonabiding, free from the extremes of acting and action, and beyond the scope of thought and nonthought.[579]

d.div: [911] sde dge_128_bka'/ mdo sde/ da_chos nyid mi g.yo ba'i mdo/ shog_172_ba3
[579] Dharmatāsvabhāvaśūnyatācalapratisarvālokasūtra, Toh 128 Kangyur, mdo sde, da, 172b3.

f.d:
des na sems de sus kyang ma mthong bas na/ rang rig rang gsal du brjod pa don med do/ / byang chub spyod 'jug las kyang /
gang tshe 'gas kyang mthong med na/ gsal ba'am ni mi gsal ba/ / mo gsham bu yi 'gying bag bzhin/ / de ni brjod kyang don med do/[912] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Since no one has ever witnessed mind, it is pointless to speak of it in terms of apperception and self-illumination. As Guide to the Bodhisattva Way of Life states:
Since none has ever seen it at any time, to ask whether it is self-illuminating is as meaningless as discussing the elegance of a barren woman’s child.[580]

d.div: [912] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_rgyal sras zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 9_sh+loka_23_shog_31_ba5
[580] Śāntideva, Bodhicaryāvatāra 9:22, Toh 3871 Tengyur, dbu ma, la, 31b5.

f.d:
te lo pas kyang /
kye ho 'di ni rang rig ye shes te/ / ngag gi lam 'das yid kyi spyod yul min/[913] / zhes gsungs so//

d.div: [913] sde dge_2281_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ zhi_grub chen te lo pa/ do ha mdzod/ shog_136_ba2_tshig ji bzhin mi snang / te lo pa'i gsungs de yang dpal spungs dpar mar mi snang bas brtag

[581] This is not verbatim but based on Tilopa’s Treasury of Dohas (Dohakoṣa), Toh 2281 Tengyur, rgyud ’grel, zhi, 136b2. Tilopa is found in the Tengyur and other sources under the similar-sounding names of Tillipa, Tailikapada, Talika, and Tilopada.

f.d: don gsum pa bshad na/ yang gong du bshad pa ltar gzugs la sogs pa phyi'i yul ma grub pas na/ de 'dzin pa'i nang gi sems kyang ma grub ste/

(3) The third point—the nonexistence of the perceiving mind because no objective reality exists—is explained as follows. Since, as was demonstrated above, visual forms and so forth—the outer objective reality—have no substantial existence, the inner mind that perceives them cannot have substantial existence either.

chos kyi dbyings kyi rang bzhin dbyer med par bstan pa'i le'u las kyang /
sems 'di ni sngon po'am/ ser po'am/ dmar po'am/ dkar po'am/ btsod kha'am/ shel gyi kha dog lta bu'am/ yang dag pa'am/ yang dag pa ma yin pa'am/ rtag ces bya ba'am/ mi rtag ces bya ba'am/ gzugs can nam/ gzugs can ma yin pa zhig ces so sor rtogs shig / sems ni gzugs can ma yin pa/ bstan du med pa/ snang ba med pa/ thogs pa med pa/ rnam par rig byed ma yin pas/ nang na mi gnas/ phyi rol na mi gnas/ gnyis ka'i bar na mi gnas pa'i phyir/ yongs su dag pa/ yongs su ma grub pa yin zhing de la rnam par grol ba med de chos kyi dbyings kyi rang bzhin no/[914] / zhes gsungs so/ /

In the Sutra on the Indivisibility of the Dharmadhātu, it says:
Investigate whether this thing you call “mind” is blue, yellow, red, white, maroon, or transparent; whether it is pure or impure, “permanent” or “impermanent,” and whether or not it is endowed with form. Mind has no physical form; it cannot be shown. It does not manifest, it is intangible, it does not cognize, it resides neither inside, outside, nor anywhere in between. Thus it is utterly pure, totally nonexistent. There is nothing of it to liberate; it is the very nature of the dharmadhātu.[582]

d.div: [914] sde dge_52_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ kha_chos kyi dbyings kyi rang bzhin dbyer med par bstan pa'i mdo/ shog_143_na3
[582] Dharmadhātuprakṛtyasambhedanirdeśasūtra, Toh 52 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, kha, 143a3.

f.d:
byang chub spyod 'jug las kyang /
shes bya med na ci rig nas/ / gang gis shes pa de rjod byed/[915] / ces pa dang /
des na shes bya nyer gnas pa/ / med par shes pa med ces nges/[916] / zhes gsungs so//

Furthermore, Guide to the Bodhisattva Way of Life says: /198/
When there is nothing to be known, what is the point of speaking of knowing?[583] and
It is certain, therefore, that without the presence of something knowable, there can be no knowledge.[584]

d.div: [915] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 9_sh+loka_61_shog_33_na4
[916] gong mtshungs/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 9_sh+loka_62_shog_33_na5
[583] Śāntideva, Bodhicaryāvatāra 9:60cd, Toh 3871 Tengyur, dbu ma, la, 33a4.
[584] Ibid. 9:61cd, Toh 3871 Tengyur, dbu ma, la, 33a5.

f.d: de dag gis nang 'dzin pa'i sems ma grub par bstan te/
Through the above points, it has been demonstrated that the perceiving mind, a subjective mind, has no ultimate existence.
de ltar dngos por 'dzin pa bkag nas/
This concludes the section discussing the belief in substantial reality.
don gnyis pa dngos med du 'dzin pa dgag pa la/

d.i: B. Refutation of belief in unreality

f.d: gal te bdag gnyis po de dngos po cir yang ma grub pas dngos med cig yin nam zhe na/ de ni dngos med du yang ma grub ste/ ci ltar zhe na/ bdag gnyis po'am/ sems de sngar dngos por yod pa la/[917] phyis med pa yin na dngos med ces byar rung ste/ bdag gnyis sam/ sems shes bya ba'i chos ye nas rang bzhin gyis ma grub pas na/[918] dngos por yod pa dang med pa'i mtha' las 'das so/ /

If the two types of self have no authentic existence as real things, could they be nonexistent, unreal? In fact, they do not even exist as unrealities. Why? Were one or the other to have had true existence in the first place, as something real, and then to have ceased existing, a “nonexistence” would be feasible. However, since neither the two kinds of self or mind ever had substantial existence in the first place, they cannot be classed in either of these extreme definitions of existing or nonexisting.

d.div: [917] bdag gnyis po de dngos por yod pa las/ dpal spungs/
[918] bdag gnyis zhes bya ba'i chos/ dpal spungs/

f.d:
sa ra ha pas/
dngos por 'dzin pa phyugs dang 'dra ba ste/ / dngos med 'dzin na de bas kyang ni blun/[919]/zhes gsungs so//

Saraha said:
To believe in reality is to be like cattle. But to believe in unreality is even more stupid![585]

d.div: [919] sde dge_2264_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ zhi_grub chen sa ra ha/ mi zad pa'i gter mdzod man ngag gi glu/ shog_29_na4
[585] Song of an Inexhaustible Treasure of Instruction (Dohakoṣopadeśagīti), Toh 2264 Tengyur, rgyud ’grel, zhi, 29a4.

f.d:
lang kar gshegs pa las kyang /
phyi rol dngos po yod med min/ / sems kyang yongs su bzung ba med/ / lta ba thams cad rab spangs pa/ / de ni skye med mtshan nyid do/[920] / zhes gsungs so/ /

The Sutra on Going to Laṅka says:
Externals are neither existent nor nonexistent. Mind cannot be truly apprehended either. The characteristic of the unborn is to be utterly other than all these views.[586]

d.div: [920] sde dge_107_bka'/ mdo sde/ ca_lang kar gshegs pa'i mdo/ le'u/ 10_sh+loka_595_shog_180_ba3
[586] Laṅkāvatārasūtra, Toh 107 Kangyur, mdo sde, ca, 180b3.

rin chen 'phreng ba las kyang /
gang tshe dngos po mi rnyed pa/ / de tshe dngos med ga la 'gyur/[921] / zhes gsungs so//

The Precious Garland says,
When no substantial reality can be found, how can there be unrealities?[587]

d.div: [921] sde dge_4158_bstan/ spring yig_ge_mgon po klu sgrub/ rin chen phreng ba/ le'u/ 1_sh+loka_98_shog_10_ba2
[587] Nāgārjuna, Ratnāvalī 1:98cd, Toh 4158 Tengyur, spring yig, ga, 10b2.

f.d: don gsum pa med par 'dzin pa'i skyon 'chad pa la/

d.i: C. The mistake of belief in nonexistence

f.d:
'o na don dngos por 'dzin pa ni 'khor ba'i rtsa bar 'dug na/[922] dngos med du bltas na 'khor ba las grol bar 'gyur ba min nam zhe na/ snga ma bas phyi ma skyon che ste/ sa ra has/
dngos por 'dzin pa phyugs dang 'dra ba ste// dngos med 'dzin na de bas kyang ni blun/[923] / zhes gsungs so/ /

If belief in existence is the root of samsara, will those who hold a view of nonexistence become liberated from samsara? In fact, this mistake is even worse than the one explained above. As [already mentioned,] Saraha said:
To believe in reality is to be like cattle. But to believe in unreality is even more stupid![588]

d.div: [922] don dngos por lta ba ni/ dpal spungs/

[923] sde dge_2264_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ zhi_grub chen sa ra ha/ mi zad pa'i gter mdzod man ngag gi glu/ shog_29_na4 sa ra ha'i gsung dngos por 'dzin zhes pa'i lung 'di dpal spungs dpar mar mi byung ba brtag
[588] Song of an Inexhaustible Treasure of Instruction (Dohakoṣopadeśagīti), Toh 2264 Tengyur, rgyud ’grel, zhi, 29a4.

f.d:
ji skad du dkon mchog brtsegs pa las/
'od srungs gang zag tu blta ba ri rab tsam la gnas pa ni sla yi/ mngon pa'i nga rgyal stong pa nyid du blta ba ni de lta ma yin no/[924] / zhes gsungs so/ / yang ji skad du/[925]
stong pa nyid la blta nyes pas/ / shes rab chung rnams phung bar 'gyur/[926] / zhes gsungs so/[927] /

It also says in the Heap of Jewels [in the Kāśyapa Chapter Sutra]:
Kāśyapa, the view of personality—even if it is as big as Mount Meru—is relatively easy [to abandon], but not so for a decidedly arrogant view of emptiness. And, furthermore it is stated:
Flawed views concerning emptiness will be the downfall of those of little wisdom.[589]

d.div: [924] sde dge_87_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ cha_'od srung gis zhus pa'i le'u/ shog_132_ba1
[925] ji skad du/ rtsa ba shes rab las/ dpal spungs/
[926] sde dge_3824_bstan/ dbu ma/ tsa_mgon po klu sgrub/ rtsa ba shes rab/ rab byed/ 24_sh+loka_11_shog_15_na2
[927] zhes dang / gang dag stong pa nyid lta ba// dpal spungs/
[589] Kāśyapaparivartasūtra, Toh 87 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, cha, 132b1.

f.d:
rtsa ba shes rab las kyang /
gang dag stong pa nyid blta ba/ / de dag gsor mi rung bar gsungs/[928] / zhes gsungs so/ /

In the Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way, it says:
Those who believe in emptiness are said to be incurable.[590]

d.div: [928] sde dge_3824_bstan/ dbu ma/ tsa_mgon po klu sgrub/ rtsa ba shes rab/ rab byed/ 13_sh+loka_8_shog_8_na6
[590] Nāgārjuna, Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 13:8cd, Toh 3824 Tengyur, dbu ma, tsa, 8a6.

f.d: gsor ci ltar mi rung zhe na/ dper na nad pa la 'khru sman btang bas/ nad dang 'khru sman gnyis char 'khrus na nad sos pa yin la/[929] nad 'khrus nas 'khru sman ma zhu na/ nad pa gsor mi rung ste 'chi bar 'gyur ro/ / de bzhin du dngos por blta ba de stong nyid bsgoms pas bud kyang /[930] stong nyid la zhen cing blta na/ stong pa'i bdag po stong par 'gro ste/ ngan 'gror phyogs par 'gyur ba'o/ /

Why are they incurable? Take the example of a strong purgative: if both the constipation and the medicine are eliminated, the patient will recover. /199/ If the blockage is removed but the patient fails to cleanse the purgative itself from his system, he may not recover and may even die. Likewise, belief in substantial reality is eliminated by cultivating the notion of emptiness, but if the person clings to emptiness and makes it a “view,” the “master of emptiness” will annihilate himself and be on his way to the lower states.

d.div: [929] 'khrus sman/ dpal spungs/
[930] bsgom/ dpal spungs/

f.d:
rin chen phreng ba las kyang /
yod pa po ni bde 'gror 'gro / med pa po ni ngan 'gror 'gro[931] / zhes gsungs so/ /

d.div: [931] sde dge_4158_bstan/ spring yig_ge_mgon po klu sgrub/ rin chen phreng ba/ le'u/ 1_sh+loka_57_shog_109_na2
[591] Nāgārjuna, Ratnāvalī 1:57ab, Toh 4158 Tengyur, spring yig, ge, 109a2

f.d: de la snga ma bas phyi ma skyon che'o/[932] /
Thus the latter mistake is worse than the former.

d.div: [932] des na snga ma las/ dpal spungs/

f.d: don bzhi pa 'dzin pa gnyis char gyi skyon 'chad pa la/

d.i: D. The mistake of both beliefs

f.d:
don la yod par 'dzin pa dang / med par 'dzin pa gnyis char skyon can yin te/ rtag chad gnyis kyi mthar ltung ba'i phyir/[933] / rtsa ba shes rab las kyang /
yod ces bya ba rtag par lta/ / med ces bya ba chad par lta/[934] / zhes gsungs so/ /

In fact, belief in existence and belief in nonexistence are both mistakes because they are beliefs that have fallen into the two extremes of eternalism and nihilism. The Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way says:
“Exists” is the view of eternalism, and “does not exist” is the view of nihilism.[592]

d.div: [933] phyir ro/ dpal spungs/
[934] sde dge_3824_bstan/ dbu ma/ tsa_mgon po klu sgrub/ rtsa ba shes rab/ rab byed/ 15_sh+loka_10_shog_9_na2
[592] Nāgārjuna, Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 15:10ab, Toh 3824 Tengur, dbu ma, tsa, 9a2.

f.d:
rtag chad kyi mthar lhung ba ni rmongs pa'o/ / rmongs pa ni 'khor ba las grol bar mi 'gyur ba'o/[935] / de ltar yang rin chen phreng ba las kyang /
de ltar smig rgyu lta bu yi/ 'jig rten yod pa'am med pa zhes/ / 'dzin pa de ni rmongs pa ste/ / rmongs pa yod na mi grol lo/[936] / zhes gsungs so//

To fall into the extremes of eternalism or nihilism is confused ignorance, and while there is such confused ignorance there will be no liberation from samsara. The Precious Garland says:
To believe that this mirage-like world either “exists” or “does not exist” is confused ignorance. With [such] confusion, there is no liberation.[593]

d.div: [935] rmongs pas/ dpal spungs/
[936] sde dge_4158_bstan/ spring yig_ge_mgon po klu sgrub/ rin chen phreng ba/ le'u/ 1_sh+loka_56_shog_109_na2
[593] Nāgārjuna, Ratnāvalī 1:56, Toh 4158 Tengyur, spring yig, ge, 109a2.

f.d: don lnga pa grol bar 'gyur ba'i lam 'chad pa las/

'o na gang gis grol zhe na/ mtha' la mi gnas pa dbu ma'i lam gyis grol bar 'gyur ro/[937] / de ltar yang rin chen phreng ba las/
yang dag ci bzhin (chos thams cad ye nas skye med du/) yongs shes pa/ / gnyis (rtag chad/) la mi brten thar ('khor ba las/) bar 'gyur/[938] / zhes pa dang /
des na gnyis (rtag chad gnyis kyi mtha' la/[939] )mi brten pa grol/[940] / zhes gsungs so/ /

“Well, then, what does bring liberation?” It is a middle way that does not abide in extremes and that leads to liberation. As the Precious Garland says:
Those who fully understand the truth just as it is (that each and every phenomenon is and always has been nonproduced) and do not depend on the two (eternalism and nihilism) will become liberated (from samsara).[594]
Thus someone who does not resort to them (the extremes of eternalism and nihilism) is liberated, so it is taught.

d.div: [937] mtha' gnyis la/ dpal spungs/
[938] sde dge_4158_bstan/ spring yig_ge_mgon po klu sgrub/ rin chen phreng ba/ le'u/ 1_sh+loka_57_shog_109_na3
[939] gong du yig chung nang du byung ba'i mchan cha tshang dpal spungs dpar mar mi byung ba brtag
[940] sde dge_4158_bstan/ spring yig_ge_mgon po klu sgrub/ rin chen phreng ba/ le'u/ 1_sh+loka_57_shog_109_na3
[594] Ibid. 1:57cd, 109a3. The text in parentheses corresponds to the smaller letters within the quoted text in the Tibetan edition.

f.d:
rtsa ba shes rab las kyang /
de phyir yod dang med pa la/ / mkhas pas gnas par mi bya'o/[941] / zhes gsungs so//

The Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way, too, says:
Therefore the wise should not dwell on existence or nonexistence.[595]

d.div: [941] sde dge_3824_bstan/ dbu ma/ tsa_mgon po klu sgrub/ rtsa ba shes rab/ rab byed/ 15_sh+loka_10_shog_9_na2
[595] Nāgārjuna, Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 15:10cd, Toh 3824 Tengur, dbu ma, tsa, 9a2.

f.d:
'o na mtha' gnyis spang ba'i dbu ma nyid ci lta bu yin snyam na/[942] 'phags pa dkon mchog brtsegs pa las/
'od srungs byang chub sems dpas tshul bzhin du chos la sbyor ba gang zhe na/ 'di lta ste/ dbu ma'i lam chos rnams la so so yang dag par rtog go / 'od srungs dbu ma'i lam chos rnams la so sor rtog pa gang zhe na/ de bzhin du sbyar te/ 'od srungs rtag ces bya ba ni mtha' gcig go / mi rtag ces bya ba ni mtha' gnyis so/ / mtha' de gnyis kyi dbus gang yin pa de ni dpyad du med pa/ bstan du med pa/ snang ba med pa/ rnam par rig pa med pa ste/ 'od srungs 'di ni/ dbu ma'i lam chos rnams la yang dag par so sor rtog pa zhes bya'o/ / 'od srungs bdag ces bya ba ni mtha' gcig go / bdag med ces bya ba ni mtha' gnyis so/ / de bzhin du sbyar te/ 'od srung 'khor ba zhes bya ba 'di ni mtha' gcig go / mya ngan las 'das pa 'di ni mtha' gnyis so/ / mtha' de gnyis kyi dbus ma gang yin pa de ni dpyad du med pa bstan du med pa/ snang ba med pa/ rnam par rig pa med pa ste/ 'od srungs 'di ni dbu ma'i lam chos rnams la yang dag par so sor rtog pa zhes bya'o/[943] / zhes gsungs so/ /

What is the “Middle Way” that abolishes the two extremes? The Heap of Jewels [in the Three Vows Chapter] answers:
Kāśyapa! What is the correct way for bodhisattvas to approach phenomena? It is this. It is the middle way; the correct, discerning appreciation of phenomena. Kāśyapa! What is this middle way that is a proper, discerning appreciation of phenomena? Kāśyapa! “Permanence” makes one extreme. /200/ “Impermanence” makes a second extreme. Whatever lies between these two extremes cannot be analyzed, cannot be shown, is not apparent, and is totally unknowable. Kāśyapa! This is the “middle way that is a correct, discerning appreciation of phenomena.” Kāśyapa! “Self” is one extreme. “Selfless” is a second extreme. . . [etc.]. Kāśyapa! “Samsara” is one extreme. This nirvana is a second extreme. Whatever lies between these two extremes cannot be analyzed, cannot be shown, is not apparent, and is totally unknowable. This is the “middle way that is a correct, discerning appreciation of phenomena.”[596]

d.div: [942] spangs/ dpal spungs/
[943] sde dge_45_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ ka_'od srung gis zhus pa'i le'u/ shog_130_ba1
[596] Trisaṃvaranirdeśaparivarta, Toh 45 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, ka, 130b1.

f.d:
zhi ba lhas kyang /
nang yang sems min phyi min zhing / / gzhan du yang ni rnyed ma yin/ / 'dres min logs su 'gar med de/ / 'di ni cung zad min de'i phyir/ / sems can rang bzhin mya ngan 'das/[944] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Also, Master Śāntideva has taught:
Neither inside nor outside, nor elsewhere can the mind be found. It is not a combination [with the body], and neither is it something other. It is not the slightest thing. The very nature of sentient beings is nirvana.[597]

d.div: [944] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 9_sh+loka_103_shog_34_ba7
[597] Guide to the Bodhisattva Way of Life (Bodhicaryāvatāra) 9:102cd and 103b–d, Toh 3871 Tengyur, dbu ma, la, 34b7.

f.d:
des na mtha' gnyis la mi rtog cing dbu ma'i lam byas kyang / dbu ma nyid la yang brtag tu med de/[945] don la der 'dzin gyi shes pa dang bral ba blo las 'das par gnas pa'o/ / jo bos kyang /
de yang 'di ltar 'das pa'i sems ni 'gags shing zhig / ma 'ongs pa'i sems ni mi skye zhing mi 'byung / da ltar gyi sems ni shin tu brtags dka' ste/ kha dog med pa/ dbyibs dang bral ba ni nam mkha' dang 'dra bar ma grub bo/[946] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Therefore, even though someone may practice this middle way that does not consider things in terms of the two extremes, the middle itself is never something that can be examined. It abides beyond the intellect, free from understanding that believes sense data to be this or that. Atiśa has said:
Likewise, the past mind has ceased and is destroyed. The future mind is not born and has not yet occurred. The present mind is exceedingly hard to investigate, is colorless, without form, and, like space, without concrete existence.[598]

d.div: [945] dbu ma nyid la'ang rtag tu/ dpal spungs/
[946] sde dge_3929_bstan/ dbu ma/ ki_mar me mdzad/ dbu ma'i man ngag_shog_95_ba5_jo bos kyang zhes pa'i lung 'di cha tshang dpal spungs dpar mar mi byung ba brtag
[598] Instructions on Madhyamaka (Madhyamakopadeśa), Toh 3929 Tengyur, dbu ma, ki, 95b5. This entire quotation from Atiśa is missing in the Palpung edition of the text.

f.d:
mngon rtogs rgyan las kyang /
tshu rol pha rol mtha' la min/ / de dag bar na mi gnas pa/ / dus rnams mnyam pa nyid shes phyir/ / shes rab pha rol phyin par 'dod/[947]/ ces gsungs so//

The Ornament of Clear Realization also says:
Not in the extremes of this shore or that nor abiding between the two. And since it perceives all times to be the same, it is held to be the perfection of wisdom.[599]

d.div: [947] sde dge_3786_bstan/ sher phyin/ ka_byams mgon/ mngon rtogs rgyan/ skabs/ 3_sh+loka_1_shog_6_ba4
[599] Maitreya, Abhisamayālaṃkāra 3:1, Toh 3786 Tengyur, shes phyin, ka, 6b4.

f.d: don drug pa grol ba'i rang bzhin mya ngan las 'das pa'i rang bzhin 'chad pa la/[948]

d.div: [948] mya ngan las 'das pa 'chad pa la/ dpal spungs/

f.d:
'o na 'khor ba'i chos thams cad dngos po'am/ dngos med gang du yang ma grub pa yin na/ mya ngan las 'das pa zhes bya ba de dngos po cig yin nam/[949] dngos med zhig yin zhe na/ dmigs pa can la la dag myang 'das dngos por yod snyam du sems so/ / de ma yin te rin chen 'phreng ba las/
mya ngan 'das pa dngos med pa'ang / / min na dngos po ga la yin/[950] / zhes gsungs so/ /

If all the phenomena of samsara have no true existence, either as things substantial or insubstantial, then is “nirvana” something that has substantial or insubstantial reality? Some philosophers do consider nirvana actually to have some concrete existence. However, this is not correct, as the Precious Garland explains:
Since nirvana is not even unreal, how could it be substantially real?[600] /201/

d.div: [949] yin nam 'on te/ dpal spungs/
[950] sde dge_4158_bstan/ spring yig_ge_mgon po klu sgrub/ rin chen phreng ba/ le'u/ 1_sh+loka_42_shog_108_ba2
[600] Nāgārjuna, Ratnāvalī 1:42ab, Toh 4158 Tengyur, sprin yig, ge, 108b2.

f.d:
gal te dngos po yin na mya ngan las 'das pa 'dus byas su 'gyur ro/ / 'dus byas yin na mthar 'jig par 'gyur ro/ / des na rtsa ba shes rab las/
gal te mya ngan 'das dngos na/ / mya ngan 'das pa 'dus byas 'gyur/[951] / zhes pa la sogs pa gsungs so/ /

Were nirvana something substantial, it would have to be a composite thing, and whetever is composite will eventually disintegrate. Hence the Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way states, among other things:
Were nirvana to be substantially real, it would be a composite thing.[601]

d.div: [951] sde dge_3824_bstan/ dbu ma/ tsa_mgon po klu sgrub/ rtsa ba shes rab/ rab byed/ 25_sh+loka_5_shog_16_na7
[601] Nāgārjuna, Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 25:5ab, Toh 3824 Tengur, dbu ma, tsa, 16a7.

f.d:
dngos po med pa'ang ma yin te/ de nyid las/
de la dngos med yod ma yin/[952] / zhes gsungs so/ /

It is also not the case that it is something unreal. The same work says:
There is no unreality in it.[602]

d.div: [952] gong mtshungs/ rtsa ba shes rab/ rab byed/ 25_sh+loka_7_shog_16_ba2

f.d: 'o na ci tsam la bya zhe na/ dngos por 'dzin pa dang / dngos med du 'dzin pa'i blo thams cad zad pa/[953] blo 'das brjod bral de la mya ngan las 'das pa zhes bya'o/ /
Well then, what is it? Nirvana is “the exhaustion of all of the grasping at substantial reality and unreality. It is beyond the scope of the intellect and is beyond words.”

d.div: [953] blo thams cad zad pa de nyid la mya ngan las zhes bya'o/ /dpal spungs/ der blo 'das brjod bral zhes pa'i tshig mi byung ba _brtag

f.d:
de ltar yang / rin chen 'phreng ba las/
dngos po dngos por med 'dzin pa/ / zad pa mya ngan 'das zhes bya/[954] / zhes gsungs so/ /

The Precious Garland:
The cessation of all notions of substantial reality or unreality: that is “nirvana.”[603]

d.div: [954] sde dge_4158_bstan/ spring yig_ge_mgon po klu sgrub/ rin chen phreng ba/ le'u/ 1_sh+loka_42_shog_108_ba2
[603] Nāgārjuna, Ratnāvalī 42cd, Toh 4158 Tengyur, spring yig, ge, 108b2.

f.d:
byang chub sems dpa'i spyod pa la 'jug pa las kyang /
gang tshe dngos dang dngos med dag / blo yi mdun na mi gnas pas/ / de tshe rnam pa gzhan med pas/ / dmigs pa med par rab tu zhi/[955] / zhes gsungs so/ /

It also says, in Guide to the Bodhisattva Way of Life:
Whenever substantial reality or unreality no longer dwell before the mind, since there will be no other alternative way, free of objectification, one will be utterly at peace.[604]

d.div: [955] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug_le'u/ 9_sh+loka_35_shog_32_na4
[604] Śāntideva, Bodhicaryāvatāra 9:34, Toh 3871 Tengyur, dbu ma, la, 32a4.

f.d:
'phags pa tshangs pas zhus pa'i mdo las kyang /
yongs su mya ngan las 'das pa zhes bgyi ba ni/ gang mtshan ma thams cad rab tu zhi ba/ g.yo ba thams cad dang bral ba'o/[956] / zhes gsungs so/ /

The Questions of Brahma Viśesacinti Sutra says:
Total nirvana is the complete pacification of every distinctive characteristic and freedom from any sort of fluctuation.[605]

d.div: [956] sde dge_160_bka'/ mdo sde/ ba_tshangs pas zhus pa'i mdo/ shog_33_ba3
[605] Brahmaviśeṣacintiparipṛcchāsūtra, Toh 160 Kangyur, mdo sde, ba, 33b3.

f.d:
dam pa'i chos pad+ma dkar po las kyang /
'od srungs chos thams cad mnyam pa nyid khong du chud pa ni mya ngan las 'das pa'o/[957] / zhes gsungs so/ /

The Lotus Sutra says:
Kāśyapa! To comprehend the utter equality of all phenomena, this is nirvana.

d.div: [957] sde dge_113_bka'/ mdo sde/ ja_dam chos pad+ma dkar po'i mdo/ le'u/ 5_shog_79_ba3

f.d:
de ltar mya ngan las 'das pa de ni/ blo yi 'jug pa zhi ba tsam las ma gtogs pa'i skye 'gag gam/ spang thob la sogs chos gang du yang grub pa med do/[958] / de ltar rtsa ba shes rab las/
spangs pa med pa thob med pa/ / chad pa med pa rtag med pa/ / 'gag pa med pa skye med pa/ / de ni mya ngan 'das pa'o/[959] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Therefore, other than being the pacification of all mental activity, nirvana does not exist in terms of any phenomena, something that arises or ceases, something to be eliminated or to be attained. The Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way states:
No abandoning, no acquiring, no nihilism, no eternalism, no cessation, no arising: this is nirvana.[606]

d.div: [958] spangs/ dpal spungs/
[959] sde dge_3824_bstan/ dbu ma/ tsa_mgon po klu sgrub/ rtsa ba shes rab/ rab byed/ 25_sh+loka_3_shog_16_na6
[606] Nāgārjuna, Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 25:3, Toh 3824 Tengyur, dbu ma, tsa, 16a6.

f.d:
de ltar skye 'gag gam/[960] spang thob la sogs pa gang yang med pas na/ mya ngan las 'das pa de la rang gis byas pa'am/[961] bcos pa'am/ bsgyur ba med do/ / de ltar yang nam mkha' rin po che'i mdo las/
'di la bsal bya ci yang med/ / bzhag par bya ba cung zad med/ / yang dag nyid la yang dag lta/ / yang dag mthong na rnam par grol/[962] / zhes gsungs so/ /

d.div: [960] skye 'gag spangs thob/ dpal spungs/
[961] de gang gis kyang byas pa'am/ dpal spungs/

[962] nam mkha' rin po che'i mdo 'di ngos 'dzin ma thub la/ sh+loka 'di rje btsun byams pa mgon po'i mngon rtogs rgyan dang rgyud bla ma gnyis kar byung / mngon rtogs rgyan/ skabs/ 5_sh+loka_21_shog_10_na3_dang / rgyud blam/ skabs/ 1_shog_61_ba5

[607] The Precious Space Jewel Sutra (Nam mkha’ rin po che’i mdo) source of this famous quotation has not been identified. But the verse appears, among other places, in Maitreya’s Ornament of Clear Realization (Abhisamayālaṃkāra) 5:21, Toh 3786 Tengyur, shes phyin, ka, 10a3 and in his Uttaratantra 1:154, Toh 4024 D, sems tsam phi, 61b5.

f.d:
de ltar shes rab bam rang sems shes par bya ba'i tshig de dag kyang / rtog pas dpyad pa'i ngos nas yin la/[963] shes rab bam sems kyi don ni shes par bya ba'am/[964] brjod par bya ba las 'das pa yin no/ / de ltar yang / rab kyi rtsal gyis rnam par gnon pas zhus pa'i mdo las/[965]
shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa ni/ chos gang gis kyang brjod par bya ba ma yin te/ tshig thams cad las 'das pa'o/[966] / zhes gsungs so/ /

Therefore, although the terms “what is to be known is one’s own mind” or “what is to be known is wisdom ( prajñā)” and so forth are employed in the context of analytical investigation, in actual fact, wisdom or mind remain beyond cognition or verbal expression. /202/ As the Sutra Requested by Suvikrāntavikrami says:
As the perfection of wisdom cannot be expressed through anything phenomenal, it transcends all words.[608]

d.div: [963] de ltar shes rab ces bya ba'i tshig de dag kyang / ldog pas bcad pa'i ngos nas/ dpal spungs/
[964] shes rab kyi don ni/ dpal spungs/
[965] rab rtsal/ mi rigs dpe skrun/
[966] sde dge_14_bka'/ sher phyin/ ka_rab rtsal gyi rnam par gnon pas zhus pa'i mdo/ shog_23_na5
[608] Suvikrāntavikramiparipṛcchāsūtra, Toh 14 Kangyur, shes rab sna tshogs, ka, 23a5.

f.d:
sgra gcan 'dzin gyis yum la bstod pa las kyang /
smra bsam brjod med shes rab pha rol phyin/ / ma skyes mi 'gag nam mkha'i ngo bo nyid/ / so so rang rig ye shes spyod yul ba/ / dus gsum rgyal ba'i yum la phyag 'tshal lo/[967] / zhes shes rab ces bya ba bshad zin to//[968]

d.div: [967] phyag 'tshal lo/ /zhes gsungs so/ /dpal spungs/
[968] des shes rab shes par bya ba bshad zin to/ /dpal spungs/

[609] Sgra can ’dzin gyis yum la bstod pa. Although this verse homage to the Perfection of Wisdom attributed to the Buddha’s son Rāhula is well known, its exact source in the canonical texts remains unidentified.

f.d: da ni sems sam shes rab de goms par bya ba 'chad de/[969] 'o na chos thams cad stong pa nyid yin na/ shes pa de la goms par bya ba cang dgos sam zhe na dgos te/ dper na dngul rdo de dngul gyi rang bzhin yin yang / bzhu gtul ma byas kyi bar du dngul mi snang /[970] dngul chu 'dod na dngul rdo de bzhu btul bya dgos so/ / de bzhin du chos thams cad ye nas rang bzhin stong pa nyid spros pa thams cad dang bral ba yin yang / sems can rnams la dngos po sna tshogs su snang zhing sdug bsngal sna tshogs myong bas shes pa dang goms par bya dgos/ des na gong ltar shes par byas nas/ de goms par byed pa la bzhi ste/ sngon 'gro dang / mnyam bzhag dang / rjes thob dang / goms rtags so//

Now, I will explain the sixth point, how to cultivate deep wisdom. “If all phenomena are emptiness,” someone may wonder, “is it really nec- essary to cultivate this awareness?” Indeed it is necessary. For instance, even though silver ore has the very nature of silver, the silver itself will not be apparent until the ore has been smelted and worked on. Likewise all things have always been by their very nature emptiness, beyond every form of conceptual elaboration, and nevertheless there is a need to develop awareness of it because beings experience it in various material ways and undergo various sufferings. Therefore, having become aware of what was explained above, cultivating this awareness has four elements: A. The preliminary practices B. The meditation session [practice] C. The post-meditation [practices] D. The signs of having cultivated

d.div: [969] da ni shes rab goms par bya ba/ dpal spungs/
[970] bzhu btul ma byas kyi bar du dngul mi snang la/ dpal spungs/

f.d:
de la sngon 'gro ni/ sems rnal du dbab pa'o/ / ci lta dbab na/ shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa bdun brgya pa las/
rigs kyi bu'am/ rigs kyi bu mos dben pa'i lam stan brtan par bya/ 'du 'dzi med pa la dga' bar bya/ mtshan ma thams cad yid la mi byed par skyil krung bcas ste 'dug nas/[971] zhes pa la sogs pa dang /[972] phyag rgya chen po'i sngon 'gro ltar bya'o/[973] /

(A) The first, the preliminary practices, involves bringing your mind to a natural settled state.[610] How does one achieve this? By following what it says in the Perfection of Wisdom in Seven Hundred Lines:
Sons and daughters of this noble line should seek the path of solitude! They should delight in the absence of distractive activities. They should sit cross-legged, not bringing to their attention any extraneous signs. [611] You should do these as found in the Mahāmudrā preparatory practices.[612]

d.div: [971] sde dge_90_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ cha_sher phyin bdun brgya pa/ shog_204_na5
[972] la sogs pa gsungs pa ltar bya'o/ dpal spungs/
[973] phyag rgya chen po'i sngon 'gro ltar bya'o// zhes pa dpal spungs dpar mar med pas brtag

[610] The Tibetan for what is translated here as “natural settled state” is archaic: rnal du dbab pa. The meaning of this was defined by later Tibetan translators as “abiding within its own natural dominion, untroubled by harm from what is other.”
[611] Saptaśatikānāmaprajñāpāramitā, Toh 90 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, cha, 204a5.
[612] The Palpung edition of the text does not have this sentence.

f.d:
de nas mnyam par bzhag pa'i thabs rnams kyang /[974] phyag rgya chen po khrid lugs ltar byas nas/ yod med blang dor ci la yang mi sems par 'bad rtsol dang bral bar bzhag go / de ltar yang tai los/
mi mno mi bsam mi dpyad cing / / mi bsgom mi sems rang bab bzhag[975] / ces gsungs so//

(B) Next, as for the method of the actual meditation session [practice], following the Mahāmudrā system of instruction, place your mind free from effort or exertion, without any thought pertaining to existence or nonexistence, affirmation or rejection. Tilopa says:
Not dwelling on, not intending, not analyzing, not meditating, not contemplating, leave mind to itself.[613]

d.div: [974] de nas mnyam par bzhag pa ni yod med dam blang dor la sogs pa ci la yang mi sems par bzhag go /dpal spungs/

[975] bka' brgyud pa'i rnam thar pod dang po/ nA ro pa'i rnam thar dri med legs bshad bde chen 'brug sgra/ shog_58_na2_de ltar yang te los/ zhes pa nas/ shes pa spros dang bral bar bzhag /ces gsungs so/ /zhes pa'i bar gyi gzhung tshig cha tshang dpal spungs dpar mar mi byung /

[613] This translation of this famous six-point instruction from Tilopa follows the traditional meaning more than a strictly literal interpretation. The traditional explanation sets them into a time context as follows: “Not dwelling on [the past], not intending [about the future], not analyzing [the present, in terms of ‘being’ in the present].”

f.d:
sems nyid ngal bsor yang /
bu nyon khyod gang rnam par rtog / 'dir bdag ma bcings ma grol phyir/ / ma yengs ma bcos rang dgar ni/ / kye ho dub pa ngal sos shig[976] / ces gsungs so/ /

Also, about letting the mind rest:
Listen, child! Whatever mental activity occurs, within this there is no one bound, no one free. Therefore, O joy, shedding your fatigue, rest naturally, without contrivance or distraction.[614] /203/

d.div: [976] 'dir sems nyid ngal bso gsungs pa'i gzhung ngos 'dzin ma thub/
