d.div: [510] The shared tradition here is that of such treatises as Asaṅga’s Compendium of Higher Knowledge. The “central country” (madhyadeśa), classically conceived, is the Magadha region of the Ganges plain.

f.d: theg pa chen po thun mong ma yin pa ni sa bcu pa'i rten dang / sa bsam gtan bzhi pa shin tu rnam par dag pa'i mthar bdag rkyen rdo rje lta bu'i ting nge 'dzin las skye bar 'dod do/ / rdo rje lta bu'i ting nge 'dzin yang nyan thos kyi nyon mongs pa'i sa bon chung ngu'i mgo gnon pa sbyor lam/ rtsa ba can 'don pa bar chad med pa'i lam mo/ / byang chub sems dpa'i nyon mongs pa dang shes bya'i sgrib pa'i sa bon chung ngu'i mgo gnon pa sbyor lam/ rtsa ba nas 'don pa bar chad med pa'i lam mo//

The unshared Mahayana tradition holds that the path of complete accomplishment is based on the tenth level (bhūmi) and that it arises from the predominating condition of the vajra-like absorption at the end of the extremely pure fourth meditative concentration. Regarding that vajra-like absorption, for the śrāvaka its suppression of the small seeds of the afflictions is the path of application, and its complete uprooting of them is the immediate path. For the bodhisattva its suppression of the small seeds of the affliction and knowable things obscurations is the path of application, and its complete uprooting of them is the immediate path.

gsum pa yul gang la dmigs pa ni/ theg pa thun mong gi lugs kyis yul bden pa bzhi'am yang na 'gog pa'i bden pa'am/ mi slob pa'i chos bcu la/ rdo rje lta bu'i ting nge 'dzin gyis dmigs/ de la mi slob pa'i chos bcu ni/ yang dag pa'i lta ba dang / yang dag pa'i rtog pa dang / de bzhin du ngag dang / las kyi mtha' dang / 'tsho ba dang / rtsol ba dang / dran pa dang / ting nge 'dzin dang / rnam par grol ba dang/ rnam par grol pa'i ye shes mthong ba'o/ /

What objects it takes as its object. According to the shared tradition, the path of complete accomplishment focuses through the vajra-like absorption on the four noble truths, on the truth of cessation, or on the ten qualities of the level beyond training. Regarding the latter, the ten qualities of the level beyond training are: (1) right view, (2) right thought, (3) right speech, (4) right “ends of action” [i.e., bodily merits], (5) right livelihood, (6) right effort, (7) right mindfulness, (8) right meditative absorption, (9) liberation, and (10) seeing the gnosis of liberation.[511]

d.div: [511] The ninth quality, “liberation,” is in the sense of firm appreciation. And the final quality, “seeing the gnosis of liberation,” is the gnosis of the ārya on the path beyond training (vimuktijñānadarśana).

f.d: de dag phung pos bsdu na/ yang dag pa'i ngag dang / las kyi mtha' dang 'tsho ba ni/ tshul khrims kyi phung po'o/ / ting nge 'dzin dang / dran pa ni ting nge 'dzin gyi phung po'o/ / lta ba dang / rtogs dang / brtson 'grus ni shes rab kyi phung po'o/ / rnam par grol ba ni rnam par grol pa'i phung po'o/ / rnam par grol ba'i ye shes mthong ba ni rnam par grol pa'i ye shes mthong ba'i phung po'o/ / de la'ang rnam par mi rtog pa 'jig rten las 'das pa'i ye shes kyis bsdus pa dang / rjes las thob pa dag pa 'jig rten pa'i ye shes kyis bsdus pa'o zhes zer ro/ /

If you subsume them within the categories of Dharma, right speech, action, and livelihood make up the category of moral discipline. Meditative absorption and mindfulness make up the category of meditative absorption. View, thought, and diligence make up the category of discerning wisdom. “Liberation” makes up the category of liberation. And “seeing the gnosis of liberation” makes up the category of seeing the gnosis of liberation. With regard to the above, the nonconceptualizing [meditation session] is included within supramundane gnosis, and the postmeditative activities are included within the pure mundane gnosis. /371/
theg pa chen po thun mong ma yin pa'i lugs kyi nyan thos dang rang sangs rgyas yul mya ngan las 'das pa la dmigs/ byang chub sems dpa' ni mi gnas pa'i mya ngan las 'das pa la dmigs so//

According to the unshared Mahayana tradition, the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha [on the path of complete accomplishment] focus on nirvana as their object. The bodhisattva focuses on nirvana that is not entered into anywhere.

bzhi pa nges tshig ni/ niSh+Tha mArga zhes bya ba spang bya spangs pa dang shes bya shes pa mthar phyin par byed pas mthar phyin pa'i lam/ zag pa dang bral bas zag pa med pa dge ba'i rtsa ba spangs pa'i nyon mongs pa slar mi skye bar byed pas thag bsrid ba'i gnyen po zhes bya'o/ /

The Sanskrit etymology of “path of complete accomplishment.” The Sanskrit niṣṭhāmārga[512] is the “path of complete accomplishment” because it brings to completion the elimination of those things to be eliminated and the knowing of those things to be known. Its root of merit is without impurities because it is free of impurities. And it is known as the “distancing antidote” because it prevents the eliminated afflictions from arising again.

d.div: [512] This path is also commonly known as the path of no more training (aśaikṣamārga).

f.d:
'di dag la theg pa thun mong ba'i lugs mdzod las/
mya ngan 'das sogs gong nas gong / / thob pa la ni dbang byed phyir/ / kun shes byed dang kun shes dang / / de bzhin kun shes ldan dbang po/[365] / zhes bshad pas mthong lam la dbang sgyur ba mi shes pa kun shes par byed pa'i dbang po sbyor lam na yod/ sgom lam la dbang sgyur ba kun shes par byed pa'i dbang po mthong lam na yod/ mthar phyin pa'i lam la dbang sgyur ba kun shes pa dang ldan pa'i dbang po sgom lam na yod ces zer la/ theg pa chen po thun mong ma yin pa ni/ dbang po 'di dag gi tha snyad mi 'dogs so//

Regarding this, the tradition of the shared vehicle is explained in the Treasury of Higher Knowledge as:
For acquiring control over the higher and higher [attainments] such as nirvana, there are the faculties of [resolving] to come to know perfectly [that which is unknown], of perfect knowledge, and of the possession of perfect knowledge.[513] Thus it is taught that on the path of application there exists the faculty of resolving to know perfectly what is unknown, which brings the path of seeing under your control. On the path of seeing there exists the faculty of perfect knowledge, which brings the path of cultivation under your control. And on the path of cultivation there exists the faculty of being in possession of perfect knowledge, which brings the path of complete accomplishment under control. But the unshared Mahayana tradition does not employ such terminology for these faculties.

d.div: [365] sde dge_4089_mngon pa/ ku_dbyig gnyen/ chos mngon pa mdzod/ gnas/ 2_sh+loka_4_shog_4_na3
[513] Vasubandhu, Abhidharmakośa 2:4, Toh 4089 Tengyur, mngon pa, ku, 1a3. According to Khenpo Appey, Sapaṇ’s interpretation differs here from the usual exegesis of this verse.

f.d: sa bcu'i rnam gzhag bshad pa/

d.i: The presentation of the ten levels

f.d: gnyis pa sa bcu'i rnam gzhag la gsum ste/ mtshan nyid/ rab tu dbye ba/ so so'i rnam gzhag go /
The explanation of the ordering of the ten levels has three parts: the definition, their divisions, and the formulation of each division.
dang po ni yon tan khyad par can gyi rten byed pa'o/ /
The definition of the ten levels. The definition of level (bhūmi) is “that which acts as the basis for special excellent qualities.”

dbye na gnyis las/ mos pa spyod pa'i sa'i mtshan nyid ni 'phags pa'i chos la 'jug pa'i yon tan gyi rten byed pa'o/ / 'jig rten las 'das pa'i sa'i mtshan nyid ni/ 'phags pa'i yon tan khyad par can gyi rten byed pa'o/ /

If you divide the levels, there are two main divisions. The definition of the levels of practice through conviction is “that which acts as a basis for the virtues that engage in the qualities of the ārya.” The definition of the supramundane levels is “that which acts as the basis for the special virtues of the ārya.”

gnyis pa de'ang dbye na/ nyan thos kyi sa dang / byang chub sems dpa'i sa gnyis te/ rin chen phreng ba las/
ji ltar nyan thos theg pa las/ / nyan thos ni brgyad bshad pa/ / de bzhin theg pa chen po las/ / byang chub sems dpa'i sa bcu bstan/[366] / zhes gsungs pa ltar ro//

Their divisions. If you divide them, you get the levels of the śrāvaka and the levels of the bodhisattva. As the Precious Garland teaches:
Just as in the Śrāvaka Vehicle eight levels of the śrāvaka are taught, so in the Mahayana there is taught the ten levels of the bodhisattva.[514]

d.div: [366] sde dge_4158_bstan/ skye rabs/ ge_mgon po klu sgrub/ rin chen phreng ba/ le'u/ 5_sh+loka_40_shog_123_ba3
[514] Nāgārjuna, Ratnāvalī 5:40, Toh 4158 Tengyur, spring yig, ge, 123b3.

f.d: gsum pa so so'i rnam par gzhag pa la/ nyan thos kyi sa dang / byang chub sems dpa'i sa gnyis las/ dang po la brgyad de/ dkar po rnam par mthong ba'i sa/ rigs kyi sa/ brgyad pa'i sa/
The formulations of each of those divisions. The levels are formulated in two ways, that of the śrāvaka and that of the bodhisattva. /372/
bsrabs pa'i sa/ 'dod chags dang bral ba'i sa/ byas pa rtogs pa'i sa/ nyan thos kyi sa/ rang sangs rgyas kyi sa'o/ / 'on kyang 'di dag skabs kyi don ma yin pas re zhig bzhag go/

The formulation of the levels of the śrāvaka. These are eight in number: (1) the level of seeing the wholesome, (2) the level of “spiritual lineage,” (3) the level of the eighth,[515] (4) the level of thinning, (5) the level that is freed from desire, (6) the level of mastery, (7) the level of the śrāvaka, and (8) the level of the pratyekabuddha.[516] However, since these are not our relevant topic here, I will leave off this subject.

d.div: [515] “Eighth” here refers to the stream-enterer trainee, who is the lowest in the list of eight realized beings enumerated in the non-Mahayana sources, the remaining ones being: (2) the one abiding in the fruit of stream entry and the trainees and the ones abiding in the fruits of (3–4) a once-returner, (5–6) a nonreturner, and (7–8) an arhat.

[516] The list diverges in some respects from its usual explanation in the Abhisamayālaṃkāra commentaries. Cf. R. Sakaki, Mahāvyutpatti, nos. 1141–46. Khenpo Appey referred me also to Nyawön’s Dispelling Mental Darkness, vol. 1: 608; and Ngulchu Thokmé Sangpo’s Precious Garland, 497 (fol. 249).

f.d: gnyis pa byang chub sems dpa'i sa la'ang bzhi ste/ rab tu dbye ba/ grangs nges pa/ so so'i yon tan/ ming gi don to/ /

The formulation of the levels of the bodhisattva. The explanation of this has four parts: their divisions, their having a fixed number, their individual excellent qualities, and [the Sanskrit etymology of] the terms.

dang po la yang bcu ste/ sa dang po rab tu dga' ba/ gnyis pa dri ma med pa/ gsum pa 'od byed pa/ bzhi pa 'od 'phro ba/ lnga pa sbyang dka' ba/ drug pa mngon du gyur pa/ bdun pa ring du song ba ste/ bdun ni ma dag pa'i sa/ brgyad pa mi g.yo ba/ dgu pa legs pa'i blo gros/ bcu pa chos kyi sprin/ gsum po dag pa'i sa'o/ /

Their divisions. There are ten: (1) the Joyous, (2) the Stainless, (3) the Shining, (4) the Blazing, (5) Difficult to Master, (6) the Manifested, (7) the Far-Reaching, (8) the Unshakable, (9) the Excellent Intelligence, and (10) the Cloud of Dharma. The first seven are the impure levels, and the last three are the pure levels.
de'ang mos pa spyod pa'i sa nga rgyal mang / ma dag pa'i sa bdun nga rgyal phra/ dag pa'i sa gsum nga rgyal med do/ /
Moreover, the level of practice through conviction has much pride. The impure levels have slight pride. And the three pure levels are without pride.

mdo sde rgyan las/
nga rgyal mang dang nga rgyal phra/ / nga rgyal med pa dag tu 'dod/[367] / ces gsungs pa ltar ro//

For as the Ornament of Mahayana Sutras teaches:
These are held to be prideful, with slight pride, and without pride.[517]

d.div: [367] sde dge_4020_bstan/ sems tsam/ phi_byams pa mgon po/ mdo sde rgyan/ le'u/ 12_sh+loka_75_shog_16_na5
[517] Maitreya, Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra 12:75, Toh 4020 Tengyur, sems tsam, phi, 16b5.

f.d: gnyis pa grangs nges pa ni/ pha rol tu phyin pa bcus sa bcu ste/ pha rol tu phyin pa drug gis sa drug_thabs/ stobs/ smon lam/ ye shes bzhis sa bzhi ste bcur nges so//

Their having a fixed number. The levels are definitely determined as ten because they correspond to the ten perfections. The six perfections correspond to the first six levels, and the four perfections of method, strength, resolution, and gnosis correspond to the remaining four levels.
gsum pa so so'i yon tan la gnyis las/
Their individual excellent qualities have two parts: the qualities of being free from something undesirable and the excellent qualities that consist of a positive attainment.

bral ba'i yon tan ni/ sdug bsngal gyi chu bo chen po bzhi brgal te/ rgyud bla ma las/
'phags pa 'chi dang na ba dang / / rga ba'i sdug bsngal rtsad nas spangs/ / las dang nyon mongs dbang gis skye/ / de la de med phyir de med/[368] / ces gsungs pa ltar ro/ /

[Bodhisattvas who have the qualities of being free from something undesirable] have crossed over the four great rivers of suffering. For as the Uttaratantra teaches:
The [Mahayana] ārya has completely eliminated the sufferings of death, sickness, and old age. No birth through the power of past karma and afflictions exists for him. He does not possess such birth because he lacks those [causes].[518]

d.div: [368] sde dge_4024_bstan/ sems tsam/ phi_byams pamagon po/ rgyud bla ma/ skabs/ 1_sh+loka_67_shog_57_ba3
[518] Maitreya, Uttaratantra 1:67, Toh 4024 Tengyur, sems tsam, phi, 57b3.

f.d:
yang 'jigs pa lnga las grol te/ sangs rgyas phal po che las/
'tsho ba med dang 'chi dang mi bsngags ngan 'gro dang / / 'khor gyi 'jigs bral de la bag tsha'i rnam pa med/[369] / ces gsungs pa ltar/

Also they are freed from the five fears, for as the Flower Ornament Sutra teaches:
That person who is free of the fears of no livelihood, death, ill repute, the lower miserable destinies, and assemblies possesses no form of timidity.[519]

d.div: [369] sde dge_44_bka'/ phal chen/ kha_mdo sde sa bcu pa/ le'u/ 31_shog_186_na5
[519] Avataṃsakasūtra, Toh 44 Kangyur, phal chen, kha, 186b5.

f.d: 'tsho ba med pa dang / dus ma yin par 'chi ba dang / gtam ngan dang / ngan song dang / 'khor la mi spobs pa'i 'jig pa lnga dang bral pa'o/ / gzhan yang 'jigs pa bsam gyis mi khyab pa las grol ba/ mdo sde sa bcu pa las/ ji skad gsungs pa bzhin no/[370] / de dag kyang sa dang po nas sa bcu pa'i bar la rim gyis 'phel bar 'gyur ba don gyis shes par bya'o/ /

Such a one is free from the five fears of lack of livelihood, untimely death, disrepute, the lower miserable destinies, and the lack of confident presence of mind amid an assembly. Moreover, he or she is freed from unthinkably many fears [or dangers], just as the Ten Levels Sutra teaches.[520] You should also understand by implication that those qualities increase gradually from the first level until the tenth.

d.div: [370] gong mtshungs/ mdo sde sa bcu pa/ le'u/ 31_shog_200_na4
[520] Daśabhūmikasūtra, Toh 44 Kangyur, phal chen, kha, 200a4.

f.d:
'jigs pa las grol yang skye rga na 'chi'i sdug bsngal yod pa ltar ston pa ni/ sems can gyi don du bsams bzhin du srid par skye ba ste/
ji bzhin yang dag mthong ba'i phyir/ / skye sogs rnams las 'das gyur kyang / / snying rje'i bdag nyid skye ba dang / / 'chi dang na dang rga bar ston/[371] / zhes gsungs pa ltar ro//

Even though they are freed from fears, they show the appearance of experiencing birth, old age, sickness, and death. Regarding this, [bodhisattvas on these levels] are born into cyclic existence according to their own wishes in order to benefit sentient beings. /373/ For as the Uttaratantra teaches:
Even though he has transcended birth and the rest, because he sees reality exactly as it is, the person of compassionate nature shows the appearance of birth, death, illness, and aging.[521]

d.div: [371] sde dge_2024_bstan/ sems tsam/ phi_byams pa mgon po/ rgyud bla ma/ skabs/ 1_sh+loka_68_shog_4_ba4
[521] Maitreya, Uttaratantra 1:68, Toh 4024 Tengyur, sems tsam, phi, 4b4.

f.d: gnyis pa thob pa'i yon tan ni/ mdo sde sa bcu pa las/ skad cig ma gcig la skye ba'i phyir yon tan brgya phrag bcu gnyis gsungs te/ ting nge 'dzin brgya 'thob/ de la snyoms par 'jug sangs rgyas brgya mthong / de dag gi byin rlabs shes/ 'jig rten gyi khams brgya g.yo/ zhing brgyar 'gro/ 'jig rten gyi khams brgya snang bar byed/ sems can brgya yongs su smin par byed/ bskal pa brgyar gnas/ bskal pa brgya'i sngon dang phyi ma'i mthar 'jug / chos kyi sgo brgya 'byed/ lus brgya ston/ lus re re la'ang 'khor byang chub sems dpa' brgya brgya dang ldan par ston pa'o/[372] /

The excellent qualities that consist of a positive attainment. The Ten Levels Sutra explains them as twelve sets of a hundred virtues [on the first level] because[522] these virtues arise in a single moment: you attain a hundred meditative absorptions and dwell in them, you see a hundred buddhas, you understand their sustaining powers, one hundred world realms quake, you visit a hundred pure realms, you illuminate a hundred world realms, you bring to spiritual maturity one hundred sentient beings, you dwell for a hundred eons, [your knowledge] penetrates up to the ends of the previous and following hundred eons, you open one hundred “doors of Dharma,” you display a hundred bodies, and each of those bodies manifests a retinue of a hundred bodhisattvas.[523]

d.div: [372] sde dge_44_bka'/ phal chen/ kha_mdo sde sa bcu pa/ le'u/ 31_shog_185_na7
[522] Omit phyir?
[523] Daśabhūmikasūtra, Toh 44 Kangyur, phal chen, kha, 185a7.

f.d: yon tan de dag sa gnyis pa la stong 'gyur ro/ / sa gsum pa la 'bum 'gyur/ bzhi pa la bye ba phrag brgya/ lnga pa la bye ba phrag stong / drug pa la bye ba phrag 'bum/ bdun pa la bye ba khrag khrig 'bum/ brgyad pa la 'jig rten gyi khams 'bum gyi rdul phra rab dang mnyam pa/ dgu pa la 'bum phrag bcu'i rdul phra rab dang mnyam pa/ bcu pa la sangs rgyas kyi zhing brjod du med pa'i rdul dang mnyam pa thob cing de las gzhan pa'i yon tan yang 'byung / gzhan sa'i yon tan rgyas par mdo sde sa bcu pa nyid dang / dgongs 'grel dang / mdo sde rgyan la sogs par shes par bya'o//

Those excellent qualities become a thousand [instead of the previous hundred] on the second level. On the third level they become one hundred thousand. On the fourth level, a billion. On the fifth level, ten billion. On the sixth level, a trillion. On the seventh level, a hundred quadrillion. On the eighth level their number is equal to the number of “atoms” in one hundred thousand world realms. On the ninth level they are equal to the “atoms” of a million world realms. On the tenth level you attain a number equal to the “atoms” in inexpressibly many buddhafields, and there also arise other excellent qualities besides. Learn about the excellent qualities of the spiritual levels in more detail from such scriptures as the Ten Levels Sutra, the Sutra Definitely Elucidating the Noble Intention, and the Ornament of Mahayana Sutras.
bzhi pa ming gi don la gnyis las/
The Sanskrit etymology of the terms has two parts, [the meaning of the term bhūmi and the meanings of the terms for the individual levels].

thun mong gi ming don ni/ sa la b+hU mI zhes zer la/ de'i sgra las drangs nas/ mdo sde rgyan las/
'byung po dpag med 'jigs med phyir/ / dpag tu med pa de dag la/ / phyi bzhin gong du bgrod ldan phyir/ / de dag nyid ni sar 'dod do/[373] / zhes gsungs so/ /

The meaning of the common term. “Level” in Sanskrit is bhūmi. If you trace its etymological derivation, it is said in the Ornament of Mahayana Sutras:
Those are held to be “levels” because they remove the fear of infinite beings, and because they entail ascending further and further upward to those infinite [excellent qualities].[524]

d.div: [373] sde dge_4020_bstan/ sems tsam/ phi_byams pa mgon po/ mdo sde rgyan/ le'u/ 21_sh+loka_40_shog_38_na1
[524] Maitreya, Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra 21:40, Toh 4020 Tengyur, sems tsam, phi, 38a1. See also Ngulchu Thokmé Sangpo, Precious Garland, 519 (fol. 269).

f.d: b+hU ta 'byung po/ mi/ a mi ta dpag med/ ab+ha ya 'jigs med/ mi/ a mi ta na dpag med/ b+hu ya phyi bzhin/ ur+d+haM ga ma na gong du bgrod ldan no/ /

[The bhū is for] bhūta, “creature”; mi is from amita, “infinite”; [bhū is for] abhaya, “fearless”; mi is for amita, “infinite”; [bhū is for] bhuya[s], “more and more”; ūrdhvaṃgamana [yogita] is “possessing upward movement.”

so so'i sgra don ni/
byang chub la ni nye ba dang / / sems can don grub mthong ba la/ / rab tu dga' ba skye 'gyur bas/ / sa de rab tu dga' bar bshad/[374] / ces bya ba la sogs ltar ro//

(2) The etymological meanings of the individual terms. This is such as is as stated in the passage beginning:
The [first] level is taught as Joyous because joy will arise for one who sees the closeness to awakening and the accomplishment of the welfare of sentient beings.[525] /374/

d.div: [374] gong mtshungs/ mdo sde rgyan/ le'u/ 21_sh+loka_33_shog_37_ba3
[525] Maitreya, Ornament of Mahayana Sutras (Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra) 21:32, Toh 4020 Tengyur, sems tsam, phi, 37b3. The remaining levels are glossed in verses 33–38.

f.d: deng sang bod 'di na sa lam mi bgrod par 'tshang rgya bar 'dod pa dang / yon tan med par mthong lam skye bar 'dod pa mthong ste/ mdo rgyud bstan bcos thams cad nas de lta bu bshad pa ma mthong bas sangs rgyas kyi bstanapa ma yin no/ /

Nowadays here in Tibet, I see some who maintain that buddhahood can be reached without traveling over the paths and levels[526] and who hold that the path of seeing arises without accompanying excellent qualities.[527] But this is not the doctrine of the Buddha because such a teaching is not seen in any sutra, tantra, or great treatise.

d.div: [526] This was a special mahāmudrā teaching of Shang Tsalpa. See also Sapaṇ, Clear Differentiation 3:376; Rhoton, A Clear Differentiation, 193n81, and Gorampa, Detailed Commentary, 140b.

[527] Sapaṇ, Clear Differentiation 3:190–92; Rhoton, A Clear Differentiation, 187n41. See also Jackson, “Birds in the Egg and Newborn Lion Cubs,” and Gorampa’s Detailed Commentary, 113a, and Dispelling Errors, 46.

f.d: de lta bu'i lam dang sa de dag kyang / don dam sems bskyed la brten nas/ shes rab stong pa nyid bsgoms pas nyer len gyi rgyu dang / thabs snying rje chen pos lhan cig byed pa'i rkyen byas nas lam lnga 'grub/ kun rdzob sems bskyed la brten nas thabs snying rjes nyer len gyi rgyu dang / shes rab stong pa nyid kyis lhan cig byed pa'i rkyen byas nas/ sa bcu thob la/ sangs rgyas pa na yang lam mthar thug pa chos sku dang / sa mthar thug pa gzugs sku yin no/ /

Furthermore, regarding those paths and levels, the five paths will be accomplished based on the ultimate thought of awakening, with discerning wisdom (the meditative realization of emptiness as the appropriating cause) and method (the great compassion) as the immediately acting condition. The ten levels are attained based on the relative thought of awakening, with method (the great compassion) as the appropriating cause and discerning wisdom (emptiness) as the immediately acting condition. And when you awaken to buddhahood, the ultimate path is the Dharma body and the ultimate level is the form body.
mthar thug gi 'bras bu bshad pa/
12. The Ultimate Fruit

de dag gis/ skyon med pa la 'jug pa dang / /zhing yongs su dag pa bshad nas/ bdun pa mi gnas mya ngan 'das pa dang / /byang chub mchog dang ston pa'o/[375] /zhes bya ba'i don mthar thug gi 'bras bu ste/ de yang mi gnas pa'i mya ngan las 'das pa ni/ shes rab kyis 'khor ba/ snying rjes mya ngan las 'das pa la mi gnas pa yin te/ mngon rtogs rgyan las/
shes pas srid la mi gnas shing / / snying rjes zhi la mi gnas pa/[376] / zhes pa ltar ro/ /

Having thus explained the words “entering into the faultless levels and the pure fields,” I will now explain the seventh key phrase: “nonsituated nirvana, the highest awakening, and the displaying.”[528] The sense indicated here is the ultimate fruit. Moreover, “nonsituated nirvana” refers to not being situated in cyclic existence because of discerning wisdom, and not being situated in nirvana because of compassion. For as the Ornament of Clear Realization teaches:
Because of understanding, he does not remain in worldly existence. Because of compassion, he does not remain in quiescence.[529]

d.div: [375] gong mtshungs/ mdo sde rgyan/ le'u/ 20_sh+loka_64_shog_35_na5
[376] sde dge_3786_bstan/ sher phyin/ ka_byams pa mgon po/ mngon rtogs rgyan/ skabs/ 1_sh+loka_10_shog_2_na7
[528] This is a reference to the seventh key theme listed in the lines quoted from Ornament of Mahayana Sutras 20:61–62 in the opening section of the text.
[529] Maitreya, Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1:10, Toh 3786 Tengyur, shes phyin, ka, 2b7.

f.d: byang chub mchog ni/ sangs rgyas kyi thun mong dang / thun mong ma yin pa'i yon tan mtha' dag lhun gyis grub pa yin no/ / ston pa ni mya ngan las 'das pa chen po ston pa ste/ de'ang nyan thos kyi mya ngan las 'das pa ltar zad pa dang / mi skye ba shes pa tsam ma yin gyi/ mya ngan las 'das kyang / sems can gyi don rgyun mi 'chad par 'gyur ba'o// de dag gi don bstan pa la gsum ste/ sangs rgyas kyi mtshan nyid/ sku'i rnam gzhag_yon tan gyi chos phye ste bshad pa'o/ /

The “highest awakening” is all the spontaneously achieved shared and unique excellent qualities of buddhahood. “Displaying” is the displaying of the great nirvana. That, too, is not merely the exhaustion of the afflictions or the knowledge that those afflictions will not arise again, in the manner of the nirvana of the śrāvaka. Rather, even though nirvana has been attained, there is the uninterrupted arising of benefits for sentient beings. The teaching of these points has three parts: the definition of buddhahood, the formulation about the bodies of buddhahood, and the explanation of the excellent qualities of buddhahood.
dang po [mtshan nyid]
['di ]ni spangs pa dang / ye shes phun sum tshogs pa'o/ /
The definition of buddhahood is “perfectly complete elimination and gnosis.”
de la spangs pa ni nyon mongs pa dang shes bya'i sgrib pa bag chags dang bcas pa spangs pa'o/ /
Here “elimination” means elimination of the affliction and knowledge obscurations together with the propensities toward those obscurations. /375/

ye shes ni shes bya ji lta ba dang / ji snyed pa mkhyen pa ste/ slob dpon ma ti tsi tras/
thams cad mkhyen la yon tan kun/ / mnga' la de yang nyams mi mnga'/ / nyes pa bag chags dang bcas te/ / skyob pa gcig bu la mi mnga'/[377] / zhes gsungs pa ltar ro//

“Gnosis” is the cognition of objects of knowledge exactly as they are and in their full variety and extent. As Ācārya Maticitra said:
The Omniscient One possesses all excellent qualities and also possesses no defects. The Sole Protector does not possess the faults or their propensities.[530]

d.div: [377] sde dge_1147_bstan/ bstod chogs/ ka_rta dbyangs/ bstod pa brgya lnga bcu pa/ le'u/ 1_shog_110_na4
[530] Aśvaghoṣa, Praise in Hundred and Fifty Stanzas (Śatapañcāśatakastotra), Toh 1147 Tengyur, bstod tshogs, ka, 110a4.

f.d: gnyis pa sku'i rnam gzhag

d.i: The formulation about the bodies of buddhahood

f.d: ['di ]la gsum ste/ sku gsum du dbye ba/ gnyis su bsdu ba/ de la ye shes yod med dpyad pa'o/ /
This has three main parts: the division into three bodies, their inclusion within two bodies, and the investigation of whether or not gnosis exists in those.
dang po la gsum las/
The division into three bodies. The “bodies” of buddhahood can be divided into three.

ngo bo nyid kyi sku ni dbyings rang bzhin gyis rnam par dag pa spang bya glo bur gyi dri ma las grol ba dag pa gnyis dang ldan pa ste/ mngon rtogs rgyan las/
thub pa'i ngo bo nyid sku ni/ / zag pa med pa'i chos gang dag / thob gyur rnam kun rnam dag pa/ / de dag rang bzhin mtshan nyid can/[378] / zhes gsungs pa ltar ro//

(1) The body of ultimate nature (svabhāvakāya) possesses the two purities: the natural purity of the “origin” (dhātu), and the purity of the freedom from the adventitious stains of the things that are to be eliminated. As the Ornament of Clear Realization teaches:
Those [twenty-one classes of] qualities without impurity of the ultimate-nature body of the Sage that have been acquired are in every respect pure, and they possess the characteristic of being naturally [pure from the beginning].[531]

d.div: [378] sde dge_3786_bstan/ sher phyin/ ka_byams pa mgon po/ mngon rtogs rgyan/ skabs/ 8_sh+loka_1_shog_11_na7
[531] Maitreya, Abhisamayālaṃkāra 8:1, Toh 3786 Tengyur, shes phyin, ka, 11a7.

f.d:
gnyis pa longs spyod rdzogs pa'i sku ni/ gnas stug po bkod pa'i zhing khams na/ sku mtshan dang dpe byad kyis brgyan pa/ gsung theg pa chen po'i chos kyi 'khor lo rgyun mi 'chad par bskor ba/ thugs ye shes bzhi'i rang bzhin can/ 'khor byang chub sems dpa' sa bcu pa rnams tshim par mdzad ba ste/
mtshan ni sum cu rtsa gnyis dang / / dpe byad brgyad cu gang ldan pa/ / theg chen nye bar longs spyod phyir/ / thub pa'i longs spyod rdzogs skur bzhed/[379] / ces gsungs pa ltar ro//

(2) The body of enjoyment (sambhogakāya). The dwelling place of this body is in the divine realm of Akaniṣṭha. Its physical body is adorned with the bodily signs and characteristics. Its speech is the continual preaching of the Mahayana teachings. Its mind has the nature of the four gnoses. Its retinue of disciples is made up of bodhisattvas of the tenth level whom [that Buddha] satisfies. As it is taught:
Because it possesses the thirty-two signs and the eighty characteristics and partakes of the Mahayana, it is held to be the enjoyment body of the Sage.[532]

d.div: [379] gong mtshungs/ mngon rtogs rgyan/ skabs/ 8_sh+loka_12_shog_11_ba7

f.d:
gsum pa sprul pa'i sku ni/ ngo bo longs sku'i bdag rkyen las byung ba/ yul nam mkha'i mtha' dang mnyam pa'i gdul bya gang na gnas pa na/ dus rgyun mi 'chad pa dang / phrin las sems can gyi don 'ba' zhig mdzad pa ste/ de la'ang dbye na sprul pa gsum las/ skye ba'i sprul pa dga' ldan du bzhugs pa la sogs pa/ mchog gi sprul pa shAkya thub pa la sogs pa sangs rgyas kyi rnam 'phrul du ma/ bzo'i sprul pa dri za'i rgyal po rab dga' gdul ba'i don du pi wang len pa la sogs pa du ma ste/ de'ang /
gang gis srid pa ji srid par/ / 'gro la phan pa sna tshogs dag / mnyam du mdzad pa'i sku de ni/ / thub pa'i sprul sku rgyun mi 'chad/[380] / ces gsungs pa ltar ro/ /

(3) The emanation body (nirmānakāya). Its nature is to have arisen through the predominating condition of the enjoyment body. Its place is wherever the beings to be trained dwell, who are as infinite as the bounds of the sky. Its period is unceasing. Its activities are solely the work of benefitting sentient beings. Moreover, if you divide the emanation body, you get three types: born emanations, dwelling in such divine realms as Tuṣita; the highest emanations, which are the numerous manifestations of buddhahood such as Śākyamuni; and fashioned emanations, which are numerous and include such things as the vina player manifested [by Śākyamuni] for the sake of Supriya, the king of the gandharvas. Moreover, as it is taught:
That body that simultaneously accomplishes manifold benefits for living beings for as long as existence continues is the unceasing emanation body of the Sage.[533]

d.div: [380] gong mtshungs/ mngon rtogs rgyan/ skabs/ 8_sh+loka_33_shog_12_ba6

f.d: mdo rgyud 'ga' zhig las sku bzhir bshad pa ltar na 'dir bshad pa'i ngo bo nyid kyi sku la chos skur 'dogs/ de lta bu'i sku gsum dbyer mi phyed pa'i khyad par 'ga' ngo bo nyid kyi skur bzhed do/[381] / 'on kyang 'di gsang sngags kyi rgyud sde las gtso cher grags pas 'dir ma bshad do//

Some sutras and tantras explain the bodies of buddhahood as being four, and according to them, that which is here taught as the ultimate-nature body is designated as the “Dharma body” (dharmakāya). And some maintain the special feature consisting of the indivisibility of those three bodies to be the ultimate-nature body. /376/ But since this classification is mainly recognized in the tantras of the mantra tradition, I will not explain it here.

d.div: [381] khyad par 'ga' zhig ngo bo nyid kyi skur bzhed do/ /zha lu/

f.d: gnyis pa bsdu na/ sku gsum po de yang chos sku dang gzugs sku gnyis so/ / de la rang don gyi sku gzhan don gyi sku zhes bshad pa'ang yod do/ / chos sku don dam/ gzugs sku kun rdzob kyi sku zhes kyang grags so//

Their inclusion within two bodies. If you subsume those three bodies within a briefer classification, they consist of the two: the Dharma body (dharmakāya) and material form body (rūpakāya). With reference to those, there also exists the explanation of the two as “the body for the benefit of self” and “the body for the benefit of others.” Also, the Dharma body is known as the “ultimately real body,” and the form body is known as the “surface-level body.”

gsum pa de la ye shes yod med dpyad pa la gsum las/ dang po gzhan gyi lugs dgag na/ kha cig sangs rgyas la rang rgyud kyis bsdus pa'i ye shas yod de thams cad mkhyen pa yin pa'i phyir dang / tshogs gnyis kyi rnam smin gyi sku yin pa'i phyir dang / ye shes med pa dngos med dam bems por 'gyur ba'i phyir dang / nyan thos 'gog pa dang mtshungs par thal ba dang mu stegs chad lta ba dang mtshungs par thal ba la sogs pa lung dang rigs pa du ma'i sgo nas ye shes med pa bkag nas rang rgyud la ye shes yod pa bsgrub bo/ /

Whether or not gnosis exists in buddhahood entails three parts. (1) Refuting the tradition of others. Some prove the existence of the gnosis of the Buddha and refute the nonexistence of gnosis by means of many scriptural passages and reasonings, such as by saying that a buddha possesses a gnosis that is included within his own mental continuum because he is the Omniscient One, because he is the body that is the fruition of the two preparatory assemblages, because without gnosis the Buddha would become a nonexistent (abhāva) or an inanimate thing, because [an absence of gnosis] would entail the consequence that buddhahood would be the same as the cessation (nirodha) of the śrāvaka, and because there would be the consequence that [to maintain the contrary] would be equal to the tīrthika nihilist view.

yang kha cig ye shes yod na 'khrul snang can dang ngar 'dzin can du 'gyur ba dang / sems tsam pa dang mtshungs pa dang / mu stegs rtag smra ba dang khyad par med par 'gyur ba la sogs pa lung rigs pa du ma'i sgo nas rang rgyud la ye shes med par bsgrub bo/ /

Also, some prove the nonexistence of gnosis in the Buddha’s own mental continuum, saying, for instance, that if such gnosis existed, it would possess illusory appearances and a positing of self, and that to say so would be the same as the Yogācāra adherent’s theory and would be no different from the tīrthika eternalist view.[534]

d.div: [534] See the detailed study on the existence of gnosis on the level of buddhahood in Almogi, Rong-zom-pa’s Discourses on Buddhology.

f.d: de gnyis ka mi 'thad de/ ye shes rang rgyud la bden par grub pa yod na mu stegs rtag smra dang mtshungs pa dang / ngar 'dzin can dang mi rtag par 'gyur ba la sogs pa ye shes med par 'dod pas brjod pa'i skyon 'byung ste yod par 'dzin par mtshungs pa'i phyir ro/ / ye shes rang rgyud la med par gzhan snang yin na sangs rgyas la yon tan med par 'gyur ro/ /

Both these opinions are unacceptable, for if, first, gnosis were to exist as something veridically established in a buddha’s own mental continuum, there would occur the faults mentioned by the person who maintains the nonexistence of gnosis, such as that this would be equivalent to the tīrthika eternalist’s view, that this would be the possession of self-postulation, and that this would be the view of permanence, for this would be equivalent to positing an existent entity. Second, if the gnosis does not exist in the mental continuum of the Buddha himself but is only something appearing in the experiences of others around him, the Buddha would be without excellent qualities.
yang sangs rgyas yod med brtag med na lam bsgoms pa don med du 'gyur zhing / yod na sangs rgyas ni yod ye shes med pas bems por 'gyur ro/[382] /

Furthermore, let us critically examine whether or not “the Buddha” exists. If he does not exist, the cultivation of the path would be pointless, and if he does exist but has no gnosis, he would be an inanimate thing.

d.div: [382] yod na sangs rgyas ni yod ye shes ni med pas/ zha lu dgon/

f.d: gal te sangs rgyas la ye shes med kyang smon lam gyis gzhan don 'grub bo zhe na/ smon lam grub na 'tshang rgya bar smon lam btab pa de ci'i phyir mi 'grub ste/ 'tshang rgya ba'i smon lam mi 'grub la/ gzhan don gyi smon lam 'grub pa'i rgyu mtshan med de/ grub na grub mnyam/ mi 'grub na mi 'grub mnyam pa'i phyir ro/ / yang sangs rgyas med la smon lam yod ces zer ba ni rigs pas bsgrub dka' 'o//

[Objection:] Though gnosis does not exist in the Buddha, the benefitting of others is achieved by him through his past aspirations. [Reply:] If an aspiration has here been realized, then why would the aspiration to become a buddha not also be achieved? There is no reason that the aspiration to become a buddha would not be achieved while the aspiration to achieve benefits for others would be achieved. For if the one is achieved, they are equally achievable, and if the one is not achieved, both are equally unachievable. Also the assertion, “The Buddha does not exist, but the aspiration exists,” is difficult to establish through reasoning. /377/
gnyis pa rang gi lugs la/ don dam dang kun rdzob gnyis las/
(2) Our own tradition. In our own tradition there are two levels of truth: the ultimately real, and the surface level.

dang po ni blo'i yul las 'das pa'i phyir/ yod med kyi mtha' thams cad las grol ba ste/ de la dgongs nas mdo ting nge 'dzin rgyal po las/
mya ngan 'das pa'i chos la chos med de/ / gang phyir de med nam yang yod mi 'gyur/ / rtog can dag gis yod dang med ces bstan/ / de ltar brtags pas sdug bsngal zhi mi 'gyur/[383] / ces bya ba dang /

The ultimately real. The first of these, the ultimate, is free from all extremes of existence and nonexistence, for it is beyond the range of mind. With that sense in mind, the King of Meditation Sutra teaches:
In the factor of existence of nirvana there exists no factor of existence, for it is nonexistent and never will exist [independently]. Those who possess [dualistic] conceptual thought teach existence and nonexistence. By conceptualizing in that way, suffering will not be pacified.[535]

d.div: [383] sde dge_127_bka'/ mdo sde/ da_ting nge 'dzin rgyal po'i mdo/ le'u/ 9_shog_26_ba7
[535] Samādhirājasūtra 9:26, Toh 127 Kangyur, mdo sde, da, 26b7.

f.d:
slob dpon 'phags pas/
yod ces bya ba rtag par 'dzin/ / med ces bya ba chad par lta/[384] / zhes bya ba la sogs pa dang /
yod dang med pa la sogs bzhi/ / zhi ba 'di la ga la yod/[385] / ces bya ba la sogs pa gsungs shing / rab gyi rtsal gyis rnam par gnon pa'i mdo las kyang / ye shes yod med gnyis ka las grol bar bshad do//[386]

And as Ācārya Ārya [Nāgārjuna] said:
To say “It exists” is the view of eternalism. To say “It does not exist” is the view of annihilationism.[536] And also, for instance:
How could there exist the four of existence, nonexistence, and the others in this quiescence?[537] In the Sūtra Requested by Suvikrāntavikrami, it is also explained that gnosis is free from both existence and nonexistence.[538]

d.div: [384] sde dge_3824_bstan/ dbu ma/ tsa_mgon po klu sgrub/ rtsa ba shes rab/ rab byed/ 15_sh+loka_10_shog_9_na2
[385] gong mtshungs/ rtsa ba shes rab/ rab byed/ 22_sh+loka_12_shog_13_ba2
[386] sde dge_14_bka'/ sher phyin sna tshogs/ ka_rab rtsal rnam gnon pas zhus pa/ le'u/ 1_shog_23_ba5
[536] Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā) 15:10ab, Toh 3824 Tengyur, dbu ma, tsa, 9a2.
[537] Ibid. 22:12ab, 13b2. In the Dergé edition of the Fundamental Verses, the two lines read: “How could the four—eternal, noneternal, and so on—exist in that which is free of intrinsic nature?”
[538] Suvikrāntavikramiparipṛcchāsūtra, Toh 14 Kangyur, shes rab sna tshogs, ka, 23b5.

f.d: gnyis pa kun rdzob tu yang sems dang sems las byung ba la ye shes su 'dogs na/ med de 'khrul pa zad pa'i phyir ro/ / shes bya ma lus pa mkhyen pa la ltos nas ye shes yod de/ gnas gyur gyi sku brnyes pa'i phyir ro/ /

The surface-level truth. On the surface level, too, if you designate mind or the mental factors as gnosis, it does not exist, for this is merely deluded error. But for someone who knows all objects of knowledge without exception, gnosis exists, for he has gained the body of transformation.

gnas gyur pa de yang slob dpon tsan+d+ra go mis sangs rgyas kyi sa las/
kun gzhi'i rnam shes gang yin pa/ / de ni me long ye shes gyur/ / de yang chos kyi dbyings nyid kyi/ / ngo bo nyid du yang dag gsal/ /
nyon mongs can yid gnas gyur pa/ / mnyam nyid ye shes dag tu 'dod/ /
yid kyi ye shes gnas gyur pa/ / so sor rtog pa can zhes bya/ /
sgo lnga'i rnam shes gnas gyur pa/ / de ni don kun grub pa nyid/[387] / ces pa ltar ro/ /

That transformation, moreover, is explained by Candragomin in his Buddha Levels:
That which is the “store cognition” (ālayavijñāna) has become the mirror-gnosis, and it shines forth as the nature of the sphere of reality (dharmadhātu).
The transformation of defiled mind (kliṣṭamanas) is held to be the gnosis of equality.
The transformation of nonsensory cognition (manovijñāna) is the gnosis possessing discrimination.
The transformation of the five sensory cognitions is the gnosis that accomplishes all aims.[539]

d.div: [387] sa paN gyis slob dpon tsan+d+ra go mi'i gsung 'di gang las drangs gzhung ngos 'dzin ma thub/
[539] Candragomin, Buddhabhūmi (Sangs rgyas kyi sa). Not located.

f.d:
des na kun rdzob 'khor ba/ don dam pa mya ngan las 'das pa ste/ sangs rgyas mi gnas pa'i mya ngan las 'das pa zung 'jug gi sku yin te/ slob dpon 'phags pas/
'khor ba dang ni mya ngan 'das/ / so so'i char ni shes gyur nas/ / gang du yang dag 'dres gyur pa/ / zung du 'jug par de bshad do/[388] / zhes gsungs pa dang/
zung 'jug ting 'dzin la gnas nas/ / slar zhing gang la'ang mi slob bo/ / 'di ni rdzogs pa'i rnal 'byor pa/ / rdo rje 'dzin pa chen po 'dir/ / rnam pa kun gyi mchog ldan pa/ / thams cad mkhyen par de nas 'gyur/[389] / ces gsungs pa ltar ro/ /

Therefore the surface level of truth is cyclic existence. The ultimately real is nirvana, and the Buddha’s nonsituated nirvana is the body of integration. As Ācārya Ārya [Nāgārjuna] said:
After you have understood in their separate aspects cyclic existence and nirvana, where these are completely mixed is explained as “the integration.”[540] And as it is also said:
Dwelling in the absorption of the integration, he does not train himself anymore in anything. This is the yogin of the completion stage. Here the great vajra-holder stage there then occurs that omniscience possessing the highest of all qualities.[541]

d.div: [388] sde dge_1802_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ ngi _mgon po klu sgrub/ rim lnga/ rim pa/ 5_shog_56_na2
[389] gong mtshungs/ rim lnga/ rim pa/ 1_shog_45_ba1
[540] Nāgārjuna, Pañcakrama, Toh 1802 Tengyur, rgyud, ngi, 56a2; P 2667, rgyud ’grel, gi, 62b6. The quote appears above on page 518 with a slightly different wording.

f.d: des na slob dpon 'phags pa'ang lta ba'i skabs su mthar thug de bzhin nyid rtogs pa spros bral mdzad la/[390] sgom pa'i skabs su mthar thug don dam dang mi 'gal ba'i thabs mkhas pa nyams su len pa/ 'bras bu'i skabs su mthar thug mi gnas pa'i mya ngan las 'das pa'i zung 'jug la mdzad pa yin no//

Therefore Ācārya Ārya [Nāgārjuna], too, on the level of theory held the ultimate to be the understanding of reality as devoid of conceptual elaborations. /378/ On the level of meditative cultivation, he maintained the ultimate to be the practice of skillful means that does not conflict with ultimate reality. And on the level of the result, he held the ultimate to be the integration of nonsituated nirvana.

d.div: [390] spros bral la mdzad la/ zha lu/ lu phu/

f.d: gsum pa rtsod pa spang ba ni/ ye shes de rang snang yin na ye shes yod pa la brjod pa'i skyon 'ong zhing / gzhan snang yin na ye shes med pa la brjod pa'i skyon mtshungs so zhe na/ rang snang gzhan snang du 'dzin na gzung 'dzin yin la/ gzung 'dzin gnas gyur pas gzung 'dzin las grol ba'i ye shes 'grub ste/ de'i phyir me long lta bu'i ye shes la sogs pa'i ming 'thob bo/ /

(3) The elimination of objections. [Doubt:] The previously expressed faults will occur about the existence of gnosis if you maintain that gnosis [is an existent thing that] appears [to its possessor], and the expressed fault about the nonexistence of gnosis will equally occur if it exists merely in the appearances experienced by others. [Reply:] If you hold gnosis to be something manifested to yourself or manifesting to others, that is the apprehended object and apprehending subject. However, through the transformation of subject-object duality, you will achieve the gnosis that is freed from subject and object and that has hence gained designations such as “mirror-like gnosis.”

des na mdo sde rgyan las/
me long ye shes nga yi med/ / yongs su ma chad rtag par ldan/[391] / zhes bya ba la sogs pa dang / ye shes grub pa las/
de bzhin gshegs kun ye shes ni/ / rang nyid dang ni 'gro ba yang / / dngos kun gcig par thugs chud pas/ / mnyam nyid ye shes zhes bshad do/[392] / zhes gsungs pa ltar ro/ /

Therefore, as the Ornament of Mahayana Sutras teaches:
The mirror gnosis is without “mine.” It always possesses nondifferentiation.[542] And in Achieving Pristine Awareness:
The gnosis of all the tathāgatas understands all entities—yourself and other living beings— as the same, and thus it is explained as being the “gnosis of equality.”[543]

d.div: [391] sde dge_4020_bstan/ sems tsam/ phi_byams pa mgon po/ mdo sde rgyan/ le'u/ 10_sh+loka_68_shog_11_ba4
[392] sde dge_2219_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ wi_in+d+ra b+hu di/ ye shes grub pa zhes bya ba'i sgrub pa'i thabs/ shog_38_ba7
[542] Maitreya, Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra 10:68a, Toh 4020 Tengyur, sems tsam, phi, 11b4.
[543] Indrabhūti, Jñānasiddhisādhanopāyikā, Toh 2219 Tengyur, rgyud, wi, 38b7.

f.d:
nyon mongs pa can gyi yid rang bzhin mnyam pa nyid kyi ye shes su gnas gyur pas na rang rgyud gzhan rgyud kyi tha snyad las grol lo/ / rnam 'grel las kyang /
gzugs sogs dang ni sems de ltar/ / gzung ba'i mtshan nyid dpyod pa 'di/ / ma dag blo can la yin gyi/ / rnal 'byor rtogs pa bsam mi khyab/[393] / ces bya ba dang / rgyud gzhan grub pa las/ gnas gyur pa'i ye shes bsam gyis mi khyab par gsungs pa ltar ro//[394]

Because of the transformation of defiled mind (kliṣṭamanas) into the gnosis of equality by nature, you have transcended the conventional terminology of your mind and another’s mind. As it is also stated in the Thorough Exposition of Valid Cognition:
The investigation of visible form and so on and of mind, whose defining mark is to apprehend thus, is something that pertains to those of impure minds. The realized understanding of the Yogin is impossible to encompass with the mind.[544] And as taught in Establishing the Minds of Others, the gnosis that results from transformation is impossible to encompass with the mind.[545]

d.div: [393] sde dge_4210_bstan/ tshad ma/ ce_tshad ma rnam 'grel/ mngon sum le'u/ sh+loka_532_shog_138_ba6
[394] sde dge_4219_bstan/ tshad ma/ che_chos grags/ rgyud gzhan grub pa/ shog_359_na6
[544] Dharmakīrti, Pramāṇavārttika 3:532, Toh 4210 Tengyur, tshad ma, ce, 138b6.
[545] Dharmakīrti, Saṃtānāntarasiddhi, Toh 4219 Tengyur, tshad ma, che, 359a6.

f.d: gsum pa yon gyi chos phye ste bshad pa

d.i: The different shared and special properties of the excellent qualities of buddhahood

f.d: ['di ]la gnyis/ thun mong dang thun mong ma yin pa'o/[395]/
These are of two sorts: those that are held in common with others and those that are unique [to the Buddha].[546]

d.div: [395] dang po la gsum ste/ rnam thar/ zil gnon/ zad pa/ mngon shes lnga ste/ 'jig rten pa dang thun mong dang / zag pa zad pa'i mngon shes/ nyon mongs med pa/ smon pa shes pa/ so so yang dag par rig pa la sogs slob ma thun mong ba dang / mtshan dpe dang / dbang bcu dang / gzungs kyi sgo la sogs pa byang chub sems dpa'i sa la gnas pa dang thun mong ba'o// gnyis pa thun mong ma yin pa ni/ stobs bcu/ mi 'jigs pa bzhi/ sangs rgyas kyi chos ma 'dres pa bco brgyad/ bag chags yang dag par bcom pa la sogs sangs rgyas kho na la mnga' ba'i ma 'dres pa'i chos thun mong ma yin pa'o/ /zha lu / lu phu/

[546] I have added the following introductory paragraph that was missing from the Dergé edition on the basis of the Shalu and Luphu manuscripts, as noted in ITC, 470n395. The existence of this passage in both independent manuscripts is proof that it was probably omitted in the main manuscript upon which Dergé was based. I could not yet check this in the Sakya xylograph or other sources. Proof that the Shalu manuscript belongs to an independent textual tradition is also given by the following and final notes (nn. 396 and 427).

f.d: dang po la gsum ste/

Concerning the first, the qualities of buddhahood held in common with others, there exist three kinds: those held in common with [meditators of] the worldly sphere, those held in common with the śrāvakas, and those held in common with a bodhisattva who dwells on one of the levels.

rnam thar/ zil gnon/ zad par/ mngon shes lnga ste/ 'jig rten pa dang thun mong dang / zag pa zad pa'i mngon shes/ nyon mongs pa med pa/ smon pa shes pa/ so so yang dag par rig pa la sogs slob ma dang thun mong ba dang / mtshan dpe dang / dbang bcu dang / gzungs kyi sgo la sogs pa byang chub sems pa'i sa la gnas pa dang thun mong ba'o/ /

Those held in common with [meditators of] the worldly sphere are the emancipations, the bases of mastery, the bases of totality (kṛtsna), and five of the six supernatural perceptions. Those held in common with the śrāvakas are such qualities as the sixth supernatural perception, that which knows the exhaustion of the impurities, the lack of afflictions, knowledge from aspiration, and the four analytical knowledges. Those held in common with a bodhisattva who dwells on one of the bodhisattva levels include such qualities as the bodily characteristics and marks, the ten controlling powers, and the doors of dhāraṇī.

gnyis pa thun mong ma yin pa ni/ stobs bcu/ mi 'jigs pa bzhi/ sangs rgyas kyi chos ma 'dres pa bco brgyad/ bag chags yang dag par bcom pa la sogs sangs rgyas kho na la mnga' ba'i ma 'dres pa'i chos thun mong ma yin pa'o//

Those qualities that are unique to a buddha include the ten powers, the four modes of fearlessness, the eighteen characteristics unique to a buddha, and the thorough destruction of the propensities toward the afflictions.[547]

d.div: [547] This classification into shared and special qualities is treated by Sapaṇ on page 577 below. The principal Indian sources for the list of these qualities of a buddha include Maitreya’s Ornament of Clear Realizations (chapter 4), Asaṅga’s Compendium of Higher Knowledge (chapter 4), Vasubhandu’s Treasury of Higher Knowledge (chapter 7), and Candrakīrti’s Entering the Middle Way (chapter 10).

f.d: de lta ba'i thun mong dang thun mong ma yin pa'i yon tan de dag rang gzhan gyi rgyud la bsod nams chen po thob par 'dod pas tshigs su bcad pa'i dbyangs kyis bstod par bya ste/ de'ang thog mar mdo sde rgyan las 'byung ba ltar brjod la/ der cung zad ma rdzogs pa bdag nyid kyis tshigs su bcad pas kha bskang ste brjod par bya'o/ / de dag kyang 'di lta ste/[396]

Here I will praise those shared and exclusive excellent qualities through versified song so that great merit may be acquired in my own mind and in the minds of others. Moreover, I will state their praises first of all as they appear in the Ornament of Mahayana Sutras and then add more praises, supplementing what is slightly incomplete there with verses of my own composition.[548]

d.div: [396] de la thog mar tshad med pa bzhi/ zha lu/ lu phu/

[548] Beginning here, for several folios Sapaṇ follows word for word Drolungpa’s Great Tenrim, which likewise includes the same praises of the Buddha from chapter 21 of the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra (as was first pointed out to me by Mr. Kazuo Kano when we read this passage together in Hamburg). After seventeen such verses, Sapaṇ begins the praises of his own composition.

f.d: de la thog mar tshad med pa bzhi/

sems can rnams la brtse ba can/ / phrad dang bral ba'i dgongs pa can/ / mi 'bral bde ba'i dgongs pa can/ / phan dgongs khyod la phyag 'tshal lo/[397] / tshad med pa bzhi yang bsdu na phan bde gnyis las/ bde ba'i dgongs pa ni/ bde ba dang phrad par 'dod pa byams pa/ sdug bsngal dang bral bar 'dod pa snying rje/ de gnyis dang mi 'bral bar 'dod pa dga' ba ste gsum mo/ /

You’re compassionate toward sentient beings; you wish them to meet [with happiness] and part [from suffering], and that they be never separated [from happiness]— I pay homage to you whose wish is to help and benefit.[549] The four immeasurables can be subsumed within the two: intended benefits and intended happiness. /379/ From among them, the intention [that all living beings have] happiness is threefold: loving kindness, which is the desire that living beings come into contact with happiness; compassion, which is the desire that they be parted from suffering; and sympathetic joy, which is the desire that they never be parted from the above two [desirable states, i.e., the possession of happiness and the freedom from suffering].

d.div: [397] sde dge_4020_bstan/ sems tsam/ phi_byams pa mgon po/ mdo sde rgyan/ le'u/ 21_sh+loka_44_shog_38_na3

[549] Maitreya, Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra 21:43, Toh 4020 Tengyur, sems tsam, phi, 38a3. This verse is also quoted and explained above on page 466. The four immeasurables are wholesome attitudes cultivated toward all beings: (1) benevolence or loving kindness (byams pa), (2) compassion (snying rje), (3) sympathetic joy (dga’ ba), and (4) equanimity (btang snyom). In Maitreya’s Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra and Asaṅga’s Abhidharmasamuccaya, equanimity has a special Mahayana sense of wishing benefit; see also Boin-Webb, Abhidharmasamuccaya, 223.

f.d: phan pa'i dgongs pa ni/ btang snyoms kyi bde ba la chags/ sdug bsngal la sdang ba'i kun nas nyon mongs pa gnyis snyoms pas gtan du phan par dgongs pa'o/ /

The intention [that all living beings] benefit is the constant intent that, through equanimity, [they may come to view] both the affliction of attachment to happiness and the affliction of aversion to suffering equally.
rnam thar zil gnon zad par gyi skye mched ni/

d.i: The emancipations, the bases of mastery, and the bases of totality

d.div: thub pa sgrib kun nges par grol/ / 'jig rten thams cad zil gyis gnon/ / khyod kyi mkhyen pas shes byar khyab// thugs grol khyod la phyag 'tshal lo//[398]
O Sage, you are emancipated from all obscurations. You have mastery over the whole world. Your knowledge encompasses all objects of knowledge. Homage to you, whose mind is liberated![550]
[398] gong mtshungs/ mdo sde rgyan/ le'u/ 21_sh+loka_45_shog_38_na4
[550] Maitreya, Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra 21:44, Toh 4020 Tengyur, sems tsam, phi, 38a4.

f.d: gzugs can gzugs la lta ba'i rnam par thar pa la sogs pa brgyad ni/ 'jig rten pa'i sgrib pa gnyis ka las ma grol/ nyan thos dang rang rgyal gyis nyon mongs pa'i sgrib pa spangs/ sangs rgyas kyis shes bya'i sgrib pa las kyang grol/

Concerning the eight emancipations,[551] such as the first emancipation, in which [the meditator begins still perceiving himself] as possessing physical form while relating to outer forms, here the person of the mundane sphere is not free from either obscuration. The śrāvaka [arhat] and pratyekabuddha have eliminated the affliction obscuration. The Buddha is freed from that, and also from the knowledge obscuration.

d.div: [551] On the emancipations (rnam par thar) of yogic concentration practice, see also Vasubandhu, Abhidharmakośa 8:32, and Boin-Webb, Abhidharmasamuccaya, 223, “deliverances.” In his commentary Sapaṇ does not explain what these three special yogic practices or attainments are, but he establishes the Buddha’s qualities as superior to those of the others who might possess them.

f.d: zil gyis gnon pa la/ 'jig rten pas rang gi spyod yul tsam zil gyis gnon/ nyan thos kyis stong gnyis bar ma/ rang rgyal gyis stong gsum/ sangs rgyas kyis 'jig rten thams cad zil gyis gnon/

Concerning the bases of mastery,[552] a person of the mundane sphere [who reaches this yogic attainment] has dominion merely over his own sphere of experience (gocara). The śrāvaka has dominion over world systems numbering one million. The pratyekabuddha has dominion over world systems numbering one billion. And the Buddha has dominion over all world systems.

d.div: [552] On the eight bases of mastery (zil gyis gnon pa skye mched brgyad ), see also Vasubandhu, Abhidharmakośa 8:35, and Boin-Webb, Abhidharmasamuccaya, 224, “spheres of mastery.”

f.d: zad par bcu ni/ 'jig rten pas rgya chung ngu shes/ nyan thos dang rang rgyal rgya che/ sangs rgyas shes bya thams cad la ye shes khyab par gzigs shing / 'jig rten pa ma grol zhing / nyan thos dang rang rgyal/ nyon mongs pa'i bag chags dang shes bya'i sgrib pa las ma grol la/ 'di grol ba yin no/ /

Concerning the ten bases of totality,[553] a person of the mundane sphere knows to a small extent. The śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha know on a vaster scale. The Buddha sees, encompassing all objects of knowledge with his gnosis. And [concerning the words “whose mind is liberated”], the person of the world is not liberated [from the afflictions]. The śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha are not liberated from the propensities toward the afflictions and from the knowledge obscurations. But this one, [the Buddha], is liberated.

d.div: [553] The ten bases of totality (zad par gyi skye mched, kṛtsnāyatana, Pali kaṣina) are explained by Nārada in A Manual of Abhidhamma, 117n7, as a series of concentration exercises in which you concentrate in sequence on ten different circular objects: (1) the elements earth, (2) water, (3) fire, and (4) air; the colors (5) blue, (6) yellow, (7) red, and (8) white; and (9) light and (10) space. The outer physical object of concentration is first concentrated on long enough to be able to visualize it with closed eyes. This inner visualization is then focused on until it develops into a purified, abstract concept. Concentrating on this final abstracted image eventually results in proximate and ecstatic concentrations (samādhi). See also Vasubandhu, Abhidharmakośa 8:36, and Boin-Webb, Abhidharmasamuccaya, 225, and note 105, “spheres of totalization.”

f.d: 'di gsum gyis ni/ yon tan gyi mi mthun pa'i phyogs thams cad las rnam par grol bas na thugs grol lo/ /
Since by means of these three [attainments, the Buddha] is completely liberated from all factors opposed to the excellent qualities, he is therefore one whose mind is liberated.
rgyal ba'i nyon mongs pa med pa ni/

d.div: sems can rnams ni ma lus pa'i/ / nyon mongs ma lus thams cad 'dul/ / nyon mongs 'joms mdzad nyon mongs la/ / thugs rjer bcas khyod la phyag 'tshal/[399] /
Homage to you who tame absolutely the afflictions of all beings without exception, to you who destroy [latent] afflictions and are compassionate toward the afflicted!
[399] gong mtshungs/ mdo sde rgyan/ le'u/ 21_sh+loka_46_shog_38_na4

f.d: sems can thams cad kyi nyon mongs 'dul ba dang / nyon mongs pa'i gnyen po mdzad pa dang / skye bo nyon mongs pa can la brtse bar mdzad pa ste/ nyan thos la sogs pa gzhan gyis ni rang la dmigs nas/ nyon mongs pa skye ba tsam spong gi gzhan gyi sel bar mi byed do/[400] /

The Buddha tames the afflictions of all sentient beings and applies the antidote to the afflictions and acts kindly toward those people who possess the afflictions. Those like the śrāvakas, thinking of themselves, eliminate merely the arising of their own afflictions but do not remove those of others.[554]

d.div: [400] nyon mongs pa skye ba tsam spong gi gzhan ni sel bar mi byed do/ /zha lu/

[554] Maitreya, Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra 21:45, Toh 4020 Tengyur, sems tsam, phi, 38a4. On “lack of afflictions” (nyon mongs med, araṇā), see also Vasubandhu, Abhidharmakośa 7:35, and Boin-Webb, Abhidharmasamuccaya, 226, “non-contention.”

f.d: smon nas mkhyen pa ni/

lhun gyis grub cing chags mi mnga'/ / thogs pa mi mnga' rtag par yang / / mnyam par gzhag cing 'dri kun gyi/ / lan ldon khyod la phyag 'tshal lo/[401] / nyan thos kyi smon nas mkhyen pa ni/ 'bad pa dang snyoms 'jug la brten nas nyi tshe ba tsam shes kyi/ the tshom thams cad gcod mi nus la/ sangs rgyas ni lhun gyis grub pa dang / chags pa mi mnga' ba dang / shes bya la thogs pa med pa dang / rtag tu mnyam par gzhag pa dang / 'dri ba thams cad kyi the tshom gcod pa'o//

Homage to you [whose knowledge] is spontaneous, is not attached, is unhindered, is always in the meditative equipoise, and can answer all questions![555] /380/ The knowledge from aspiration that is possessed by the śrāvaka [arhat] understands merely an approximation, being based on effort and meditative practice, though it is unable to remove all doubts. But that of a buddha is spontaneously realized, is not attached, is unhindered in knowing all objects of knowledge, is always in the meditative state, and removes the doubts of all questions [posed by others].

d.div: [401] sde dge_4020_bstan/ sems tsam/ phi_byams pa mgon po/ mdo sde rgyan/ le'u/ 21_sh+loka_47_shog_38_na5

[555] Maitreya, Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra 21:46, Toh 4020 Tengyur, sems tsam, phi, 38a5. On “knowledge from aspiration” (smon nas shes pa, praṇidhijñāna), see also Vasubandhu, Abhidharmakośa 7:35, 8:37ab, and Boin-Webb, Abhidharmasamuccaya, 226, “knowledge of the aspiration (resolution).”

f.d: so so yang dag par rig pa ni/

rten dang brten pa bshad bya dang/ / gsung dang mkhyen pa 'chad byed la/ / blo gros rtag thogs mi mnga' bas/ / legs ston khyod la phyag 'tshal lo/[402] / rten chos mtshan gzhi dang / de la brten pa don mtshan nyid gnyis ni bshad par bya ba'o/ / gsungs nges pa'i tshig sgra don dang / mkhyen pa spobs pa gnyis ni 'chad byed do//

Homage to you, who are an excellent teacher because your intelligence can never be hindered about the “support” and the “supported,” the things to be explained, and about speech and knowledge, the means of explaining![556] The “support” refers to the Dharma [as verbal expression], which is the exemplification bearing the defining mark. “That which is supported” refers to its sense, which is the defining mark. These first two are the content to be taught. “Speech” refers to etymological explanation, which is the explanation of the meaning of Sanskrit words. “Knowledge” refers to confident presence of mind. These last two are the means of teaching.

d.div: [402] gong mtshungs/ mdo sde rgyan/ le'u/ 21_sh+loka_48_shog_38_na5
[556] Maitreya, Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra 21:47, Toh 4020 Tengyur, sems tsam, phi, 38a5.

f.d: mngon par shes pa ni/

d.div: gshegs nas spyod pa mkhyen par mdzad/ / de dag skad kyis sems can gyi/ / 'ong dang 'gro dang nges 'byung la/ / legs 'doms khyod la phyag 'tshal lo/[403]/
Homage to you who go and understand the conduct of others, and who, by your speech, give excellent instruction about the coming, going, and release of sentient beings![557]
[403] gong mtshungs/ mdo sde rgyan/ le'u/ 21_sh+loka_49_shog_38_na6
[557] Ibid. 21:48, 38a6. On the superknowledges (mngon par shes pa, mngon shes rnam drug), see also Vasubandhu, Abhidharmakośa 7:42.

f.d: sku'i cho 'phrul rdzu 'phrul gyi mngon shes kyis gdul bya gang na gnas pa der gshegs pa'o/ / thugs kyi kun brjod pa'i cho 'phrul gyis gzhan gyi sems mkhyen pa'o/ / gsung gi rjes su bstan pa'i cho 'phrul bzhi las/ lha'i rna bas de dag gi so so'i skad mkhyen pa'o// gnyis pa don gyi dbye ba ste/[404] sngon gyi gnas rjes su dran pas sngon gyi mtha' nas 'dir 'ong ba dang / 'chi 'pho dang skye ba shes pa lha'i mig gis ji ltar 'di nas phyi ma'i mthar 'gro ba dang / zag pa zad pa mkhyen pas 'khor ba las nges par 'byung ba/ mkhyen pa ltar gdams ngag stsol bas dus gsum la rmongs pa spangs pa nyid kyi phyir ro/ /

Through the bodily miracle,[558] the superknowledge of (1) magical power, he goes to wherever his disciples are staying. By the mental miracle of knowing others’ minds,[559] he (2) understands the minds of others. There are four verbal miracles of instruction:[560] The first knows through (3) the divine ear their separate languages. The second through fourth consist of a division of the object of knowledge. The reason for this division is that he gives instructions according to his knowledge of how a being has come into this life from a previous time through (4) remembering past states of existence. He shows beings how they go from this life into future lives through (5) his divine eye that knows deaths and births. And he explains the escape from cyclic existence into liberation through (6) knowing the exhaustion of the impurities. And therefore he has eliminated ignorance about the three times.

d.div: [404] gsum pa don gyi dbye ba ste/ zha lu/ lu phu/

[558] Sapaṇ here classifies the six superknowledges as types of the three miracles (cho ’phrul), of the Buddha—the bodily miracle (magical power), the mental miracle of knowing others’ minds (clairvoyance), and the verbal miracle of instruction (the last four superknowledges).

[559] Zhang et al., Extensive Tibetan-Tibetan-Chinese Dictionary, classifies this not as pertaining to the mind (thugs) but as the all-expressing miracle of speech (gsung kun tu brjod pa’i cho ’phrul), defining it: gzhan gyi sems shes pa’i sgo nas nyes dmigs dang legs pa’i yon tan gang yin pa de dag gzhan gyi sems dang mthun par ston pa/.

[560] Zhang et al., Extensive Tibetan-Tibetan-Chinese Dictionary, calls this not speech (gsung) but mind (thugs) and defines it: rjes su bstan pa’i cho ’phrul, sems kyi rgyud la nyon mongs pa’i shas gang che ba brtags nas gnyen po de dang de ston pa.

f.d: mngon shes snga ma lnga ni zag bcas 'jig rten pa dang thun mong ba yin la/ phyi ma drug pa ni/ zag med slob pa dang thun mong ma yin no//
The first five superknowledges are impure and are held in common with people of the mundane sphere. The last—that is, the sixth—is free from impurity and not held in common with the trainee.[561]

d.div: [561] Śaikṣa. In other words, one who is on the lower seven śrāvaka levels before reaching the eighth, that of the arhat.

f.d: mtshan dang dpe byad ni/

lus can kun gyis khyod mthong na/ / skyes bu dam pa lags par 'tshal/ / mthong ba tsam gyis rab dang bar/ / mdzad pa khyod la phyag 'tshal lo/[405] / skyes bu chen por mtshon pa'i mtshan sum cu rtsa gnyis dang / de mdzes par byed pa dpe byad bzang po brgyad cus brgyan pas de'i phrin las mthong ba tsam gyis thams cad dad par mdzad pa'o//

When all embodied beings see you, they know you to be a great being. Homage to you who inspire intense faith merely by being seen![562] Because he is ornamented with the thirty-two bodily characteristics that indicate a great being (satpuruṣa) and the eighty excellent marks that beautify him, he inspires faith in all beings by the mere sight of his activities.

d.div: [405] sde dge_4020_bstan/ sems tsam/ phi_byams pa mgon po/ mdo sde rgyan/ le'u/ 21_sh+loka_50_shog_38_na7
[562] Maitreya, Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra 21:49, Toh 4020 Tengyur, sems tsam, phi, 38a7: bodily characteristics and marks (mtshan dang dpe byed ). This verse is also quoted above at the end of chapter 6.

f.d: yongs su dag pa bzhi ni/

d.div: len dang gnas dang gtong ba dang / / sprul dang yongs su bsgyur ba dang / / ting nge 'dzin dang ye shes la/ / mnga' brnyed khyod la phyag 'tshal lo/[406] /
Homage to you who have achieved dominion over assuming [of new existence], its duration and its abandonment, over emanations and transformation, and over meditative absorptions and gnosis![563] /381/
[406] gong mtshungs/ mdo sde rgyan/ le'u/ 21_sh+loka_51_shog_38_na7
[563] Ibid. 21:50, 38a7: the four purities (yongs su dag pa bzhi, pariśuddha/pariśuddhi). This verse is also quoted above at the end of chapter 8.

f.d: yongs su dag pa bzhis dbang bzhi bstan te/ rten yongs du dag pa ni/ nyon mongs ba'i bag chags thams cad rten las ma lus par spangs pas lus gang bzhed pa len pa dang/ ci bzhed par sku tshe gnas pa dang / nam 'dod pa na gtong ba gsum la dbang ba'o/ / dmigs pa yongs su dag pa ni/ med pa sprul ba dang/ yod pa bsgyur ba la dbang 'byor ba dang / thugs yongs su dag pa ni/ gnas ngan len thams cad dang bral zhing dge ba thams cad bsags pas/ rnam pa thams cad du ting nge 'dzin thams cad la dbang ba'o// shes rab yongs su dag pa ni/ ma rig pa rgyun bcad pas shes bya thams cad la ye shes sgrib pa med pa la dbang ba'o/ /

The four purities reveal four powers: 1. The purity of basis [that is, of the body] has three powers: the power to assume any form desired, the power to live for whatever lifespan is desired, and the power to abandon that existence whenever desired because he has eliminated from the basis absolutely all dispositions toward the afflictions. 2. The purity of object is the power that can project emanations of non-existing things and transform existing things. 3. The purity of mind is the constant mastery and control of all meditative absorptions since he is free from all evils and has accumulated all merits. 4. The purity of discerning wisdom is mastery and control of a gnosis, free from obscurations, that embraces all knowable things because he has brought ignorance to an end.
stobs bcu ni/

d.div: thabs dang skyabs dang dag pa dang / / theg chen nges par 'byung ba las/ / sems can rnams ni rab bslu ba'i/ / bdud 'joms khyod la phyag 'tshal lo/[407] /
Homage to you who vanquish evil ones who lead sentient beings astray from correct method, refuge, purity, and the true liberation of the Mahayana![564]
[407] gong mtshungs/ mdo sde rgyan/ le'u/ 21_sh+loka_52_shog_38_ba1

f.d: gnas dang gnas ma yin pa mkhyen pa'i stobs dang / las bdag gir bya ba mkhyen pa'i stobs dang / khams sna tshogs mkhyen pa'i stobs dang / mos pa sna tshogs pa mkhyen pa'i stobs dang / dbang po mchog dang mchog ma yin pa mkhyen pa'i stobs dang / thams cad du 'gro ba'i lam mkhyen pa'i stobs dang / dbang po dang stobs dang byang chub kyis yan lag dang rnam par thar pa dang / ting nge 'dzin dang / snyoms par 'jug pa dang / kun nas nyon mongs pa dang / rnam par byang ba'i rnam par bkod pa mkhyen pa'i stobs dang / sngon gyi gnas rjes su dran pa mkhyen pa'i stobs dang / lha'i mig gis 'chi 'pho ba dang skye ba mkhyen pa'i stobs dang / zag pa zad pa mkhyen pa'i stobs so/ /

[The ten powers (bala) are:] 1. The power consisting of the knowledge of what is possible and impossible.[565] 2. The power of the knowledge of individual heritages of karma [and their results].[566] 3. The power of the knowledge of various dispositions [of disciples]. 4. The power of the knowledge of the various spiritual aspirations [of disciples]. 5. The power of the knowledge to which degree, higher or lower, the moral faculties [are present in disciples]. 6. The power of the knowledge of the paths leading to rebirths everywhere 7. The power of the knowledge of the system of the moral faculties, powers, limbs of awakening, meditative concentrations, emancipations, absorptions, meditative attainments, the defiled, and the purified. 8. The power of the knowledge that remembers former states of existence. 9. The power of the knowledge of future deaths and rebirths through the divine eye. 10. The power of the knowledge of the extinction of the impurities.

d.div: [565] Chim Jampaiyang, Detailed Abhidharma Commentary, 617, explains gnas dang gnas min pa in this context as “possible and impossible” (srid pa dang mi srid pa).

[566] Chim Jampaiyang, Detailed Abhidharma Commentary, 617, calls this power zag bcas gyi las dang ’bras bu rnam par smin pa sna tshogs mkhyen pa’i stobs, and Zhang et al., Extensive Tibetan-Tibetan-Chinese Dictionary, gives simply las kyi rnam smin mkhyen pa’i stobs. Sapaṇ here calls it las kyi bdag gir bya ba mkhyen pa’i stobs, as in Asvabhāva’s Detailed Commentary on the Ornament of Mahayana Sutras (Sūtrālaṃkāraṭīkā), Toh 4029 Tengyur, sems tsam, bi, 171b6.

f.d: gnas las khams mos dbang po dang / / kun 'gro bkod dang sngon gyi gnas/ / 'chi 'pho zag pa med mkhyen pa/ / 'di dag thub pa'i stobs bcu yin/ / bsdu ba'i tshig bcad do//

Or, in a summarizing verse:
Knowledge of the possible, of karma, dispositions, aspirations, moral faculties, leading everywhere, the system, former dwellings, deaths and rebirths, and the extinction of impurities—these are the ten powers of the Sage.
'dir ni de dag gi las phyogs gcig tu gsungs te/ de'ang don bzhi las sems can slu ba'i bdud 'joms pa'o/ /

Here [in the above quote from the Ornament of Mahayana Sutras] the function of these powers is explained from one perspective. That is, they are explained as vanquishing the evil ones who deceive sentient beings by leading them away from four things.

de la thabs las slu ba ni/ gsod pa'i mchod sbyin dang chu la lceb pa la sogs pas mtho ris dang thar pa thob par ston pa ni gnas dang gnas ma yin pa mkhyen pas bzlog ste/ rgyu 'bras phyin ci ma log pa gzigs pas dge ba las mtho ris su 'gro ba'i gnas yod/ sdig pa la gnas med pa la sogs pa mkhyen pa'o/ /

(1) Leading away from correct method. This is to teach that higher existences and liberation can be attained by such things as sacrificing living animals and committing suicide in water. /382/ This deception is averted by the [first power,] knowledge of what is possible and impossible. Through seeing cause and effect correctly, a buddha knows, for example, that through virtuous deeds you go to higher existences but that through evil deeds this would be impossible.

skyabs las slu ba ni/ sdig pa byas bsod nams ma byas kyang dbang phyug dang khyab 'jug la sogs pa mgu bar byas na ngan 'gro las skyob pa la sogs pa smra ba ni las bdag gir bya ba mkhyen pas 'joms te/ sbyin pa la sogs pa'i bsod nams kyi las kyis bde bar 'gyur gyi/ dbang phyug la sogs pas bde ba'i rgyur mi 'gyur te/ mdo sde rgyan las/
sbyin sogs rdzogs pa'i byang chub kyi/ / rten yin dbang phyug sogs ma yin/[408] / zhes gsungs so/ /

(2) Leading away from the correct refuge. This is to assert such things as that even if you commit evil deeds and do not do virtuous deeds, you will be protected from lower miserable destinies if you propitiate such deities as Īśvara and Viṣṇu. This deception is vanquished by the [second power,] knowledge of the individual heritages of karma [and their results]. You will become happy through deeds of merit such as generosity, but the causes of happiness will not come about through such deities as Īśvara. For as the Ornament of Mahayana Sutras teaches:
Generosity and the others are bases for perfect awakening. Īśvara and the rest are not.[567]

d.div: [408] gong mtshungs/ mdo sde rgyan/ le'u/ 12_sh+loka_66_shog_15_ba7
[567] Maitreya, Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra 12:66, Toh 4020 Tengyur, sems tsam, phi, 15b7.

f.d: dag pa las slu ba ni/ zag pa dang bcas pa'i las khrus dang / dka' thub la sogs pas dag par smra mod/ de ni lam ma yin te/ bsam gtan la sogs pa rnam par dag pa'i lam du ston pa/ bsam gtan dang ting nge 'dzin dang snyoms 'jug mkhyen pa'i stobs kyis bzlog go /

(3) Leading away from real purity. Some profess that you can become purified through impure actions such as ritual purification and physical mortification. But that is not a correct path. The teaching of such things as meditative concentrations as being the completely correct and sufficient path is averted by [the seventh power,] knowledge of the meditative concentrations, absorptions, and meditative attainments.
nges par 'byung ba las slu ba ni/ snod dang mi mthun pa'i lam ston pa'o/ / de ni dbang po mchog dang mchog ma yin pa mkhyen pa la sogs pa stobs lhag ma bdun gyis 'joms te/ 'di ltar

(4) Leading away from salvation, or escape into liberation. This is to teach a spiritual path that is inappropriate for the person receiving the teachings. That deception is destroyed by the knowledge of higher and lower degrees of the moral faculties and by the remaining six powers. Those seven powers are the following:
dbang po mchog dang mchog ma yin pa mkhyen pa ni dad pa la sogs pa lnga po chung ngu dang 'bring dang chen po mkhyen nas de dang 'tsham par chos gsung pa'o/ /

(1) [The fifth power,] knowledge of the higher and lower degrees of the moral faculties, is to know whether the five moral faculties such as faith exist to a weaker, middling, or stronger [degree in a disciple], and afterward to teach religion in consonance with that.
mos pa sna tshogs ni sems can gyi 'dod pa dang rtogs pa che 'bring gsum mkhyen pa'o/ /

(2) [The fourth power,] various spiritual aspirations, is to know to which degree—stronger, middling, or weaker—the desires and thoughts [aspiring to spiritual paths such as that of the śrāvaka are present in] sentient beings.
khams sna tshogs ni rigs can gsum dang 'dod chags la sogs pa'i spyod pa brgyad khri bzhi stong gi khams rnams mkhyen pa'o/ /

(3) [The third power,] various dispositions, is the knowledge of whether beings possess the three spiritual lineages[568] or the dispositions of the eighty-four thousand activities of desires and the other afflictions.

d.div: [568] That is, the dispotions toward the śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, and Mahayana paths. Chim Jampaiyang, Detailed Abhidharma Commentary, 618, explains khams here as a spiritual disposition or ingrained tendency of mind.

f.d: kun tu 'gro ba'i lam ni de dag nyid kyi 'jug pa'i sgo dang 'tsham pa 'dod chags kyi gnyen por mi sdug pa bsgom pa la sogs pa mkhyen pa'o/ /
(4) [The sixth power,] the paths leading everywhere, is the knowledge of what initial instructions are best for specific disciples, such as the meditation on repulsiveness as the antidote to desire.

sngon gyi gnas rjes su dran pa ni phyogs thams cad na sems can gyi rigs sna tshogs kyi ming dang brda tha dad pa/ sngon gyi gnas rnam pa du ma gzhi brgyad la brten pa'i spyod pa drug rjes su dran pa ste/ gzhi brgyad ni ming 'di zhes bya'o/ /rigs dang / rus dang / zas dang / bde sdug dang / tshe tshad dang/ yun dang / tshe 'di tsam zhig thub ces bya'o/ / de dag la brten pa'i spyod pa drug ni bod pa'i brda dang / rgyal rigs la sogs pa'i rigs dang / pha ma dang / zas skom la sogs pa'i bya ba dang / dar rgud dang / tshe'i rnam pa sna tshogs so/ / rnam pa ni spyod pa drug go /don rtags ni gzhi brgyad do//

(5) [The eighth power,] memory of previous states of existence, recalls the numerous features of previous births: the different names and original designations of the various classes of sentient beings everywhere and the six modes, which are based on the eight foundations. The eight foundations are knowing “This was his name,” “This was his lineage,” “This was his clan,” “This is what he ate,” “This was his happiness and suffering,” “This was his lifespan,” “This was his period,” and “He was able to live this long.” The six modes are the name he was called, his lineage (such as kṣatriya), his parents, his activities such as eating and drinking, his flourishing and decline, and various features of his life. /383/ The word “feature”[569] refers to the six modes, while the word “proof”[570] refers to the eight foundations.

d.div: [569] Rnam pa. The reference to “features” here is to sutra passages in which the Buddha relates his memories of previous states of existences.
[570] Dergé’s don rtags is emended here to dan rtags (“proof ”). Drolungpa, Great Ten-rim, uses exactly the same rare expression, and indeed Sapaṇ quotes from him here.

f.d: lha'i mig ni lha'i gnas su bsam gtan bzhi'i 'bras bu ste shin tu rdzogs shing dag pa'i bsam gtan la brten pas na shin tu dag pa'o/ / 'dod pa'i lha la ni de dang ming mthun pa tsam yod kyi/ mi la de yang med pas na mi las 'das pa'o/ / de'i yul ni sems can 'chi ba dang bar dor skye ba gnyis so/ / mun pa la 'jug pa phya ra nag po'am mun nag tu 'gro ba lta bu kha dog ngan pa dang / snang bar 'gro ba zla ba'i 'od dam/ wA rA Na sI'i ras lta bu kha dog bzang po/ ngan pa dang bzang po yang de dag nyid de/ ngan 'gro dang bde 'gror 'gro bas so/ /
